## The EDA Landscape

Layer 1. What electronic design automation is, the RTL-to-GDSII flow stage by stage, the representations each stage consumes and produces, PPA, the industry and its history.

Builds on: discrete math.

Topics covered:

- Electronic design automation, ECAD, computer-aided engineering
- Integrated circuit design, VLSI, ULSI
- ASIC, FPGA, SoC, semiconductor IP cores, standard cells and cell libraries as products
- Design abstraction, hierarchy, top-down and bottom-up design, hardware-software co-design
- The end-to-end flow: specification, architecture, RTL, verification, synthesis, DFT, floorplan, placement, CTS, routing, extraction, signoff, tape-out, fabrication, packaging, test
- Why real flows are iterative: timing, power and verification recur at many stages; how errors propagate downstream
- Representations and formats map: HDL/RTL, Boolean networks, BDD/AIG, gate netlists, Liberty, SDC, LEF/DEF, SPEF, GDSII/OASIS, SPICE netlists, PDK decks - what each preserves, abstracts and enables
- PPA (power, performance, area) and the cost of a respin
- Analog/mixed-signal, FPGA, PCB/package and manufacturing as adjacent branches with different flows
- Industry: the major EDA vendors and their product lines; foundry model, fabless companies, the EDA industry structure
- Major tools by role (custom layout, place and route, synthesis, logic and circuit simulation, timing signoff, physical verification, test, FPGA implementation) - what class of problem each solves
- Research communities: DAC, ICCAD, DATE, ISPD, ITC, CAV; landmark history: structured VLSI design, SPICE, the university CAD tools behind today's logic synthesis and layout
- Standards bodies for languages, formats, boards and manufacturing

Subdomains: [What EDA is](#the-eda-landscape-what-eda-is), [Stages of the flow](#the-eda-landscape-stages-of-the-flow), [Representations and formats](#the-eda-landscape-representations-and-formats), [Quality metrics](#the-eda-landscape-quality-metrics), [Branches of EDA](#the-eda-landscape-branches-of-eda), [The industry and its standards](#the-eda-landscape-the-industry-and-its-standards), [History](#the-eda-landscape-history), [Frontier: agent-first futures](#the-eda-landscape-frontier-agent-first-futures)

<a id="the-eda-landscape-what-eda-is"></a>

### What EDA is

<a id="c-flow-overview-what-is-eda"></a>

#### What electronic design automation is

`flow.overview.what_is_eda`

Electronic design automation (EDA) is the software that turns an idea for an electronic system into something a factory can build and a tester can check.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Design, analysis and verification tools
- Every tool is an algorithm on a model
- Why automation is unavoidable

Sample problem:

> A gate-sizing optimizer upsizes cells on failing paths and re-times after every few moves. What does this illustrate?
>
> A) An implementation tool calling an analysis engine inside its loop
>
> B) A verification tool proving functional correctness
>
> C) An analysis tool that never changes the design
>
> D) Two independent tools that never share data

Answer: An implementation tool calling an analysis engine inside its loop

Why: Optimizers transform the design but need an analyzer, here a timer, to score each change.

<a id="c-flow-overview-scale-vlsi"></a>

#### Integrated circuits and VLSI scale

`flow.overview.scale_vlsi`

An integrated circuit puts transistors and their wiring on one piece of silicon.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Integration levels and exponential growth
- Why exhaustive methods fail
- The design productivity gap

Sample problem:

> A chip family holds 6 billion transistors today. If the count doubles every 3 years, how many billion transistors will a chip of the same cost hold after 9 years?

Answer: 48

Why: 9 years is 3 doubling periods, so the count is $6 \cdot 2^{3} = 48$ billion.

<a id="c-flow-overview-abstraction-levels"></a>

#### Abstraction levels from system to layout

`flow.overview.abstraction_levels`

Designers describe a chip at several levels of abstraction: system, algorithm or behavior, register transfer, gate, transistor and layout.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The ladder of levels
- What each level keeps and drops
- Refinement and checking between levels

Sample problem:

> A C++ model computes a video filter with no notion of clock cycles. At which level is it?
>
> A) Behavioral or algorithmic level
>
> B) Register-transfer level
>
> C) System floorplan level
>
> D) Gate level

Answer: Behavioral or algorithmic level

Why: An untimed algorithm is a behavioral description; RTL fixes cycle-by-cycle register behaviour.

<a id="c-flow-overview-hierarchy"></a>

#### Hierarchy, top-down and bottom-up design

`flow.overview.hierarchy`

A chip is never designed as one flat list of billions of cells. It is a tree of modules: the top instantiates subsystems, which instantiate blocks, which instantiate library cells.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Definitions, instances and flattening
- Top-down and bottom-up
- What hierarchy buys and costs

Sample problem:

> The top module instantiates 6 copies of block A and 4 copies of block B. Block A contains 5 standard cells of its own plus 2 instances of block C. Block C contains 28 standard cells. Block B contains 31 standard cells. How many standard cells does the fully flattened design contain?

Answer: 490

Why: Multiply along each path from the top: $6(5 + 2 \cdot 28) + 4 \cdot 31 = 490$ cells.

<a id="c-flow-overview-asic-fpga-soc"></a>

#### ASICs, FPGAs and systems on chip

`flow.overview.asic_fpga_soc`

Three product kinds dominate digital hardware. An application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) is fabricated for one purpose.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Three ways to build digital logic
- Non-recurring and unit cost
- Choosing and combining

Sample problem:

> What does an ASIC team pay for that an FPGA team does not?
>
> A) Functional verification
>
> B) Synthesis of RTL into logic
>
> C) Static timing analysis
>
> D) A mask set and wafer fabrication for its own design

Answer: A mask set and wafer fabrication for its own design

Why: Both teams synthesize, time and verify; only the ASIC team fabricates its own masks.

<a id="c-flow-overview-ip-libraries"></a>

#### IP cores and standard-cell libraries as products

`flow.overview.ip_libraries`

Almost nothing on a modern chip is designed from scratch. Standard cells, memories, I/O cells, PHYs and processor cores are bought or reused as intellectual-property (IP) products.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Soft, firm and hard IP
- The standard-cell library
- Characterization and reuse economics

Sample problem:

> Why does hard IP give the integrator less risk but less freedom?
>
> A) It must be redesigned for every use
>
> B) It can be resynthesized at any frequency
>
> C) It contains no timing information
>
> D) Its timing and layout are proven but cannot be changed

Answer: Its timing and layout are proven but cannot be changed

Why: The more physical the delivery, the more is fixed and verified in advance, and the less the integrator can modify.

<a id="c-flow-overview-codesign"></a>

#### Hardware-software co-design

`flow.overview.codesign`

A system's function can run in software on a processor or in dedicated hardware.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Partitioning a function
- Amdahl's law
- Sizing the accelerator

Sample problem:

> Profiling shows that 65% of a program's runtime is a kernel that a hardware accelerator runs 2 times faster. The rest stays in software. What is the overall speedup? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 1.48

Why: $S = 1/((1 - 0.65) + 0.65/2) = 1.48$.

<a id="the-eda-landscape-stages-of-the-flow"></a>

### Stages of the flow

<a id="c-flow-stages-rtl-to-gds"></a>

#### The RTL-to-GDSII flow end to end

`flow.stages.rtl_to_gds`

The RTL-to-GDSII flow is the chain of tools that turns register-transfer code into the mask layout a foundry manufactures.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The stages in order
- What each stage hands the next
- What becomes known at each stage

Sample problem:

> In a standard digital implementation flow, which stage comes directly after parasitic extraction?
>
> A) Tape-out
>
> B) Packaging
>
> C) RTL design
>
> D) Signoff
>
> E) Routing

Answer: Signoff

Why: The chain runs RTL design, Logic synthesis, Scan insertion, Floorplanning, Placement, Clock tree synthesis, Routing, Parasitic extraction, Signoff, Tape-out, Fabrication, Packaging, Production test, so Signoff follows Parasitic extraction.

<a id="c-flow-stages-spec-to-rtl"></a>

#### Specification, architecture and RTL

`flow.stages.spec_to_rtl`

The front of the flow decides what the chip is before any tool decides how to build it.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The specification
- Architecture: blocks, pipelines and budgets
- RTL as the hand-off

Sample problem:

> Which of these is an interface item in a specification?
>
> A) The bus protocol and pin list a block must support
>
> B) The OPC recipe of a mask layer
>
> C) The global router's gcell size
>
> D) The number of buffers in the clock tree

Answer: The bus protocol and pin list a block must support

Why: Interfaces define how the chip or block connects to the outside world.

<a id="c-flow-stages-functional-verification"></a>

#### Functional verification in the flow

`flow.stages.functional_verification`

Functional verification asks whether the design does what the specification says.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Simulation, formal and emulation
- Coverage closes the loop
- Why late bugs cost more

Sample problem:

> A small controller has 3 input bits and 6 bits of state. An exhaustive test must apply every input combination in every state. How many (state, input) pairs is that?

Answer: 512

Why: There are $2^{6}$ states and $2^{3}$ input combinations, so $2^{9} = 512$ pairs, and reaching each state may itself take many cycles.

<a id="c-flow-stages-logic-synthesis"></a>

#### Logic synthesis

`flow.stages.logic_synthesis`

Logic synthesis translates RTL into a netlist of cells from a target library, optimizing for timing, area and power under the constraints in an SDC file.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Elaboration and generic logic
- Optimization and technology mapping
- Correctness and what synthesis cannot see

Sample problem:

> During elaboration, what does synthesis infer from an always block triggered on a clock edge?
>
> A) Clock buffers
>
> B) Registers
>
> C) Tristate buses
>
> D) Latches

Answer: Registers

Why: Edge-triggered processes describe flip-flops.

<a id="c-flow-stages-dft"></a>

#### Design for test and scan insertion

`flow.stages.dft`

A fabricated chip can have manufacturing defects that no design review could find, so each die is tested before it ships.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Scan chains
- Test time
- What DFT costs the rest of the flow

Sample problem:

> A design has 13,800 scan flip-flops, divided as evenly as possible into 16 scan chains. How many flip-flops are in the longest chain?

Answer: 863

Why: $\lceil 13800 / 16 \rceil = 863$.

<a id="c-flow-stages-floorplan"></a>

#### Floorplanning and power planning

`flow.stages.floorplan`

Floorplanning is the first physical step. It chooses the die and core size, places the large blocks (memories, analog macros, hard IP), arranges the I/O, and lays down the power distribution network.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Core area from utilization
- Shape, rows and the die
- Macros and the power grid

Sample problem:

> Synthesis reports 560,000 square microns of standard cells and macros. The floorplan targets a utilization of 0.8. What core area does that require, in square microns? Round to the nearest whole number.

Answer: 700000

Why: Core area = cell area / utilization = 560000 / 0.8 = 700000 square microns.

<a id="c-flow-stages-placement"></a>

#### Placement

`flow.stages.placement`

Placement assigns every standard cell a legal location in the rows of the floorplan.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Half-perimeter wirelength
- Total wirelength and incremental moves
- Density, legality and what goes wrong

Sample problem:

> A net connects pins at (29, 28), (27, 0), (12, 21), (22, 18), in microns. What is its half-perimeter wirelength, in microns?

Answer: 45

Why: The bounding box width plus height is 45 microns.

<a id="c-flow-stages-cts"></a>

#### Clock tree synthesis

`flow.stages.cts`

Every flip-flop needs the clock, and it needs it at nearly the same time as its neighbours.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Latency and skew
- Building the buffered tree
- Skew and timing

Sample problem:

> After clock tree synthesis, the clock latencies of a group of flip-flops are 417, 350, 437, 454, 415 ps. What is the global skew of the group, in picoseconds?

Answer: 104

Why: Global skew is the maximum minus the minimum latency: $454 - 350 = 104$ ps.

<a id="c-flow-stages-routing"></a>

#### Global and detailed routing

`flow.stages.routing`

Routing turns every net's connectivity into metal wires and vias on the available layers, without breaking design rules and without shorting nets together.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Global routing and overflow
- Detailed routing and design rules
- Detours and what routing reveals

Sample problem:

> A global router reports these gcell edges: edge 1: demand 16, capacity 14; edge 2: demand 12, capacity 13; edge 3: demand 22, capacity 17; edge 4: demand 10, capacity 8. What is the total overflow?

Answer: 9

Why: Overflow sums $\max(0, \text{demand} - \text{capacity})$ over the edges, giving 9.

<a id="c-flow-stages-extraction-signoff"></a>

#### Extraction, timing and signoff

`flow.stages.extraction_signoff`

Signoff is the set of final checks that must all pass before a design is sent to manufacturing.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Parasitic extraction
- Corners, modes and scenarios
- Signoff slack with real parasitics

Sample problem:

> A chip is signed off in 2 functional modes, at 5 process-voltage-temperature corners and 3 interconnect RC corners, with every combination analyzed. How many timing scenarios must be run?

Answer: 30

Why: Scenarios multiply: the product is 30.

<a id="c-flow-stages-tapeout-to-test"></a>

#### Tape-out, fabrication, packaging and test

`flow.stages.tapeout_to_test`

Tape-out is the moment the design team releases final layout to the foundry. After it, the design leaves the EDA world for the factory: mask making, wafer fabrication, wafer test, dicing, packaging and final test.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Tape-out and mask data preparation
- Fabrication
- Packaging and production test

Sample problem:

> What does the design team deliver to the foundry at tape-out?
>
> A) Final layout in GDSII or OASIS with its documentation
>
> B) Only the gate-level netlist
>
> C) The Liberty files and SDC
>
> D) The RTL and testbenches

Answer: Final layout in GDSII or OASIS with its documentation

Why: The foundry manufactures from layout; behavioural and timing files stay with the design team.

<a id="c-flow-stages-iteration-closure"></a>

#### Why design flows iterate

`flow.stages.iteration_closure`

The flow diagram is a straight line, but no real project runs it once. Timing, power, area and verification are checked at many stages with better information each time, and when a later check fails, an earlier stage re-runs.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The same question asked many times
- Loops and their costs
- Convergence and when it fails

Sample problem:

> Why does a later stage keep finding surprises that an earlier stage did not?
>
> A) Each stage optimized against an estimate that the next stage computes more accurately
>
> B) Later tools use different logic functions
>
> C) Earlier tools ignore constraints
>
> D) The process changes between stages

Answer: Each stage optimized against an estimate that the next stage computes more accurately

Why: Estimation error at one stage becomes a violation discovered at the next.

<a id="c-flow-stages-error-propagation"></a>

#### How poor decisions propagate downstream

`flow.stages.error_propagation`

A flow is a directed sequence of stages, and an error made in one stage is inherited by every stage after it.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Re-running the descendants
- Adding up the cost
- Iterations that may fail

Sample problem:

> A flow runs synthesis, scan insertion, floorplanning, placement, CTS, routing, extraction, signoff in that order, and a change to a stage invalidates that stage and every later one. An engineer changes the floorplanning step. How many stages must re-run, counting the changed one?

Answer: 6

Why: floorplanning is stage 3 of 8, so stages 3 through 8 re-run: 6 stages.

<a id="the-eda-landscape-representations-and-formats"></a>

### Representations and formats

<a id="c-flow-repr-format-map"></a>

#### The map of design representations and formats

`flow.repr.format_map`

A design passes through a dozen representations on its way from RTL to masks, and each one is stored in a file format that tools exchange.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The main formats and what they keep
- Who writes and who reads each format
- Choosing the format for a computation

Sample problem:

> Which format keeps power domains, supply nets, isolation and retention intent?
>
> A) Liberty (.lib)
>
> B) VCD or SAIF activity file
>
> C) SDF
>
> D) UPF

Answer: UPF

Why: UPF keeps power domains, supply nets, isolation and retention intent.

<a id="c-flow-repr-netlist"></a>

#### Netlists as the shared currency of the flow

`flow.repr.netlist`

A netlist is the list of component instances in a design and the nets that connect their pins.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Instances, pins and nets
- The netlist as a hypergraph
- Graph models of a hypergraph

Sample problem:

> A netlist has these nets, each written with its driver pin first: n1: U7/Y U5/A; n2: U2/Y U6/C U3/C U12/C U1/B U9/B; n3: U11/Y U3/C U4/A U10/B U6/A U9/B; n4: U1/Y U8/B U11/C; n5: U2/Y U11/C; n6: U3/Y U8/C U7/B U5/A U1/A U11/A. What is the total fanout, summed over all nets?

Answer: 19

Why: Each net's fanout is its pin count minus the driver; the sum is 19.

<a id="c-flow-repr-boolean-networks"></a>

#### Boolean networks, BDDs and AIGs

`flow.repr.boolean_networks`

Before logic becomes cells it lives in a technology-independent representation of Boolean functions.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Truth tables and their size
- And-inverter graphs
- BDDs and canonicity

Sample problem:

> How many rows does the truth table of a 6-input Boolean function have?

Answer: 64

Why: $2^{6} = 64$ rows.

<a id="c-flow-repr-liberty"></a>

#### Liberty cell libraries

`flow.repr.liberty`

Liberty is the format that tells synthesis, timing and power tools how each library cell behaves.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What a Liberty file contains
- Reading and interpolating a table
- Power, leakage and what tables miss

Sample problem:

> A Liberty cell_rise table has index_1 (input slew) 0.02, 0.05, 0.1 ns and index_2 (output load) 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.04 pF. Its rows are slew 0.02 ns: 0.0585, 0.078, 0.117, 0.195; slew 0.05 ns: 0.0765, 0.096, 0.135, 0.213; slew 0.1 ns: 0.1065, 0.126, 0.165, 0.243. What rise delay does it give, in ns, at an input slew of 0.05 ns and a load of 0.02 pF?

Answer: 0.135

Why: The point lies on the grid, so the delay is the table entry 0.135 ns.

<a id="c-flow-repr-sdc"></a>

#### SDC timing constraints

`flow.repr.sdc`

SDC is the Tcl-based format in which designers state timing intent: which clocks exist and at what period, when inputs arrive and outputs are required relative to those clocks, and which paths are exceptions.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Clocks
- Input and output delays
- Exceptions

Sample problem:

> An SDC file contains create_clock -name core_clk -period 2 [get_ports clk], with times in ns. What is the clock frequency, in MHz? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 500

Why: $1000/2 = 500$ MHz.

<a id="c-flow-repr-lef-def"></a>

#### LEF and DEF physical exchange

`flow.repr.lef_def`

LEF (Library Exchange Format) and DEF (Design Exchange Format) are the text formats in which physical-design tools exchange abstract layout.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- LEF: abstracts of cells and layers
- DEF: a design in database units
- Rows, sites and capacity

Sample problem:

> A DEF file declares UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS 1000 and DIEAREA ( 0 0 ) ( 1300000 1200000 ). What is the die area, in square millimetres? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 1.56

Why: Dividing by 1000 units per micron gives a 1300 by 1200 micron die, 1.56 square millimetres.

<a id="c-flow-repr-spef"></a>

#### SPEF parasitic exchange

`flow.repr.spef`

The Standard Parasitic Exchange Format (SPEF), defined in IEEE 1481, carries the resistances and capacitances that extraction computes from routed layout.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Header and units
- A detailed net
- Resistance paths and use in timing

Sample problem:

> A SPEF file with *C_UNIT 1 FF has a *D_NET for net *8 whose *CAP section reads: 1 *8:1 2.4; 2 *8:2 0.2; 3 *8:3 3.2; 4 *8:4 2; 5 *8:2 *14:3 1.4. The last entry couples *8 to another net. What total capacitance should the *D_NET line report, in fF? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 9.2

Why: Ground and coupling capacitances add: 9.2 fF.

<a id="c-flow-repr-gdsii-oasis"></a>

#### GDSII and OASIS mask layout

`flow.repr.gdsii_oasis`

GDSII and OASIS are the formats in which final layout is handed to the foundry. They store polygons on numbered layers, organized into a hierarchy of cells, and nothing else: no nets, no timing, no logic.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- GDSII structures and units
- Polygons and file size
- OASIS and repetition

Sample problem:

> A GDSII UNITS record says one database unit is 1E-9 metres. A BOUNDARY vertex has the integer coordinate 1287153. What is that coordinate in microns? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 1287.153

Why: $1287153 \cdot 10^{-9}$ m is 1287.153 microns.

<a id="c-flow-repr-spice-pdk"></a>

#### SPICE netlists and PDK decks

`flow.repr.spice_pdk`

A process design kit (PDK) is the foundry's package that lets a design team use a process: device models, design rules, verification decks, extraction data, and often basic cells.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- SPICE netlists
- What a PDK contains
- The PDK as the root of every abstraction

Sample problem:

> Where does a SPICE netlist appear in a digital flow?
>
> A) Only in placement
>
> B) Only in RTL simulation
>
> C) In library characterization, custom design and LVS
>
> D) Only in mask fracturing

Answer: In library characterization, custom design and LVS

Why: Cells are characterized by SPICE, custom blocks are simulated in it, and LVS compares SPICE netlists.

<a id="the-eda-landscape-quality-metrics"></a>

### Quality metrics

<a id="c-flow-metrics-ppa"></a>

#### Power, performance and area

`flow.metrics.ppa`

Power, performance and area (PPA) are the three numbers by which a chip implementation, and the tools that produced it, are judged.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Dynamic and static power
- Voltage, frequency and the quadratic lever
- Performance from the critical path

Sample problem:

> A block switches an effective capacitance of 250 pF with activity factor 0.2, at 0.9 V and 0.8 GHz. What is its dynamic power $\alpha C V^2 f$, in mW? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 32.4

Why: $0.2 \cdot 250 \times 10^{-12} \cdot 0.9^2 \cdot 0.8 \times 10^9$ W is 32.4 mW.

<a id="c-flow-metrics-pareto"></a>

#### PPA trade-offs and Pareto fronts

`flow.metrics.pareto`

There is no single best implementation of a design, because power, performance and area cannot all be minimized at once.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Dominance
- The Pareto front
- Weighted costs and their limits

Sample problem:

> Two implementations of a block are A: 17 mW, 1 ns, 1.8 square mm; B: 20 mW, 1.2 ns, 2 square mm. Lower is better for power, critical-path delay and area. Which statement is true?
>
> A) A dominates B
>
> B) B dominates A
>
> C) Neither dominates the other
>
> D) Each dominates the other

Answer: A dominates B

Why: A point dominates another when it is no worse on every metric and strictly better on at least one.

<a id="c-flow-metrics-die-per-wafer"></a>

#### Dies per wafer

`flow.metrics.die_per_wafer`

A wafer is a disc, and dies are rectangles, so only a whole number of dies fit, and some area at the edge is always lost.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The area ratio
- The edge-loss correction
- Scribe lanes and die size

Sample problem:

> Ignoring edge loss, how many dies of 439 square mm fit by area on a 300 mm wafer? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 161

Why: $\pi (300/2)^2 / 439 = 161$.

<a id="c-flow-metrics-yield-cost"></a>

#### Yield and cost per good die

`flow.metrics.yield_cost`

Not every die on a wafer works. Random defects, particles and process faults kill some fraction, and the probability that a die survives falls with its area.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The Poisson yield model
- Good dies per wafer
- Cost per good die

Sample problem:

> Defects are Poisson-distributed at 0.05 per square cm. Under $Y = e^{-D_0 A}$, what fraction of 277 square mm dies is defect-free, in percent? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 87.1

Why: 277 square mm is 2.77 square cm, so $Y = e^{-0.05 \cdot 2.77} = 87.1\%$.

<a id="c-flow-metrics-respin-cost"></a>

#### The cost of a respin

`flow.metrics.respin_cost`

A respin is a second (or third) fabrication of a chip after first silicon fails.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The direct cost
- The cost of delay
- Expected cost and the value of verification

Sample problem:

> A respin needs a new mask set costing 25 million dollars and 36 engineers for 2 months at 15 thousand dollars per engineer-month. What is its direct cost, in millions of dollars? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 26.08

Why: $25 + 36 \cdot 2 \cdot 15/1000 = 26.08$ million dollars.

<a id="the-eda-landscape-branches-of-eda"></a>

### Branches of EDA

<a id="c-flow-branches-analog-ams"></a>

#### Analog and mixed-signal design flows

`flow.branches.analog_ams`

Analog and mixed-signal (AMS) circuits, such as amplifiers, data converters, PLLs, regulators and RF front ends, do not fit the RTL-to-GDSII flow.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- A schematic-driven flow
- Why analog resists automation
- Mixed-signal integration

Sample problem:

> What is the first design representation in a typical analog flow?
>
> A) A transistor-level schematic
>
> B) A gate-level netlist
>
> C) A routed DEF
>
> D) Synthesizable RTL

Answer: A transistor-level schematic

Why: Analog design starts from a schematic of devices that the designer sizes and simulates.

<a id="c-flow-branches-fpga-flow"></a>

#### The FPGA implementation flow

`flow.branches.fpga_flow`

An FPGA flow starts from the same RTL as an ASIC flow but ends in a bitstream that configures a fixed chip.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- LUTs as truth tables
- Placement and routing on a fixed fabric
- Vendor tools, open tools and trade-offs

Sample problem:

> What does FPGA technology mapping cover the logic with?
>
> A) Library cells from a Liberty file
>
> B) Mask polygons
>
> C) k-feasible cones, each with at most k inputs
>
> D) Transistor networks

Answer: k-feasible cones, each with at most k inputs

Why: Any function of k inputs fits one LUT, so mapping finds cones with at most k inputs.

<a id="c-flow-branches-pcb-package"></a>

#### PCB and package design

`flow.branches.pcb_package`

A chip is useless until it is packaged and mounted on a board. Package design connects the die to the outside world through bumps, substrate traces and balls; printed circuit board (PCB) design connects packages, passives and connectors through layers of copper.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The board flow
- Packages and advanced packaging
- Signal, power and thermal integrity

Sample problem:

> Why does advanced packaging make package design resemble chip design?
>
> A) Packages are synthesized from RTL
>
> B) Packages now contain transistors
>
> C) Packages need clock trees
>
> D) Thousands of die-to-die connections must be routed at fine pitch

Answer: Thousands of die-to-die connections must be routed at fine pitch

Why: Dense interposer and bridge wiring needs chip-like routing and verification.

<a id="c-flow-branches-manufacturing"></a>

#### Manufacturing, lithography and DFM

`flow.branches.manufacturing`

Manufacturing is the branch where geometry becomes silicon, and its tools work on the far side of tape-out: mask synthesis, lithography simulation, process modelling and yield analysis.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Printing below the wavelength
- Design for manufacturability
- Process and device modelling

Sample problem:

> A layer's pitch is too tight for one exposure. What resolution technique splits it?
>
> A) Multiple patterning onto two or more masks
>
> B) Metal fill
>
> C) Scan insertion
>
> D) Optical proximity correction alone

Answer: Multiple patterning onto two or more masks

Why: Splitting the layer into masks, a graph-colouring problem, relaxes the pitch per exposure.

<a id="the-eda-landscape-the-industry-and-its-standards"></a>

### The industry and its standards

<a id="c-flow-industry-foundry-fabless"></a>

#### The foundry and fabless model

`flow.industry.foundry_fabless`

Most chips today are designed by companies that do not own a factory. A fabless company designs chips and sells them; a foundry manufactures chips that others design.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Integrated, fabless and foundry companies
- The PDK as the interface
- Economics and consequences for EDA

Sample problem:

> Besides models and rule decks, what do foundries often supply or reference for their process?
>
> A) Validated standard-cell and memory libraries
>
> B) Board-level layouts
>
> C) The customer's testbench
>
> D) The customer's floorplan

Answer: Validated standard-cell and memory libraries

Why: Libraries characterized on the process are part of design enablement.

<a id="c-flow-industry-vendors"></a>

#### EDA vendors and industry structure

`flow.industry.vendors`

The EDA industry is small in revenue next to the semiconductor industry it serves, but it is indispensable: no advanced chip can be built without its tools.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The large digital vendors
- Specialists by domain
- How the business works

Sample problem:

> Which barrier does a new EDA entrant face that a mature vendor already cleared?
>
> A) The need for a user interface
>
> B) The need to read Verilog
>
> C) The need to run on Linux
>
> D) Foundry certification of its tool on each process

Answer: Foundry certification of its tool on each process

Why: Without certification, signoff results are not accepted for manufacturing.

<a id="c-flow-industry-tool-landscape"></a>

#### The commercial and open-source tool landscape

`flow.industry.tool_landscape`

Engineers name tools by product, but a tool designer should name them by the problem class they solve: simulation, synthesis, place and route, static timing, extraction, physical verification, test, custom layout.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Front-end tools
- Back-end and signoff tools
- The open-source landscape

<a id="c-flow-industry-open-source"></a>

#### Open-source EDA tools

`flow.industry.open_source`

Open-source EDA has grown from academic prototypes into a complete RTL-to-GDSII flow that has taped out real chips.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The digital implementation chain
- Layout, verification and simulation
- What open tools are good for

Sample problem:

> What does the open-source tool nextpnr do?
>
> A) Event-driven Verilog simulation
>
> B) RTL synthesis to a gate-level netlist
>
> C) Compiling Verilog into a fast cycle-based C++ model
>
> D) FPGA placement and routing

Answer: FPGA placement and routing

Why: nextpnr: FPGA placement and routing.

<a id="c-flow-industry-standards"></a>

#### Standards bodies and open formats

`flow.industry.standards`

EDA works only because tools from different vendors can read each other's files and agree on what a language means.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Si2, SEMI and IPC
- De facto standards

Sample problem:

> Which IEEE standard defines boundary scan (JTAG)?
>
> A) IEEE 1481
>
> B) IEEE 1801
>
> C) IEEE 1149.1
>
> D) IEEE 1364

Answer: IEEE 1149.1

Why: JTAG boundary scan is IEEE 1149.1.

<a id="the-eda-landscape-history"></a>

### History

<a id="c-flow-history-landmarks"></a>

#### Structured VLSI design, SPICE and the university CAD tools

`flow.history.landmarks`

Modern EDA grew from a few landmark ideas of the 1970s and 1980s.

Sample problem:

> How does SPICE formulate the circuit equations?
>
> A) Modified nodal analysis with sparse matrices
>
> B) A timing graph of arrival times
>
> C) An and-inverter graph
>
> D) A routing-resource graph

Answer: Modified nodal analysis with sparse matrices

Why: Modified nodal analysis gives a sparse system solved by sparse LU factorization.

<a id="c-flow-history-communities"></a>

#### EDA research conferences and communities

`flow.history.communities`

EDA research is published mainly at conferences, and each major conference has a distinct community and focus.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The general conferences
- The specialist communities
- Benchmarks and contests

Sample problem:

> Which conference is research-focused and covers the whole of EDA without a large exhibition?
>
> A) ISSCC
>
> B) ICCAD
>
> C) DAC
>
> D) SEMICON

Answer: ICCAD

Why: ICCAD is the field-wide research conference.

<a id="the-eda-landscape-frontier-agent-first-futures"></a>

### Frontier: agent-first futures

<a id="c-flow-frontier-engine-layers"></a>

#### The four-layer model across flow engines

`flow.frontier.engine_layers`

An agent that changes EDA tools on request needs to know which part of an engine a request touches.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The same four layers in every engine
- Classifying a request
- Why the core must stay small

Sample problem:

> In a router, which part is strategy rather than core?
>
> A) The definition of a short between nets
>
> B) The rip-up and reroute ordering
>
> C) The DRC-correct path model
>
> D) Grid and layer legality

Answer: The rip-up and reroute ordering

Why: How the router searches is strategy; what counts as a legal route is core.

<a id="c-flow-frontier-change-tiers"></a>

#### Routing a flow change request to a tier

`flow.frontier.change_tiers`

Requests to change a flow arrive in plain language: make placement less congested near the memories, time this block with an extra margin, route this bus on upper layers.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Three tiers
- Matching requests to tiers
- Proving a change at its tier

Sample problem:

> What defines a Tier 2 change?
>
> A) A small implementation at a defined extension point, leaving the core untouched
>
> B) A change to the foundry rule deck
>
> C) A value in a configuration file
>
> D) A change to the engine's core source

Answer: A small implementation at a defined extension point, leaving the core untouched

Why: Tier 2 adds code through a seam such as a plug-in interface.

<a id="c-flow-frontier-fast-accurate"></a>

#### Fast and accurate engines across the flow

`flow.frontier.fast_accurate`

Every analysis in the flow exists at several accuracies: a fast placer and a full placer, a quick congestion estimate and a global router, a fast timer with lumped wires and a signoff timer with extracted parasitics.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The cost of a modeling loop
- When to recurse to the accurate engine
- What the fast mode gives up

Sample problem:

> An agent runs 60 iterations of a fast place-and-time loop, each taking 15 minutes, and every 5th iteration it confirms the result with an accurate run taking 240 minutes. How many minutes does the whole loop take?

Answer: 3780

Why: $60 \cdot 15 + \lfloor 60/5 \rfloor \cdot 240 = 3780$ minutes.

<a id="c-flow-frontier-differential-qor"></a>

#### Differential QoR checks on a flow change

`flow.frontier.differential_qor`

When an agent changes a flow, by a parameter, a plug-in or a script, someone must decide whether the change did what it claimed and nothing else.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Comparing two runs
- Summary metrics and their limits
- Intended versus unintended movement

Sample problem:

> A differential timing check compares endpoint setup slacks (in ps, baseline to new) after a flow change: A: -10 to -9; B: -3 to 0; C: -5 to -3; D: 37 to 33; E: 32 to 29. With a tolerance of 5 ps, how many endpoints moved?

Answer: 0

Why: Count endpoints whose slack changed by more than 5 ps: 0.

<a id="c-flow-frontier-agentic-flow"></a>

#### Agentic closure loops across the flow

`flow.frontier.agentic_flow`

Design closure has always been a loop: read reports, decide a fix, run tools, check again.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The closure loop as an agent
- Multi-agent orchestration over the flow
- Rewards, reward hacking and the human gate

Sample problem:

> A path fails timing by 6 ps. What should a well-designed closure agent try first?
>
> A) Relaxing the clock constraint
>
> B) Changing the floorplan
>
> C) A local fix such as resizing a gate or inserting a buffer
>
> D) Re-running synthesis from RTL

Answer: A local fix such as resizing a gate or inserting a buffer

Why: The most local fix re-runs the fewest stages, as an engineer would choose.

---

## Boolean Reasoning and Complexity

Layer 1. Boolean functions, cofactors, Shannon expansion, covers and clauses, and the complexity theory that explains why every EDA problem needs heuristics.

Builds on: discrete math, abstract algebra.

Topics covered:

- Boolean algebra and Boolean functions, propositional and predicate logic as used in hardware
- Cofactors, Shannon expansion, Boolean difference, unate and binate functions, symmetry
- Cubes, covers, SOP/POS, minterms, implicants, prime implicants
- Boolean decomposition, functional dependence
- Decision diagrams overview, constraint satisfaction problems
- Partial orders and lattices in logic
- Computational complexity: P vs NP, NP-completeness, NP-hardness, reductions (SAT, 3-SAT, clique, vertex cover), approximation algorithms, heuristics, parameterized complexity, randomized algorithms, amortized analysis, algorithm analysis
- Data structures for Boolean reasoning (bit-parallel truth tables, hash-consing)

Subdomains: [Boolean functions](#boolean-reasoning-and-complexity-boolean-functions), [Decomposition](#boolean-reasoning-and-complexity-decomposition), [Covering and minimization](#boolean-reasoning-and-complexity-covering-and-minimization), [Representations (BDDs, AIGs)](#boolean-reasoning-and-complexity-representations-bdds-aigs), [Variable ordering](#boolean-reasoning-and-complexity-variable-ordering), [CNF and encodings](#boolean-reasoning-and-complexity-cnf-and-encodings), [Algorithms](#boolean-reasoning-and-complexity-algorithms), [Complexity](#boolean-reasoning-and-complexity-complexity), [Frontier: agent-first futures](#boolean-reasoning-and-complexity-frontier-agent-first-futures)

<a id="boolean-reasoning-and-complexity-boolean-functions"></a>

### Boolean functions

<a id="c-boolalg-func-truth-table"></a>

#### Boolean functions and truth tables

`boolalg.func.truth_table`

A Boolean function $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ is the object every logic tool manipulates: synthesis rewrites it, a SAT solver searches its inputs, an equivalence checker compares two of them, and a test generator looks for inputs that expose a difference.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Functions from n bits to one bit
- Counting Boolean functions
- Comparing two functions row by row

Sample problem:

> Let $f(a, b, c) = \overline{c} + ab$. On how many of the 8 rows of its truth table is $f = 1$?

Answer: 5

Why: Evaluating the expression row by row gives the ON-set m(0, 2, 4, 6, 7), which has 5 rows.

<a id="c-boolalg-func-cofactor"></a>

#### Cofactors of a Boolean function

`boolalg.func.cofactor`

The cofactor of $f$ with respect to a literal is the function left over when that variable is fixed.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Fixing one variable
- Cofactors from the truth table
- Cofactor with respect to a cube

Sample problem:

> Let $f(a, b, c) = \overline{a}c + b + \overline{b}\overline{c}$. Compute the cofactor $f_{\overline{b}}$ (set $b = 0$), a function of a, c. How many of its 4 rows are 1?

Answer: 3

Why: Setting b = 0 keeps the 4 rows with that value. Of those, 3 have f = 1.

<a id="c-boolalg-func-shannon"></a>

#### Shannon expansion

`boolalg.func.shannon`

Shannon expansion writes any Boolean function as a choice between its two cofactors: $f = x\, f_x + \overline{x}\, f_{\overline{x}}$.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Splitting a function on one variable
- Rebuilding a function from its cofactors
- Recursive expansion and distinct subfunctions

Sample problem:

> A function of a, b, c is built by Shannon expansion on $a$: $f = a\,(\overline{c} + \overline{b}) + \overline{a}\,(\overline{c} + \overline{b})$. On how many of the 8 rows of $f$ is $f = 1$?

Answer: 6

Why: The two terms are disjoint, since one needs a = 1 and the other a = 0. The positive cofactor has 3 ON rows and the negative cofactor has 3, so f has 6.

<a id="c-boolalg-func-boolean-difference"></a>

#### Boolean difference and sensitivity

`boolalg.func.boolean_difference`

The Boolean difference of $f$ with respect to $x$ is the function that is 1 exactly where changing $x$ changes $f$.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The XOR of the two cofactors
- Inputs where a variable matters
- Sensitization in test generation

Sample problem:

> Let $f(a, b, c) = \sum m(3, 4, 5, 6, 7)$. The Boolean difference $\partial f / \partial a = f_{a} \oplus f_{\overline{a}}$ is a function of b, c. On how many of its 4 rows is it 1?

Answer: 3

Why: XOR the two cofactors row by row: they differ on 3 of the 4 rows.

<a id="c-boolalg-func-unateness"></a>

#### Unate and binate functions

`boolalg.func.unateness`

A function is positive unate in $x$ when raising $x$ from 0 to 1 can never lower the output, negative unate when it can never raise it, and binate when it does both on different rows.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Comparing the two cofactors
- Classifying every variable
- Syntactic versus semantic unateness

Sample problem:

> Let $f(a, b, c) = b\overline{c} + \overline{b}c$. How does $f$ depend on $c$? Compare $f_{c}$ with $f_{\overline{c}}$.
>
> A) Independent of $c$
>
> B) Positive unate in $c$
>
> C) Binate in $c$
>
> D) Negative unate in $c$

Answer: Binate in $c$

Why: Neither cofactor implies the other: some rows rise with c and others fall, so f is binate in c.

<a id="c-boolalg-func-symmetry"></a>

#### Symmetric functions

`boolalg.func.symmetry`

A function is symmetric in a pair of variables when swapping them never changes the output, and totally symmetric when any permutation of its inputs leaves it unchanged.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Totally symmetric functions
- Symmetry in a pair of variables
- Counting symmetric functions

Sample problem:

> A totally symmetric function of 3 inputs is 1 exactly when the number of inputs at 1 is one of {1, 2}. How many of its 8 rows are 1?

Answer: 6

Why: Count the rows of each allowed weight: C(3,1) + C(3,2) = 6.

<a id="c-boolalg-func-quantification"></a>

#### Existential and universal quantification

`boolalg.func.quantification`

Quantifying a Boolean variable removes it from a function. The existential quantification $\exists x\, f$ asks whether some value of $x$ makes $f$ true; the universal quantification $\forall x\, f$ asks whether every value does.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Existential quantification as an OR of cofactors
- Universal quantification as an AND of cofactors
- Nested quantifiers in hardware properties

Sample problem:

> Let $f(a, b, c) = b + a + a\overline{c}$. The property "there exists a value of $b$ that makes $f$ true" is $\exists b\, f$, a function of a, c. On how many of its 4 rows is it 1?

Answer: 4

Why: Existential quantification is the OR of the cofactors: f with b = 0 OR f with b = 1. That OR is 1 on 4 rows.

<a id="boolean-reasoning-and-complexity-decomposition"></a>

### Decomposition

<a id="c-boolalg-decomp-support"></a>

#### Support and functional dependence

`boolalg.decomp.support`

The support of a function is the set of variables it really depends on. Expressions routinely mention variables the function ignores, and netlists routinely compute signals that are functions of other signals.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The true support of a function
- Vacuous variables in a redundant expression
- When one function is a function of others

Sample problem:

> Let $f(a, b, c, d) = \sum m(0, 2, 4, 6)$. How many variables are in the true support of $f$, the variables whose Boolean difference is not identically 0?

Answer: 2

Why: Compare the two cofactors of each variable. They differ only for a, d, so the support has 2 variables.

<a id="c-boolalg-decomp-disjoint"></a>

#### Simple disjoint decomposition

`boolalg.decomp.disjoint`

A decomposition writes a function as a composition of smaller ones. The simple disjoint form is $f(A, B) = h(g(A), B)$: a sub-function $g$ reads only the bound set $A$, and the rest of the logic sees $A$ only through that single wire.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The decomposition chart
- How many intermediate signals
- Searching for a good bound set

Sample problem:

> Let $f(a, b, c, d) = \sum m(0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 10, 11, 14, 15)$. Draw the decomposition chart with bound set $\{a, d\}$ (one column per assignment of the bound set) and free set $\{b, c\}$. What is the column multiplicity, the number of distinct columns?

Answer: 3

Why: Each column is the cofactor of f with respect to one assignment of (a, d), a function of b, c. There are 3 distinct cofactors. A simple disjoint decomposition f = h(g(a, d), b, c) exists exactly when this is at most 2.

<a id="boolean-reasoning-and-complexity-covering-and-minimization"></a>

### Covering and minimization

<a id="c-boolalg-cover-cubes"></a>

#### Cubes and their minterms

`boolalg.cover.cubes`

A cube is a product of literals, such as $a\overline{c}d$, and also the set of minterms it covers, a subcube of the Boolean hypercube.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Cubes as products of literals
- Intersection and union of cubes
- Distance and consensus

Sample problem:

> In positional notation over 5 variables (one position per variable, 0 for a complemented literal, 1 for a true literal, - for an absent variable), how many minterms does the cube 0--0- contain?

Answer: 8

Why: The cube has 3 dashes, each free to be 0 or 1, so it contains 2^3 = 8 minterms.

<a id="c-boolalg-cover-sop-pos"></a>

#### Sum-of-products and product-of-sums forms

`boolalg.cover.sop_pos`

Every Boolean function has two canonical two-level forms: the sum of its minterms and the product of its maxterms.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Canonical sum of minterms
- Canonical product of maxterms
- Evaluating a product of sums

Sample problem:

> Let $f(a, b, c) = b\overline{c} + b + \overline{a}\overline{b}$. How many literals does its canonical sum of minterms contain in total?

Answer: 18

Why: There are 6 ON rows, each a minterm of 3 literals: 18 literals.

<a id="c-boolalg-cover-implicants"></a>

#### Cubes, implicants and prime implicants

`boolalg.cover.implicants`

An implicant of $f$ is a cube that lies entirely inside the ON-set, so it implies $f$.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Implicants: cubes inside the ON-set
- Prime implicants: maximal implicants
- Recognizing primes in a cover

Sample problem:

> Let $f(a, b, c) = \sum m(0, 1, 3, 6)$. Classify the cube $\overline{b}$.
>
> A) An implicant of $f$ but not prime
>
> B) Not an implicant of $f$
>
> C) An essential prime of the complement of $f$
>
> D) A prime implicant of $f$

Answer: Not an implicant of $f$

Why: Some minterm of the cube is an OFF row of f, so the cube is not contained in the ON-set.

<a id="c-boolalg-cover-essential-primes"></a>

#### Essential prime implicants

`boolalg.cover.essential_primes`

A prime implicant is essential when it is the only prime covering some ON minterm.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Generating all primes
- Essential primes
- What the essentials leave behind

Sample problem:

> Let $f(a, b, c) = \sum m(0, 7)$. How many prime implicants does $f$ have?

Answer: 2

Why: The primes are $\overline{a}\overline{b}\overline{c}$, $abc$: 2.

<a id="c-boolalg-cover-min-cover"></a>

#### Minimum covers and the covering problem

`boolalg.cover.min_cover`

Once the primes are known, two-level minimization becomes a covering problem: choose the cheapest set of primes whose union is the ON-set.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Covering the ON-set with primes
- The cyclic core
- Cost beyond cube count

Sample problem:

> Let $f(a, b, c) = \sum m(2, 6)$. What is the smallest number of product terms in any sum-of-products expression for $f$?

Answer: 1

Why: A minimum SOP uses primes only. Of the 1 primes, 1 are essential, and the cheapest set covering every ON minterm has 1 cubes.

<a id="c-boolalg-cover-dont-cares"></a>

#### Incompletely specified functions

`boolalg.cover.dont_cares`

Real specifications leave some outputs free. Inputs that never occur (an unused opcode, an unreachable state code) and outputs nobody observes are don't cares.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The ON, OFF and don't-care sets
- Minimizing with don't cares
- Primes of an incompletely specified function

Sample problem:

> An incompletely specified function of a, b, c has ON-set $\sum m(0, 3, 4, 6)$ and don't-care set $d(1, 2)$; every other row is OFF. How many completely specified functions agree with it on every care row?

Answer: 4

Why: Each of the 2 don't-care rows may be 0 or 1: 2^2 = 4.

<a id="c-boolalg-cover-tautology"></a>

#### Tautology checking of a cover

`boolalg.cover.tautology`

A cover is a tautology when its cubes together contain every minterm, so the function it represents is the constant 1.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- A cover is a tautology when nothing is missed
- Cofactoring a cover
- Cube containment as a tautology question

Sample problem:

> Over the variables a, b, c, in that order, a cover is $F = \{-0-, -00, -00, -00, 11-, 0-0, 0-1\}$ in positional notation. How many of the 8 minterms does $F$ miss? (Zero means $F$ is a tautology.)

Answer: 0

Why: The cubes together cover 8 of the 8 minterms, so 0 are missed.

<a id="boolean-reasoning-and-complexity-representations-bdds-aigs"></a>

### Representations (BDDs, AIGs)

<a id="c-boolalg-repr-bitparallel"></a>

#### Bit-parallel truth tables

`boolalg.repr.bitparallel`

For functions of up to about 16 inputs, the fastest representation is the explicit truth table packed into machine words.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- A function as one machine word
- Variable masks and word operations
- Cofactors by shifting

Sample problem:

> A tool stores $f(a, b, c) = \overline{a}\overline{c} + a + \overline{b}$ as a 8-bit truth-table word. Bit $i$ of the word holds $f$ at minterm $i$, where $i$ is written in binary as $abc$ with $a$ the most significant bit; bit 0 is the least significant bit of the word. Which word is it?
>
> A) 0xF6
>
> B) 0xEF
>
> C) 0xF7
>
> D) 0x08

Answer: 0xF7

Why: The ON-set is m(0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7); set those bits and read the word in hex from bit 7 down to bit 0: 0xF7.

<a id="c-boolalg-repr-hash-consing"></a>

#### Hash-consing and structural hashing

`boolalg.repr.hash_consing`

Hash-consing is the rule that a data structure never stores two copies of the same node: before creating a node, look up its key, the operator and its children's identifiers, in a unique table, and return the existing node if one is there.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- One node per distinct structure
- Canonical keys
- Trivial simplification before hashing

Sample problem:

> An and-inverter graph over inputs $a, b, c, d$ is built gate by gate: $g_{1} = c \land d$, $g_{2} = a \land d$, $g_{3} = g_{1} \land g_{2}$, $g_{4} = g_{1} \land g_{2}$, $g_{5} = b \land g_{2}$, $g_{6} = g_{3} \land g_{4}$. The builder hash-conses: before creating an AND node it looks up the pair of operands in a unique table. How many AND nodes does the table hold at the end?

Answer: 4

Why: Of the 6 gate definitions, 4 produce new keys; the rest are duplicates or simplify away. Hash-consing gives each distinct structure exactly one node, so equality of nodes is a pointer comparison.

<a id="c-boolalg-repr-decision-diagram"></a>

#### Decision diagrams overview

`boolalg.repr.decision_diagram`

A reduced ordered binary decision diagram (ROBDD) is the Shannon expansion tree of a function with identical subfunctions shared and pointless tests removed, under a fixed variable order.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- From the Shannon tree to a reduced diagram
- Counting reduced nodes level by level
- The order decides the size

Sample problem:

> Let $f(a, b, c) = \sum m(1, 6)$. Build its reduced ordered BDD with the order a < b < c (first variable at the top). How many internal (non-terminal) nodes does it have?

Answer: 5

Why: At each level, count the distinct subfunctions reached by fixing the variables above it that still depend on that level's variable; sum over levels: 5 nodes, plus the two terminals.

<a id="boolean-reasoning-and-complexity-variable-ordering"></a>

### Variable ordering

<a id="c-boolalg-order-boolean-lattice"></a>

#### The Boolean lattice and implication order

`boolalg.order.boolean_lattice`

Bit vectors of length $n$, ordered componentwise, form the Boolean lattice $B^n$: the hypercube with 00...0 at the bottom and 11...1 at the top.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Bit vectors ordered componentwise
- Functions ordered by implication
- Join and meet of functions

Sample problem:

> In $B^{6}$ ordered componentwise, how many vectors are comparable to 011110 (above it, below it, or equal)?

Answer: 19

Why: There are 2^2 vectors at or above and 2^4 at or below; the vector itself is counted twice: 19.

<a id="c-boolalg-order-monotone"></a>

#### Monotone functions

`boolalg.order.monotone`

A monotone function is an order-preserving map from $B^n$ to $\{0, 1\}$: raising any input never lowers the output.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Monotone means order-preserving
- Minimal true points are the primes
- Maximal false points give the clauses

Sample problem:

> The monotone function $f(a, b, c, d) = ab + ad + c$ uses only positive literals. On how many of its 16 rows is $f = 1$?

Answer: 11

Why: The ON-set is the up-set of the minimal true points: every vector at or above one of them. It has 11 rows.

<a id="c-boolalg-order-fixpoint"></a>

#### Fixpoints on the subset lattice

`boolalg.order.fixpoint`

Many verification questions are answered by iterating a set operator until it stops changing.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Iterating a monotone operator
- The least fixpoint is the reachable set
- Greatest fixpoints

Sample problem:

> A transition system has states $s_0$ to $s_6$ and transitions $s_1 \to s_4,\ s_4 \to s_4,\ s_5 \to s_1,\ s_5 \to s_5,\ s_6 \to s_2,\ s_6 \to s_4$. Reachability iterates $R_0 = \{s_1, s_5\}$, $R_{k+1} = R_k \cup \mathrm{Img}(R_k)$ until nothing changes. How many steps add at least one new state?

Answer: 1

Why: Breadth-first, each step adds the states one transition further out. The farthest reachable state is 1 transitions from the initial set, so 1 steps add states and the next step confirms the fixpoint.

<a id="boolean-reasoning-and-complexity-cnf-and-encodings"></a>

### CNF and encodings

<a id="c-boolalg-cnf-clauses"></a>

#### Conjunctive normal form and clauses

`boolalg.cnf.clauses`

Conjunctive normal form is an AND of clauses, each clause an OR of literals. It is the input language of every SAT solver (the DIMACS format), so equivalence checking, bounded model checking, test generation and many scheduling and routing problems end up as CNF.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Clauses and assignments
- What one clause forbids
- CNF size of familiar functions

Sample problem:

> Under the assignment $x_{1} = 0, x_{2} = 1, x_{3} = 0, x_{4} = 0$, how many clauses of $(\neg x_{2} \lor \neg x_{3}) \land (\neg x_{2} \lor \neg x_{4}) \land (\neg x_{1} \lor x_{2} \lor \neg x_{4}) \land (\neg x_{2} \lor \neg x_{3})$ are falsified?

Answer: 0

Why: A clause is falsified only when every one of its literals is false. 0 clauses are.

<a id="c-boolalg-cnf-tseitin"></a>

#### Tseitin encoding of a circuit

`boolalg.cnf.tseitin`

The Tseitin encoding turns a circuit into CNF of linear size by giving every gate output its own variable and writing a few clauses that force that variable to equal the gate's function of its inputs.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Clauses for one gate
- Clauses for a netlist
- Variables and the size of the encoding

Sample problem:

> Use the standard Tseitin encoding: one fresh variable per gate output, the clauses of output if and only if gate function, and no simplification. How many clauses encode a single two-input XNOR gate?

Answer: 4

Why: y = a XNOR b, like XOR, needs 4 three-literal clauses. Total: 4.

<a id="c-boolalg-cnf-model-count"></a>

#### Counting satisfying assignments

`boolalg.cnf.model_count`

Model counting, written #SAT, asks how many assignments satisfy a formula rather than whether one exists.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Model counting by enumeration
- Counting by inclusion and exclusion
- Independent components multiply

Sample problem:

> Over $x_1$ to $x_{3}$, how many assignments satisfy $(\neg x_{2} \lor \neg x_{3}) \land (x_{1} \lor \neg x_{2} \lor \neg x_{3}) \land (x_{1} \lor x_{2} \lor \neg x_{3})$?

Answer: 5

Why: Enumerate all 8 assignments and test every clause: 5 satisfy the formula.

<a id="c-boolalg-cnf-resolution"></a>

#### Resolution and variable elimination

`boolalg.cnf.resolution`

Resolution is the single inference rule behind clause-based reasoning: from $(x \lor A)$ and $(\neg x \lor B)$ infer $(A \lor B)$.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The resolution rule
- Tautological resolvents
- Eliminating a variable

Sample problem:

> Resolve $(x_{1} \lor x_{4})$ with $(\neg x_{1} \lor x_{4})$ on $x_{1}$. How many distinct literals does the resolvent contain?

Answer: 1

Why: Drop the clashing pair and take the union of what remains, merging repeated literals: $(x_{4})$, 1 literals.

<a id="c-boolalg-cnf-csp"></a>

#### Constraint satisfaction problems in CNF

`boolalg.cnf.csp`

A constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) has variables with finite domains and constraints over subsets of them.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- One-hot encoding of a finite domain
- Graph coloring as a CSP
- Binary encoding of a domain

Sample problem:

> A CSP has 11 variables, each with a domain of 3 values, encoded one-hot with an at-least-one clause and pairwise at-most-one clauses per variable. How many domain clauses are there in total, before any constraint clauses?

Answer: 44

Why: Each variable needs 1 + C(3, 2) = 4 clauses; times 11 variables gives 44.

<a id="c-boolalg-cnf-tractable"></a>

#### Tractable classes of SAT

`boolalg.cnf.tractable`

SAT is NP-complete, but several syntactic classes are solvable in polynomial time, and a surprising share of the constraints that EDA tools generate fall into them.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- 2-SAT and the implication graph
- Horn clauses and forward chaining
- XOR constraints and where hardness begins

Sample problem:

> In a 2-SAT implication graph, $x$ and $\neg x$ lie in the same strongly connected component. What follows?
>
> A) The formula has exactly two models
>
> B) $x$ is true in every model
>
> C) $x$ can be removed as a pure literal
>
> D) The formula is unsatisfiable

Answer: The formula is unsatisfiable

Why: Paths $x \to \dots \to \neg x$ and $\neg x \to \dots \to x$ force $x$ to equal its own negation, so no assignment works.

<a id="boolean-reasoning-and-complexity-algorithms"></a>

### Algorithms

<a id="c-boolalg-algo-analysis"></a>

#### Algorithm analysis for Boolean tools

`boolalg.algo.analysis`

Boolean tools live on the edge between polynomial and exponential cost. A tool designer must predict, before writing code, whether an approach scales: how much memory an explicit representation takes, how many calls a recursion makes, and how a measured runtime will extrapolate to the next design size.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Memory of an explicit truth table
- Recurrences of recursive Boolean algorithms
- Extrapolating exponential running time

Sample problem:

> A tool stores the complete truth table of a 17-variable function bit-parallel in 64-bit machine words. How many words does it need?

Answer: 2048

Why: The table has 2^17 bits; dividing by 2^6 bits per word leaves 2^11 = 2048 words. Each extra variable doubles it, which is why explicit tables stop near 16 to 20 inputs.

<a id="c-boolalg-algo-amortized"></a>

#### Amortized analysis

`boolalg.algo.amortized`

Amortized analysis bounds the total cost of a sequence of operations, even when single operations are occasionally expensive.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The binary counter
- Doubling hash tables
- Cost per operation

Sample problem:

> A binary counter starts at 0 and is incremented 147 times. Each increment flips the trailing 1s to 0 and one 0 to 1. How many bit flips happen in total?

Answer: 290

Why: Bit j flips once every 2^j increments, so the total is 2N minus the number of 1s in N: 2(147) - 4 = 290, under 2 flips per increment.

<a id="c-boolalg-algo-randomized"></a>

#### Randomized algorithms and random simulation

`boolalg.algo.randomized`

Randomized algorithms use coin flips to be faster or simpler than any known deterministic method, at the price of a bounded probability of error or a random running time.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The chance that random vectors miss a difference
- How many vectors are enough
- Expected time to the first counterexample

Sample problem:

> Two 6-input functions differ on exactly 1 of the $2^{6}$ input vectors. A simulator applies 19 independent, uniformly random vectors. What is the probability that none of them exposes the difference? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 0.7414

Why: Each vector misses with probability 1 - 1/64. Independence gives (1 - p)^19 = 0.7414.

<a id="boolean-reasoning-and-complexity-complexity"></a>

### Complexity

<a id="c-boolalg-complexity-p-np"></a>

#### P, NP and coNP

`boolalg.complexity.p_np`

Complexity classes tell a tool designer what kind of algorithm to look for. A problem in P has an algorithm whose time is polynomial in the input size.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Decision problems and polynomial time
- Certificates and NP
- coNP and the shape of verification problems

Sample problem:

> Which of these is a decision problem?
>
> A) Find the smallest circuit computing this truth table
>
> B) List all satisfying assignments of this CNF
>
> C) Count the models of this formula
>
> D) Is there an input vector that sets this circuit's output to 1?

Answer: Is there an input vector that sets this circuit's output to 1?

Why: A decision problem has a yes or no answer. The others ask for an object, a list or a number.

<a id="c-boolalg-complexity-reduction"></a>

#### Polynomial-time reductions

`boolalg.complexity.reduction`

A reduction from problem A to problem B is a polynomial-time transformation of every instance of A into an instance of B with the same yes or no answer.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What a reduction must preserve
- 3-SAT to independent set
- Choosing the direction

Sample problem:

> What must a polynomial-time many-one reduction from problem A to problem B do?
>
> A) Run in polynomial time on yes-instances only
>
> B) Map instances of B to instances of A
>
> C) Map yes-instances of A to yes-instances of B and no-instances to no-instances, in polynomial time
>
> D) Preserve the number of solutions exactly

Answer: Map yes-instances of A to yes-instances of B and no-instances to no-instances, in polynomial time

Why: The reduction is a polynomial function f with x in A exactly when f(x) is in B. Counting solutions is a stronger, parsimonious requirement.

<a id="c-boolalg-complexity-np-complete"></a>

#### NP-completeness

`boolalg.complexity.np_complete`

A problem is NP-complete when it is in NP and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The Cook-Levin theorem
- Proving a new problem NP-complete
- NP-hard, NP-complete and the problems a tool meets

Sample problem:

> Why does the Cook-Levin proof turn a verifier into a circuit?
>
> A) A polynomial-time verifier on inputs of fixed size unrolls into a polynomial-size circuit, and asking whether some certificate makes it accept is a satisfiability question
>
> B) Circuits remove the need for certificates
>
> C) Circuits run faster than Turing machines
>
> D) Only circuits can express polynomial time

Answer: A polynomial-time verifier on inputs of fixed size unrolls into a polynomial-size circuit, and asking whether some certificate makes it accept is a satisfiability question

Why: The circuit's free inputs are the certificate bits; satisfiability of the circuit is exactly the existence of an accepted certificate.

<a id="c-boolalg-complexity-sat-to-3sat"></a>

#### From SAT to 3-SAT

`boolalg.complexity.sat_to_3sat`

3-SAT, where every clause has at most three literals, is the standard starting point for NP-hardness proofs because its instances are uniform and small gadgets can simulate a clause.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Splitting one long clause
- Fresh variables for a whole formula
- Size of the 3-CNF

Sample problem:

> The standard SAT-to-3-SAT reduction splits a clause of 5 literals into a chain of three-literal clauses. How many fresh linking variables does it introduce?

Answer: 2

Why: A chain of k - 2 = 3 clauses has k - 3 = 2 links between consecutive clauses, one fresh variable each.

<a id="c-boolalg-complexity-graph-reductions"></a>

#### Vertex cover, independent set and clique

`boolalg.complexity.graph_reductions`

Vertex cover, independent set and clique are three faces of one problem, and they appear throughout EDA: vertex cover in test-point selection and in breaking cycles, independent sets in conflict-free scheduling and in register binding, cliques in compatibility-based resource sharing.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Covers and independent sets are complements
- 3-SAT to vertex cover
- Clique through the complement graph

Sample problem:

> A graph $G$ has 26 vertices and its maximum independent set has 21 vertices. How large is the minimum vertex cover of $G$?

Answer: 5

Why: Complement the largest independent set to get the smallest cover: 26 - 21 = 5.

<a id="c-boolalg-complexity-approximation"></a>

#### Approximation algorithms and heuristics

`boolalg.complexity.approximation`

When a problem is NP-hard, a tool still has to return an answer quickly. An approximation algorithm runs in polynomial time and comes with a proven ratio: its cost is never worse than $\rho$ times the optimum.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The matching-based vertex cover
- What a ratio guarantees
- Greedy set cover and heuristics without guarantees

Sample problem:

> A graph on vertices 1 to 6 has edges (1,6), (3,6), (2,6), (1,4), (1,2), (4,6), (4,5), (1,3), (2,3), (1,5). The 2-approximation for vertex cover scans the edges in this order and, whenever an edge has neither endpoint in the cover, adds both endpoints. How many vertices does it return?

Answer: 6

Why: The edges it picks form a maximal matching of 3 edges, and it returns both endpoints of each: 6 vertices.

<a id="c-boolalg-complexity-parameterized"></a>

#### Parameterized complexity

`boolalg.complexity.parameterized`

Parameterized complexity measures running time in two quantities: the input size $n$ and a parameter $k$ such as the solution size or the treewidth.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Bounded search trees
- Kernelization: forced vertices
- The kernel size bound

Sample problem:

> A refined vertex-cover search branches on a vertex $v$ of degree at least 3: take $v$ (budget drops by 1) or take all its neighbours (budget drops by at least 3). Its leaf count satisfies $L(k) = L(k-1) + L(k-3)$ with $L(0) = L(1) = L(2) = 1$. What is $L(9)$?

Answer: 19

Why: Iterating gives L(9) = 19, against 2^9 = 512 for plain edge branching. Better branching lowers the base of the exponent, not the dependence on n.

<a id="boolean-reasoning-and-complexity-frontier-agent-first-futures"></a>

### Frontier: agent-first futures

<a id="c-boolalg-frontier-reasoning-tools"></a>

#### SAT and BDD engines as agent tools

`boolalg.frontier.reasoning_tools`

In an agent-first flow, SAT solvers, BDD packages and simulators are not libraries buried inside one program; they are skills an agent calls through a typed tool interface, the way engines are exposed over MCP.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Typed inputs and outputs
- What the manifest advertises
- Trusting the answer

Sample problem:

> A SAT tool takes a CNF in DIMACS form. What else must each call carry so that results are reproducible?
>
> A) The solver's source code
>
> B) The resource limits and the random seed
>
> C) The expected answer
>
> D) The agent's chat history

Answer: The resource limits and the random seed

Why: CDCL runs depend on seeds and limits; recording them makes a verdict, and especially an UNKNOWN, repeatable.

<a id="c-boolalg-frontier-fast-exact-modes"></a>

#### Fast and exact Boolean reasoning modes

`boolalg.frontier.fast_exact_modes`

Every Boolean engine has a fast mode and an exact mode. Random or guided simulation, structural hashing and cheap signatures run in microseconds and can only refute; SAT, BDDs and proof-producing checkers are complete but can take arbitrarily long.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Simulation as the fast mode
- Exact engines as the accurate mode
- When the agent must recurse

Sample problem:

> An agent proposes a rewrite of a 13-input block and runs 3072 independent uniformly random vectors through the original and the rewrite with no mismatch. Suppose the rewrite were in fact wrong on 8 of the $2^{13}$ inputs. Which statement is correct?
>
> A) A difference that size would escape with probability about 0.9503, so equivalence is still unproven
>
> B) A difference that size would escape with probability about 0.0497, so equivalence is still unproven
>
> C) The clean run proves equivalence, so the exact check can be skipped
>
> D) A difference that size would escape with probability about 0.001, so equivalence is still unproven

Answer: A difference that size would escape with probability about 0.0497, so equivalence is still unproven

Why: Each vector misses with probability 1 - 8/2^13, so all 3072 miss with probability (1 - p)^3072 = 0.0497. Simulation can refute equivalence, never prove it; an exact SAT or BDD check must follow.

<a id="c-boolalg-frontier-equivalence-golden"></a>

#### Equivalence checking as the golden test

`boolalg.frontier.equivalence_golden`

When an agent proposes a logic transform, a rewrite, a resynthesized cone, a remapped block, the golden test is a combinational equivalence check between the original and the proposal.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The miter
- The size of the check
- Equivalence up to don't cares

Sample problem:

> Over a, b, c, an agent proposes replacing $f = \overline{a}c + \overline{a}\overline{b}$ by $g = c + \overline{a}\overline{b}$. The golden test builds the miter $f \oplus g$ and asks a SAT solver for inputs that make it 1. How many of the 8 input vectors satisfy the miter? (Zero means the transform is correct.)

Answer: 2

Why: Compare the two truth tables: they differ on m(5, 7). Any one of these is a counterexample the solver can return, and the transform is rejected unless the count is 0.

<a id="c-boolalg-frontier-change-tiers"></a>

#### Change tiers in a Boolean reasoning engine

`boolalg.frontier.change_tiers`

When an agent or a user asks for a change in a SAT solver or BDD package, the first decision is where the change belongs.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Core, policy, parameters and hooks
- Landing a request in a tier
- Seams for Boolean engines

Sample problem:

> In a BDD package, the unique table and the canonicity invariant (no duplicate nodes, no node with equal children) belong to which layer?
>
> A) Parameters
>
> B) Policy
>
> C) Observation hooks
>
> D) The core

Answer: The core

Why: Canonicity is what makes equivalence a pointer comparison; nothing outside the core may break it.

<a id="c-boolalg-frontier-tool-grounded-reward"></a>

#### Tool-grounded rewards for logic transforms

`boolalg.frontier.tool_grounded_reward`

Training a model to propose logic rewrites with reinforcement learning needs a reward, and the natural reward comes from tools: an equivalence checker says whether the rewrite is correct, structural hashing and a node count say whether it helps.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Scoring a proposed transform
- How a reward gets gamed
- From proxy to signoff

Sample problem:

> A proven-equivalent rewrite raises logic depth from 18 to 26 levels on a timing-critical block. What should the reward include?
>
> A) The number of SAT conflicts
>
> B) A bonus for the added depth
>
> C) Nothing more, since equivalence is enough
>
> D) A depth or delay term alongside the node count

Answer: A depth or delay term alongside the node count

Why: A reward that sees only area will trade delay for nodes; the objective must contain what the design cares about.

---

## Graph Algorithms for EDA

Layer 1. Netlists as hypergraphs, partitioning (KL, FM, multilevel, spectral), shortest paths and A*, flows, Steiner trees and the graph machinery under placement, routing and timing.

Builds on: discrete math, graph theory, linear algebra.

Topics covered:

- Directed graphs, DAGs, hypergraphs; netlists as hypergraphs; clique and star net models
- Topological sorting, strongly connected components, graph traversal
- Graph partitioning, hypergraph partitioning, min-cut, Kernighan-Lin, Fiduccia-Mattheyses, multilevel partitioning (coarsen, partition, uncoarsen), spectral partitioning, graph Laplacian, spectral graph theory
- Graph coloring, graph matching, bipartite matching
- Network flow, maximum flow, minimum cut, minimum-cost flow
- Shortest paths: Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, A* search; longest paths in DAGs
- Minimum spanning tree, Steiner tree problem, rectilinear Steiner tree, Hanan grid
- Traveling salesman problem (scan-chain ordering), graph embedding, planarity, graph drawing

Subdomains: [Graph models of circuits](#graph-algorithms-for-eda-graph-models-of-circuits), [DAG algorithms](#graph-algorithms-for-eda-dag-algorithms), [Shortest paths](#graph-algorithms-for-eda-shortest-paths), [Partitioning](#graph-algorithms-for-eda-partitioning), [Spectral methods](#graph-algorithms-for-eda-spectral-methods), [Network flow](#graph-algorithms-for-eda-network-flow), [Steiner trees](#graph-algorithms-for-eda-steiner-trees), [Graph coloring](#graph-algorithms-for-eda-graph-coloring), [Frontier: agent-first futures](#graph-algorithms-for-eda-frontier-agent-first-futures)

<a id="graph-algorithms-for-eda-graph-models-of-circuits"></a>

### Graph models of circuits

<a id="c-graphs-model-hypergraph"></a>

#### Netlists as hypergraphs

`graphs.model.hypergraph`

A netlist is a set of cells joined by nets, and a net can join any number of cells.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Cells, nets and pins
- Degrees and neighbourhoods
- What the hypergraph abstracts away

Terms: pin, degree, neighbours.

Sample problem:

> A netlist has cells c1 to c6 and nets n1 = {c2, c4, c6}; n2 = {c1, c3, c6}; n3 = {c1, c3, c4, c6}; n4 = {c1, c2, c4, c5}. Seen as a hypergraph, how many pins (vertex-hyperedge incidences) does it have?

Answer: 14

Why: Each net contributes one pin per cell it touches. The net sizes are 3, 3, 4, 4, which sum to 14.

<a id="c-graphs-model-pin-graph"></a>

#### Directed pin graphs of drivers and sinks

`graphs.model.pin_graph`

Timing analysis, levelization and loop detection need to know which way signals flow.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- From nets to driver-to-sink arcs
- Fan-in, fanout and cones
- Direction as a source of structure

Terms: pin graph, fanout, fan-in, transitive fanout cone.

Sample problem:

> Each cell has one output pin. The nets are: n1 driven by c2, sinks c4; n2 driven by c5, sinks c7; n3 driven by c6, sinks c7. Build the directed pin graph with one arc from each net's driver to each of its sinks. How many arcs does the graph have?

Answer: 3

Why: A net with k pins has one driver and k - 1 sinks, so it contributes k - 1 arcs. Summing the sink counts gives 3.

<a id="c-graphs-model-net-models"></a>

#### Clique and star models of a net

`graphs.model.net_models`

Many algorithms, from spectral partitioning to quadratic placement, need an ordinary weighted graph rather than a hypergraph.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Clique and star expansions
- Weighting clique edges
- Choosing a model

Terms: clique model, star model.

Sample problem:

> A netlist has nets with 7, 2, 8, 8 pins. Expanding every net as a clique, how many graph edges result (count parallel edges between the same pair separately)?

Answer: 78

Why: A k-pin clique has k(k - 1)/2 edges. Summing over the nets gives 78. Large nets dominate: the clique count grows quadratically.

<a id="c-graphs-model-csr"></a>

#### Compressed incidence storage for netlists

`graphs.model.csr`

A million-cell netlist has several million pins, and every pass of a partitioner or placer walks them.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Offsets and pin arrays
- The transpose: cell-to-net incidence
- Why compressed storage wins

Sample problem:

> Nets: n1 = {c3, c4, c5}; n2 = {c2, c6}; n3 = {c1, c3, c4}; n4 = {c1, c2, c3, c4}. The tool stores net-to-pin incidence in compressed form: an offset array netStart of length m + 1 and a pin array listing each net's cells in order, so net j's pins are pin[netStart[j]] up to pin[netStart[j+1] - 1], with nets indexed from 0 (n1 is index 0). What is netStart[1]?

Answer: 3

Why: netStart[1] is the number of pins in nets 0 to 0, which is 3. The offsets are 0, 3, 5, 8, 12.

<a id="graph-algorithms-for-eda-dag-algorithms"></a>

### DAG algorithms

<a id="c-graphs-tree-rooted-traversal"></a>

#### Pre-order and post-order traversal of a rooted tree

`graphs.tree.rooted_traversal`

Routed nets, clock trees, Steiner trees and buffer trees are rooted trees: a driver at the root, sinks at the leaves.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Pre-order: parent before children
- Post-order: children before parent
- Two passes on an RC tree

Terms: pre-order, post-order.

Sample problem:

> A rooted tree has nodes 1 to 6 with root 1 and parent(2) = 1, parent(3) = 1, parent(4) = 1, parent(5) = 1, parent(6) = 2. Children are visited in increasing label order. Which node is visited in position 6 of the pre-order traversal? Answer with its label.

Answer: 5

Why: Pre-order visits a node before its children: 1, 2, 6, 3, 4, 5. Position 6 holds node 5.

<a id="c-graphs-dag-topo-sort"></a>

#### Topological sorting of a DAG

`graphs.dag.topo_sort`
