- Iterating to the fixpoint
- Rounds, cost and trust

Sample problem:

> An agent proposes candidate invariants for a system with states s0 to s7, initial state s0 and transitions s0 → s4, s5; s1 → s7; s2 → s0; s3 → s5, s7; s4 → s1, s2; s5 → s4; s6 → s2, s5; s7 → s0. Candidates (each is the set of states it allows): c1 = {s0, s1, s2, s4, s5, s7}; c2 = {s0, s1, s5, s6, s7}; c3 = {s0, s1, s2, s4, s5}; c4 = {s0, s1, s2, s3, s5, s6, s7}; c5 = {s0, s1, s2, s4, s5, s6, s7}. Houdini runs rounds: it takes the conjunction (intersection) of all surviving candidates, and removes every candidate that excludes s0 or that some state of the conjunction can leave in one transition; it repeats until a round removes nothing. How many candidates survive the first round?

Answer: 2

Why: In round 1 the conjunction is the intersection of all 5 candidates; checking each candidate against its successors leaves 2.

<a id="c-fv-frontier-llm-sva-checking"></a>

#### Checking machine-written SVA with the prover

`fv.frontier.llm_sva_checking`

Language models can turn specifications into SystemVerilog assertions quickly, but a generated assertion can be malformed, vacuous, trivially true or simply wrong.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Syntax and elaboration gates
- Vacuity and covers
- Does the assertion have teeth

Sample problem:

> A language model writes 200 SVA properties from a spec. What is the cheapest first filter before any proof?
>
> A) Prove every property with IC3
>
> B) Ask the model whether each property is correct
>
> C) Simulate each property for a million cycles
>
> D) Parse and elaborate each property against the RTL, rejecting syntax errors and unknown signals

Answer: Parse and elaborate each property against the RTL, rejecting syntax errors and unknown signals

Why: Front-end checks are fast and deterministic, and they remove a large share of broken output before expensive engines run.

<a id="c-fv-frontier-proof-guided-repair"></a>

#### Counterexample-guided agent repair

`fv.frontier.proof_guided_repair`

When a property fails, the prover returns a counterexample trace, which is unusually good input for an agent: short, precise and reproducible.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Reading the counterexample
- Proposing and checking a fix
- Guardrails on the repair loop

Sample problem:

> The counterexample comes from the induction step, not the base case. How should the agent read it?
>
> A) As a reset bug
>
> B) As a possibly unreachable start state, which may need a helper invariant rather than an RTL change
>
> C) As proof that the RTL is wrong
>
> D) As a vacuous result

Answer: As a possibly unreachable start state, which may need a helper invariant rather than an RTL change

Why: Step-case traces start from arbitrary states satisfying the assertions, so they often show a weak property, not a bug.

<a id="c-fv-frontier-formal-reward"></a>

#### Formal results as a tool-grounded reward

`fv.frontier.formal_reward`

Formal engines give verdicts that are deterministic and checkable, which makes them attractive as the reward signal when a model is trained, by reinforcement learning, to write RTL fixes, assertions or invariants.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Prover outcomes as reward
- How the reward gets hacked
- Designing a robust reward

Sample problem:

> A team trains a model to write RTL fixes, rewarding it when the prover proves the target assertion. What makes the prover a good reward source?
>
> A) Its verdicts are deterministic and checkable, so the reward is grounded in ground truth
>
> B) It never times out
>
> C) It explains why a fix is wrong in natural language
>
> D) It is cheaper than any test

Answer: Its verdicts are deterministic and checkable, so the reward is grounded in ground truth

Why: Tool-grounded rewards come from engines whose answers can be re-checked, unlike scores from another model.

<a id="c-fv-frontier-engine-seams"></a>

#### Seams and certificates in a formal engine

`fv.frontier.engine_seams`

An agent that customizes or extends a formal engine needs to know which parts it may touch.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The four layers of a formal engine
- Which tier a request lands in
- Certificates as golden checks

Sample problem:

> An agent wants to watch an IC3 run and stop it if frames are not converging. Which layer provides that?
>
> A) The proof format
>
> B) The parameter layer
>
> C) The immutable core
>
> D) Observation hooks that report frame sizes and clause counts

Answer: Observation hooks that report frame sizes and clause counts

Why: Hooks expose live state without letting the observer change the engine's correctness logic.

---

## Functional Verification and Simulation

Layer 4. Event-driven and compiled simulation, testbenches, constrained random, coverage, UVM, emulation and CDC.

Builds on: HDLs and Hardware Compilers, Digital Logic Design, Graph Algorithms for EDA, Variability, Yield and Reliability Statistics, Boolean Reasoning and Complexity.

Topics covered:

- Hardware verification, functional verification, the verification gap
- Logic simulation: event-driven simulation, delta cycles, scheduling regions, four-state logic and X-propagation, cycle-based simulation, compiled simulation (Verilator)
- Testbenches, stimulus, checkers, scoreboards, reference models
- Constrained-random verification, constraint solving for stimulus
- Coverage-driven verification: code coverage, functional coverage, covergroups, coverage closure
- Assertion-based verification in simulation
- UVM and OVM: agents, sequences, drivers, monitors, the phasing model
- Transaction-level modeling, SystemC TLM
- Hardware emulation, FPGA prototyping, hardware acceleration for verification
- Clock-domain crossing and reset-domain crossing verification
- cocotb, Verilator, Icarus Verilog, GHDL in practice

Subdomains: [Event-driven simulation](#functional-verification-and-simulation-event-driven-simulation), [Cycle-based simulation](#functional-verification-and-simulation-cycle-based-simulation), [Testbenches](#functional-verification-and-simulation-testbenches), [Constrained-random stimulus](#functional-verification-and-simulation-constrained-random-stimulus), [Coverage](#functional-verification-and-simulation-coverage), [Assertions](#functional-verification-and-simulation-assertions), [UVM methodology](#functional-verification-and-simulation-uvm-methodology), [Clock-domain crossing](#functional-verification-and-simulation-clock-domain-crossing), [Acceleration and emulation](#functional-verification-and-simulation-acceleration-and-emulation), [Frontier: agent-first futures](#functional-verification-and-simulation-frontier-agent-first-futures)

<a id="functional-verification-and-simulation-event-driven-simulation"></a>

### Event-driven simulation

<a id="c-sim-event-event-driven"></a>

#### Event-driven logic simulation

`sim.event.event_driven`

A logic simulator answers one question millions of times: given a change on some input, what changes next, and when?

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Events and evaluations
- Counting events after an input toggle
- Activity and why event-driven wins

Terms: event, evaluation, activity factor.

Sample problem:

> A netlist has inputs a, b, c, d and gates n1 = NAND(a, d); n2 = XOR(c, n1); n3 = XOR(n1, n2); n4 = OR(n2, n3). Every gate has a delay of one time unit. The circuit is stable with a = 0, b = 0, c = 1, d = 0. At time 0 input c toggles. An event-driven simulator applies the net changes of each time step, evaluates every fanout gate of a changed net once in that step, and schedules an output change one unit later only if the new value differs. How many events (net value changes) occur in total, counting the input toggle?

Answer: 3

Why: Propagating the toggle step by step, nets change 3 times in total, the input toggle included, over 3 time steps.

<a id="c-sim-event-event-wheel"></a>

#### The event wheel and time queue

`sim.event.event_wheel`

An event-driven simulator spends much of its time inserting and removing events from a time-ordered queue.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Slots indexed by time modulo the wheel size
- The overflow list for far-future events
- Advancing time in jumps

Terms: timing wheel, overflow.

Sample problem:

> A simulator keeps near-future events in a timing wheel of 64 slots, one per time unit; an event for absolute time t goes into slot t mod 64. The current time is 730. A gate with delay 51 schedules its output change. Which slot index receives the event?

Answer: 13

Why: The event is due at 730 + 51 = 781, and 781 mod 64 = 13.

<a id="c-sim-event-delta-cycles"></a>

#### Delta cycles

`sim.event.delta_cycles`

Real gates have delay, but RTL is usually written with none: continuous assignments and always blocks update in zero simulated time.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Ordering zero-delay updates in delta steps
- Counting deltas to settle
- Zero-time glitches and loops

Terms: delta cycles.

Sample problem:

> A module contains the zero-delay continuous assignments assign w1 = ~a; assign w2 = ~w1; assign w3 = ~w2; Input a is changed by the testbench at time 10 ns. Counting the delta cycle in which a itself changes as delta 1, how many delta cycles at time 10 ns contain at least one net change?

Answer: 4

Why: Each assignment reads a net that changed in the previous delta and updates in the next one. The change of a is delta 1, w1 changes in delta 2, and w3 changes in delta 4. No simulated time passes.

<a id="c-sim-event-scheduling-regions"></a>

#### Verilog scheduling regions

`sim.event.scheduling_regions`

The Verilog and SystemVerilog standard does not leave the order of events within a time step entirely to the simulator.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The region order of a time step
- Blocking versus nonblocking results
- Races between processes

Terms: regions, NBA.

Sample problem:

> After the NBA region applies updates, those updates wake further always blocks. What does the scheduler do?
>
> A) It discards the new events until the next clock edge
>
> B) It advances simulation time by one unit
>
> C) It returns to the Active region in the same time step, which is another delta cycle
>
> D) It runs them in the Postponed region

Answer: It returns to the Active region in the same time step, which is another delta cycle

Why: Regions iterate: new Active events after NBA cause another pass through the region loop at the same simulated time.

<a id="c-sim-event-delay-models"></a>

#### Inertial and transport delay

`sim.event.delay_models`

A gate delay in a simulator is not just a number added to a timestamp. The simulator must decide what happens when an input changes again before the previous output change has matured.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Transport and inertial delay
- Computing the output of a pulse train
- Consequences for gate-level simulation

Terms: transport, inertial.

Sample problem:

> A buffer with an transport delay of 3 ns sees its input rise at 28 ns and fall at 32 ns, a pulse 4 ns wide. How many transitions appear on its output?

Answer: 2

Why: A transport delay shifts every input change by the delay, so both edges appear.

<a id="c-sim-event-four-state"></a>

#### Four-state logic and X propagation

`sim.event.four_state`

Real wires are 0 or 1, but a simulator must also represent what it does not know.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Four values and what they mean
- Truth tables with X and Z
- Expressions and driver resolution

Terms: 0, 1, controlling value.

Sample problem:

> In a four-state Verilog simulation, a = X and b = X. What is the value of a ^ b?
>
> A) Z
>
> B) 0
>
> C) 1
>
> D) X

Answer: X

Why: A Z input to a logic operator is treated as unknown, X. XOR has no controlling value, so any X or Z input gives X.

<a id="c-sim-event-x-pessimism"></a>

#### X-pessimism and X-optimism

`sim.event.x_pessimism`

An X in simulation should mean "this could be 0 or 1". Simulators do not track that exactly: they apply local truth tables, which lose correlations between signals.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- X-pessimism at gate level
- X-optimism in RTL control flow
- Consequences and mitigations

Sample problem:

> A 2:1 mux is coded as assign y = s ? a : b; The select s is X, a = 1 and b = 0. What does a four-state simulator produce for y?
>
> A) 1
>
> B) Z
>
> C) X
>
> D) 0

Answer: X

Why: The conditional operator with an unknown select combines both data inputs bit by bit: equal bits pass through and differing bits become X.

<a id="functional-verification-and-simulation-cycle-based-simulation"></a>

### Cycle-based simulation

<a id="c-sim-cycle-levelization"></a>

#### Levelization of combinational logic

`sim.cycle.levelization`

Levelization assigns every combinational gate a level so that evaluating gates in level order guarantees each gate sees settled inputs.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Levels as longest paths from sources
- Computing levels in topological order
- Why level order works and when it fails

Sample problem:

> A combinational block reads primary inputs a, b, c and the flip-flop output q. Its gates are n1 = NAND(b, c); n2 = NOR(c, n1); n3 = XOR(a, n1); n4 = XOR(c, n3); n5 = AND(a, b); n6 = NAND(n1, n4). Inputs and flop outputs are level 0, and a gate's level is one more than the highest level among its inputs. What is the level of n4?

Answer: 3

Why: n4 reads c (level 0) and n3 (level 2), so its level is 3.

<a id="c-sim-cycle-compiled"></a>

#### Cycle-based and compiled simulation

`sim.cycle.compiled`

Event-driven simulation pays for flexibility: every change goes through a queue.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Evaluating once per cycle in levelized order
- Cost model and break-even activity
- What compilation adds and what it loses

Terms: compiled.

Sample problem:

> A design has two asynchronous clock domains. How does a cycle-based simulator typically handle it?
>
> A) It cannot simulate registers at all
>
> B) It evaluates each domain's logic on that domain's edges, scheduling edges from both clocks in time order
>
> C) It falls back to analog simulation
>
> D) It merges both clocks into one

Answer: It evaluates each domain's logic on that domain's edges, scheduling edges from both clocks in time order

Why: Edges are still scheduled in time; between edges each domain's combinational logic is evaluated in levelized order.

<a id="c-sim-cycle-verilator"></a>

#### Verilator's compilation model

`sim.cycle.verilator`

Verilator is the most widely used open-source fast simulator for SystemVerilog. It is a compiler, not an interpreter: it translates synthesizable RTL into C++ (or SystemC) classes, which a host compiler turns into an executable model.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- From RTL to a C++ model
- Two-state values and X handling
- Threads, lint and circular logic

Sample problem:

> In a C++ harness around a Verilated model, what must the harness do after changing the clock input?
>
> A) Call the simulator's event queue
>
> B) Call the model's eval() so it recomputes its state and outputs
>
> C) Restart the model
>
> D) Nothing: the model updates on assignment

Answer: Call the model's eval() so it recomputes its state and outputs

Why: The model only computes when eval() is called; the harness drives inputs, calls eval() and reads outputs.

<a id="c-sim-cycle-parallel"></a>

#### Parallel simulation: work and span

`sim.cycle.parallel`

A large SoC simulates slowly on one core, so simulators try to use many. A partitioned design is a task graph: each partition is work, and data dependences between partitions are edges.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Work and span of a cycle's task graph
- Speedup bounds
- Why synchronization dominates

Terms: work, span, parallelism.

Sample problem:

> One simulated cycle of a partitioned design is a task graph: T1 (5 us); T2 (4 us); T3 (7 us) after T2 and T1; T4 (3 us) after T2; T5 (5 us) after T1 and T3; T6 (2 us) after T2; T7 (1 us) after T3. What is the total work W of one cycle, in microseconds?

Answer: 27

Why: Work is the sum of all task costs, 27 us: the time one thread needs.

<a id="functional-verification-and-simulation-testbenches"></a>

### Testbenches

<a id="c-sim-tb-verification-gap"></a>

#### The verification gap and exhaustive simulation

`sim.tb.verification_gap`

Functional verification asks whether an RTL design does what its specification says.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The verification gap
- Counting input and state spaces
- Exhaustive simulation time and sampled coverage

Sample problem:

> A controller has 11 flip-flops and no other state. How many distinct states can its register contents take?

Answer: 2048

Why: Each flip-flop holds one of two values, so there are 2^11 = 2048 states, whether or not all are reachable.

<a id="c-sim-tb-testbench"></a>

#### Testbench architecture

`sim.tb.testbench`

A testbench is the program that exercises a design under test (DUT) and decides whether it behaved correctly.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Components of a layered testbench
- Directed, self-checking and random testbenches
- Driving and sampling without races

Terms: stimulus generator, driver, monitor, reference model, scoreboard, coverage collector, directed, self-checking, constrained-random, clocking blocks.

Sample problem:

> In a layered testbench, which component converts a transaction into pin-level activity on the DUT interface?
>
> A) The coverage collector
>
> B) The monitor
>
> C) The driver
>
> D) The scoreboard

Answer: The driver

Why: The driver turns abstract transactions into signal wiggles; the monitor does the reverse.

<a id="c-sim-tb-scoreboard"></a>

#### Scoreboards and reference models

`sim.tb.scoreboard`

A scoreboard is the testbench component that decides pass or fail. It holds the expected results produced by a reference model and matches them against what monitors observe at the DUT outputs.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- In-order scoreboards
- Out-of-order matching
- Sizing queues and choosing reference models

Sample problem:

> An in-order scoreboard pops one expected transaction from its queue for every DUT output and compares them. The reference model predicted 83, 23, 54, 73, 51, 18; the DUT produced 83, 54, 54, 73, 51, 65, in that order. How many comparisons fail?

Answer: 2

Why: Comparing position by position, 2 position(s) differ.

<a id="c-sim-tb-cocotb"></a>

#### cocotb and open-source simulators

`sim.tb.cocotb`

cocotb is an open-source framework for writing testbenches in Python. It does not simulate anything itself: it attaches to an HDL simulator through that simulator's procedural interface and runs Python coroutines alongside the simulation.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Python coroutines over the simulator interface
- The open-source simulators underneath
- Reading values at the right moment

Terms: trigger, Icarus Verilog, GHDL.

Sample problem:

> A cocotb test uses await Timer(10, 'ns'). What happens?
>
> A) Every signal is delayed by 10 ns
>
> B) The coroutine resumes after 10 ns of simulated time
>
> C) The coroutine resumes after 10 ns of real time
>
> D) The DUT clock period becomes 10 ns

Answer: The coroutine resumes after 10 ns of simulated time

Why: Timer waits on simulation time, not wall-clock time.

<a id="functional-verification-and-simulation-constrained-random-stimulus"></a>

### Constrained-random stimulus

<a id="c-sim-random-constrained"></a>

#### Constrained-random stimulus

`sim.random.constrained`

Constrained-random verification replaces hand-written stimulus with random values restricted to legal inputs.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Random variables and constraints define a solution space
- Counting solutions
- Uniform over solutions, not uniform per variable

Terms: solution space.

Sample problem:

> A class declares rand bit [1:0] x; rand bit [1:0] y; constraint c { x >= 2 * y; }. Arithmetic in the constraint does not overflow. How many (x, y) pairs satisfy the constraints?

Answer: 6

Why: Enumerating the 4 x 4 grid of values and keeping the pairs that satisfy every constraint leaves 6 legal solutions.

<a id="c-sim-random-dist-solve-before"></a>

#### Distribution weights and solve-before

`sim.random.dist_solve_before`

Uniform sampling over the solution space is a precise rule, and often the wrong distribution for verification.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Weights with := and :/
- solve...before changes the distribution, not the space
- Combining ordering and weights

Sample problem:

> A variable is constrained by x dist { 0 := 3, [1:9] := 5 }; and has no other constraints. What is the probability that x == 0? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 0.062

Why: With :=, every value in the range gets weight 5, so the total weight is 3 + 9 x 5. The probability is 0.062.

<a id="c-sim-random-corner-probability"></a>

#### Probability of hitting a corner case

`sim.random.corner_probability`

Random stimulus finds a bug only if it reaches the scenario that triggers it. Corner cases, such as a full FIFO during a flush or an address at the top of a range with a zero length, often have tiny per-test probabilities.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The probability of a corner per draw
- At least one hit in N tests
- Tests needed for a target confidence

Sample problem:

> A transaction has an unconstrained 8-bit field addr and an unconstrained 4-bit field len, each uniform and independent. The corner of interest is addr at its maximum value and len == 0 in the same transaction. On average, how many transactions are drawn until the first one hits the corner?

Answer: 4096

Why: The corner probability is p = 2^-8 x 2^-4 = 2^-12. The number of draws to the first hit is geometric with mean 1/p = 4096.

<a id="c-sim-random-constraint-solving"></a>

#### Constraint solvers for stimulus

`sim.random.constraint_solving`

Behind every call to `randomize()` is a constraint solver that must find a legal assignment quickly and, ideally, sample uniformly over all legal assignments.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- BDD-based and SAT-based solvers
- The cost of rejection sampling
- Performance pitfalls for constraint writers

Terms: SAT, SMT.

Sample problem:

> What does a SAT- or SMT-based stimulus solver find easily, and what does it not give for free?
>
> A) It finds a legal solution quickly, but uniform sampling over all solutions is not automatic
>
> B) It counts all solutions exactly
>
> C) It gives uniform samples, but finding any solution is slow
>
> D) It only works on unconstrained variables

Answer: It finds a legal solution quickly, but uniform sampling over all solutions is not automatic

Why: SAT search returns some solution biased by its heuristics; near-uniform sampling needs extra techniques such as random hashing constraints.

<a id="c-sim-random-seeds"></a>

#### Seeds and random stability

`sim.random.seeds`

A constrained-random test is deterministic once its seed is fixed: the seed and the code determine every random value.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Seeds make runs reproducible
- Random stability in SystemVerilog
- Managing seeds in regression

Terms: random stability.

Sample problem:

> Why should every regression log record the seed of each test?
>
> A) So the simulator runs faster
>
> B) So any failure can be rerun exactly for debugging
>
> C) So coverage merges correctly
>
> D) So that seeds are never reused

Answer: So any failure can be rerun exactly for debugging

Why: Without the seed, a random failure may never be seen again.

<a id="functional-verification-and-simulation-coverage"></a>

### Coverage

<a id="c-sim-cov-code-coverage"></a>

#### Code coverage

`sim.cov.code_coverage`

Code coverage measures which parts of the RTL source a regression exercised. The simulator instruments statements, branches, toggles and state machines and counts hits.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Statement coverage
- Branch coverage
- Toggle and FSM coverage, and the limits

Sample problem:

> A coverage report says: module A has 180 statements of which 70 executed; module B has 35 statements of which 24 executed; module C has 130 statements of which 127 executed. What is the overall statement coverage of the design, in percent? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 64.1

Why: Pool the counts: 221 executed of 345 statements is 64.1%. Averaging the per-module percentages would weight a small module like a large one.

<a id="c-sim-cov-condition"></a>

#### Condition and expression coverage

`sim.cov.condition`

Branch coverage asks whether each decision went both ways. A condition such as `(a && b) || c` can take both outcomes while one of its atomic conditions never mattered.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Condition coverage
- Computing coverage from test vectors
- MC/DC and its minimum test count

Terms: Condition coverage, MC/DC, condition.

Sample problem:

> The condition of an if statement is a && b && c. The tests apply the vectors 110, 010, each listing abc in that order. Treat every condition as fully evaluated (no short-circuit masking). Condition coverage needs each of the 3 conditions to be observed both true and false. How many of the 6 condition-value pairs are observed?

Answer: 4

Why: Scanning each column of the vectors for a 0 and a 1 finds 4 of the 6 pairs.

<a id="c-sim-cov-functional-coverage"></a>

#### Functional coverage

`sim.cov.functional_coverage`

Functional coverage measures whether the scenarios in the verification plan actually happened.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Covergroups, coverpoints and bins
- Coverpoint coverage
- Covergroup coverage and weights

Terms: bins.

Sample problem:

> A coverpoint declares bins r0 = {[0:6]}; bins r1[4] = {[7:13]}; How many bins does it have?

Answer: 5

Why: A scalar bin covers its whole range as one bin, bins name[] makes one bin per value, and bins name[N] splits the values into N bins. The total is 5.

<a id="c-sim-cov-cross-coverage"></a>

#### Cross coverage

`sim.cov.cross_coverage`

Many bugs appear only in combinations: a write to the last address while a flush is pending, a short packet on the highest-priority channel.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Crosses as Cartesian products
- Removing ignored and illegal combinations
- Coverage of a cross and its cost

Sample problem:

> Coverpoints cp_op, cp_size and cp_mode have 6, 4 and 4 bins. How many bins does cross cp_op, cp_size, cp_mode have?

Answer: 96

Why: A cross has one bin per combination of its coverpoints' bins: 6 x 4 x 4 = 96.

<a id="c-sim-cov-coupon-collector"></a>

#### Expected tests to close coverage bins

`sim.cov.coupon_collector`

How many random tests does it take to cover every bin? If tests hit bins at random, coverage closure is the coupon collector problem: the first bins come quickly and the last ones take most of the time.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Waiting for one bin
- All n bins: n times the harmonic number
- The last bins dominate

Sample problem:

> A coverage bin is hit by 16 out of every 200 random tests on average, independently. What is the expected number of tests until it is first hit? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 12.5

Why: The wait is geometric with p = 16/200, so the mean is 1/p = 12.5 tests.

<a id="c-sim-cov-closure"></a>

#### Coverage closure

`sim.cov.closure`

Coverage closure is the work of driving a coverage model to completion, or to an agreed, justified stopping point.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Holes, exclusions and plateaus
- Ranking tests with greedy set cover
- The coverage-driven loop

Terms: hole, plateau, Test ranking.

Sample problem:

> What is a coverage hole?
>
> A) A bin or scenario in the coverage model that no test has hit yet
>
> B) A line of code that never runs
>
> C) A bug found by an assertion
>
> D) A test that always fails

Answer: A bin or scenario in the coverage model that no test has hit yet

Why: Holes are the gap between the coverage model and what the regression achieved.

<a id="functional-verification-and-simulation-assertions"></a>

### Assertions

<a id="c-sim-assert-in-simulation"></a>

#### Assertions in simulation

`sim.assert.in_simulation`

Assertions state properties a design must satisfy, written next to the design and checked continuously while it simulates.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Immediate, deferred and concurrent assertions
- Sampling and evaluation regions
- Engineering assertions for simulation

Terms: immediate, deferred, concurrent, sampled in the Preponed region, evaluated in the Observed region, Action blocks.

Sample problem:

> Which statement checks a property without asserting it, recording each time it is matched?
>
> A) cover property
>
> B) expect
>
> C) assume property
>
> D) restrict property

Answer: cover property

Why: cover property counts matches and contributes to functional coverage.

<a id="c-sim-assert-implication"></a>

#### Implication and sequence checking

`sim.assert.implication`

Most concurrent assertions are implications: whenever an antecedent sequence matches, a consequent must follow.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Overlapping and non-overlapping implication
- Counting failures on a trace
- Vacuous success

Terms: overlapping, non-overlapping, vacuously.

Sample problem:

> The property assert property (@(posedge clk) a |-> b); is checked against sampled values over cycles 1 to 10: a = 0 0 1 0 0 1 0 1 0 0 and b = 0 1 1 1 1 0 0 0 1 0. An attempt starts at every cycle; consider only attempts starting in cycles 1 to 10, whose checks fall inside the trace. How many attempts fail?

Answer: 2

Why: An attempt fails when a is 1 at its start cycle and b is 0 in the same cycle. That happens 2 time(s); 1 attempt(s) pass for real and 7 pass vacuously.

<a id="functional-verification-and-simulation-uvm-methodology"></a>

### UVM methodology

<a id="c-sim-uvm-architecture"></a>

#### UVM architecture

`sim.uvm.architecture`

The Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) is a SystemVerilog class library and a set of conventions for building reusable testbenches.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The component hierarchy
- Active and passive agents and reuse
- Components versus objects

Terms: test, environment, agent, scoreboard, sequencer, driver, monitor, active, passive, components, objects.

Sample problem:

> Which three components make up a typical active UVM agent?
>
> A) A sequencer, a driver and a monitor
>
> B) An environment, a test and a factory
>
> C) A sequence, a register model and a monitor
>
> D) A scoreboard, a driver and a test

Answer: A sequencer, a driver and a monitor

Why: The sequencer feeds items to the driver, the driver wiggles pins, and the monitor observes them.

<a id="c-sim-uvm-phasing"></a>

#### UVM phasing and objections

`sim.uvm.phasing`

A UVM testbench is a program with many cooperating components, and they must be built, connected, run and shut down in a coordinated order.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The phase sequence and traversal order
- Run-time phases and objections
- Using the phases correctly

Terms: build, connect, end_of_elaboration, start_of_simulation, run, extract, check, report, final, top-down, bottom-up, objection.

Sample problem:

> Why does build_phase execute top-down through the hierarchy?
>
> A) A parent must build first so that it can create and configure its children
>
> B) Leaves need no build phase
>
> C) Top-down is faster on multicore hosts
>
> D) Children are always built first

Answer: A parent must build first so that it can create and configure its children

Why: Each parent creates its children in its own build_phase, so the parent's call must come first.

<a id="c-sim-uvm-sequences"></a>

#### Sequences, sequencers and drivers

`sim.uvm.sequences`

UVM separates what traffic to generate from how to put it on the pins. Sequences describe scenarios as streams of randomized transactions; drivers implement the protocol.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The sequence, sequencer and driver handshake
- Arbitration, responses and virtual sequences
- Layering and reuse

Terms: late randomization, virtual sequence, layered.

Sample problem:

> Inside a sequence's body(), which pair of calls hands one item to the driver?
>
> A) start_item(req) then finish_item(req)
>
> B) put(req) then get(rsp)
>
> C) get_next_item(req) then item_done()
>
> D) create(req) then write(req)

Answer: start_item(req) then finish_item(req)

Why: start_item waits for the sequencer to grant access; finish_item sends the item and waits for the driver.

<a id="c-sim-uvm-factory-config"></a>

#### The UVM factory and configuration database

`sim.uvm.factory_config`

A reusable environment must let each test change behavior without editing shared code.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Factory creation and overrides
- The configuration database
- Silent failures and defensive use

Terms: factory, configuration database, type override, instance override.

Sample problem:

> How does an instance override differ from a type override?
>
> A) It applies only at matching hierarchical paths
>
> B) It only works for sequences
>
> C) It applies to every instance in the design
>
> D) It changes the class definition

Answer: It applies only at matching hierarchical paths

Why: Instance overrides are scoped by path; type overrides are global.

<a id="c-sim-uvm-tlm"></a>

#### Transaction-level modeling and TLM ports

`sim.uvm.tlm`

Transaction-level modeling (TLM) describes communication as function calls that carry whole transactions, not as signal changes on pins.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Ports, exports and analysis ports
- SystemC TLM-2.0: loosely and approximately timed
- Temporal decoupling and the quantum

Terms: port, export, imp, analysis port, generic payload, Loosely timed, Approximately timed, temporal decoupling, global quantum.

Sample problem:

> Why does a transaction-level model simulate far faster than RTL?
>
> A) It uses four-state logic
>
> B) It skips the testbench
>
> C) One function call represents a whole bus transfer instead of many signal events per cycle
>
> D) It runs on an emulator

Answer: One function call represents a whole bus transfer instead of many signal events per cycle

Why: Abstraction removes per-cycle, per-signal activity.

<a id="functional-verification-and-simulation-clock-domain-crossing"></a>

### Clock-domain crossing

<a id="c-sim-cdc-synchronizers"></a>

#### CDC verification and synchronizers

`sim.cdc.synchronizers`

Whenever a signal crosses from one clock domain to an unrelated one, the receiving flop can sample it while it changes and go metastable.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Metastability and the two-flop synchronizer
- Structural CDC checks
- Why simulation misses CDC bugs

Terms: two-flop synchronizer, combinational logic before the synchronizer, fanout of the first synchronizer stage, reconvergence, fast-to-slow pulses, metastability injection.

Sample problem:

> Why must the source of a synchronized signal come straight from a flip-flop?
>
> A) Flops are faster than gates
>
> B) Synchronizers only accept Gray code
>
> C) Combinational logic can glitch, and a glitch may be captured as a false pulse in the other domain
>
> D) It saves area

Answer: Combinational logic can glitch, and a glitch may be captured as a false pulse in the other domain

Why: The receiving domain samples at arbitrary times, so any glitch can be caught.

<a id="c-sim-cdc-mtbf"></a>

#### Synchronizer MTBF

`sim.cdc.mtbf`

A synchronizer cannot eliminate metastability, so its quality is a failure rate.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The MTBF formula
- Computing MTBF
- Adding stages and designing to a target

Sample problem:

> A synchronizer flop has resolution time constant tau = 14 ps and metastability window T0 = 40 ps. It is clocked at 400 MHz, the asynchronous data toggles at 25 MHz, and 350 ps are available for resolution. Using MTBF = e^(t_r/tau) / (T0 f_clk f_data), what is the MTBF in seconds? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 180012.2

Why: t_r/tau = 25, so e^(t_r/tau) = 72004899337. The denominator T0 f_clk f_data = 400000 per second. MTBF = 180012.2 s, far too short for a product.

<a id="c-sim-cdc-multibit"></a>

#### Multi-bit crossings, Gray codes and async FIFOs

`sim.cdc.multibit`

A two-flop synchronizer makes one bit safe. A multi-bit value is not made safe by synchronizing every bit, because the bits resolve independently and can be captured from different cycles.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Why multi-bit binary crossings fail
- Gray codes
- Asynchronous FIFOs and their depth

Sample problem:

> A pointer crossing clock domains is converted to Gray code with g = b XOR (b >> 1). What is the Gray code of b = 48, written as a decimal number?

Answer: 40

Why: b = 110000 in binary and b >> 1 = 11000; their XOR is 101000, which is 40.

<a id="c-sim-cdc-reset-domain"></a>

#### Reset synchronizers and reset-domain crossing

`sim.cdc.reset_domain`

Resets cross domains too. An asynchronous reset asserts without a clock, which is useful, but its release is a timing event relative to each flop's clock, and an asynchronous reset in one part of a design can corrupt flops elsewhere that are not reset.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Reset synchronizers
- Reset-domain crossings
- Verifying reset behavior

Terms: recovery, removal, reset synchronizer, reset-domain crossing.

Sample problem:

> Each clock domain has its own reset synchronizer. Why?
>
> A) One synchronizer cannot drive many flops
>
> B) Resets must be Gray coded
>
> C) Release must be synchronous to each domain's own clock
>
> D) To save power

Answer: Release must be synchronous to each domain's own clock

Why: Synchronous release is per clock; a single synchronizer serves only one domain.

<a id="functional-verification-and-simulation-acceleration-and-emulation"></a>

### Acceleration and emulation

<a id="c-sim-accel-emulation"></a>

#### Emulation and FPGA prototyping

`sim.accel.emulation`

Software simulation of a full SoC runs far too slowly to boot an operating system or run real workloads.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Emulators and prototypes
- Testbenches and transactors
- Choosing the platform

Terms: emulators, FPGA prototypes, emulator, FPGA prototype, transaction-based acceleration, transactors, Speed bridges.

Sample problem:

> Compared with an emulator, what is an FPGA prototype's main advantage?
>
> A) Full visibility of every signal at every cycle
>
> B) Faster compile for each change
>
> C) Higher run speed, which suits long software workloads
>
> D) No need to synthesize the design

Answer: Higher run speed, which suits long software workloads

Why: Prototypes run faster but take longer to bring up and expose fewer signals.

<a id="c-sim-accel-throughput"></a>

#### Simulation versus emulation throughput

`sim.accel.throughput`

Verification platforms differ by orders of magnitude in speed, and they also differ in setup cost: an emulator or prototype must be compiled before it runs.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Simulation speed in cycles per second
- Emulation time including compile
- The break-even test length

Sample problem:

> An SoC simulates at 1000 cycles per second. How many hours does a 36-million-cycle boot test take? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 10

Why: 36000000 cycles / 1000 cycles per second = 36000 s, which is 10 hours.

<a id="c-sim-accel-partitioning"></a>

#### Multi-FPGA partitioning and pin multiplexing

`sim.accel.partitioning`

A large SoC does not fit in one FPGA, so emulators and prototypes split it across many.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Cut nets become inter-FPGA signals
- Time-division multiplexing
- The system clock and why the cut matters

Terms: cut, Time-division multiplexing.

Sample problem:

> A design is split across two FPGAs: FPGA A holds B1, B4 and FPGA B holds B2, B3, B5. Its nets, each listing the blocks it connects, are n1 {B1, B5}; n2 {B2, B4, B5}; n3 {B5, B2, B4}; n4 {B4, B1}; n5 {B2, B3}. How many nets must cross between the FPGAs?

Answer: 3

Why: A net is cut when its blocks sit on both FPGAs. 3 nets are cut, and each needs an inter-FPGA signal.

<a id="functional-verification-and-simulation-frontier-agent-first-futures"></a>

### Frontier: agent-first futures

<a id="c-sim-frontier-coverage-agent"></a>

#### Agentic coverage-closure loops

`sim.frontier.coverage_agent`

Coverage closure is a loop of reading holes, changing stimulus and rerunning, which makes it a natural job for an agent driving the simulator as a tool.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The closure loop
- Reward design and how it is gamed
- Change tiers for closure

Terms: Tier 1, Tier 2.

Sample problem:

> An agent proposes a new constraint that it claims will hit a hole. What is the cheapest check before a full regression?
>
> A) Synthesize the design
>
> B) Ask the agent to rate its confidence
>
> C) Randomize the constrained item many times without simulation and count how often the target bin values appear
>
> D) Run the full nightly regression

Answer: Randomize the constrained item many times without simulation and count how often the target bin values appear

Why: Solver-only sampling is a fast surrogate that filters bad proposals before expensive runs.

<a id="c-sim-frontier-llm-testbench"></a>

#### LLM-generated testbenches checked by simulation

`sim.frontier.llm_testbench`

Language models can write testbenches, assertions and reference models quickly. The question is how to trust them.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Compile, run and actually check
- Mutation score
- Failure modes and safe use

Terms: Mutation testing, killed, equivalent, mutation score.

Sample problem:

> An LLM generates a testbench that compiles and prints PASS on the original RTL. What has been shown?
>
> A) That coverage is complete
>
> B) Only that it runs; whether it would detect bugs is still unknown
>
> C) That the testbench is equivalent to the spec
>
> D) That the RTL is correct

Answer: Only that it runs; whether it would detect bugs is still unknown

Why: A testbench that never fails gives no evidence; its checking strength must be measured separately.

<a id="c-sim-frontier-debug-agent"></a>

#### Debug agents and waveform root cause

`sim.frontier.debug_agent`

When a regression fails, an engineer reproduces it, finds the first wrong value, and traces back to the cause.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Inputs and the first divergence
- Bisection over time and cones
- Tools, hypotheses and review

Sample problem:

> Why are waveform queries exposed to the agent as typed tool calls rather than raw VCD text?
>
> A) VCD files cannot be read
>
> B) Typed queries return only the requested signals and time ranges, which fits context limits and avoids parsing errors
>
> C) Typed calls change the waveform
>
> D) Agents cannot use tools

Answer: Typed queries return only the requested signals and time ranges, which fits context limits and avoids parsing errors

Why: A narrow interface (for example over MCP) lets the agent ask precise questions of a huge database.

<a id="c-sim-frontier-differential-sim"></a>

#### Simulation as a differential test for agent edits

`sim.frontier.differential_sim`

When an agent edits RTL, a testbench or the simulator itself, the change must be shown to do what was intended and nothing else.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Golden and differential runs
- What the diff must prove
- Differential testing across simulators

Terms: golden test, differential run.

Sample problem:

> Why must races be removed from a design before it is used in differential simulation?
>
> A) Races are illegal syntax
>
> B) Races hide coverage
>
> C) Races slow simulation
>
> D) A race makes outputs depend on process ordering, so differences appear without any real change

Answer: A race makes outputs depend on process ordering, so differences appear without any real change

Why: Nondeterminism produces false alarms that drown out real regressions.

<a id="c-sim-frontier-simulator-seams"></a>

#### Seams and change tiers in a simulator

`sim.frontier.simulator_seams`

A simulator is an engine like a placer or a timer, and the four-layer model applies to it: an immutable core, policies, parameters and observation hooks.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The four layers of a simulator
- Classifying change requests
- Designing seams that keep compiled speed

Terms: core, policy, Observation hooks, Tier 1, Tier 2, Tier 3.

Sample problem:

> Where does an agent read live simulation state, such as signal values or coverage counts, during a run?
>
> A) Through observation hooks such as VPI callbacks and coverage or assertion monitors
>
> B) By editing the scheduler
>
> C) From the synthesis log
>
> D) From the compiled C++ source

Answer: Through observation hooks such as VPI callbacks and coverage or assertion monitors

Why: Hooks are the observation layer: read state and inject behavior without core changes.

---

## Circuit Simulation

Layer 4. Modified nodal analysis, Newton with companion models, transient integration and step control, AC, PSS, Monte Carlo and model order reduction.

Builds on: Numerical Methods for EDA, Circuits and Electromagnetics, Semiconductor Devices and Compact Models, CMOS Circuits and Cell Libraries, Variability, Yield and Reliability Statistics, linear algebra.

Topics covered:

- Electronic circuit simulation, SPICE and its history, SPICE netlists, device models
- Modified nodal analysis: element stamps for R, C, L, sources, controlled sources
- DC operating point: Newton-Raphson on circuit equations, linearized companion models, convergence aids (gmin stepping, source stepping, damping, limiting)
- Transient analysis: companion models for C and L under backward Euler and trapezoidal, BDF/Gear, timestep control from local truncation error, ringing of trapezoidal
- AC small-signal analysis, noise analysis
- Periodic steady state: shooting, harmonic balance; RF circuit simulation
- Sensitivity analysis, corner analysis (PVT), Monte Carlo circuit simulation, device mismatch
- Model order reduction for interconnect (AWE, PRIMA), behavioral macromodeling
- Fast SPICE, mixed-signal simulation, co-simulation
- ngspice and Xyce: running decks, reading output, what numerical machinery each exposes

Subdomains: [Simulators and netlists](#circuit-simulation-simulators-and-netlists), [Modified nodal analysis](#circuit-simulation-modified-nodal-analysis), [DC analysis](#circuit-simulation-dc-analysis), [Transient analysis](#circuit-simulation-transient-analysis), [AC and noise analysis](#circuit-simulation-ac-and-noise-analysis), [Periodic steady state](#circuit-simulation-periodic-steady-state), [Variation analysis](#circuit-simulation-variation-analysis), [Model order reduction](#circuit-simulation-model-order-reduction), [Fast simulation](#circuit-simulation-fast-simulation), [Frontier: agent-first futures](#circuit-simulation-frontier-agent-first-futures)

<a id="circuit-simulation-simulators-and-netlists"></a>

### Simulators and netlists

<a id="c-csim-tool-spice-netlist"></a>

#### SPICE netlists

`csim.tool.spice_netlist`

SPICE set the input format that nearly every circuit simulator still reads: the netlist.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Elements, nodes and the ground node
- Which elements add branch currents
- From netlist lines to unknowns

Sample problem:

> A SPICE deck contains these element cards (node 0 is ground): R3 drv 0 1meg; C1 n7 0 100f; V1 out 0 DC 3.3; R1 out drv 2.2k; I1 0 n7 DC 10u; R2 drv n7 10k. How many distinct non-ground nodes does the circuit have?

Answer: 3

Why: Collect every node name on the cards and drop 0. The names are out, drv, n7, so there are 3.

<a id="c-csim-tool-scale-suffixes"></a>

#### SPICE values and scale suffixes

`csim.tool.scale_suffixes`

SPICE numbers are written with scale suffixes: 2.2k, 470p, 1meg. The parser reads a number, then the letters after it, takes the first one or three letters as a scale factor and ignores the rest as decoration.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Reading scale suffixes
- The M and MEG trap
- Computing with netlist values

Sample problem:

> A SPICE card reads L1 a b 47u. What is the element value in nanohenries? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 47000

Why: The suffix u scales by $10^{-6}$, so in nanohenries the value is 47 times 1000, which is 47000.

<a id="c-csim-tool-model-cards"></a>

#### Model cards and device instances

`csim.tool.model_cards`

A netlist separates what a device is from where it is. An instance card, such as M1 d g s b nch W=1u L=0.1u, places one transistor and sets its geometry.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Instances and model cards
- Model levels and parameter sets
- Libraries, corners and subcircuits

Sample problem:

> Two hundred diodes in a deck name the same .model dmod d (is=1e-14 n=1.05). An engineer edits is on the model card. What changes?
>
> A) Only the first diode that names dmod
>
> B) Nothing until each instance line is edited too
>
> C) Only diodes whose instance line also sets is
>
> D) The saturation current of all two hundred diodes

Answer: The saturation current of all two hundred diodes

Why: A model card is shared state: every instance that names it is evaluated with its parameters, which is what makes process changes a one-line edit.

<a id="c-csim-tool-ngspice-xyce"></a>

#### Running decks in ngspice and Xyce

`csim.tool.ngspice_xyce`

ngspice and Xyce are the two open-source simulators a tool designer is most likely to read, run and extend.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Analysis cards and what they compute
- Options that steer the numerical engine
- Reading output and choosing a simulator

Sample problem:

> A deck contains .tran 1p 2n. What do the two numbers mean in SPICE?
>
> A) The minimum and maximum internal step
>
> B) The start time and the stop time
>
> C) The fixed integration step and the stop time
>
> D) The suggested print step and the stop time; the internal step is still chosen by error control

Answer: The suggested print step and the stop time; the internal step is still chosen by error control

Why: In .tran tstep tstop, tstep is the output (and initial suggested) step. The simulator adapts its own internal steps from truncation error estimates.

<a id="circuit-simulation-modified-nodal-analysis"></a>

### Modified nodal analysis

<a id="c-csim-mna-stamps"></a>

#### Modified nodal analysis stamps

`csim.mna.stamps`

Modified nodal analysis (MNA) is how SPICE turns a netlist into a linear system.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The resistor stamp
- Off-diagonal entries and the ground row
- Assembling the whole matrix

Sample problem:

> A resistor network has nodes 1 to 3 and ground: R1 between nodes 1 and 2, 5 k$\Omega$; R2 between nodes 1 and 3, 0.25 k$\Omega$; R3 from node 1 to ground, 2 k$\Omega$; R4 between nodes 1 and 3, 0.5 k$\Omega$. In the nodal conductance matrix $G$ (unknowns ordered by node number, ground row and column removed), what is the diagonal entry $G_{33}$ in mS? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 6

Why: A diagonal entry sums the conductances of every resistor touching the node, including those to ground: $G_{33} = 6$ mS.

<a id="c-csim-mna-current-sources"></a>

#### Current source stamps

`csim.mna.current_sources`

Independent current sources are the simplest stamps in MNA: they touch only the right-hand side vector $b$.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Injected current on the right-hand side
- The SPICE current-source convention
- Sources that touch ground

Sample problem:

> A circuit with nodes 1 to 4 and ground has resistors and these current sources: a source drawing 2 mA out of node 3 into ground; a source pushing 2 mA into node 2, drawn from node 1. With KCL written as currents leaving through elements equal to source currents injected, what is the right-hand-side entry $b_2$, in mA? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 2

Why: Add every current pushed into node 2 and subtract every current drawn out of it: $b_2 = 2$ mA.

<a id="c-csim-mna-voltage-sources"></a>

#### Voltage sources in MNA

`csim.mna.voltage_sources`

Plain nodal analysis cannot express a voltage source: its current is not a function of its terminal voltages.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Why a voltage source needs a branch current
- The augmented stamp
- The sign of the branch current

Sample problem:

> A circuit has 5 non-ground nodes, 9 resistors, 1 capacitors (open at DC), 2 independent current sources and 1 independent voltage sources. How many unknowns does the DC modified nodal analysis system have?

Answer: 6

Why: Every node voltage is an unknown, and each voltage source adds its branch current, because its current cannot be written from its terminal voltages. Resistors, capacitors and current sources add none: 5 + 1 = 6.

<a id="c-csim-mna-vccs"></a>

#### Voltage-controlled current source stamps

`csim.mna.vccs`

Controlled sources are how small-signal device models enter MNA: a transistor's transconductance is a voltage-controlled current source.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Four entries off the controlling nodes
- Adding a VCCS to a resistive matrix
- Controlled sources break symmetry

Sample problem:

> A VCCS card G1 n+ n- nc+ nc- gm drives a current $g_m (v_{nc+} - v_{nc-})$ from n+ through the source into n-. A circuit with nodes 1 to 3 contains G1 2 0 1 0 1m (gm in mS, 0 is ground). Which entries does this card alone stamp into the nodal matrix entry $G_{21}$, in mS? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 1

Why: The VCCS stamps $+g_m$ at (n+, nc+), $-g_m$ at (n+, nc-), $-g_m$ at (n-, nc+) and $+g_m$ at (n-, nc-), dropping any ground row or column. Entry (2, 1) is 1 mS.

<a id="c-csim-mna-vcvs"></a>

#### VCVS stamps and controlled branch rows

`csim.mna.vcvs`

A voltage-controlled voltage source forces an output voltage proportional to a controlling voltage.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The VCVS branch row
- Counting unknowns with controlled sources
- Solving an ideal amplifier stage

Sample problem:

> A circuit with nodes 1 to 3 contains E1 2 0 1 0 20 (E1 n+ n- nc+ nc- gain). Unknowns are $v_1, \ldots, v_3$ followed by the branch currents in card order, so E1's branch current is unknown 4 and its constraint is row 4. What is the entry in row 4, column 3 contributed by these cards? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 0

Why: The E1 row encodes $v_{n+} - v_{n-} - \mu (v_{nc+} - v_{nc-}) = 0$: $+1$ at n+, -1 at n-, $-\mu$ at nc+, $+\mu$ at nc-. Its branch column has $+1$ at n+ and -1 at n-. Entry (4, 3) is 0.

<a id="c-csim-mna-solve-small"></a>

#### Solving a small MNA system

`csim.mna.solve_small`

After stamping comes solving. A simulator factors the sparse MNA matrix with LU and substitutes; by hand, a two-node system yields to Cramer's rule.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Two-node nodal equations
- Solving for the second node
- A system with a voltage source row

Sample problem:

> A current source pushes 1 mA into node 1. R1 = 0.5 k$\Omega$ connects node 1 to ground, R2 = 2.5 k$\Omega$ connects nodes 1 and 2, and R3 = 0.5 k$\Omega$ connects node 2 to ground. Writing $G v = b$ in mS, mA and V, what is $v_1$ in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 0.429

Why: $G = \begin{pmatrix} 2.4 & -0.4 \\ -0.4 & 2.4 \end{pmatrix}$, $b = (1, 0)$, $\det G = 5.6$. By Cramer's rule $v_1 = 0.4286$ V and $v_2 = 0.0714$ V.

<a id="c-csim-mna-structure"></a>

#### Sparsity and structure of the MNA matrix

`csim.mna.structure`

Circuit matrices are extremely sparse: a node connects to a handful of neighbours, so a row of a million-node matrix holds perhaps five nonzeros.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Counting structural nonzeros
- Nonzeros of the augmented matrix
- Zero diagonals and pivoting

Sample problem:

> A circuit on nodes 1 to 4 has R1 between nodes 1 and 2, 2.5 k$\Omega$; R2 between nodes 1 and 3, 2.5 k$\Omega$; R3 between nodes 3 and 4, 1 k$\Omega$; R4 from node 4 to ground, 2 k$\Omega$; R5 between nodes 4 and 3, 2 k$\Omega$; R6 between nodes 3 and 1, 10 k$\Omega$. How many structurally nonzero entries does its nodal conductance matrix have (ground removed)?

Answer: 10

Why: Every node has a nonzero diagonal, and each distinct pair of non-ground nodes joined by a resistor adds two symmetric off-diagonal entries. Parallel resistors share a position. Total 10.

<a id="circuit-simulation-dc-analysis"></a>

### DC analysis

<a id="c-csim-dc-op-reduction"></a>

#### The DC operating point problem

`csim.dc.op_reduction`

The DC operating point is the first thing almost every analysis computes: transient starts from it, AC and noise linearize around it.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Capacitors open, inductors short
- Currents at the operating point
- The DC system a simulator actually builds

Sample problem:

> V1 drives node in at 1.5 V. R1 = 1 k$\Omega$ runs from in to node a, capacitor C1 from a to ground, inductor L1 from a to node b, R2 = 1 k$\Omega$ from b to ground, and capacitor C2 from b to node c with R4 = 2 k$\Omega$ from c to ground. What is the DC operating-point voltage at node a, in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 0.75

Why: At DC the capacitors are open and the inductor is a short, so a and b are one node and c sees no current through C2. The divider R1 into 1 k$\Omega$ gives $v_a = v_b = 0.75$ V, and $v_c = 0$.

<a id="c-csim-dc-diode-companion"></a>

#### Linearized diode companion model

`csim.dc.diode_companion`

Nonlinear devices enter MNA through linearization. At each Newton iterate, a diode is replaced by its tangent line: a conductance in parallel with a current source.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Conductance at the iterate
- The equivalent current source
- What the linear model predicts

Sample problem:

> A diode with $I_S$ = 100 fA and $V_T = 0.025$ V obeys $I = I_S(e^{V/V_T} - 1)$. Newton's current iterate is $V_k = 0.66$ V. What companion conductance $g_d$ does the simulator stamp, in mS? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 1168

Why: $I_d(V_k) = 29.19943$ mA, $g_d = (I_S/V_T)e^{V_k/V_T} = 1167.97706$ mS, $I_{eq} = I_d - g_d V_k = -741.66543$ mA.

<a id="c-csim-dc-newton-companion"></a>

#### Newton-Raphson with companion models

`csim.dc.newton_companion`

Newton-Raphson on circuit equations has an elegant implementation: linearize every device at the current iterate, stamp the companion models, solve the resulting linear circuit, and repeat.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Stamping the linearized diode
- One Newton iterate
- The KCL residual

Sample problem:

> A source of 1 V drives a 2 k$\Omega$ resistor into node d; a diode from d to ground has $I_S$ = 5 fA, $V_T = 0.025$ V and $I = I_S(e^{V/V_T}-1)$. The current Newton iterate is $v_d = 0.63$ V. Work in mS, mA and V. What is the single entry of the linearized MNA matrix for node d, in mS? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 18.09

Why: At $V_k$: $I_d = 0.43973$ mA, $g_d = 17.5894$ mS, $I_{eq} = -10.64158$ mA. The linearized KCL row is $(1/R + g_d)\, v = V_s/R - I_{eq}$, so $18.0894\, v = 11.14158$ and $v_{k+1} = 0.61592$ V.

<a id="c-csim-dc-newton-convergence"></a>

#### Newton convergence tests

`csim.dc.newton_convergence`

Newton never reaches the exact solution; a simulator must decide when to stop. SPICE's convergence tests combine relative and absolute tolerances on both node voltages and device currents, and their defaults are worth memorizing because they set the accuracy of every result.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The voltage tolerance band
- Quadratic convergence in iterations
- The current tolerance

Sample problem:

> Two successive Newton iterates of a node voltage are 4.2172 V and 4.2182 V. With SPICE defaults RELTOL = $10^{-3}$ and VNTOL = 1 uV, the voltage test passes when $|v_k - v_{k-1}| \le \text{RELTOL} \cdot \max(|v_k|, |v_{k-1}|) + \text{VNTOL}$. What is the allowed band, in microvolts? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 4219.2

Why: $10^{-3} \times 4.2182$ V $= 4218.2$ uV, plus 1 uV, gives 4219.2 uV. The actual change is 1000 uV.

<a id="c-csim-dc-mosfet-linearization"></a>

#### Linearizing a MOSFET at a Newton iterate

`csim.dc.mosfet_linearization`

A MOSFET is a three-port nonlinearity: its drain current depends on both gate-source and drain-source voltages.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Transconductance from the square law
- Output conductance
- The MOSFET equivalent current

Sample problem:

> An NMOS in saturation follows $I_D = \tfrac{k}{2}(V_{GS} - V_T)^2 (1 + \lambda V_{DS})$ with $k = 1.9$ mA/V$^2$, $V_T = 0.35$ V and $\lambda = 0.08$ 1/V. Newton's iterate has $V_{GS} = 0.95$ V and $V_{DS} = 1.5$ V (source grounded). What transconductance $g_m = \partial I_D/\partial V_{GS}$ is stamped, in mS? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 1.2768

Why: $V_{ov} = 0.6$ V. $I_D = 0.38304$ mA, $g_m = k V_{ov}(1 + \lambda V_{DS}) = 1.2768$ mS, $g_{ds} = \tfrac{k}{2} V_{ov}^2 \lambda = 0.02736$ mS, $I_{eq} = I_D - g_m V_{GS} - g_{ds} V_{DS} = -0.87096$ mA.

<a id="c-csim-dc-junction-limiting"></a>

#### Junction voltage limiting

`csim.dc.junction_limiting`

An exponential device turns a modest Newton overshoot into a catastrophe: evaluating a diode at 5 V gives a current of order $e^{200}$.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The critical voltage
- Limiting a forward step
- When limiting does nothing

Sample problem:

> A diode has $I_S$ = 1 fA and $V_T = 0.025$ V. SPICE's junction limiter switches on above the critical voltage $v_{crit} = V_T \ln(V_T/(\sqrt{2} I_S))$, the voltage where the diode's current-voltage curve has its minimum radius of curvature. What is $v_{crit}$ in volts? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 0.7626

Why: $V_T/(\sqrt{2} I_S) = 1.7678 \times 10^{13}$, its natural log is 30.5033, times 0.025 gives 0.7626 V.

<a id="c-csim-dc-damping"></a>

#### Damped Newton steps

`csim.dc.damping`

Newton converges quadratically near a root and can diverge or cycle far from one.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Clipping the step
- Uniform damping of a vector update
- Backtracking on the residual

Sample problem:

> A Newton solve at iterate $v = 0.9$ V proposes the update $\Delta v = 2$ V. The simulator clips any node update to at most 0.3 V in magnitude. What is the next iterate, in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 1.2

Why: The applied step is 0.3 V, so the iterate becomes 1.2 V. Clipping keeps the step in the region where the linearization is trustworthy.

<a id="c-csim-dc-gmin-stepping"></a>

#### Gmin stepping

`csim.dc.gmin_stepping`

Gmin stepping is SPICE's main continuation method for hard operating points. It attaches a conductance gmin from every node to ground, large at first so the circuit is nearly linear and well conditioned, solves, then shrinks gmin step by step, using each solution as the starting guess for the next.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- A conductance to ground at every node
- The stepping schedule
- The error left by the final gmin

Sample problem:

> A current source pushes 0.4 mA into a node that has a 1 k$\Omega$ resistor to ground. During gmin stepping the simulator also attaches $g_{min} = 0.01$ mS from every node to ground. What node voltage does that intermediate solve produce, in volts? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 0.396

Why: The node sees $1/R + g_{min} = 1.01$ mS, so $v = 0.4 / 1.01 = 0.396$ V, against 0.4 V once gmin is removed. Each stepping solve starts from the previous one as gmin shrinks.

<a id="c-csim-dc-convergence-aids"></a>

#### DC convergence aids

`csim.dc.convergence_aids`

When plain Newton fails on an operating point, simulators fall back on a toolbox of convergence aids: junction limiting, damping, gmin stepping, source stepping, pseudo-transient continuation and user-supplied nodesets.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Why Newton fails on circuits
- Choosing an aid
- What each aid costs and hides

Sample problem:

> An operating point oscillates between two iterates and never meets the tolerance. Which property of Newton explains this?
>
> A) Newton converges only locally; far from a solution the full step can overshoot back and forth
>
> B) Newton is globally convergent, so the matrix must be wrong
>
> C) LU factorization introduces the oscillation
>
> D) The tolerance is applied only to currents

Answer: Newton converges only locally; far from a solution the full step can overshoot back and forth

Why: Quadratic convergence holds only near a root. Far away, full Newton steps can cycle, which damping and limiting are designed to stop.

<a id="circuit-simulation-transient-analysis"></a>

### Transient analysis

<a id="c-csim-tran-dae"></a>

#### Transient equations as a DAE

`csim.tran.dae`

Transient analysis integrates the circuit equations in time, but those equations are not an ordinary differential equation.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Resistive and reactive parts
- Algebraic constraints and singular C
- Stiffness and why SPICE is implicit

Sample problem:

> Why do accurate simulators prefer integrating a MOSFET's terminal charges rather than its voltage-dependent capacitances?
>
> A) Charges make the matrix symmetric
>
> B) Capacitances cannot be stamped into MNA
>
> C) Integrating C(v) dv/dt with a numerical rule can create or destroy charge, while integrating q(v) conserves it
>
> D) Charge formulations need no Newton iteration

Answer: Integrating C(v) dv/dt with a numerical rule can create or destroy charge, while integrating q(v) conserves it

Why: For a nonlinear capacitance, the discretized C(v) dv/dt does not equal the exact change in charge, so charge leaks numerically. A charge-based model avoids that.

<a id="c-csim-tran-companion-c"></a>

#### Capacitor companion models

`csim.tran.companion_c`

Transient analysis turns every capacitor into a resistor and a current source for the duration of one time step.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Backward Euler capacitor
- Trapezoidal capacitor
- Recovering the capacitor current

Sample problem:

> A 5 pF capacitor is integrated with backward Euler at step $h = 0.01$ ns. Units: C/h with C in pF and h in ns is in mS; currents are in mA. The companion is $i_C(t_{n+1}) = G_{eq} v_{n+1} - I_{eq}$. What is $G_{eq}$ in mS? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 500

Why: Backward Euler replaces $C\,dv/dt$ by $C(v_{n+1} - v_n)/h$, so $G_{eq} = C/h = 500$ mS.

<a id="c-csim-tran-companion-l"></a>

#### Inductor companion models

`csim.tran.companion_l`

Inductors get companion models too, by discretizing $v = L\, di/dt$ instead of $i = C\, dv/dt$.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Backward Euler inductor
- Trapezoidal inductor conductance
- The trapezoidal history current

Sample problem:

> A 1 uH inductor carries 1 mA at $t_n$. Backward Euler at $h = 0.05$ ns gives a voltage of 0.2 V across it at $t_{n+1}$. With h in ns and L in uH, h/L is in mS; currents are in mA. The companion is $i_{n+1} = G_{eq} v_{n+1} + I_{eq}$. What is $i_{n+1}$ in mA? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 1.01

Why: $i_{n+1} = i_n + (h/L) v_{n+1} = 1 + 0.05 \times 0.2 = 1.01$ mA.

<a id="c-csim-tran-be-step"></a>

#### One backward-Euler transient step

`csim.tran.be_step`

One transient step is one companion-model solve. For a linear circuit there is no Newton iteration: stamp the companions, solve once, advance.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Assembling the step equation
- Marching two steps
- Error against the exact exponential

Sample problem:

> A source steps to 2.5 V at $t = 0$ and drives R = 2 k$\Omega$ into a node with C = 5 pF to ground. The step is $h = 5$ ns (k$\Omega$ times pF is ns; 1/R is in mS and C/h in mS). The capacitor voltage at $t_n$ is 0.8 V. Which value does one backward-Euler step give for $v_{n+1}$, in volts? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 1.3667

Why: $(1/R + C/h) v_{n+1} = V_s/R + (C/h) v_n$: $(0.5 + 1) v_{n+1} = 1.25 + 0.8$, so $v_{n+1} = 1.3667$ V.

<a id="c-csim-tran-trap-step"></a>

#### One trapezoidal transient step

`csim.tran.trap_step`

The trapezoidal rule is SPICE's default integrator because it is second-order accurate and A-stable at the same cost per step as backward Euler.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The trapezoidal step equation
- Updating the capacitor current
- Two trapezoidal steps

Sample problem:

> A source steps to 4 V at $t = 0$ and drives R = 5 k$\Omega$ into a node with C = 0.5 pF to ground. The step is $h = 0.25$ ns (k$\Omega$ times pF is ns; 1/R is in mS and C/h in mS). At $t_n$ the capacitor is at 3.7 V, so its current is $i_n = (V_s - v_n)/R = 0.06$ mA. Which value does one trapezoidal step give for $v_{n+1}$, in volts? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 3.7286

Why: $(1/R + 2C/h) v_{n+1} = V_s/R + (2C/h) v_n + i_n$: $(0.2 + 4) v_{n+1} = 0.8 + 14.8 + 0.06$, so $v_{n+1} = 3.72857$ V and $i_{n+1} = (2C/h)(v_{n+1} - v_n) - i_n = 0.05429$ mA.

<a id="c-csim-tran-trap-ringing"></a>

#### Trapezoidal ringing

`csim.tran.trap_ringing`

The trapezoidal rule is A-stable, yet on stiff circuits it produces a sawtooth that alternates in sign from step to step.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The trapezoidal amplification factor
- Ringing over several steps
- Damping with a backward Euler step

Sample problem:

> A capacitor discharges through a resistor with time constant $\tau = 0.05$ ns (source-free, $x' = -x/\tau$). The simulator takes steps of $h = 0.25$ ns with the trapezoidal rule, whose one-step factor is $(1 - h/2\tau)/(1 + h/2\tau)$. What is the factor multiplying $x$ at each step? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: -0.4286

Why: $h/\tau = 5$, so the factor is $(1 - 2.5)/(1 + 2.5) = -0.4286$. It is negative whenever $h > 2\tau$, which flips the sign every step: ringing.

<a id="c-csim-tran-gear-bdf"></a>

#### BDF and Gear integration

`csim.tran.gear_bdf`

Backward differentiation formulas (BDF), introduced to circuit simulation by Gear, approximate the derivative at the new time point from several past points.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The BDF2 derivative formula
- The BDF2 history current
- One BDF2 step on an RC node

Sample problem:

> Second-order BDF (Gear 2) at constant step uses $x'_{n+1} \approx (3x_{n+1} - 4x_n + x_{n-1})/(2h)$, so the capacitor companion is $i_{n+1} = G_{eq} v_{n+1} - I_{eq}$. For C = 4 pF and $h = 1$ ns, what is $G_{eq}$ in mS? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 6

Why: $G_{eq} = 3C/(2h) = 6$ mS, larger than backward Euler's $C/h$ by half.

<a id="c-csim-tran-lte-estimate"></a>

#### Estimating local truncation error

`csim.tran.lte_estimate`

A simulator cannot compare its result with the exact solution, so it estimates the local truncation error (LTE) of each step from the solution itself.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Derivatives from divided differences
- Backward Euler error estimate
- Trapezoidal error estimate

Sample problem:

> A node voltage has been accepted at four equally spaced time points, $h = 0.4$ ns apart: 1.580301, 1.883508, 2.086753, 2.222992 V. Using the first three samples, estimate the second derivative $x'' \approx (v_2 - 2v_1 + v_0)/h^2$ in V/ns$^2$. Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: -0.6248

Why: $v_2 - 2v_1 + v_0 = -0.099962$ V; divided by $h^2 = 0.16$ gives -0.6248 V/ns$^2$. This is twice the second divided difference.

<a id="c-csim-tran-timestep-control"></a>

#### Timestep control

`csim.tran.timestep_control`

Transient analysis spends most of its effort deciding how long the next step should be.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The next step for trapezoidal
- The next step for backward Euler
- Rejecting a step

Sample problem:

> A trapezoidal step of $h = 2$ ns was accepted with an estimated local truncation error of 0.25 mV against a tolerance of 2 mV. Since the trapezoidal error scales as $h^3$, what step $h_{new} = h(\varepsilon/|LTE|)^{1/3}$ should the simulator try next, in ns? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 4

Why: $\varepsilon/LTE = 8$; its cube root is 2; $h_{new} = 4$ ns.

<a id="c-csim-tran-breakpoints"></a>

#### Breakpoints and step restarts

`csim.tran.breakpoints`

Step control assumes smooth waveforms. Circuits are full of corners: PWL and PULSE sources, switching events, the start of the simulation.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Breakpoints at source corners
- Restarting after a discontinuity
- Initial conditions and UIC

Sample problem:

> A digital-heavy deck has many fast PULSE sources with unrelated periods. What happens to the timestep?
>
> A) Nothing; breakpoints only affect output
>
> B) It becomes fixed at tstep
>
> C) It grows, because breakpoints relax tolerances
>
> D) It is repeatedly cut to hit breakpoints, so the run takes many small steps even where signals are idle

Answer: It is repeatedly cut to hit breakpoints, so the run takes many small steps even where signals are idle

Why: Every source corner forces a step boundary. Many unsynchronized edges pack breakpoints densely, which is one reason fast SPICE uses event-driven methods.

<a id="circuit-simulation-ac-and-noise-analysis"></a>

### AC and noise analysis

<a id="c-csim-ac-linearize-op"></a>

#### Small-signal models from the operating point

`csim.ac.linearize_op`

AC analysis begins where the DC operating point ends. Every nonlinear device is replaced by its small-signal model, the derivatives of its currents and charges at the bias point, which are exactly the conductances Newton already computed in its last iteration.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Transconductance at the bias point
- Output resistance
- Intrinsic gain

Sample problem:

> After the DC operating point, an NMOS in saturation (square law) carries $I_D = 0.9$ mA with overdrive $V_{ov} = 0.14$ V and channel-length modulation $\lambda = 0.08$ 1/V. What transconductance $g_m$ does AC analysis use, in mS? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 12.857

Why: For the square law $g_m = 2 I_D / V_{ov} = 2 \times 0.9 / 0.14 = 12.857$ mS.

<a id="c-csim-ac-complex-mna"></a>

#### The complex MNA system

`csim.ac.complex_mna`

AC analysis solves the linearized circuit at each frequency in a sweep. In the phasor domain a capacitor's current is $j\omega C$ times its voltage, so MNA becomes a complex linear system $(G + j\omega C)x = b$, with $G$ and $C$ the same matrices transient analysis uses.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Admittance entries
- Solving one complex node
- Phase of the response

Sample problem:

> AC analysis stamps a capacitor as the admittance $j\omega C$. A 1 pF capacitor connects node 1 to ground. At 10 MHz, what is the imaginary part of its contribution to the diagonal entry $Y_{11}$, in microsiemens? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 62.83

Why: $\omega C = 2\pi \times 10 \times 10^6 \times 1 \times 10^{-12} = 62.83$ uS.

<a id="c-csim-ac-small-signal"></a>

#### AC small-signal analysis

`csim.ac.small_signal`

AC small-signal analysis combines the two previous ideas: linearize every device at the operating point, then solve the complex MNA system over frequency.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Low-frequency gain
- Gain at a frequency
- The pole frequency

Sample problem:

> AC analysis linearizes a common-source stage at its operating point: $g_m = 3$ mS, drain resistor $R_D = 50$ k$\Omega$, $r_o = 20$ k$\Omega$, load $C_L = 1$ pF. The gain is $A(j\omega) = -g_m R_{out}/(1 + j\omega R_{out} C_L)$ with $R_{out} = R_D \parallel r_o$. What is the low-frequency gain magnitude in dB? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 32.64

Why: $R_{out} = 14.286$ k$\Omega$, $|A_0| = 42.857$, $20\log_{10} 42.857 = 32.64$ dB.

<a id="c-csim-ac-noise"></a>

#### Noise analysis

`csim.ac.noise`

Noise analysis is a small-signal frequency sweep with a twist: instead of one input, every resistor and transistor contributes a random noise source, and the simulator sums their powers at the output.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Thermal noise of a resistor
- Summing independent noise at the output
- Integrated kT/C noise

Sample problem:

> Noise analysis models a resistor's thermal noise as a voltage source with density $4kTR$ in V$^2$/Hz. For R = 5 k$\Omega$ at T = 300 K ($k = 1.380649 \times 10^{-23}$ J/K), what is the noise voltage density in nV/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 9.102

Why: $4kTR = 8.2839 \times 10^{-17}$ V$^2$/Hz; its square root is 9.102 nV/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$.

<a id="circuit-simulation-periodic-steady-state"></a>

### Periodic steady state

<a id="c-csim-pss-shooting"></a>

#### Shooting for periodic steady state

`csim.pss.shooting`

Many circuits are judged in periodic steady state: oscillators, mixers, switching converters, clocked comparators.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The periodic boundary condition
- One shooting Newton step
- Why brute-force transient is slow

Sample problem:

> Integrating a linear circuit driven by a periodic source over one period T maps its capacitor voltage as $x(T) = 0.75\, x(0) + 0.65$ V. Periodic steady state requires $x(T) = x(0)$. What is that initial voltage, in volts? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 2.6

Why: Solve $x = 0.75 x + 0.65$: $x = 0.65/(1 - 0.75) = 2.6$ V. Starting there, one period returns to the same state.

<a id="c-csim-pss-harmonic-balance"></a>

#### Harmonic balance

`csim.pss.harmonic_balance`

Harmonic balance (HB) finds the periodic steady state in the frequency domain. Each circuit unknown is represented by its Fourier coefficients up to some harmonic, linear elements are stamped harmonic by harmonic exactly as in AC analysis, and nonlinear devices are evaluated in the time domain and transformed back with FFTs.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Unknowns in the frequency domain
- Harmonics of a quadratic nonlinearity
- Harmonics of a cubic nonlinearity

Sample problem:

> Harmonic balance represents each of a circuit's 39 MNA unknowns by a DC term and the cosine and sine amplitudes of harmonics 1 to 5. How many real unknowns does the harmonic-balance system have?

Answer: 429

Why: Each unknown carries $2K + 1 = 11$ real coefficients, so $39 \times 11 = 429$. The Jacobian couples harmonics through every nonlinear device, which is why large HB uses matrix-free Krylov solvers.

<a id="c-csim-pss-rf-methods"></a>

#### RF simulation beyond periodic steady state

`csim.pss.rf_methods`

Periodic steady state is the base on which RF simulation builds. Mixers, oscillators and switched circuits need small-signal and noise analyses that account for a large periodic drive, and multitone or modulated signals need methods that avoid simulating millions of carrier cycles.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Periodic small-signal analyses
- Multitone and envelope methods
- Choosing shooting or harmonic balance

Sample problem:

> Periodic noise analysis of a mixer reports noise at the IF output that originated near the image frequency. What phenomenon is this?
>
> A) Thermal noise that is independent of the LO
>
> B) A numerical artifact of harmonic balance
>
> C) Noise folding: the time-varying operating point converts noise from sidebands of the LO harmonics to the output frequency
>
> D) Aliasing from the transient timestep

Answer: Noise folding: the time-varying operating point converts noise from sidebands of the LO harmonics to the output frequency

Why: Cyclostationary analysis tracks how a periodically modulated circuit mixes noise from every sideband onto the output, which stationary noise analysis cannot.

<a id="circuit-simulation-variation-analysis"></a>

### Variation analysis

<a id="c-csim-var-sensitivity"></a>

#### Direct sensitivity analysis

`csim.var.sensitivity`

Sensitivity analysis asks how much an output moves when a parameter moves. Simulators compute it exactly, without finite differences, by differentiating the circuit equations themselves and reusing the factorization of the nominal solve.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Differentiating the circuit equations
