Sample problem:

> Each iteration of a loop reads a[i+1], a[i+3], a[i+6], a[i+7]. The array is partitioned cyclically into 4 banks numbered from 0. In the iteration with i = 15, which bank does the read a[i+1] use?

Answer: 0

Why: The read touches element 15 + 1 = 16, and 16 mod 4 = 0.

<a id="c-hls-mem-interfaces"></a>

#### Interface synthesis: handshakes, streams and buses

`hls.mem.interfaces`

A synthesized kernel must exchange data with the rest of the system, and C function arguments say nothing about how.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Port-level protocols
- Streams, memories and buses
- How interfaces bound performance

Sample problem:

> A scalar argument becomes an input port with no handshake. What must the surrounding design guarantee?
>
> A) The value arrives with a valid strobe
>
> B) The block acknowledges every read
>
> C) The value changes every cycle
>
> D) The value stays stable for as long as the block may read it

Answer: The value stays stable for as long as the block may read it

Why: With no protocol the block samples the port whenever its schedule needs it, so the environment must hold it steady.

<a id="c-hls-mem-dataflow"></a>

#### Task-level dataflow

`hls.mem.dataflow`

Loop pipelining overlaps iterations of one loop. Dataflow overlaps whole tasks: a function body made of several sub-functions or loops runs as a pipeline of processes connected by channels, so the second task works on frame $k$ while the first starts frame $k + 1$.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Tasks, channels and the slowest stage
- Total time for many frames
- Speedup and the rules that make it possible

Sample problem:

> A dataflow region chains tasks through ping-pong buffers: T1 (latency 120, interval 70), T2 (latency 200, interval 200), T3 (latency 200, interval 200), in cycles per frame. A task's interval is how often it can accept a new frame. Model the region as starting a new frame every max-interval cycles, with the first frame taking the sum of the latencies. How many cycles separate successive frames at the output in steady state?

Answer: 200

Why: The slowest stage sets the rate: T2 with interval 200 cycles.

<a id="c-hls-mem-line-buffers"></a>

#### Line buffers and data reuse

`hls.mem.line_buffers`

Stencil computations, such as convolutions and filters over images, read each input many times.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- How many pixels to keep
- Block RAMs for the buffers
- Latency to the first output

Sample problem:

> A 3×3 convolution streams an image of width 720 pixels in raster order, one pixel per cycle, and reads each pixel from external memory only once. How many pixels must the line buffers hold?

Answer: 1440

Why: To form a 3-row window the design keeps the previous 2 rows: 2 × 720 = 1440 pixels. The newest row streams in directly.

<a id="high-level-synthesis-hls-systems-and-tools"></a>

### HLS systems and tools

<a id="c-hls-sys-codesign"></a>

#### Hardware-software partitioning

`hls.sys.codesign`

HLS is usually applied to part of a program: the kernel that dominates run time is moved to an accelerator while the rest stays in software.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- New run time after offloading
- Overall speedup and Amdahl's limit
- The break-even speedup

Sample problem:

> A program takes 660 ms in software. A kernel accounting for 88% of that time is moved to an HLS accelerator that runs it 28 times faster, and moving data to and from the accelerator adds 98.7 ms. What is the new run time in ms? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 198.64

Why: Software part (1 - 0.88) × 660 = 79.2 ms, accelerated part 580.8 / 28 = 20.74 ms, plus 98.7 ms of transfer: 198.64 ms.

<a id="c-hls-sys-dse"></a>

#### Design-space exploration of HLS directives

`hls.sys.dse`

One C kernel admits thousands of microarchitectures through its directives: unroll factors, pipeline settings, partition factors, inlining, resource limits.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The size of the directive space
- Pareto-optimal designs
- Measuring a front with hypervolume

Sample problem:

> A kernel has 3 loops; each can take one of 3 unroll factors and may be pipelined or not. It has 3 arrays; each can take one of 4 partitioning choices. All choices are independent. How many configurations does the pragma design space contain?

Answer: 13824

Why: Each loop has 3 × 2 = 6 settings and each array 4, so the space has 6^3 × 4^3 = 13824 points.

<a id="c-hls-sys-tools"></a>

#### HLS tools and IRs: Vitis HLS, Bambu, CIRCT, Calyx

`hls.sys.tools`

HLS is now built on compiler infrastructure. Commercial HLS tools use LLVM-based front ends and expose the concepts of this domain as directives.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Directives in a commercial flow
- Open tools and intermediate languages
- Static versus dynamic scheduling and MLIR-based HLS

Sample problem:

> A loop of 64 iterations has one multiplication in its body. What does fully unrolling it tend to do, with no other directive?
>
> A) Turn the loop into a FIFO
>
> B) Reduce the design to a single multiplier
>
> C) Halve the latency with no change in area
>
> D) Expose 64 multiplications at once, which can cost up to 64 multipliers unless resources are limited

Answer: Expose 64 multiplications at once, which can cost up to 64 multipliers unless resources are limited

Why: Unrolling replicates the body. The parallelism is real only if units and memory ports keep up, and it is paid for in area.

<a id="high-level-synthesis-frontier-agent-first-futures"></a>

### Frontier: agent-first futures

<a id="c-hls-frontier-seams"></a>

#### Seams and change tiers in an HLS engine

`hls.frontier.seams`

An HLS engine built for agents separates what must never change casually, the rules that make every schedule and binding correct, from what customers and agents tune: priorities, cost functions, directive values and observation points.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The four layers of an HLS engine
- Which tier a request lands in
- Designing the seams and proving changes

Sample problem:

> A user sets a 4 ns target clock and II = 2 on a loop. Which layer do these values sit in?
>
> A) Parameters
>
> B) Immutable core
>
> C) Observation hooks
>
> D) Strategy or policy

Answer: Parameters

Why: They are values the engine reads, changed without recompiling anything.

<a id="c-hls-frontier-pragma-agent"></a>

#### Pragma-search agents

`hls.frontier.pragma_agent`

Choosing HLS directives is a search over a huge discrete space with an expensive, noisy evaluator, exactly the kind of loop an agent can run.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The search problem
- Reading the report to choose the next move
- Rewards, proxies and verification

Sample problem:

> What should a pragma-search agent read after each HLS run to choose the next experiment?
>
> A) Only the pass or fail exit code
>
> B) The achieved II, latency and resource use, and the reported reason a loop missed its target II
>
> C) The generated Verilog line by line
>
> D) The host CPU load

Answer: The achieved II, latency and resource use, and the reported reason a loop missed its target II

Why: The report names the binding constraint, which tells the agent which pragma could actually help.

<a id="c-hls-frontier-llm-to-hlsc"></a>

#### LLM-to-HLS-C translation loops

`hls.frontier.llm_to_hlsc`

Language models can translate a reference algorithm, written in Python, MATLAB or plain C, into synthesizable HLS-C with directives.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What makes generated code synthesizable
- The harness loop
- Measuring and bounding the system

Sample problem:

> An LLM writes 'while (err > tol)' for an iterative solver. What should be added for HLS?
>
> A) A bound on the trip count so the tool can budget and report worst-case latency
>
> B) Nothing, because HLS ignores while-loops
>
> C) A switch to double precision
>
> D) A directive to unroll it fully

Answer: A bound on the trip count so the tool can budget and report worst-case latency

Why: A data-dependent loop can be synthesized, but without a bound its latency is unknown and it may never terminate on bad data.

<a id="c-hls-frontier-cosim-golden"></a>

#### Co-simulation as the golden test

`hls.frontier.cosim_golden`

In an HLS flow the C model is the specification, and C/RTL co-simulation is the test that checks the generated hardware against it.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What co-simulation checks
- Golden and differential tests for engine changes
- Where the golden test is weak

Sample problem:

> Co-simulation passes. What has it not shown?
>
> A) That the RTL finishes on those inputs
>
> B) That the interface handshakes work on those tests
>
> C) That outputs match the C model on the tested vectors
>
> D) That the design meets timing after implementation

Answer: That the design meets timing after implementation

Why: Co-simulation is functional and cycle-level at RTL; physical timing needs implementation and static timing analysis.

<a id="c-hls-frontier-qor-surrogate"></a>

#### Fast QoR surrogates for exploration

`hls.frontier.qor_surrogate`

Every HLS run costs minutes; every implementation run costs far more. Design-space explorers therefore use surrogate models that predict latency, II and resources from a configuration in milliseconds, and spend real runs only on promising points.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Error of a single prediction
- Mean absolute percentage error
- Ranking quality matters more than error

Sample problem:

> A fast QoR surrogate predicts 3980 cycles of latency for a pragma configuration; full HLS synthesis reports 3700 cycles. What is the absolute percentage error of the prediction? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 7.6

Why: |3980 - 3700| / 3700 × 100 = 7.6%.

---

## Static Timing Analysis

Layer 5. Timing graphs, delay models, clocks and constraints, OCV, AOCV, POCV and SSTA, incremental timing and timing closure.

Builds on: CMOS Circuits and Cell Libraries, Graph Algorithms for EDA, Digital Logic Design, Variability, Yield and Reliability Statistics, Circuits and Electromagnetics, Optimization for EDA.

Topics covered:

- Static timing analysis as graph propagation: timing graph, arcs, arrival time, required time, slack, WNS, TNS
- Setup and hold checks, clock-to-q, recovery/removal, latches and time borrowing
- Delay models: Elmore delay, NLDM table interpolation (slew and load), effective capacitance, slew propagation, wire delay
- Clocks: definitions, generated clocks, clock latency and uncertainty, skew, jitter, CPPR/CRPR
- Timing constraints and SDC: create_clock, set_input_delay, set_output_delay, false paths, multicycle paths, clock groups
- Critical paths, path-based vs graph-based analysis, path enumeration
- Corners and modes: PVT corners, MCMM
- On-chip variation: flat OCV derates, AOCV, POCV, LVF; statistical STA (canonical first-order form, sum and max)
- Incremental timing, timing closure, timing ECOs
- OpenSTA: Liberty + Verilog netlist + SDC + SPEF in, reports out

Subdomains: [The timing graph](#static-timing-analysis-the-timing-graph), [Delay calculation](#static-timing-analysis-delay-calculation), [Timing checks](#static-timing-analysis-timing-checks), [Clocks](#static-timing-analysis-clocks), [Constraints](#static-timing-analysis-constraints), [Path analysis](#static-timing-analysis-path-analysis), [Variation-aware timing](#static-timing-analysis-variation-aware-timing), [Incremental timing](#static-timing-analysis-incremental-timing), [Timing closure](#static-timing-analysis-timing-closure), [Frontier: agent-first futures](#static-timing-analysis-frontier-agent-first-futures)

<a id="static-timing-analysis-the-timing-graph"></a>

### The timing graph

<a id="c-sta-graph-timing-graph"></a>

#### The timing graph

`sta.graph.timing_graph`

A static timer never simulates a circuit. It turns the netlist into a directed graph and propagates numbers along it.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Pins as nodes, arcs as edges
- Counting cell arcs and net arcs
- Loops, disabled arcs and why a DAG matters

Sample problem:

> Where do the delays on cell arcs come from?
>
> A) The SPEF file alone
>
> B) The Verilog netlist
>
> C) The Liberty timing arcs of each cell, evaluated at the pin's slew and load
>
> D) The SDC file

Answer: The Liberty timing arcs of each cell, evaluated at the pin's slew and load

Why: Liberty describes each input-to-output timing arc with delay and slew tables. Parasitics feed the load, and SDC sets clocks and constraints.

<a id="c-sta-graph-unateness"></a>

#### Timing sense and unateness of arcs

`sta.graph.unateness`

A timer does not propagate one arrival time per pin but two, one for a rising and one for a falling transition.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Positive, negative and non-unate arcs
- Following a transition through a chain
- Non-unate arcs propagate both edges

Sample problem:

> A falling transition enters a chain of gates in this order: buffer. It passes through one input of each gate, and side inputs may hold any value. Which output transitions must the timer propagate at the end of the chain?
>
> A) No transition, because the side inputs block it
>
> B) A falling transition only
>
> C) Both a rising and a falling transition
>
> D) A rising transition only

Answer: A falling transition only

Why: Positive-unate arcs keep the direction, negative-unate arcs flip it, and a non-unate arc such as XOR can produce either, after which both directions travel on. The result is: a falling transition only.

<a id="c-sta-graph-levelization"></a>

#### Levelizing the timing graph

`sta.graph.levelization`

Before a timer propagates anything it levelizes the graph: it assigns every node a level so that each arc goes from a lower level to a higher one.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The level of a node
- Depth is the longest path in arcs
- Levels as batches of independent work

Sample problem:

> A timing graph has the arcs L→B, N→B, Q→N, T→F, T→M, N→M, Q→L. Sources are at level 0, and every other node is at one plus the largest level among its fanins. What is the level of node B?

Answer: 2

Why: Sources sit at level 0 and every other node at one more than its deepest fanin. Levels: T = 0, Q = 0, F = 1, L = 1, N = 1, B = 2, M = 2.

<a id="c-sta-graph-arrival-time"></a>

#### Forward propagation of arrival times

`sta.graph.arrival_time`

The arrival time at a pin is when the signal there settles, measured from the launching clock edge.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The max-plus recurrence
- Propagating to the endpoints
- Early arrivals for hold

Sample problem:

> A timing graph has the arcs Q→M (9 ps), U→A (10 ps), A→M (8 ps), Q→U (16 ps). Signals leave the sources Q at 20 ps. What is the latest arrival time at node M, in ps?

Answer: 54

Why: Visit nodes in topological order and take the max over fanins of arrival plus arc delay. Arrivals: Q = 20, U = 36, A = 46, M = 54. At M the latest arrival is 54 ps.

<a id="c-sta-graph-arrival-required"></a>

#### Arrival and required times

`sta.graph.arrival_required`

Arrival times say when data settles; required times say when it must settle. A timer computes the first forward from the startpoints and the second backward from the endpoints, and their difference is slack.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Required time at an endpoint
- Backward propagation with a minimum
- Why the minimum governs

Sample problem:

> A capture flip-flop is clocked with period 700 ps. Its clock pin sees the capturing edge 5 ps late (clock latency), and its setup time is 44 ps. Data launches from a flop on the edge at 0 ps with ideal latency. What is the required time at the capture flop's D pin, in ps?

Answer: 661

Why: Required time is the capturing edge plus its latency minus setup: 700 + 5 - 44 = 661 ps.

<a id="c-sta-graph-slack-meaning"></a>

#### What slack measures

`sta.graph.slack_meaning`

Static timing analysis reduces a chip's timing to one signed number per endpoint: slack.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Required minus arrival
- The sign of slack
- Hold slack runs the other way

Sample problem:

> A path launches on a clock edge at 0 ps. The capture edge is at 800 ps, setup time is 30 ps and data arrives at 790 ps. What is the setup slack?
>
> A) -20 ps
>
> B) -50 ps
>
> C) 10 ps
>
> D) 20 ps

Answer: -20 ps

Why: Required time is 800 - 30 = 770 ps. Slack is required minus arrival: 770 - 790 = -20 ps.

<a id="c-sta-graph-node-slack"></a>

#### Node slack and the critical path

`sta.graph.node_slack`

Slack is defined at every pin, not only at endpoints. Once arrivals and required times are known everywhere, the slack of a pin is the slack of the worst path through it.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Slack at an endpoint
- Slack at an internal node
- The critical path shares one slack

Sample problem:

> A timing graph has the arcs D→S (22 ps), R→W (26 ps), E→R (36 ps), R→D (13 ps), G→S (12 ps). Sources launch E at 10 ps, G at 10 ps. Endpoint required times are W at 82 ps, S at 56 ps. What is the slack at endpoint S, in ps?

Answer: -25

Why: Arrivals (forward max): E = 10, G = 10, R = 46, D = 59, W = 72, S = 81. Required times (backward min): E = -15, G = 44, R = 21, D = 34, W = 82, S = 56. Slack is required minus arrival: E = -25, G = 34, R = -25, D = -25, W = 10, S = -25.

<a id="c-sta-graph-wns-tns"></a>

#### Worst and total negative slack

`sta.graph.wns_tns`

A chip has millions of endpoints, each with a slack. Two summary numbers reduce them to something a team can track from run to run: worst negative slack and total negative slack.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Worst negative slack
- Total negative slack
- How a fix changes TNS

Sample problem:

> The setup slacks of a design's endpoints, in ps, are E1: -12, E2: 44, E3: -6, E4: 34, E5: -31, E6: -5, E7: -2. What is the worst negative slack (WNS), in ps?

Answer: -31

Why: WNS is the most negative endpoint slack, -31 ps.

<a id="static-timing-analysis-delay-calculation"></a>

### Delay calculation

<a id="c-sta-delay-elmore"></a>

#### Elmore delay of an RC tree

`sta.delay.elmore`

A routed net is not a wire with one delay. It is a tree: one driver, a trunk, branches and several sinks, each piece carrying resistance along its length and capacitance to ground.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The first moment of the impulse response
- Shared resistance times downstream capacitance
- Computing it in one tree traversal

Sample problem:

> An RC chain runs from the driver through $R_1 = 250\ \Omega$ then $C_1 = 35$ fF, $R_2 = 250\ \Omega$ then $C_2 = 25$ fF, $R_3 = 250\ \Omega$ then $C_3 = 15$ fF, each capacitor to ground. What is the Elmore delay at the far end, node 3, in picoseconds?

Answer: 32.5

Why: Each capacitor sees all the resistance between it and the driver. Summing shared resistance times capacitance gives 32500 ohm-femtofarads, which is 32.5 ps.

<a id="c-sta-delay-wire-rc"></a>

#### Delay of a distributed RC wire

`sta.delay.wire_rc`

A wire is not a lumped resistor and capacitor: its resistance and capacitance are spread along its length.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The distributed line halves the lumped delay
- Driver, wire and load together
- Quadratic growth and repeaters

Sample problem:

> A wire of length 350 um has resistance 1 ohm/um and capacitance 0.2 fF/um, distributed uniformly. Ignoring the driver and any load, what is its Elmore delay from one end to the other, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 12.25

Why: A distributed line has Elmore delay $rcL^2/2$, half the lumped value: 1 x 0.2 x 350^2 / 2 = 12250 ohm-fF, which is 12.25 ps.

<a id="c-sta-delay-nldm-interpolation"></a>

#### Interpolating NLDM tables

`sta.delay.nldm_interpolation`

Liberty's non-linear delay model stores each timing arc as small tables of delay and output slew, indexed by the input slew and the output load.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Linear interpolation along one axis
- Bilinear interpolation in a window
- Extrapolation beyond the table

Sample problem:

> A Liberty cell_rise table is indexed by input slew (index_1) and output load (index_2). Its window around the query holds: at slew 20 ps, load 4 fF the delay is 39 ps; at slew 20 ps, load 8 fF it is 60 ps; at slew 40 ps, load 4 fF it is 48 ps; at slew 40 ps, load 8 fF it is 71 ps. Using bilinear interpolation (extrapolating linearly from this window if the point lies outside it), what delay does the timer compute at slew 20 ps and load 5 fF? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 44.25

Why: The fractional positions are $t_s = 0$ along slew and $t_c = 0.25$ along load. Interpolate along load at each slew, then along slew: the result is 44.25 ps.

<a id="c-sta-delay-stage-delay"></a>

#### Stage delay: cell arc plus net arc

`sta.delay.stage_delay`

A timing path alternates cell arcs and net arcs. A stage is one driving cell plus the net it drives up to a sink pin, and its delay is what a delay calculator computes in one call.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Cell delay from drive resistance and load
- Adding the net arc
- Summing stages into a path arrival

Sample problem:

> Model each cell delay as intrinsic delay plus drive resistance times its total load (wire plus pin), and each wire as a pi model whose Elmore delay is wire resistance times (half the wire capacitance plus the pin capacitance). One kohm times one fF is one ps. Stage 1: the cell has intrinsic delay 7 ps and drive resistance 0.5 kohm; its output wire has capacitance 2 fF and resistance 0.2 kohm; the sink pin it drives has capacitance 3 fF. What is the cell delay of stage 1, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 9.5

Why: Cell delay = 7 + 0.5 x (2 + 3) = 9.5 ps.

<a id="c-sta-delay-slew-propagation"></a>

#### Slew propagation: worst slew versus path slew

`sta.delay.slew_propagation`

Delay depends on input slew, so every stage's output slew must be carried to the next stage.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Worst-slew merging at a pin
- Downstream arrival under graph-based analysis
- Path-based re-timing removes the pessimism

Sample problem:

> Gate G has inputs A and B. Input A arrives at 60 ps with slew 150 ps; input B arrives at 160 ps with slew 150 ps. The arc from input X has delay $a_X + 0.4 s_X$ and output slew $b_X + 0.6 s_X$, where $s_X$ is the input slew, with $a_A = 28$, $a_B = 17$, $b_A = 28$, $b_B = 25$ (all ps). G drives gate H, whose arc delay is $22 + 0.3 s$ for input slew s. A graph-based timer keeps one slew per pin, the worst over all arcs into it. What slew does it store at G's output, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 118

Why: The arc from A gives output slew 118 ps and the arc from B gives 115 ps. Worst-slew merging keeps the larger, 118 ps, even though it may not belong to the latest-arriving input.

<a id="c-sta-delay-effective-capacitance"></a>

#### Effective capacitance of a resistive load

`sta.delay.effective_capacitance`

Liberty tables assume a cell drives a pure capacitor. A real routed net has resistance between the driver and the far capacitance, which shields part of it: during the fast output transition the driver does not see the full load.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Resistive shielding
- Charge matching over a ramp
- Iterating with the cell table

Sample problem:

> A driver sees a pi load: 11 fF at its pin, then 850 ohm of wire resistance, then 42 fF at the far end. The resistance shields the far capacitance with time constant $\tau = R C_2$. What is $\tau$, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 35.7

Why: 850 ohm x 42 fF = 35700 ohm-fF, which is 35.7 ps. A ramp much shorter than this sees mostly the near capacitance.

<a id="static-timing-analysis-timing-checks"></a>

### Timing checks

<a id="c-sta-check-setup-hold"></a>

#### Setup and hold checks

`sta.check.setup_hold`

Every flop-to-flop path is checked twice. The setup check asks whether the slowest data reaches the capture flop before the next capturing edge; the hold check asks whether the fastest data stays away long enough not to corrupt the value being captured on the current edge.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The setup required time
- Setup slack
- Hold slack

Sample problem:

> A flop-to-flop path is clocked with period 850 ps. The launch flop's clock arrives at 145 ps and the capture flop's clock at 75 ps after the source edge. Clock-to-Q is 74 ps, the longest combinational delay is 740 ps and the shortest is 113 ps. The capture flop's setup time is 55 ps and its hold time is 50 ps. What is the setup required time at the capture flop's D pin, in ps?

Answer: 870

Why: The next capturing edge reaches the capture flop at 850 + 75 ps; setup must be met 55 ps before it: 870 ps.

<a id="c-sta-check-max-frequency"></a>

#### Minimum clock period of a register path

`sta.check.max_frequency`

The setup check can be turned around: instead of asking whether a path meets a given period, ask for the smallest period it meets.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The smallest period one path meets
- The design's minimum period
- Converting to frequency

Sample problem:

> In a register-to-register path, path 1 has clock-to-Q 72 ps, logic delay 440 ps, setup 58 ps and skew +30 ps. Skew is the capture clock arrival minus the launch clock arrival. What is the smallest clock period this path meets, in ps?

Answer: 540

Why: Setup holds when $T \ge t_{cq} + d + t_{su} - skew$ = 72 + 440 + 58 - (+30) = 540 ps.

<a id="c-sta-check-half-cycle"></a>

#### Half-cycle paths between opposite edges

`sta.check.half_cycle`

Not every path runs between rising edges. A path from a rising-edge flop to a falling-edge flop, or the reverse, has only part of a cycle for setup, and an unusually easy hold check.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Time between launch and capture edges
- Setup slack of a half-cycle path
- Hold is easy for half-cycle paths

Sample problem:

> A clock has period 700 ps and is high for the first 315 ps of each cycle (rising at 0). A path launches on the rising edge at 0 ps and is captured by a falling-edge flop. Clock-to-Q is 38 ps, the longest logic delay 100 ps and the shortest 76 ps; setup is 47 ps and hold 22 ps. Clocks are ideal. How much time separates the launch edge from the setup capture edge, in ps?

Answer: 315

Why: The setup capture edge is the first opposite edge after launch, 315 ps later.

<a id="c-sta-check-recovery-removal"></a>

#### Recovery and removal checks

`sta.check.recovery_removal`

Asynchronous set and reset pins act immediately, without the clock, but releasing them is not instantaneous in effect: if a reset deasserts too close to a clock edge, the flop may not leave reset cleanly on that edge, and different flops may leave reset on different cycles.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The recovery required time
- Recovery slack
- Removal slack

Sample problem:

> A reset synchronizer flop, clocked at period 1150 ps with clock arrival 140 ps, drives the asynchronous reset pin of a capture flop whose clock arrives at 130 ps. The synchronizer's clock-to-Q is 48 ps, and the reset net delay is at most 720 ps and at least 147 ps. The capture flop's recovery time is 36 ps and its removal time is 39 ps. What is the required time for the reset deassertion at the capture flop (the recovery check), in ps?

Answer: 1244

Why: Recovery is setup for the deasserting edge: 1150 + 130 - 36 = 1244 ps.

<a id="c-sta-check-latch-borrowing"></a>

#### Latches and time borrowing

`sta.check.latch_borrowing`

A level-sensitive latch is transparent while its clock is active, so data may arrive after the latch opens and still pass through.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Borrowing past the opening edge
- The maximum borrow
- Charging the next stage

Sample problem:

> A rising-edge flop launches data at 0 ps into a positive level-sensitive latch. The clock has period 700 ps with a 50% duty cycle, so the latch opens at 700 ps and closes at 1050 ps; the latch setup time before closing is 43 ps. Data arrives at the latch D pin at 880 ps. How much time does the path borrow from the next stage, in ps?

Answer: 180

Why: Borrowing is the time past the opening edge: max(0, 880 - 700) = 180 ps.

<a id="c-sta-check-check-types"></a>

#### Choosing the right timing check

`sta.check.check_types`

A timer applies different checks at different pins: setup and hold at flop data pins, recovery and removal at asynchronous controls, clock-gating checks at gates that combine a clock with an enable, minimum pulse width at clock pins, and data-to-data checks where two signals must stay aligned.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Data and asynchronous checks
- Clock-pin and gating checks
- Matching checks to failures

Sample problem:

> A reset signal deasserts close to a clock edge at a flop's asynchronous clear pin. Which check makes sure the flop leaves reset cleanly on that edge?
>
> A) Minimum pulse width on the clear pin only
>
> B) Setup on the D pin
>
> C) No check: asynchronous pins are untimed
>
> D) Recovery, with removal as its hold-like partner

Answer: Recovery, with removal as its hold-like partner

Why: Deassertion of an asynchronous control is timed against the clock: recovery is the setup-like check and removal the hold-like one.

<a id="static-timing-analysis-clocks"></a>

### Clocks

<a id="c-sta-clock-waveform"></a>

#### Clock waveforms and create_clock

`sta.clock.waveform`

Every check in a timer is measured against clock edges, and those edges come from the clock definitions in SDC.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Period and duty cycle
- Edges in later cycles
- Finding the next edge after a time

Sample problem:

> The SDC command `create_clock -name clk -period 16 -waveform {4 8} [get_ports clk]` defines a clock in ns. What is its duty cycle, in percent? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 25

Why: The clock is high from 4 to 8 ns, 4 ns of every 16 ns: 25%.

<a id="c-sta-clock-latency"></a>

#### Clock source and network latency

`sta.clock.latency`

A clock edge does not reach every flop at the same time. It first travels from its true origin, an oscillator or PLL, to the point where the clock is defined, and then through the on-chip clock tree to each sink.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Clock arrival at a sink
- Skew between two sinks
- Propagated clocks in the setup check

Sample problem:

> A clock has source latency 120 ps. Its tree first passes through shared buffers with delays 49 ps. One branch then passes buffers of 21 ps to the launch flop FF1; the other passes buffers of 56, 23, 38 ps to the capture flop FF2. With propagated clocks, when does the clock edge launched at 0 ps reach FF1, in ps?

Answer: 190

Why: Clock arrival is source latency plus network latency, the sum of buffer delays along the path to FF1: 190 ps.

<a id="c-sta-clock-skew-jitter"></a>

#### Clock skew and jitter

`sta.clock.skew_jitter`

Two effects move clock edges away from their ideal times: skew, a fixed spatial difference in arrival between two flops, and jitter, a random temporal variation of the edges themselves.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Signed skew
- Setup slack with skew and jitter
- Hold slack with skew

Sample problem:

> A flop-to-flop path is clocked with period 700 ps. The launch flop's clock arrives at 65 ps and the capture flop's clock at 105 ps after the source edge. Clock-to-Q is 51 ps, the longest combinational delay is 750 ps and the shortest is 24 ps. The capture flop's setup time is 52 ps and its hold time is 44 ps. What is the clock skew of this path (capture arrival minus launch arrival), in ps?

Answer: 40

Why: Skew = 105 - 65 = 40 ps. Positive skew gives setup more time and hold less.

<a id="c-sta-clock-uncertainty"></a>

#### Clock uncertainty in setup and hold

`sta.clock.uncertainty`

set_clock_uncertainty is the SDC knob that reserves margin on clock edges. Setup uncertainty makes the capturing edge effectively earlier; hold uncertainty makes the hold requirement larger.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Building a pre-CTS uncertainty
- Setup slack with uncertainty
- Hold slack with uncertainty

Sample problem:

> Before clock tree synthesis, a team budgets setup uncertainty as jitter plus an estimate of the skew the tree will add plus a design margin. The jitter is 29 ps, the skew estimate 65 ps and the margin 20 ps. What value should set_clock_uncertainty -setup carry, in ps?

Answer: 114

Why: The terms add: 29 + 65 + 20 = 114 ps. After CTS, propagated clocks model the real skew, so the skew term is removed.

<a id="c-sta-clock-generated-clocks"></a>

#### Generated clocks

`sta.clock.generated_clocks`

Many clocks on a chip are derived from others: divided by a counter, multiplied by a PLL, or shaped by selecting particular master edges.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Dividing a master clock
- Building a waveform from master edges
- Latency through the generating logic

Sample problem:

> A master clock has period 14 ns. A divider output is declared with create_generated_clock -source [get_ports clk] -divide_by 2. What is the generated clock's period, in ns?

Answer: 28

Why: Dividing by 2 multiplies the period: 2 x 14 = 28 ns.

<a id="c-sta-clock-launch-capture-edges"></a>

#### Setup and hold relationships between clocks

`sta.clock.launch_capture_edges`

When launch and capture flops are clocked by different but synchronous clocks, there is no single period to plug into the setup check.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Integer-multiple periods
- General periods over the common period
- Deriving the hold relationship

Sample problem:

> Data launches from a rising-edge flop on clock CLKA (period 12 ns) and is captured by a rising-edge flop on clock CLKB (period 6 ns). Both clocks come from one source and rise together at 0 ns. Over all launch edges, the setup check uses the nearest later capture edge. What is the most restrictive setup relationship (capture time minus launch time), in ns?

Answer: 6

Why: The edge pattern repeats every lcm(12, 6) = 12 ns. For each CLKA edge in that window, find the first CLKB edge strictly later; the smallest gap is 6 ns.

<a id="c-sta-clock-cppr"></a>

#### Clock reconvergence pessimism removal

`sta.clock.cppr`

Under on-chip variation, a timer takes the launch clock path late and the capture clock path early for setup.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The common point and its arrivals
- The pessimism credit
- Slack after CPPR

Sample problem:

> A clock tree is analyzed with early/late (min/max) delays per buffer, written early/late in ps. The common segment from the clock root to the branch point has buffers 29/40, 26/31, 46/50. The launch branch adds 53/57 to FF1, and the capture branch adds 26/38 to FF2. What is the late arrival of the clock at the branch point (the common point), in ps?

Answer: 121

Why: Sum the late delays of the common buffers: 121 ps.

<a id="static-timing-analysis-constraints"></a>

### Constraints

<a id="c-sta-constraint-sdc"></a>

#### SDC timing constraints

`sta.constraint.sdc`

A timer knows nothing about intent until it reads constraints. The SDC format is a set of Tcl commands that define clocks, the environment at the block boundary, and the exceptions to single-cycle timing.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Defining clocks
- Constraining the block boundary
- Object queries and units

Sample problem:

> Which SDC command defines a clock with a period and waveform on a port?
>
> A) set_input_delay
>
> B) set_clock_latency
>
> C) create_generated_clock
>
> D) create_clock

Answer: create_clock

Why: create_clock names a clock source, its period and its edge times. Generated clocks are derived from a master with create_generated_clock.

<a id="c-sta-constraint-io-delay"></a>

#### Input and output delays

`sta.constraint.io_delay`

A block is timed in isolation, but its ports connect to logic outside it. Input and output delays describe that outside logic as time budgets relative to a clock, so paths that enter or leave the block get proper setup checks.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Input paths
- Output paths
- Budgeting a feedthrough

Sample problem:

> create_clock -period 700 sets the clock in ps, and clocks are ideal. Input port din has set_input_delay 280 -clock clk. From din, logic of 240 ps reaches a flop with setup 56 ps. What is the setup slack of this input path, in ps?

Answer: 124

Why: The input delay models the external launch: data reaches din at 280 ps. Slack = 700 - 56 - (280 + 240) = 124 ps.

<a id="c-sta-constraint-exceptions"></a>

#### False and multicycle paths

`sta.constraint.exceptions`

By default a timer assumes every path launched on one edge must be captured on the next.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- False paths and clock groups
- Multicycle paths and absolute delays
- Exceptions as claims

Sample problem:

> A mux selects either clkA or clkB onto one clock net, never both at once. Which constraint fits?
>
> A) set_false_path from clkA to clkA
>
> B) set_clock_groups -asynchronous
>
> C) A single clock with the faster period
>
> D) set_clock_groups -logically_exclusive between clkA and clkB

Answer: set_clock_groups -logically_exclusive between clkA and clkB

Why: Exclusive clocks cannot coexist, so paths between them are not real. Asynchronous would also stop timing but misdescribes the design and changes crosstalk analysis.

<a id="c-sta-constraint-multicycle-edges"></a>

#### Multicycle paths and the hold adjustment

`sta.constraint.multicycle_edges`

A multicycle path gives data more than one cycle to settle. The setup half of the exception is intuitive; the hold half is where mistakes happen, because moving the setup check also moves the default hold check.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Moving the setup edge
- The default hold check moves too
- Pulling the hold check back

Sample problem:

> A path between two flops on clock clk (period 700 ps, ideal) has clock-to-Q 59 ps, longest logic delay 1040 ps and shortest 117 ps; setup is 35 ps and hold 34 ps. The SDC has set_multicycle_path 2 -setup -from [get_cells FF1] -to [get_cells FF2]. What is the setup slack, in ps?

Answer: 266

Why: Setup now captures at edge 2, at 1400 ps. Slack = 1400 - 35 - (59 + 1040) = 266 ps.

<a id="static-timing-analysis-path-analysis"></a>

### Path analysis

<a id="c-sta-path-path-count"></a>

#### Counting paths in a timing graph

`sta.path.path_count`

Why can a timer not simply list every path and time each one? Because the number of paths grows exponentially with depth while the graph grows only linearly.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Counting with one forward pass
- Paths through a node
- Exponential growth with reconvergence

Sample problem:

> A timing graph has the arcs Q→L, G→J, G→B, U→A, J→B, G→A, L→U, A→E, J→L. How many distinct paths run from the sources to node E?

Answer: 3

Why: Count in topological order: a source has one path and every other node sums its fanins. Counts: G = 1, Q = 1, J = 1, L = 2, U = 2, B = 2, A = 3, E = 3.

<a id="c-sta-path-k-worst"></a>

#### Enumerating the k worst paths

`sta.path.k_worst`

Block-based propagation gives each endpoint its worst arrival, but reports, path-based re-timing and optimizers need actual paths, and often more than one per endpoint.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The worst path to an endpoint
- The second-worst path
- Priority-queue enumeration and reporting

Sample problem:

> A timing graph with a single source R has the arcs R→A (12 ps), R→E (26 ps), D→H (27 ps), A→E (32 ps), B→H (31 ps), R→B (29 ps), E→T (26 ps), T→D (10 ps). What is the delay of the worst (longest) path from R to H, in ps?

Answer: 107

Why: The path delays into H, from worst down, are 107, 89, 60.

<a id="c-sta-path-gba-vs-pba"></a>

#### Graph-based versus path-based analysis

`sta.path.gba_vs_pba`

A timer can analyze in two modes. Graph-based analysis keeps one worst value per pin and times the whole design in one pass.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What graph-based analysis merges
- What path-based analysis recovers
- Using both in a flow

Sample problem:

> A design has billions of paths but only a few million pins. Which analysis can time the whole design in one linear pass?
>
> A) Path-based analysis of every path
>
> B) Graph-based analysis
>
> C) Exhaustive path enumeration with exact slews
>
> D) Monte Carlo SPICE of every path

Answer: Graph-based analysis

Why: GBA keeps one value per pin and transition, so its work grows with the graph, not with the exponential number of paths.

<a id="c-sta-path-path-report"></a>

#### Reading a timing path report

`sta.path.path_report`

A path report is the timer's explanation of one slack. It lists the launch clock, every cell and net increment along the data path, and then the capture clock with its adjustments.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Data arrival time
- Data required time
- Slack and what to read next

Sample problem:

> A setup path report lists these increments in ps:
>
> clock clk (rise edge) 0
> clock network delay (propagated) 125
> FF1/CK -> FF1/Q (DFF_X1) 43
> U1 (BUF_X4) 12 + 75 (net + cell)
> U2 (XOR2_X1) 22 + 40 (net + cell)
> U3 (INV_X2) 17 + 37 (net + cell)
> U4 (BUF_X4) 3 + 64 (net + cell)
> FF2/D net 22
> ---
> clock clk (rise edge) 1050
> clock network delay (propagated) 190
> clock reconvergence pessimism 19
> clock uncertainty -20
> library setup time -45
>
> What is the data arrival time at FF2/D, in ps?

Answer: 460

Why: Add the launch clock network delay, clock-to-Q and every net and cell increment: 460 ps.

<a id="static-timing-analysis-variation-aware-timing"></a>

### Variation-aware timing

<a id="c-sta-var-corners"></a>

#### PVT corners

`sta.var.corners`

A chip must work across manufacturing variation, supply voltage and temperature.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Slack at one corner
- The worst setup corner
- The worst hold corner

Sample problem:

> A flop-to-flop path with ideal clocks at period 1100 ps is characterized at several PVT corners (path delays include clock-to-Q): ff_0p88v_m40c: max path 392 ps, min path 41 ps, setup 22 ps, hold 15 ps; ss_0p72v_m40c: max path 694 ps, min path 73 ps, setup 39 ps, hold 26 ps; ss_0p72v_125c: max path 706 ps, min path 75 ps, setup 40 ps, hold 27 ps. What is the setup slack at corner ff_0p88v_m40c, in ps?

Answer: 686

Why: Per corner, setup slack = T - setup - max path and hold slack = min path - hold: ff_0p88v_m40c setup 686, hold 26; ss_0p72v_m40c setup 367, hold 47; ss_0p72v_125c setup 354, hold 48 (ps).

<a id="c-sta-var-mcmm"></a>

#### Multi-corner multi-mode analysis

`sta.var.mcmm`

A chip has several modes, functional, test, low-power, each with its own clocks and constraints, and must work at several PVT and extraction corners.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Counting scenarios
- Merging an endpoint's slack
- Merged TNS

Sample problem:

> A chip has 3 functional and test modes and is signed off at 5 PVT and extraction corners. 0 mode-corner pairs are pruned because they can never dominate. How many scenarios does the MCMM run analyze?

Answer: 15

Why: Scenarios are mode-corner pairs: 3 x 5 - 0 = 15.

<a id="c-sta-var-ocv-derate"></a>

#### On-chip variation derates

`sta.var.ocv_derate`

Corners model chip-to-chip variation: a whole die is slow or fast. Within one die, delays still vary from cell to cell, because of local process variation, voltage drop and temperature gradients.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Derating the launch side
- Derated setup slack
- Removing pessimism on the common clock path

Sample problem:

> A setup check uses a late derate of 1.09 on the launch clock path and data path and an early derate of 0.97 on the capture clock path. The launch clock path is 300 ps, the data path (including clock-to-Q) 500 ps, the capture clock path 210 ps, the period 850 ps and setup 36 ps (setup is not derated). What is the derated data arrival time at the capture flop, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 872

Why: (300 + 500) x 1.09 = 872 ps.

<a id="c-sta-var-aocv"></a>

#### Advanced OCV derates by depth and distance

`sta.var.aocv`

Flat OCV applies the same derate to a one-cell path and a forty-cell path. But random variation partly cancels along a path: the relative spread of a sum of $N$ independent delays shrinks like $1/\sqrt{N}$.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Looking up the derate by depth
- Interpolating between depths
- Depth and distance together

Sample problem:

> An AOCV late-derate table by logic depth reads depth 1: 1.15, depth 2: 1.13, depth 4: 1.12, depth 8: 1.11, depth 16: 1.1. A data path of depth 4 has a non-derated delay of 330 ps. What is its derated delay, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 369.6

Why: Depth 4 is on the table axis, so the derate is 1.12: 330 x 1.12 = 369.6 ps.

<a id="c-sta-var-pocv"></a>

#### Parametric OCV and LVF sigma accumulation

`sta.var.pocv`

Parametric OCV models each arc's delay not as a number scaled by a derate but as a distribution with a mean and a sigma.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Path sigma from independent arcs
- The n-sigma arrival
- Why per-arc margins are pessimistic

Sample problem:

> A data path has 3 arcs. Their LVF (mean, sigma) delays in ps are (43, 5), (61, 8), (31, 8), and their random variations are independent. What is the sigma of the path delay, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 12.37

Why: Independent variances add: $\sigma = \sqrt{153}$ = 12.37 ps.

<a id="c-sta-var-ssta"></a>

#### Statistical static timing analysis

`sta.var.ssta`

POCV treats each path's random variation statistically but keeps corners for correlated variation.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The canonical form and its sigma
- Adding canonical forms
- Correlation through shared sources

Sample problem:

> In first-order canonical form, $X_1$ and $X_2$ are shared global variation sources and each R is a private random term; all are independent standard normals, and coefficients are in ps. An arrival time is $A = 250 + 9 X_1 + 10 X_2 + 1 R$. What is its standard deviation, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 13.49

Why: $\sigma_A = \sqrt{9^2 + 10^2 + 1^2}$ = 13.49 ps.

<a id="c-sta-var-clark-max"></a>

#### Clark's max of two Gaussian arrivals

`sta.var.clark_max`

Sums keep canonical forms Gaussian; maxima do not. At every merge pin a statistical timer must take the max of two random arrivals and approximate the result again by a Gaussian in canonical form.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The spread of the difference
- The tightness probability
- The mean of the max

Sample problem:

> Two arrival times converge at a gate: A has mean 450 ps and sigma 7 ps, B has mean 480 ps and sigma 20 ps, and their correlation is 0.2. Clark's method uses $\theta = \sqrt{\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2 - 2\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B}$ and $\alpha = (\mu_A - \mu_B)/\theta$. What is $\theta$, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 19.82

Why: $\theta^2$ = 49 + 400 - 2 x 0.2 x 7 x 20 = 393, so $\theta$ = 19.82 ps.

<a id="c-sta-var-timing-yield"></a>

#### Timing yield from a Gaussian delay

`sta.var.timing_yield`

Statistical timing changes the question from whether a path passes to how many dies pass.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The z-score of a period
- Yield at a given period
- The period for a target yield

Sample problem:

> SSTA gives a circuit delay with mean 850 ps and sigma 16 ps. The clock period is 861 ps. What is the z-score of the period? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 0.69

Why: z = (861 - 850) / 16 = 0.69.

<a id="static-timing-analysis-incremental-timing"></a>

### Incremental timing

<a id="c-sta-incremental-update"></a>

#### Incremental timing analysis

`sta.incremental.update`

An optimizer changes a design thousands of times, resizing a cell, inserting a buffer, moving an instance, and after each change it needs new slacks.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Arrivals change in the forward cone
- Required times change in the backward cone
- Slack changes in the union, lazily

Sample problem:

> A timing graph has the arcs N→J, W→L, W→U, W→R, U→N, T→R, R→L, J→G. An ECO resizes a cell, and only the delay of arc N→J changes. How many nodes can have a changed arrival time (count every node whose arrival must be re-evaluated)?

Answer: 2

Why: Arrivals flow forward, so only J and its fanout cone can change: J, G (2 in all).

<a id="c-sta-incremental-early-termination"></a>

#### Early termination in incremental propagation

`sta.incremental.early_termination`

The fanout cone of a change is an upper bound on what must be recomputed, not the actual amount.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The new arrival at the changed node
- Counting the nodes that actually change
- Arrivals at downstream endpoints

Sample problem:

> A timing graph has the arcs N→W (28 ps), E→W (25 ps), E→B (40 ps), N→A (16 ps), F→E (35 ps), H→N (6 ps), and sources launch H at 0 ps, F at 0 ps. An ECO changes the delay of arc H→N from 6 ps to 11 ps. What is the new arrival time at N, in ps?

Answer: 11

Why: Arrivals before: H = 0, F = 0, N = 6, A = 22, E = 35, W = 60, B = 75. After: H = 0, F = 0, N = 11, A = 27, E = 35, W = 60, B = 75. Propagation stops wherever a node's new arrival equals its old one, because a max that did not change hides the edit from everything downstream.

<a id="static-timing-analysis-timing-closure"></a>

### Timing closure

<a id="c-sta-closure-timing-closure"></a>

#### Timing closure

`sta.closure.timing_closure`

Timing closure is the iterative process of bringing a design from its first timing estimate to a netlist and layout that pass signoff in every scenario.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Reading the shape of the problem
- Choosing the fix
- Late-stage closure

Sample problem:

> Why do teams carry extra margin, such as a tighter clock, in early implementation stages?
>
> A) To make the tools run faster
>
> B) Because Liberty data is less accurate at signoff
>
> C) Later stages add delay the early models cannot see, so early slack must cover it
>
> D) To create hold violations deliberately

Answer: Later stages add delay the early models cannot see, so early slack must cover it

Why: Each stage's estimate is optimistic relative to the next. Over-constraining early leaves room for routing, crosstalk and variation effects.

<a id="c-sta-closure-gate-sizing-eco"></a>

#### Gate sizing in a timing ECO

`sta.closure.gate_sizing_eco`

Upsizing a gate on a failing path is the most common timing fix, and the one most often over-estimated.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The resized gate gets faster
- The driver gets slower
- The net change in slack

Sample problem:

> On a failing path, driver D (drive resistance 1 kohm) drives only gate G's input (3 fF). G has intrinsic delay 15 ps and drive resistance 4 kohm and drives a load of 36 fF. Cell delay is intrinsic delay plus drive resistance times load (kohm times fF is ps). The ECO replaces G with a size 2x larger, which divides its drive resistance by 2 and multiplies its input capacitance by 2; the intrinsic delay is unchanged. What is G's new delay, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 87

Why: 15 + 4 / 2 x 36 = 87 ps, down from 159 ps.

<a id="c-sta-closure-hold-fixing"></a>

#### Hold fixing with delay buffers

`sta.closure.hold_fixing`

Hold violations are fixed by adding delay to the short paths, usually by inserting delay buffers.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Buffers needed at the fast corner
- Setup cost at the slow corner
- The feasibility bound

Sample problem:

> A path fails hold by 58 ps at the fast corner (hold slack -58 ps) and has 108 ps of setup slack at the slow corner. A delay buffer adds 18 ps at the fast corner and 23 ps at the slow corner. What is the fewest buffers that fixes the hold violation?

Answer: 4

Why: Each buffer adds 18 ps at the fast corner: ceil(58 / 18) = 4.

<a id="c-sta-closure-useful-skew"></a>

#### Useful skew

`sta.closure.useful_skew`

Zero skew is not the goal of a clock tree; meeting timing is. Deliberately delaying or advancing the clock of a flop moves time between the stages before and after it.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Shifting slack between two stages
- The balancing shift
- The hold limit

Sample problem:

> In a pipeline FF1 → FF2 → FF3, the stage into FF2 has setup slack -40 ps and the stage out of FF2 has setup slack 112 ps. Delaying FF2's clock by $\delta$ gives the first stage $\delta$ more and the second stage $\delta$ less. With $\delta$ = 35 ps, what is the worse of the two setup slacks, in ps?

Answer: -5

Why: Stage 1: -40 + 35 = -5 ps. Stage 2: 112 - 35 = 77 ps. The worse is -5 ps.

<a id="c-sta-closure-opensta-flow"></a>

#### The OpenSTA flow: inputs and reports

`sta.closure.opensta_flow`

OpenSTA is the open-source static timer used inside OpenROAD and in many research flows.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The four inputs
- Running the analysis and reading results
- A timer embedded in a flow

Sample problem:

> Which OpenSTA command loads the cell timing models that give arcs their delays?
>
> A) read_spef
>
> B) read_sdc
>
> C) read_liberty
>
> D) read_verilog

Answer: read_liberty

Why: Liberty files hold the cells' timing arcs, delay and slew tables, pin capacitances and checks.

<a id="static-timing-analysis-frontier-agent-first-futures"></a>

### Frontier: agent-first futures

<a id="c-sta-frontier-derate-provider"></a>

#### The DerateProvider seam

`sta.frontier.derate_provider`

Timing derating is the clearest example of where an agent-first timer needs a seam.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The question the core asks
- Computing with a custom provider
- Keeping the seam fast and safe

Sample problem:

> What does a POCV provider return through the seam, compared with a flat OCV provider?
>
> A) The same factor for every arc
>
> B) A mean and sigma adjustment rather than a single multiplicative factor
>
> C) A list of false paths
>
> D) A required time

Answer: A mean and sigma adjustment rather than a single multiplicative factor

Why: Flat OCV and AOCV scale a delay. POCV works with distributions, so the seam must carry a mean and a sigma that the core combines statistically.

<a id="c-sta-frontier-change-tiers"></a>

#### Change tiers for timing requests

`sta.frontier.change_tiers`

Requests to change a timer arrive constantly: a new sigma count, a different derate scheme, a margin rule from silicon correlation, a reporting change.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Tier 1: configuration
- Tier 2: a plug-in at the seam
- Tier 3: a core edit

Sample problem:

> A customer asks the timer to report the 20 worst paths per endpoint instead of 5. Which tier is this?
>
> A) Tier 3, a change to propagation
>
> B) Tier 2, a new path enumerator plug-in
>
> C) It requires a new SDC command
>
> D) Tier 1, a reporting parameter

Answer: Tier 1, a reporting parameter

Why: Which paths and how many to report is part of the timer's change surface, set by parameters.

<a id="c-sta-frontier-differential-timing"></a>

#### Differential timing reports as golden tests

`sta.frontier.differential_timing`

How do you prove that a change to a timer did what it claimed and nothing else? Not by checking that the worst slack improved, and not by checking that the code compiles.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Which endpoints moved
- Unexpected movers
- Intended endpoints and the promotion rule

Sample problem:

> A new derate provider should lower the slack of the paths ending at E1, E2, E4, E6, E8, E9 by exactly 5 ps and leave every other endpoint unchanged, with a tolerance of 0.5 ps. The differential report lists before → after slacks in ps: E1: 42 → 35, E2: 32 → 27, E3: 72 → 72, E4: -10 → -15, E5: -6 → -8, E6: 31 → 26, E7: 27 → 27, E8: 64 → 59, E9: 72 → 67. How many endpoints moved by more than the tolerance?

Answer: 7

Why: Compare after with before at each endpoint: 7 moved.

<a id="c-sta-frontier-surrogate-timer"></a>

#### Surrogate fast timers in an agent loop

`sta.frontier.surrogate_timer`

An agent exploring placements, sizings or ECOs may evaluate thousands of candidates, too many for a signoff timer.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Uncertain endpoints
- Bounding the true WNS
- Choosing the error bound

Sample problem:

> A fast surrogate timer inside an agent's optimization loop predicts these endpoint setup slacks, in ps: E1: -36.5, E2: -13.5, E3: 32.5, E4: 56.5, E5: -18.5, E6: 50.5, E7: 7.5, E8: 54.5. Validation shows its error never exceeds 12 ps. An endpoint must be re-timed by the accurate timer when its true slack could have either sign. How many endpoints must be re-timed?

Answer: 1

Why: True slack lies within 12 ps of the prediction, so the sign is uncertain when |predicted slack| < 12 ps: 1 endpoints.

<a id="c-sta-frontier-agentic-eco-loop"></a>

#### Agentic timing ECO loops

`sta.frontier.agentic_eco_loop`

An agentic ECO loop reads timing reports, proposes fixes, applies them through the engines, verifies the result and iterates, with a human approving the final change.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What the loop reads and proposes
- What the loop verifies
- Authority, containment and reuse

Sample problem:

> Why must the loop re-time incrementally after each proposed change?
>
> A) To change the clock definitions
>
> B) Each change shifts arrivals and slews in its cone, and the next proposal must see the updated state
>
> C) To recompute the whole netlist from RTL
>
> D) Because reports are cached forever otherwise

Answer: Each change shifts arrivals and slews in its cone, and the next proposal must see the updated state

Why: Incremental timing gives the updated slacks cheaply, so the loop proposes against the real current state.

<a id="c-sta-frontier-slack-reward"></a>

#### Tool-grounded rewards from slack

`sta.frontier.slack_reward`

Training a model to fix timing needs a reward, and a static timer can provide one: deterministic, cheap enough to run per episode, and grounded in the same numbers signoff uses.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- A slack-based reward
- Computing it from endpoint slacks
- Reward hacking and the grounded check

Sample problem:

> An RL environment scores an agent's timing ECO with reward $R = 2 \min(WNS, 0) + 0.01\,TNS - 10\,\Delta A$, where WNS and TNS are in ps and $\Delta A$ is the area increase in percent. The signoff timer reports WNS 3 ps and TNS 0 ps, and area grew 2.4%. What is the reward? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: -24

Why: R = 2 x 0 + 0.01 x 0 - 10 x 2.4 = -24.

---

## Test and Design for Test

Layer 5. Fault models, fault simulation, ATPG, scan and compression, BIST, JTAG, diagnosis and yield learning.

Builds on: Digital Logic Design, Logic Synthesis, Formal Verification, Functional Verification and Simulation, Variability, Yield and Reliability Statistics, Graph Algorithms for EDA.

Topics covered:

- Design for testing, semiconductor testing, manufacturing defects vs faults
- Fault models: stuck-at, transition, path delay, bridging, cell-aware
- Fault simulation (serial, parallel, deductive, concurrent), fault coverage, test coverage, fault collapsing, equivalence and dominance
- ATPG: D-algorithm, PODEM, FAN, SAT-based ATPG, controllability/observability (SCOAP)
- Scan design: scan cells, scan chains, scan insertion, scan chain ordering, launch-on-capture vs launch-on-shift
- Scan compression (EDT-style decompressors and compactors)
- BIST: LFSRs, MISRs, logic BIST, memory BIST (March tests)
- Boundary scan, JTAG, IEEE 1149.1, IEEE 1500, IEEE 1687, STIL
- Automatic test equipment, wafer probing, burn-in, yield analysis, diagnosis, silicon debug, post-silicon validation
- Error correction, redundancy and repair (memory repair)

Subdomains: [Fault models](#test-and-design-for-test-fault-models), [Fault simulation](#test-and-design-for-test-fault-simulation), [Test pattern generation](#test-and-design-for-test-test-pattern-generation), [Scan design](#test-and-design-for-test-scan-design), [Test compression](#test-and-design-for-test-test-compression), [Logic BIST](#test-and-design-for-test-logic-bist), [Memory BIST](#test-and-design-for-test-memory-bist), [Boundary scan (JTAG)](#test-and-design-for-test-boundary-scan-jtag), [Test equipment](#test-and-design-for-test-test-equipment), [Frontier: agent-first futures](#test-and-design-for-test-frontier-agent-first-futures)

<a id="test-and-design-for-test-fault-models"></a>

### Fault models

<a id="c-dft-fault-defects-vs-faults"></a>

#### Defects, faults, errors and failures

`dft.fault.defects_vs_faults`

Manufacturing test exists because fabrication is imperfect: particles, missing vias, shorts and drifted devices make some dies bad.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The causal chain
- Why tools need fault models
- Yield, quality and reliability

Terms: defect, fault, error, failure, defect level.

Sample problem:

> A metal particle shorts two adjacent wires on one die. In test terminology, what is the particle and what is the stuck-at or bridging description?
>
> A) Both are failures
>
> B) The particle is a defect; the logical description is a fault model
>
> C) The particle is a fault; the logical description is a defect
>
> D) The particle is an error; the description is a failure

Answer: The particle is a defect; the logical description is a fault model

Why: A defect is the physical imperfection. A fault is its abstraction at a level the tools can reason about, such as a bridge or a stuck line.

<a id="c-dft-fault-stuck-at"></a>

#### The stuck-at fault model

`dft.fault.stuck_at`

The single stuck-at model is the workhorse of digital test: each line of a gate-level netlist may be permanently fixed at logic 0 or logic 1, one line at a time.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Lines, stems and branches
- Single versus multiple faults
- Activation and the excitation condition

Terms: line, stem, fanout branch, single fault assumption, activate.

Sample problem:

> Inputs a, b, c; g1 = NOR(a, c); g2 = OR(b, g1); g3 = NAND(a, g2); g4 = NOR(c, g3); primary output g4. Treat every fanout branch of a signal that feeds two or more gate inputs as a line of its own. How many single stuck-at faults does the circuit have?

Answer: 22

Why: There are 7 stems (3 inputs and 4 gate outputs) and 4 fanout branches, so 11 lines. Each line can be stuck-at-0 or stuck-at-1: 22 faults.

<a id="c-dft-fault-transition"></a>

#### Transition faults

`dft.fault.transition`

Many real defects do not fix a line at a constant: a resistive via or a weak transistor makes a signal switch too slowly.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Slow-to-rise and slow-to-fall
- Two-pattern tests
- What the model misses

Terms: slow-to-rise, slow-to-fall, initialization, launch.

Sample problem:

> Inputs a, b, c; g1 = NOR(b, c); g2 = NAND(a, g1); g3 = AND(a, g1); primary outputs g2 and g3. Counting every fanout branch as its own line, how many transition faults (slow-to-rise and slow-to-fall) does the transition fault model define?
>
> A) 12
>
> B) 40
>
> C) 10
>
> D) 20

Answer: 20

Why: Each of the 10 lines gets a slow-to-rise and a slow-to-fall fault: 20, the same count as single stuck-at faults.

<a id="c-dft-fault-path-delay"></a>

#### Path delay faults

`dft.fault.path_delay`

A path delay fault says that the cumulative delay along one specific path from an input to an output exceeds the clock period, even if no single gate is grossly slow.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Counting paths
- Exponential growth
- Robust and non-robust tests

Terms: path, selected, robust, non-robust.

Sample problem:

> Inputs a, b, c; g1 = OR(b, c); g2 = NAND(a, c); g3 = OR(g1, g2); g4 = AND(a, g3); g5 = AND(b, g4); primary output g5. A path runs from a primary input through gates to a primary output. Each path carries a rising and a falling path delay fault. How many path delay faults does the circuit have?

Answer: 12

Why: Counting paths by dynamic programming (paths into a gate are the sum over its inputs) gives 6 input-to-output paths, so 12 path delay faults.

<a id="c-dft-fault-bridging"></a>

#### Bridging faults

`dft.fault.bridging`

Shorts between neighbouring wires are among the most common real defects, and they do not behave like a stuck line: the shorted nets fight, and the result depends on their values and on the drivers' strengths.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Wired and dominant models
- Excitation and candidate counts
- Detection in practice

Terms: wired-AND, wired-OR, dominant, non-feedback, opposite.

Sample problem:

> A block has 21 nets and no layout data, so every unordered pair of distinct nets is a candidate bridge, each modeled as a wired-AND and as a wired-OR. How many bridging faults is that?

Answer: 420

Why: $\binom{21}{2} = 210$ pairs times 2 models is 420. Real flows extract only physically adjacent pairs from the layout, which cuts this quadratic count to roughly linear.

<a id="c-dft-fault-cell-aware"></a>

#### Cell-aware fault models

`dft.fault.cell_aware`

Stuck-at and transition faults sit on cell pins, but many defects sit inside cells: a short between transistor terminals, an open in a diffusion contact, a resistive bridge in local interconnect.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Characterizing a cell
- Finding the detecting pattern
- Sequential and delay behaviour

Terms: layout, user-defined fault model, stuck-open.

Sample problem:

> Why is cell-aware characterization done once per library cell and not per design instance?
>
> A) Each instance has a different layout
>
> B) The defect behaviour depends on the cell's layout and function, which every instance shares
>
> C) Characterization requires the full chip netlist
>
> D) Instances never contain defects

Answer: The defect behaviour depends on the cell's layout and function, which every instance shares

Why: Characterization is expensive transistor-level simulation; amortizing it over every instance of the cell is what makes it practical.

<a id="c-dft-fault-collapsing"></a>

#### Fault collapsing

`dft.fault.collapsing`

A raw fault list has two faults per line, but many of them are indistinguishable or implied by others.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Equivalence
- Dominance
- Checkpoints and the collapse ratio

Terms: equivalent, controlling, dominates, checkpoint theorem, collapse ratio.

Sample problem:

> Inputs a, b, c; g1 = NAND(a, c); g2 = NOT(g1); g3 = NAND(b, c); g4 = AND(g2, g3); primary output g4. Count every fanout branch as its own line, so the circuit has 18 single stuck-at faults. Collapse gate by gate: an input stuck at the controlling value is equivalent to the output stuck at the resulting value, and a NOT gate's input and output faults pair up with inverted values; equivalence is transitive. How many equivalence classes remain?

Answer: 10

Why: Merging the gate-local equivalences reduces 18 faults to 10 classes; one representative per class is enough for test generation.

<a id="test-and-design-for-test-fault-simulation"></a>

### Fault simulation

<a id="c-dft-fsim-fault-detection"></a>

#### Detecting a fault with a test vector

`dft.fsim.fault_detection`

Fault simulation answers one question many times: does this input vector detect this fault?

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Activation and propagation
- Counting detected faults
- Counting detecting vectors

Terms: sensitive, undetectable.

Sample problem:

> Inputs a, b, c; g1 = NAND(b, c); g2 = AND(a, c); g3 = NAND(g1, g2); g4 = AND(c, g3); primary output g4. Apply a=0, b=0, c=1. Of the faults g2 stuck-at-0; g4 stuck-at-1; b stuck-at-1; c stuck-at-0; b stuck-at-0, how many does this vector detect?

Answer: 1

Why: A fault is detected when its line carries the opposite of the stuck value and the difference reaches an output. Detected: c stuck-at-0.

<a id="c-dft-fsim-serial"></a>

#### Serial fault simulation and fault dropping

`dft.fsim.serial`

The simplest fault simulator copies the circuit, injects one fault, simulates every pattern, and repeats for every fault.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The serial algorithm
- Fault dropping
- Coverage as a by-product

Terms: run, dropped, coverage curve, diagnosis, n-detect.

Sample problem:

> A serial fault simulator applies 6 patterns to 5 faults. One run simulates one faulty circuit for one pattern. The first pattern that detects each fault is: f1 at pattern 5, f2 at pattern 4, f3 never, f4 at pattern 1, f5 at pattern 3. With fault dropping (a fault is removed after its first detection), how many faulty-circuit runs are needed?

Answer: 19

Why: A detected fault costs runs up to and including its first detecting pattern; an undetected fault costs all 6. The sum is 19, against 30 without dropping.

<a id="c-dft-fsim-parallel"></a>

#### Parallel-fault and parallel-pattern simulation

`dft.fsim.parallel`

A machine word holds 32 or 64 bits, and a bitwise AND evaluates all of them at once.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Parallel-fault simulation
- Parallel-pattern single-fault simulation
- Bitwise evaluation

Terms: parallel-fault, PPSFP.

Sample problem:

> A parallel-fault simulator packs machines into 32-bit words, one bit for the fault-free circuit and the rest for faulty circuits. With 1698 faults and 48 patterns and no fault dropping, how many simulation passes over the circuit are needed?

Answer: 2640

Why: Each pass carries 31 faults, so a pattern needs $\lceil 1698/31 \rceil = 55$ passes; for 48 patterns that is 2640.

<a id="c-dft-fsim-deductive"></a>

#### Deductive fault simulation

`dft.fsim.deductive`

Deductive fault simulation computes, in one pass of the fault-free circuit, the complete set of faults that each pattern detects.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Fault lists
- Propagation rules
- Strengths and limits

Terms: fault list, no input, every, none.

Sample problem:

> In deductive fault simulation, a 2-input AND gate has inputs a = 0 with $L_a = \{5, 7\}$, b = 0 with $L_b = \{1, 2, 7\}$. Each list holds the faults (numbered 1 to 7) that complement that input under the current vector. Which faults are in the output list, ignoring the output's own local fault? Answer with the fault numbers separated by commas.

Answer: 7

Why: Inputs at the controlling value 0: the output flips only if a fault flips all of them and none of the others, so intersect the controlling inputs' lists and remove the other lists. Result: {7}.

<a id="c-dft-fsim-concurrent"></a>

#### Concurrent fault simulation

`dft.fsim.concurrent`

Concurrent fault simulation keeps the fault-free circuit and, at each gate, a list of faulty copies of that gate that differ from it.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Faulty gate records
- Divergence and scheduling
- Where it fits

Terms: record, local, converged, diverged.

Sample problem:

> What is the main cost of concurrent fault simulation?
>
> A) It cannot drop detected faults
>
> B) It needs SAT solving per pattern
>
> C) Memory: the fault lists at busy gates can grow large and change dynamically
>
> D) It needs one pass per fault

Answer: Memory: the fault lists at busy gates can grow large and change dynamically

Why: Storage per gate grows with the number of divergent faults, and list management dominates run time in large designs.

<a id="c-dft-fsim-coverage"></a>

#### Fault simulation and coverage

`dft.fsim.coverage`

Coverage is the number a test program is judged by: what fraction of the modeled faults the pattern set detects.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Fault classes after ATPG
- Fault coverage and test coverage
- ATPG efficiency

Terms: Not detected, Fault coverage, Test coverage, ATPG efficiency.

Sample problem:

> After ATPG on 29753 collapsed stuck-at faults: 28029 detected, 1071 proven untestable (redundant or blocked by tied logic), 267 aborted at the backtrack limit, and 386 not detected for other reasons. What is the fault coverage, detected faults over all faults, in percent? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 94.21

Why: FC = 28029/29753 = 94.21 percent.

<a id="test-and-design-for-test-test-pattern-generation"></a>

### Test pattern generation

<a id="c-dft-atpg-d-calculus"></a>

#### D-calculus and five-valued logic

`dft.atpg.d_calculus`

Automatic test pattern generation needs to reason about two circuits at once, the fault-free one and the faulty one, while most lines are still unassigned.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The five values
- Evaluating gates
- Multi-gate evaluation

Terms: activated.

Sample problem:

> In the five-valued D-calculus, what is the output of a NAND gate with a = X, b = D?
>
> A) 1
>
> B) 0
>
> C) X
>
> D) $\overline{D}$
>
> E) D

Answer: X

Why: Evaluate the fault-free and faulty machines separately: (X, 1) and (X, 0) give X.

<a id="c-dft-atpg-sensitization"></a>

#### Fault activation and path sensitization

`dft.atpg.sensitization`

Every test for a stuck-at fault does two jobs: it activates the fault by driving the line to the opposite of the stuck value, and it sensitizes a path so that the resulting error reaches an output.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Activation
- Sensitizing a path
- Branch faults and choosing a test

Terms: justification, side inputs, branch.

Sample problem:

> Inputs a, b, c; g1 = OR(b, c); g2 = NOR(a, g1); g3 = AND(b, g2); g4 = OR(g2, g3); primary output g4. Inputs in the order abc. Which vector activates (excites) g1 stuck-at-1, ignoring whether the error reaches an output?
>
> A) 011
>
> B) 110
>
> C) 000
>
> D) 001

Answer: 000

Why: Activation needs the fault-free value of g1 to be 0, the opposite of the stuck value.

<a id="c-dft-atpg-d-algorithm"></a>

#### The D-algorithm

`dft.atpg.d_algorithm`

The D-algorithm was the first complete algorithm for combinational test generation: for any detectable stuck-at fault it finds a test, and for an undetectable one it eventually proves none exists.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The D-frontier
- The J-frontier
- Search and completeness

Terms: primitive D-cube of failure, propagation D-cube, justified, implication.

Sample problem:

> Inputs a, b, c; g1 = NOR(b, c); g2 = NAND(a, g1); g3 = OR(a, g2); g4 = OR(g1, g3); primary output g4. Targeting a stuck-at-0, the D-algorithm has reached the assignment a = 1, b = X, c = 0 and implied every value it can. What is the D-frontier?
>
> A) {g2, g3, g4}
>
> B) {g2, g3}
>
> C) {g1, g2, g3}
>
> D) {g1}

Answer: {g2, g3}

Why: The D-frontier is the set of gates whose output is still X while at least one input carries D or $\overline{D}$; they are the places where the error can be pushed forward.

<a id="c-dft-atpg-scoap"></a>

#### SCOAP testability measures

`dft.atpg.scoap`

ATPG and test-point insertion need a cheap estimate of how hard it is to set a line to 0 or 1.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Combinational controllability
- Computing a value
- What the numbers mean

Sample problem:

> Inputs a, b, c; g1 = NAND(a, c); g2 = NAND(c, g1); g3 = NAND(b, g2); primary output g3. Using SCOAP combinational controllability (inputs have CC0 = CC1 = 1, and each gate adds 1), what is CC1 of g2?

Answer: 2

Why: Propagating (CC0, CC1) forward in topological order: g1 (3, 2); g2 (4, 2).

<a id="c-dft-atpg-scoap-observability"></a>

#### SCOAP observability

`dft.atpg.scoap_observability`

Controllability says how hard it is to set a line; observability says how hard it is to see it, that is, to propagate a change on the line to a primary output.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Backward propagation
- Fanout stems
- Detection difficulty

Sample problem:

> Inputs a, b, c; g1 = NAND(a, b); g2 = OR(c, g1); g3 = AND(a, g2); g4 = NOR(b, g3); primary output g4. SCOAP (CC0, CC1): a (1, 1); b (1, 1); c (1, 1); g1 (3, 2); g2 (5, 2); g3 (2, 4); g4 (2, 4). Primary outputs have CO = 0; an input of an AND or NAND has CO = CO(output) + the CC1 of the other inputs + 1 (CC0 for OR and NOR); NOT adds 1; a fanout stem takes the minimum over its branches. What is CO(b)?

Answer: 3

Why: Working backward from the outputs: CO(g4) = 0, CO(g3) = 2, CO(g2) = 4, CO(g1) = 6, CO(c) = 8, CO(b) = 3, CO(a) = 5.

<a id="c-dft-atpg-podem"></a>

#### PODEM

`dft.atpg.podem`

PODEM, path-oriented decision making, reformulated test generation so that decisions are made only on primary inputs.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Objectives
- Backtrace
- Implication and backtracking

Terms: objective, backtrace, easiest, hardest.

Sample problem:

> Inputs a, b, c; g1 = NAND(a, b); g2 = NAND(b, c); g3 = OR(a, g1); g4 = AND(g2, g3); g5 = OR(c, g4); primary output g5. PODEM targets g1 stuck-at-0. The current input assignment is a = X, b = 1, c = 1, with all values implied. If the fault is activated, PODEM chooses the first D-frontier gate in netlist order and its first X input. What objective does PODEM set next?
>
> A) g4 = 0
>
> B) g3 = 1
>
> C) g1 = 1
>
> D) g1 = 0

Answer: g1 = 1

Why: The fault is not yet activated, so the objective is to set the fault site to the opposite of the stuck value.

<a id="c-dft-atpg-fan"></a>

#### The FAN algorithm

`dft.atpg.fan`

FAN, fanout-oriented test generation, kept PODEM's idea of deciding only where decisions are safe, but noticed that most decisions are wasted inside fanout-free regions where justification can never fail.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Head lines and bound lines
- Unique sensitization and implication
- Multiple backtrace

Terms: bound, free, head line, Immediate implication, Unique sensitization, multiple backtrace.

Sample problem:

> Why can FAN stop backtrace at head lines instead of primary inputs?
>
> A) The cone feeding a head line is fanout-free, so any value on it can later be justified without conflict
>
> B) Head lines are always primary inputs
>
> C) Head lines carry D values
>
> D) Head lines are never observable

Answer: The cone feeding a head line is fanout-free, so any value on it can later be justified without conflict

Why: With no reconvergent fanout behind a head line, justification is guaranteed to succeed, so deciding there shrinks the search.

<a id="c-dft-atpg-sat-based"></a>

#### SAT-based ATPG

`dft.atpg.sat_based`

SAT-based ATPG turns test generation into Boolean satisfiability: build a formula that is satisfiable exactly when some input vector makes the fault-free and faulty circuits differ at an output, and hand it to a CDCL solver.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Encoding the circuit
- The ATPG miter
- Why it works well

Terms: redundant.

Sample problem:

> Inputs a, b, c; g1 = XOR(a, c); g2 = OR(b, g1); g3 = AND(a, g2); g4 = NOR(a, g3); g5 = AND(a, g4); primary output g5. Tseitin encoding: a k-input AND, NAND, OR or NOR gives k + 1 clauses, a NOT gives 2, a two-input XOR gives 4. How many clauses encode the fault-free circuit?

Answer: 16

Why: Summing per gate gives 16 clauses; the encoding is linear in circuit size.

<a id="c-dft-atpg-random-pattern"></a>

#### Random-pattern testability

`dft.atpg.random_pattern`

Many faults are detected by almost any pattern, and some by almost none. The detection probability of a fault under uniformly random patterns decides how many random patterns a test needs, whether logic BIST is practical, and where ATPG must take over.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Detection probability
- Patterns for a target confidence
- Expected coverage

Terms: detection probability, random-pattern resistant.

Sample problem:

> Inputs a, b, c, d; g1 = NAND(a, d); g2 = OR(b, g1); g3 = NOR(c, g2); g4 = NOR(c, d); primary outputs g3 and g4. Inputs are independent and uniformly random. What is the probability that one random vector detects d stuck-at-0? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 0.25

Why: 4 of the 16 vectors detect it, so $p = 4/16 = 0.25$.

<a id="c-dft-atpg-compaction"></a>

#### Test compaction

`dft.atpg.compaction`

ATPG generates one test cube per targeted fault, with many inputs left as don't-cares.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Merging test cubes
- Minimum covering sets
