- Reverse-order fault simulation

Terms: test cube, compatible, Static compaction, Dynamic compaction, set cover, reverse.

Sample problem:

> ATPG produced test cubes t1 = 11XXXX, t2 = X1XXXX, t3 = X001XX, t4 = X1XX01, t5 = 1XXX0X (X is don't care). Static compaction processes them in order and merges each cube into the first already-merged cube it is compatible with (no position where one has 0 and the other 1), otherwise it starts a new pattern. How many patterns result?

Answer: 2

Why: Merged patterns: 11XX01, X001XX. Unspecified bits are what make compaction possible.

<a id="test-and-design-for-test-scan-design"></a>

### Scan design

<a id="c-dft-scan-chain"></a>

#### Scan chains

`dft.scan.chain`

Sequential ATPG is hard because flip-flop states can only be reached through many clock cycles.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The mux-D scan cell
- A scan test cycle
- Test time

Terms: mux-D scan flip-flop, scan chain, shift, capture, shift out.

Sample problem:

> A design has 7424 mux-D scan flip-flops stitched into 8 equal-as-possible chains. With scan enable held at 1, how many shift clock cycles does it take to load one complete pattern into every chain?

Answer: 928

Why: Chains shift in parallel, so the load takes as many cycles as the longest chain: $\lceil 7424/8 \rceil = 928$.

<a id="c-dft-scan-insertion"></a>

#### Scan insertion and chain balancing

`dft.scan.insertion`

Scan insertion is the synthesis-stage transformation that replaces flip-flops with scan cells, fixes scan design-rule violations, and stitches the cells into chains.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Design rules and stitching
- Balancing
- Choosing the chain count

Terms: scan DRC, lockup latch.

Sample problem:

> Scan insertion must stitch 9850 scan flip-flops into 37 chains as evenly as possible. How long is the longest chain?

Answer: 267

Why: Balanced chains differ by at most one flop: $\lceil 9850/37 \rceil = 267$.

<a id="c-dft-scan-ordering"></a>

#### Scan-chain ordering

`dft.scan.ordering`

Which flop follows which in a chain has no effect on test quality, so the order is free to minimize the chain's routing.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Wirelength of an order
- Greedy and exact ordering
- Constraints and consequences

Terms: Hamiltonian path, nearest-neighbour.

Sample problem:

> Scan-in is at (0, 0) and scan-out at (11, 7). The flops are F1 (8, 12), F2 (11, 9), F3 (8, 5), F4 (0, 1), F5 (5, 11). Wirelength is the Manhattan distance summed along the chain from scan-in, through every flop, to scan-out. What is the wirelength of the order F4, F1, F3, F5, F2?

Answer: 46

Why: Summing the Manhattan hops gives 46.

<a id="c-dft-scan-loc-los"></a>

#### Launch-on-capture and launch-on-shift

`dft.scan.loc_los`

A transition test needs two vectors applied at speed, but a scan design can only load one state at a time.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Launch-on-shift
- Launch-on-capture
- Choosing between them

Terms: launch-on-shift, launch-on-capture.

Sample problem:

> A scan chain runs scan-in → $Q_1$ → ... → $Q_3$ → scan-out. In functional mode $D_1$ = $Q_2 + Q_3$, $D_2$ = $\overline{Q_2 Q_3}$, $D_3$ = $Q_1 Q_2$. The last shift leaves $V_1 = Q_1 \ldots Q_3$ = 100, and the scan-in pin holds 0. Under launch-on-shift, what launch state $V_2 = Q_1 \ldots Q_3$ does the final at-speed shift create?
>
> A) 010
>
> B) 000
>
> C) 100
>
> D) 011

Answer: 010

Why: Launch-on-shift makes the second vector by shifting once more: $Q_1$ takes the scan-in bit and each other flop takes its predecessor's value.

<a id="c-dft-scan-compression"></a>

#### Scan compression

`dft.scan.compression`

Tester channels are few and expensive, while designs have millions of scan flops.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Architecture
- Data volume and ratio
- Pattern inflation

Terms: decompressor, compactor.

Sample problem:

> A design has 174809 scan flops and 16 scan-in channels on the tester. Without compression the channels drive 16 chains directly; with an EDT-style decompressor they feed 160 internal chains. By what factor does the shift length per pattern fall? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 10

Why: Uncompressed chains are $\lceil 174809/16 \rceil = 10926$ long, internal chains $\lceil 174809/160 \rceil = 1093$; the ratio is 10.

<a id="test-and-design-for-test-test-compression"></a>

### Test compression

<a id="c-dft-compress-decompressor"></a>

#### Linear decompressors

`dft.compress.decompressor`

A linear decompressor turns a few tester bits per cycle into many scan-cell values, each a GF(2) linear combination (an XOR) of the free variables the tester injected.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Cells as XORs of variables
- Encoding a test cube
- Capacity

Sample problem:

> A linear decompressor drives scan cells with XORs of the free variables: $s_1 = x_2 \oplus x_3 \oplus x_4$, $s_2 = x_2 \oplus x_3 \oplus x_4$, $s_3 = x_4$, $s_4 = x_1 \oplus x_2 \oplus x_4$. With $x_1 = 1$, $x_2 = 0$, $x_3 = 1$, $x_4 = 0$, what values do $s_1 \ldots s_4$ receive? Answer with the bits in order.

Answer: 1101

Why: Each cell is the parity of the variables it lists: 1101.

<a id="c-dft-compress-compactor"></a>

#### Response compactors and X-masking

`dft.compress.compactor`

On the output side of a compressed design, many internal chains feed a few tester channels through a compactor.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- XOR space compaction
- Aliasing
- Unknown values and masking

Sample problem:

> A space compactor folds 8 scan-chain outputs c1 to c8 into 3 tester outputs: $z_1$ = XOR(c1, c5, c8); $z_2$ = XOR(c3, c4, c7); $z_3$ = XOR(c2, c6). In one shift cycle the chains present c1 to c8 = 11011000. What do $z_1 \ldots z_3$ show? Answer with the bits in order.

Answer: 011

Why: Each output is the parity of its group: 011.

<a id="test-and-design-for-test-logic-bist"></a>

### Logic BIST

<a id="c-dft-bist-lfsr-misr"></a>

#### LFSRs and MISRs

`dft.bist.lfsr_misr`

Built-in self-test puts the pattern generator and the response checker on the chip.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The external-XOR LFSR
- The MISR
- Polynomials over GF(2)

Terms: external-XOR, internal-XOR, MISR, signature, characteristic polynomial.

Sample problem:

> An external-XOR LFSR with 6 stages shifts $Q_1 \to Q_2 \to \ldots \to Q_6$ on each clock while $Q_1$ takes the feedback $Q_3 \oplus Q_6$. The state $Q_1 \ldots Q_6$ is 000110. What is the state after one clock? Answer with the 6 bits in order.

Answer: 000011

Why: Feedback = 0, which enters $Q_1$; the rest shift right: 000011.

<a id="c-dft-bist-lfsr-period"></a>

#### LFSR periods and primitive polynomials

`dft.bist.lfsr_period`

A pattern generator is only useful if it cycles through many states before repeating.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Maximal period
- Period by stepping
- How many primitive polynomials

Terms: maximal-length, primitive, order.

Sample problem:

> An LFSR with 12 stages has a primitive characteristic polynomial and starts from a nonzero state. How many clocks pass before its state first repeats?

Answer: 4095

Why: A primitive polynomial makes the LFSR visit every nonzero state once: $2^{12} - 1 = 4095$. The all-zero state is excluded because it maps to itself.

<a id="c-dft-bist-aliasing"></a>

#### Signature aliasing

`dft.bist.aliasing`

A MISR compresses millions of response bits into a few dozen, so information is lost.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The basic estimate
- Sizing the signature
- Escapes at volume

Sample problem:

> A long response stream is compressed into a MISR of 11 bits. Assuming every faulty response is equally likely, what is the aliasing probability, in parts per million? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 488.281

Why: Aliasing approaches $2^{-11}$ for long streams: 488.281 ppm.

<a id="c-dft-bist-lbist"></a>

#### Logic BIST and test points

`dft.bist.lbist`

Logic BIST applies pseudorandom patterns from an on-chip generator to the scan chains and compacts the responses in a MISR, with no tester data beyond a seed and a signature.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- STUMPS and test time
- Test points
- Weighted random patterns

Terms: STUMPS, phase shifter, observation point, control point.

Sample problem:

> A STUMPS logic BIST controller applies 100000 pseudorandom patterns. Each pattern shifts 53 cycles to fill the longest internal chain (the unload of the previous response into the MISR overlaps) and takes one capture cycle. At 100 MHz, how long is the session, in milliseconds? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 54

Why: $100000 \times (53 + 1)$ cycles at 100 MHz is 54 ms.

<a id="test-and-design-for-test-memory-bist"></a>

### Memory BIST

<a id="c-dft-mbist-memory-faults"></a>

#### Memory fault models

`dft.mbist.memory_faults`

Embedded memories occupy a large share of a modern die and are built at the tightest design rules, so they collect a large share of defects.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Cell faults
- Coupling faults
- Decoder and other faults

Terms: stuck-at fault, transition fault, data retention fault, read destructive fault, deceptive read, aggressor, victim, inversion, idempotent, state, address decoder fault, Neighbourhood pattern-sensitive faults.

Sample problem:

> A cell can be written to 1 but a write of 0 after a 1 leaves it at 1. Which memory fault is this?
>
> A) A down transition fault
>
> B) An inversion coupling fault
>
> C) A stuck-at-1 fault
>
> D) An address decoder fault

Answer: A down transition fault

Why: The cell can hold either value from initialization but cannot make the 1 to 0 transition; a stuck-at-1 cell could never be 0 at all.

<a id="c-dft-mbist-march"></a>

#### March tests for memories

`dft.mbist.march`

A March test applies a fixed sequence of reads and writes to every address in a fixed order, then the same for the next element.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- March notation
- Test time
- What each element buys

Terms: March elements, March C-, 10n, word-oriented, data backgrounds.

Sample problem:

> A March test is written $\{\Updownarrow(w0);\ \Downarrow(r0,w1,r1,w0,w1);\ \Downarrow(r1,w0,w1,w0,w1);\ \Uparrow(r1,w0);\ \Updownarrow(r0)\}$, where $\Uparrow$ and $\Downarrow$ are ascending and descending address orders and $\Updownarrow$ means either. How many operations does it apply per memory cell (its complexity is that number times n)?

Answer: 14

Why: Each element applies all its operations to every address, so the complexity is the total operation count, 14n.

<a id="c-dft-mbist-march-simulation"></a>

#### Simulating a March test on a faulty memory

`dft.mbist.march_simulation`

Knowing which faults an algorithm detects is a theorem about March tests; checking it is a simulation.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Executing the algorithm
- Cell faults
- Coupling faults and order

Terms: stuck-at, down transition fault.

Sample problem:

> March X, $\{\Updownarrow(w0);\ \Uparrow(r0,w1);\ \Downarrow(r1,w0);\ \Updownarrow(r0)\}$, runs on a memory of 6 one-bit cells at addresses 0 to 5 ($\Uparrow$ ascending; $\Updownarrow$ also taken ascending). Operations are numbered from 1 in execution order: element by element, address by address, operation by operation. The memory powers up holding all 0s, and cell 4 cannot make a 1 to 0 transition (down transition fault). Which operation number is the first read that returns the wrong value? Answer 0 if no read fails.

Answer: 35

Why: Simulating the memory, operation 35 is r0 at address 4 in element 4 and reads 1.

<a id="c-dft-mbist-repair"></a>

#### Redundancy allocation and memory repair

`dft.mbist.repair`

Large embedded memories rarely come out of the fab perfect, so they are built with spare rows and spare columns.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Must-repair analysis
- Minimum cover
- Repair with limited rows

Terms: must, vertex cover, König's theorem, repair yield.

Sample problem:

> Memory BIST on an 8 by 8 array logs faulty cells at (row, column) (1, 2), (1, 7), (2, 5), (5, 5), (6, 3). The array has spare rows: 2, spare columns: 1. In the first must-repair pass, a row with more faulty cells than there are spare columns must take a spare row, and a column with more faulty cells than spare rows must take a spare column. How many lines are must-repair in that pass?

Answer: 1

Why: Rows with more than 1 faults: 1. Columns with more than 2 faults: 0. Total 1.

<a id="c-dft-mbist-ecc"></a>

#### Error-correcting codes for memories

`dft.mbist.ecc`

Some memory errors appear after test: soft errors from particle strikes, retention loss, and wear.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Check bits for SEC-DED
- Decoding the syndrome
- Uncorrectable words

Terms: SEC-DED, syndrome, scrub.

Sample problem:

> A memory word holds 26 data bits. How many check bits does a SEC-DED code (single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting extended Hamming code) need?

Answer: 6

Why: SEC needs the smallest r with $2^r \ge m + r + 1$: r = 5 for m = 26. One overall parity bit adds double-error detection: 6.

<a id="test-and-design-for-test-boundary-scan-jtag"></a>

### Boundary scan (JTAG)

<a id="c-dft-jtag-boundary-scan"></a>

#### Boundary scan and JTAG

`dft.jtag.boundary_scan`

Boundary scan, standardized as IEEE 1149.1 and known as JTAG, puts a scan cell on every digital pin of a chip and links them into a shift register reached through a four- or five-wire test access port.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The architecture
- Interconnect testing
- Test time

Terms: test access port, instruction register, data registers, boundary register, bypass register, device identification register.

Sample problem:

> A board's JTAG chain links U1 (boundary register 586 cells) in BYPASS, U2 (boundary register 181 cells) in EXTEST, U3 (boundary register 284 cells) in EXTEST, U4 (boundary register 262 cells) in BYPASS. How many bits long is the selected data-register path from TDI to TDO?

Answer: 467

Why: EXTEST selects a device's boundary register; BYPASS selects its 1-bit bypass register. The sum is 467.

<a id="c-dft-jtag-tap-fsm"></a>

#### The TAP controller state machine

`dft.jtag.tap_fsm`

Every IEEE 1149.1 device contains the same 16-state finite-state machine, clocked by TCK and steered only by the value of TMS on each rising edge.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The state graph
- Following a TMS sequence
- Scan cycle counts

Sample problem:

> A TAP controller is in Select-DR-Scan. TMS takes the values 1, 1, 0 on successive rising edges of TCK. Which state is it in afterwards?
>
> A) Pause-DR
>
> B) Run-Test/Idle
>
> C) Update-IR
>
> D) Test-Logic-Reset

Answer: Run-Test/Idle

Why: Following the 1149.1 state diagram edge by edge from Select-DR-Scan ends in Run-Test/Idle.

<a id="c-dft-jtag-instructions"></a>

#### JTAG instructions and registers

`dft.jtag.instructions`

What the TAP controller shifts depends on the instruction loaded into each device's instruction register.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The standard instructions
- Path lengths
- Conventions that tools rely on

Terms: BYPASS, SAMPLE/PRELOAD, EXTEST, IDCODE, INTEST, CLAMP, HIGHZ.

Sample problem:

> What does the BYPASS instruction select, and why does it exist?
>
> A) The instruction register, for reloading
>
> B) A 1-bit register, so devices not under test add only one bit to the chain
>
> C) The full boundary register, for safety
>
> D) No register: TDI connects to TDO by a wire

Answer: A 1-bit register, so devices not under test add only one bit to the chain

Why: Bypass shortens long board chains; the single flop also keeps TDO registered for timing.

<a id="c-dft-jtag-ieee1500-1687"></a>

#### Core wrappers and IJTAG networks

`dft.jtag.ieee1500_1687`

A modern SoC holds dozens of reused cores and hundreds of embedded instruments: BIST engines, sensors, PLL controls, debug blocks.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- IEEE 1500 wrappers
- IEEE 1687 networks
- Description and retargeting

Terms: wrapper boundary register, wrapper instruction register, wrapper bypass, wrapper serial port, wrapper parallel port, internal test, external test, SIB, ICL, PDL, retargeting.

Sample problem:

> A core vendor ships a core with an IEEE 1500 wrapper and its test patterns. What does the integrator gain?
>
> A) The patterns can be reused at chip level by mapping them through the wrapper, without regenerating them
>
> B) The chip needs no scan chains
>
> C) The core no longer needs testing
>
> D) ATPG must be run on the whole chip anyway

Answer: The patterns can be reused at chip level by mapping them through the wrapper, without regenerating them

Why: Test reuse is the point: the wrapper defines a known boundary at which core-level patterns are valid.

<a id="test-and-design-for-test-test-equipment"></a>

### Test equipment

<a id="c-dft-ate-test-flow"></a>

#### Wafer probe, final test and burn-in

`dft.ate.test_flow`

Patterns become quality only on the test floor. A die is tested on the wafer by a prober, tested again after packaging, and, for high-reliability parts, stressed in burn-in.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Cost per die at probe
- Final test throughput
- Burn-in

Terms: wafer probe, touchdown, multi-site, final test.

Sample problem:

> Wafer probe applies 5404131 scan cycles at 50 MHz plus 222 ms of parametric and handling overhead per touchdown, testing 2 dies in parallel. The tester and prober cost 3 cents per second. What is the test cost per die, in cents? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 0.495

Why: Touchdown time = 108.083 ms + 222 ms = 330.083 ms; cost per touchdown = 0.9902 cents, shared by 2 dies: 0.495 cents.

<a id="c-dft-ate-stil"></a>

#### Test pattern languages: STIL

`dft.ate.stil`

ATPG tools and testers come from different vendors and speak different languages, so patterns travel in a standard interchange format.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What a STIL file describes
- Stimulus, response and masks
- Translation to the tester

Terms: scan memory.

Sample problem:

> Why does STIL describe scan with procedures such as load_unload and shift instead of listing every shift cycle as a vector?
>
> A) Procedures are required by the netlist
>
> B) A scan load is a repeated shift; describing it once and passing chain data keeps files compact and lets the tester use scan memory
>
> C) Scan chains have no timing
>
> D) Testers cannot apply individual vectors

Answer: A scan load is a repeated shift; describing it once and passing chain data keeps files compact and lets the tester use scan memory

Why: Expanding every shift would multiply file size by the chain length; procedures capture the repetition explicitly.

<a id="c-dft-ate-defect-level"></a>

#### Defect level and the Williams-Brown model

`dft.ate.defect_level`

Customers buy quality, not coverage. The defect level, the fraction of shipped parts that are defective, is usually quoted in defective parts per million (DPPM), and it depends on two quantities a test engineer knows: process yield and fault coverage.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The model
- Coverage for a target
- Connecting to defect density

Sample problem:

> A process yields 50 percent good dies and the test set has 95.73 percent fault coverage. Using the Williams-Brown model, what is the defect level of shipped parts, in defective parts per million? Round to the nearest integer.

Answer: 29164

Why: $DL = 1 - Y^{1-T} = 1 - 0.5^{0.0427} = 0.029164$, which is 29164 DPPM.

<a id="c-dft-ate-diagnosis"></a>

#### Fault diagnosis and yield learning

`dft.ate.diagnosis`

When a die fails, the tester log says which patterns failed at which outputs. Diagnosis turns that log into candidate defect locations, and volume diagnosis across thousands of failing dies turns those candidates into the yield-learning signal that tells the fab which layer and mechanism to fix.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Dictionary matching
- Effect-cause analysis
- Yield learning

Terms: pass/fail dictionary, Volume diagnosis.

Sample problem:

> A failing die fails patterns {P1, P5, P8} out of P1 to P8. A pass/fail fault dictionary lists the failing patterns each candidate fault predicts: C1 predicts {P1}; C2 predicts {P1, P2, P3, P5, P8}; C3 predicts {P1, P2, P3, P5, P8}; C4 predicts {P1, P3, P5, P8}. Scoring each candidate by the number of patterns where prediction and observation disagree, which candidate number matches best?

Answer: 4

Why: Mismatch counts (size of the symmetric difference): C1: 2, C2: 2, C3: 2, C4: 1.

<a id="c-dft-ate-silicon-debug"></a>

#### Silicon debug and post-silicon validation

`dft.ate.silicon_debug`

First silicon runs real software at full speed, billions of cycles per second, and finds bugs that pre-silicon simulation never reached.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Validation versus manufacturing test
- Seeing inside: traces and triggers
- Scan dumps and reproduction

Terms: Post-silicon validation, shmoo plots, observability, trace buffer, trigger, Trace signal selection, scan dump.

Sample problem:

> A failure appears at low voltage and high frequency but disappears at nominal. What kind of issue is suspected?
>
> A) A logic design bug independent of conditions
>
> B) An electrical or timing marginality, often investigated with shmoo plots
>
> C) A March test failure
>
> D) A broken scan chain

Answer: An electrical or timing marginality, often investigated with shmoo plots

Why: Condition-dependent failures point to speed paths, noise or power integrity; shmoo plots map pass and fail across voltage and frequency.

<a id="test-and-design-for-test-frontier-agent-first-futures"></a>

### Frontier: agent-first futures

<a id="c-dft-frontier-atpg-skill"></a>

#### ATPG as a callable skill

`dft.frontier.atpg_skill`

In an agent-first flow, ATPG is not a program an engineer babysits but a skill that agents select and call: a compiled engine with golden tests and a manifest that states what it does, what it takes, what it returns and what may be tuned.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The manifest and the typed interface
- Core, policy and parameters
- Safety and reward

Terms: immutable core.

Sample problem:

> An ATPG skill is exposed as a typed tool to other agents. Which output field matters most for a downstream test-time agent?
>
> A) The license server address
>
> B) The ATPG run's log verbosity
>
> C) The source file names of the engine
>
> D) The pattern count and per-pattern shift length, alongside the coverage achieved

Answer: The pattern count and per-pattern shift length, alongside the coverage achieved

Why: Test time is pattern count times shift cycles; a typed result lets the next agent compute cost without parsing logs.

<a id="c-dft-frontier-dft-insertion-agent"></a>

#### Agents that insert and verify test logic

`dft.frontier.dft_insertion_agent`

DFT insertion, scan stitching, compression, test points and wrappers, is a natural target for agents: it is configuration-driven, it has clear rules, and it has strong automatic checks.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What the agent must prove
- The harness loop
- Invariants versus proxies

Terms: chain integrity.

Sample problem:

> An agent inserts scan into a netlist. Which check proves it did not change the design's function?
>
> A) Static timing analysis alone
>
> B) Running ATPG and looking at coverage
>
> C) Comparing file sizes
>
> D) Combinational equivalence checking between the pre- and post-insertion netlists with scan enable tied to functional mode

Answer: Combinational equivalence checking between the pre- and post-insertion netlists with scan enable tied to functional mode

Why: With scan enable at 0 the scan muxes are transparent, so the two netlists must be equivalent; a miter-based checker proves it.

<a id="c-dft-frontier-golden-coverage-tests"></a>

#### Golden tests on coverage and pattern counts

`dft.frontier.golden_coverage_tests`

When an agent changes an ATPG or DFT skill, the evidence that it helped and did not hurt is a golden suite: reference designs with known baseline coverage and pattern counts, and tolerances the new run must meet.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Per-design limits
- Computing the thresholds
- What the metric can hide

Sample problem:

> An agent changed the ATPG skill's fault-ordering policy. The golden suite fails a design if test coverage drops by more than 0.1 percentage points or the pattern count grows by more than 3 percent. Results: D1: baseline 99.83 percent with 18380 patterns, new 99.84 percent with 19262 patterns; D2: baseline 97.78 percent with 18419 patterns, new 97.8 percent with 18234 patterns; D3: baseline 98.09 percent with 5590 patterns, new 98.18 percent with 5550 patterns; D4: baseline 98.27 percent with 15385 patterns, new 98.28 percent with 15661 patterns; D5: baseline 99.36 percent with 7488 patterns, new 99.36 percent with 8019 patterns. How many designs fail?

Answer: 2

Why: Failing: D1, D5. Both limits are checked per design; a gain on one design does not excuse a regression on another.

<a id="c-dft-frontier-diagnosis-agent"></a>

#### Diagnosis agents that read failure logs

`dft.frontier.diagnosis_agent`

Volume diagnosis produces thousands of candidate lists, and someone must decide which dies go to physical failure analysis, a slow and destructive lab step.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Posterior ranking
- Choosing what to send
- Likelihoods from mismatches

Terms: prior, likelihood.

Sample problem:

> A diagnosis agent reads a failure log and ranks candidate defects. Prior weights (proportional, not yet normalized) come from layout-weighted defect statistics; likelihoods from how well each candidate accounts for the log. C1: prior weight 3, likelihood 0.3; C2: prior weight 4, likelihood 0.81; C3: prior weight 6, likelihood 0.7; C4: prior weight 1, likelihood 0.51. What is the posterior probability of the most probable candidate, in percent? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 47.46

Why: Posterior is prior times likelihood, normalized: C3 gets 47.46 percent.

<a id="c-dft-frontier-fast-coverage-estimate"></a>

#### Fast fault-sampled coverage in an agent loop

`dft.frontier.fast_coverage_estimate`

An agent exploring DFT configurations cannot afford full fault simulation of millions of faults for every candidate.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Sampled coverage
- Confidence
- When to recurse

Sample problem:

> Inside an agent's DFT exploration loop, a fast mode fault-simulates a uniform random sample of 2000 faults out of 833243 instead of all of them, and 1902 of the sample are detected. What coverage does the fast mode report, in percent? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 95.1

Why: The sample proportion 1902/2000 = 95.1 percent is an unbiased estimate of the full coverage.

---

## Floorplanning and Placement

Layer 6. Floorplan representations, wirelength models, quadratic and electrostatic placement, legalization, detailed and timing-driven placement.

Builds on: Graph Algorithms for EDA, Computational Geometry for Layout, Optimization for EDA, Numerical Methods for EDA, Static Timing Analysis, Technology Mapping and Sizing, CMOS Circuits and Cell Libraries, Fabrication and Design-Technology Co-optimization.

Topics covered:

- Physical design overview; floorplanning objectives; die, core, rows and sites; LEF/DEF as the physical representation (what LEF abstracts, what DEF records)
- Floorplan representations: slicing floorplans, Polish expressions, sequence pairs, B*-trees; floorplanning by simulated annealing
- Macro placement, pin assignment, I/O placement, power planning handoff
- Wirelength models: HPWL, clique/star, Steiner estimates; partitioning-based (min-cut) placement
- Global placement: quadratic placement (B2B net model), force-directed placement, analytical nonlinear placement (log-sum-exp and weighted-average wirelength, density penalty), electrostatics-based placement (ePlace/RePlAce, FFT Poisson solve, Nesterov), DREAMPlace
- Legalization (Tetris, Abacus) and detailed placement (cell swapping, sliding windows, independent-set matching)
- Timing-driven placement (net weighting), congestion-driven and routability-driven placement
- Placement optimization: buffering and sizing during placement

Subdomains: [Overview](#floorplanning-and-placement-overview), [Placement formats](#floorplanning-and-placement-placement-formats), [Wirelength models](#floorplanning-and-placement-wirelength-models), [Floorplanning](#floorplanning-and-placement-floorplanning), [Macro placement](#floorplanning-and-placement-macro-placement), [Global placement](#floorplanning-and-placement-global-placement), [Legalization](#floorplanning-and-placement-legalization), [Detailed placement](#floorplanning-and-placement-detailed-placement), [Timing- and congestion-driven placement](#floorplanning-and-placement-timing--and-congestion-driven-placement), [Frontier: agent-first futures](#floorplanning-and-placement-frontier-agent-first-futures)

<a id="floorplanning-and-placement-overview"></a>

### Overview

<a id="c-place-overview-flow"></a>

#### The physical design flow

`place.overview.flow`

Physical design turns a gate-level netlist into geometry. Floorplanning fixes the chip outline, the core, the rows, the macros and the I/O; placement gives every standard cell a legal location; clock tree synthesis buffers the clock to the placed flip-flops; routing draws the wires.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Floorplan, place, clock, route
- Global, legal, detailed
- Why placement mistakes propagate

Sample problem:

> What does placement take as input that floorplanning produced?
>
> A) The core area, rows, fixed macros, I/O pins and placement blockages
>
> B) The clock tree and its skew targets
>
> C) The gate-level netlist's logic function only
>
> D) The routed nets and their parasitics

Answer: The core area, rows, fixed macros, I/O pins and placement blockages

Why: Placement works inside the region the floorplan defined, around the macros and pins it fixed.

<a id="c-place-overview-rows-sites"></a>

#### Rows, sites and the placement region

`place.overview.rows_sites`

Standard cells are not placed anywhere on the die. They sit in horizontal rows inside the core, each row divided into sites, the smallest legal horizontal step.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Die, core, rows and sites
- Counting rows and sites
- Rows as the legality grid

Sample problem:

> A standard-cell library has a site 0.19 um wide and rows 1.4 um tall. The core region is 59.114 um wide and 68.82 um tall, and rows are stacked from the bottom edge of the core with no gaps. How many complete placement rows fit in the core?

Answer: 49

Why: Rows = floor(68.82 / 1.4) = 49. The leftover 0.22 um at the top cannot hold a full row.

<a id="c-place-overview-utilization"></a>

#### Core utilization, aspect ratio and die size

`place.overview.utilization`

Before any cell is placed, the floorplan must decide how big the core is. Too small and the cells do not fit or cannot be routed; too large and the wires grow long and the die costs more.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Utilization from cell area
- Aspect ratio and core dimensions
- From core to die

Sample problem:

> The standard cells of a block have a total area of 133000 um^2. The floorplan targets a core utilization of 70%. What core area is needed, in um^2? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 190000

Why: Utilization is cell area over core area, so the core is 133000 / 0.7 = 190000 um^2.

<a id="floorplanning-and-placement-placement-formats"></a>

### Placement formats

<a id="c-place-format-lef-def"></a>

#### LEF and DEF

`place.format.lef_def`

A placer never sees transistors. It reads LEF, which abstracts the technology and each cell into the geometry a placer and router need, and DEF, which records the design: the die, rows, instances and their locations, pins, nets and special wiring.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What LEF abstracts
- What DEF records
- What a tool can compute from them

Sample problem:

> What does a technology LEF record that a cell LEF does not?
>
> A) The netlist connectivity
>
> B) Routing layers with direction, pitch, width and spacing, plus via definitions and sites
>
> C) Placement coordinates of every instance
>
> D) Timing constraints for the clocks

Answer: Routing layers with direction, pitch, width and spacing, plus via definitions and sites

Why: Technology LEF describes the metal stack and rules shared by all cells.

<a id="c-place-format-orientation"></a>

#### DEF units, orientations and pin coordinates

`place.format.orientation`

Every pin coordinate a placer uses comes from combining a cell's LEF pin offset with the instance's DEF location and orientation.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Database units and the placement point
- Transforming a pin offset
- Why orientation matters to the placer

Sample problem:

> A LEF macro has SIZE 2.36 BY 2.8 (um) and a pin whose shape is centred at (1.7, 1.91) um in the macro's own coordinates. The DEF file says UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS 1000 and places the instance with PLACED ( 20190 47600 ) N. In DEF the placement point is the lower-left corner of the instance after orientation; FN mirrors about the vertical axis, FS mirrors about the horizontal axis and S rotates by 180 degrees. What is the pin's absolute x coordinate on the die, in um? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 21.89

Why: Divide by 1000 to get the origin (20.19, 47.6) um. Under N the pin offset (1.7, 1.91) becomes (1.7, 1.91). The absolute pin is at (21.89, 49.51) um.

<a id="floorplanning-and-placement-wirelength-models"></a>

### Wirelength models

<a id="c-place-wl-hpwl"></a>

#### Half-perimeter wirelength

`place.wl.hpwl`

Half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL) is the standard estimate of a net's routed length: half the perimeter of the smallest axis-aligned box containing all its pins.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The bounding box of a net
- Total and weighted wirelength
- How good an estimate it is

Sample problem:

> A net has 3 pins at (30, 39), (59, 44), (59, 49) (um). What is its half-perimeter wirelength, in um?

Answer: 39

Why: The bounding box spans x from 30 to 59 and y from 39 to 49, so HPWL = 29 + 10 = 39 um. Only the extreme pins matter.

<a id="c-place-wl-incremental"></a>

#### Incremental HPWL after a cell move

`place.wl.incremental`

Detailed placers and annealers evaluate thousands of candidate moves per second, and each one needs the change in wirelength.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Only incident nets change
- Recomputing a box after a move
- Cost and correctness in practice

Sample problem:

> Cell c (treat it as a single pin) moves from (18, 43) to (23, 38) (um). In the placement, net n1 connects c to pins at (34, 56), (3, 43). What is the change in total HPWL, new minus old, in um?

Answer: 5

Why: Only nets incident to c can change. Recomputing their bounding boxes: n1: 44 to 49. The change is 49 - 44 = 5 um.

<a id="c-place-wl-clique-star"></a>

#### Clique and star net models

`place.wl.clique_star`

Quadratic placement works only with two-pin connections, so every multi-pin net must be replaced by a graph of weighted two-pin edges.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The clique model
- The star model
- Sparsity and choosing a model

Sample problem:

> A 3-pin net has pins at x = 17, 6, 15 (um). The clique model joins every pair of pins with a two-pin edge of weight $1/(k-1)$, where k is the pin count. What is the quadratic wirelength in x, the weighted sum of $(x_i - x_j)^2$ over all pairs, in um^2? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 103

Why: The 3 pairwise squared distances sum to 206. Times 1/2 gives 103 um^2.

<a id="c-place-wl-b2b"></a>

#### The bound-to-bound net model

`place.wl.b2b`

The bound-to-bound (B2B) net model, introduced with the Kraftwerk2 placer, replaces each net by two-pin edges chosen from the current placement so that the quadratic objective reproduces HPWL exactly at that placement.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Edges between the bounds
- Weights that reproduce HPWL
- Iterating the model

Sample problem:

> A 3-pin net has pins at x = 33, 30, 18 (um). The bound-to-bound model connects the leftmost and rightmost pins to each other and every inner pin to both of them, with edge weight $w_{ij} = 1/((k-1)|x_i - x_j|)$ computed from the current positions. What is the weight of the edge between the pin at x = 30 and the left bound? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 0.0417

Why: The left bound is x = 18. The distance is 12, so the weight is 1/(2 x 12) = 0.0417.

<a id="c-place-wl-steiner"></a>

#### Steiner and spanning-tree wirelength estimates

`place.wl.steiner`

A routed net is a rectilinear tree, and its shortest form is the rectilinear Steiner minimum tree (RSMT).

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Three pins: HPWL is exact
- Spanning trees as an upper estimate
- Steiner points on the Hanan grid

Sample problem:

> A three-pin net has pins at (28, 38), (21, 11), (22, 14) (um). What is the length of its rectilinear Steiner minimum tree, in um?

Answer: 34

Why: For three pins the RSMT joins them through the median point (median x, median y), and its length equals the HPWL: 34 um.

<a id="floorplanning-and-placement-floorplanning"></a>

### Floorplanning

<a id="c-place-floorplan-whitespace"></a>

#### Floorplan area, whitespace and aspect ratio

`place.floorplan.whitespace`

A floorplan arranges blocks, such as macros, hard IP or soft partitions, inside an outline.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Outline area and whitespace
- Packing and its bounding box
- Fixed outlines and aspect ratio

Sample problem:

> A floorplan packs 4 blocks (A is 39 x 17, B is 31 x 6, C is 8 x 5, D is 26 x 27, width x height in um) into an outline 48 um wide and 38 um tall without overlap. What percentage of the outline is whitespace? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 12.8

Why: The blocks cover 1591 um^2 of the 1824 um^2 outline, leaving 233 um^2, which is 12.8%.

<a id="c-place-floorplan-slicing"></a>

#### Slicing floorplans

`place.floorplan.slicing`

A slicing floorplan is one that can be produced by repeatedly cutting a rectangle into two with a straight horizontal or vertical line.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Cuts and the slicing tree
- Evaluating the area bottom-up
- Why slicing structures are useful and limited

Sample problem:

> Blocks have fixed shapes, width x height in um: A is 12 x 9, B is 12 x 5, C is 7 x 5. A slicing tree has root r1: node r1 is a vertical cut with block A on the left and node r2 on the right; node r2 is a horizontal cut with block B below and block C above. A vertical cut puts its children side by side (widths add, height is the larger), and a horizontal cut stacks them (heights add, width is the larger). What is the area of the floorplan's bounding box, in um^2?

Answer: 240

Why: Evaluate the tree bottom-up: the root comes out 24 um wide and 10 um tall, so the area is 240 um^2.

<a id="c-place-floorplan-polish"></a>

#### Normalized Polish expressions

`place.floorplan.polish`

A Polish expression is the post-order traversal of a slicing tree, written as a string of block names and cut operators.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- From tree to postfix string
- Evaluating with a stack
- Normalization makes the encoding unique

Sample problem:

> In a Polish expression, operands are blocks and operators are cuts: "P Q V" places P to the left of Q (widths add, height is the larger) and "P Q H" places P below Q (heights add, width is the larger). Blocks, width x height in um: 1 is 9 x 9, 2 is 6 x 9, 3 is 8 x 5. The expression is 2 1 H 3 H. What is the height of the floorplan, in um?

Answer: 23

Why: Scan left to right with a stack: push blocks, and on an operator pop two shapes and push their combination. The final shape is 9 x 23.

<a id="c-place-floorplan-polish-moves"></a>

#### The M1, M2 and M3 moves

`place.floorplan.polish_moves`

Simulated annealing over normalized Polish expressions needs a move set that can reach every slicing floorplan, changes the floorplan a little at a time and keeps expressions valid.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- M1: swap adjacent operands
- M2: complement a chain
- M3: swap an operand and an operator, with a check

Sample problem:

> In a Polish expression, operands are blocks and operators are cuts: "P Q V" places P to the left of Q (widths add, height is the larger) and "P Q H" places P below Q (heights add, width is the larger). A simulated-annealing floorplanner holds the normalized expression 4 3 2 V 1 V H. It applies move M1 to operands 3 and 2, which are adjacent in the operand sequence. What is the new expression?
>
> A) 4 3 1 V 2 V H
>
> B) 2 3 4 V 1 V H
>
> C) 4 2 3 V 1 V H
>
> D) 3 4 2 V 1 V H

Answer: 4 2 3 V 1 V H

Why: M1 swaps two operands that are adjacent once operators are ignored, leaving every operator where it was. The result is 4 2 3 V 1 V H.

<a id="c-place-floorplan-shape-curves"></a>

#### Shape functions and block orientation

`place.floorplan.shape_curves`

Blocks often have more than one allowed shape: a hard macro may rotate, and a soft block may take any aspect ratio within limits.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Shapes of one block
- Combining two blocks under a cut
- Orientation optimisation on a slicing tree

Sample problem:

> Block A is 3 x 2 um and block B is 11 x 5 um (width x height). A vertical cut places A to the left of B. Block A may be rotated by 90 degrees; block B is fixed. What is the smallest bounding-box area, in um^2, over the allowed orientations?

Answer: 65

Why: Each orientation choice gives width = sum of widths and height = max of heights. The best is 13 x 5 = 65 um^2.

<a id="c-place-floorplan-sequence-pair"></a>

#### Sequence pairs

`place.floorplan.sequence_pair`

A sequence pair encodes any packing of rectangles, slicing or not, as two permutations of the block names.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Reading relations from two sequences
- Packing by longest paths
- Annealing over sequence pairs

Sample problem:

> Blocks (width x height): A is 1 x 1, B is 1 x 2, C is 1 x 5, D is 1 x 2. A floorplan is encoded by the sequence pair $\Gamma_+$ = (B D A C), $\Gamma_-$ = (C D B A). Block a is left of b when a precedes b in both sequences, and a is below b when a follows b in $\Gamma_+$ but precedes it in $\Gamma_-$. Each block is packed as far left and as far down as these constraints allow, starting from (0, 0). What is the x coordinate of the lower-left corner of block A?

Answer: 1

Why: The coordinate is the longest path to A in the horizontal constraint graph. Packing gives x = 1, 0, 0, 0 and y = 5, 7, 0, 5 for blocks A, B, C, D in order.

<a id="c-place-floorplan-bstar"></a>

#### B*-trees and contour packing

`place.floorplan.bstar`

A B*-tree encodes a compacted floorplan as an ordered binary tree: left children sit to the right of their parent, right children sit above it at the same x.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Left children right, right children up
- Dropping blocks onto a contour
- Moves and uses

Sample problem:

> Blocks (width x height): A is 7 x 6, B is 7 x 2, C is 1 x 6, D is 6 x 2. A B*-tree has root A at (0, 0); A's left child is B, A's right child is C, C's right child is D. A left child is placed immediately to the right of its parent (x = parent x + parent width), a right child at its parent's x. Blocks are placed in pre-order, and each is dropped onto the contour: its y is the highest top edge of the already placed blocks that overlap it in x. What is the x coordinate of block B?

Answer: 7

Why: Follow the tree from A: every left edge adds the parent's width and every right edge keeps the parent's x. Block B lands at x = 7.

<a id="c-place-floorplan-annealing"></a>

#### Floorplanning by simulated annealing

`place.floorplan.annealing`

Simulated annealing is the classic search engine for floorplanning: propose a move on the representation, evaluate the new floorplan's cost, accept improvements always and worsenings with a probability that falls as the temperature cools.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- A cost that mixes area and wirelength
- The Metropolis acceptance rule
- The cooling schedule

Sample problem:

> A floorplanner's cost is $1 A + 3 W$, where A is the bounding-box area in um^2 and W the total HPWL in um. The current floorplan has A = 1141 and W = 436. A proposed move gives A = 1235 and W = 413. What is the change in cost, new minus old? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 25

Why: Old cost 2449, new cost 2474, change 25. A negative change is always accepted.

<a id="floorplanning-and-placement-macro-placement"></a>

### Macro placement

<a id="c-place-macro-placement"></a>

#### Macro placement

`place.macro.placement`

Macros (memories, register files, analog and IP blocks) are tens to thousands of times larger than standard cells, and their positions shape everything else: where connected logic can go, where routing channels form and how the power grid reaches them.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What a good macro placement looks like
- Sizing the channel between macros
- How macro placement is automated and judged

Sample problem:

> A macro's pins are all on its left edge. Which orientation choice usually helps most?
>
> A) Orientation never matters for macros
>
> B) Place it so the pins face another macro's pins with no gap
>
> C) Turn the pin edge toward the die boundary
>
> D) Turn the macro so that the pin edge faces the logic it connects to

Answer: Turn the macro so that the pin edge faces the logic it connects to

Why: Facing the pins toward their connected logic shortens nets and avoids routing around the macro.

<a id="c-place-macro-pin-assignment"></a>

#### Pin and I/O assignment

`place.macro.pin_assignment`

Pins on a block's boundary, whether chip I/O or the ports of a hierarchical partition, must be assigned to legal slots.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Pins, slots and costs
- Optimal assignment as matching
- Pin assignment in the flow

Sample problem:

> A 100 x 100 um block has 3 pins to assign to 3 legal boundary slots, one pin per slot. Pin p1 connects to a cell at (24, 85); pin p2 connects to a cell at (38, 30); pin p3 connects to a cell at (19, 44). The slots are s1 at (100, 80), s2 at (15, 100), s3 at (0, 94). The cost of an assignment is the total Manhattan distance from each pin's slot to the cell it connects to. What is the cost of the assignment p1 to s1, p2 to s2, p3 to s3, in um?

Answer: 243

Why: Sum the three distances: the cost is 243 um.

<a id="c-place-macro-power-planning"></a>

#### Power planning: rings, stripes and rails

`place.macro.power_planning`

Every cell needs VDD and VSS, so the floorplan includes a power distribution network: rings around the core and macros, stripes on upper metal layers across the core, and rails along every standard-cell row.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Rings, stripes and rails
- The routing cost of the grid
- IR drop along a rail

Sample problem:

> A core is 200 um wide. The power planner places vertical stripe pairs starting 28 um from the left core edge and repeating every 40 um, and it keeps every stripe pair whose start lies inside the core. How many stripe pairs does it place?

Answer: 5

Why: Starts are at 28, 68, ... up to 188 um: floor((200 - 28)/40) + 1 = 5.

<a id="floorplanning-and-placement-global-placement"></a>

### Global placement

<a id="c-place-global-formulation"></a>

#### The global placement problem

`place.global.formulation`

Global placement decides roughly where every standard cell goes. Stated exactly it is a huge, NP-hard, discrete problem; every practical placer solves a relaxation of it.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Variables, objective and constraint
- Three families of relaxation
- Stopping and handing off

Sample problem:

> What are the decision variables of global placement?
>
> A) The cell sizes and threshold voltages
>
> B) The order of nets in the DEF
>
> C) The x and y coordinates of every movable cell
>
> D) The routing layer of every net

Answer: The x and y coordinates of every movable cell

Why: Global placement chooses positions; sizing, routing and ordering are other problems.

<a id="c-place-global-mincut"></a>

#### Min-cut placement

`place.global.mincut`

Min-cut placement was the first scalable approach: cut the region in two, partition the netlist into two halves that minimise the nets crossing, assign each half to a side and recurse.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Bisecting the netlist and the region
- Levels of recursion
- Terminal propagation

Sample problem:

> A min-cut placer has bisected a region: cells c1, c3, c5 are on the left and c2, c4, c6 on the right. The nets are {c1, c4, c6, c5}, {c3, c6}, {c1, c4}, {c6, c4, c3}, {c3, c4, c2}, {c4, c1, c2}. How many nets cross the cut line?

Answer: 6

Why: Count the nets with at least one cell on each side: 6.

<a id="c-place-global-quadratic"></a>

#### Quadratic placement

`place.global.quadratic`

Quadratic placement replaces each net by two-pin springs and minimises the sum of squared spring lengths.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- One movable cell
- Two or three movable cells
- Why quadratic placement needs help

Sample problem:

> A quadratic placer minimises the sum over two-pin connections of $w (x_i - x_j)^2$. Coordinates are in um. One movable cell connects to fixed pins at x = 19 with weight 1, x = 82 with weight 1. What is its optimal x? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 50.5

Why: Setting the derivative to zero gives the weighted mean: 101 / 2 = 50.5.

<a id="c-place-global-laplacian-system"></a>

#### The Laplacian system of quadratic placement

`place.global.laplacian_system`

The linear system of quadratic placement has a precise structure: a weighted graph Laplacian over the movable cells plus diagonal terms from fixed connections.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Diagonal entries
- Off-diagonal entries and the right-hand side
- Positive definiteness and what breaks it

Sample problem:

> Quadratic placement in x minimises $\frac{1}{2}x^T A x - b^T x$ plus a constant for movable cells m1, m2, m3. The two-pin connections are: m2-fixed pin at x = 48 weight 4; m1-m2 weight 1; m2-m3 weight 3; m1-fixed pin at x = 30 weight 4; m2-fixed pin at x = 33 weight 3; m3-fixed pin at x = 7 weight 4; m1-m3 weight 4. What is the diagonal entry $A_{22}$?

Answer: 11

Why: A diagonal entry is the total weight of every connection at m2, to movable cells and to fixed pins alike: 11. The fixed connections make A strictly diagonally dominant in that row, which is what makes the system positive definite.

<a id="c-place-global-cg-solve"></a>

#### Solving the placement system by conjugate gradient

`place.global.cg_solve`

Every iteration of a quadratic placer solves $Ax = b$ for millions of cells. Direct factorization is too slow and memory-hungry; conjugate gradient (CG), which needs only matrix-vector products with the sparse A, is the standard solver.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The first conjugate gradient step
- Convergence and conditioning
- Making the solve fast in a placer

Sample problem:

> A two-cell placement system is $A x = b$ with $A = \begin{pmatrix} 7 & -3 \\ -3 & 6 \end{pmatrix}$ and $b = (44, 10)$. Conjugate gradient starts from $x_0 = 0$, so $r_0 = p_0 = b$. What is the first step length $\alpha_0 = r_0^T r_0 / p_0^T A p_0$? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 0.1769

Why: $r_0^T r_0$ = 2036 and $A p_0$ = (278, -72), so $p_0^T A p_0$ = 11512 and $\alpha_0$ = 0.1769.

<a id="c-place-global-spreading"></a>

#### Spreading with anchors and pseudo-nets

`place.global.spreading`

A quadratic placement solution is wirelength-optimal and hopelessly overlapped. Spreading turns it into a distributed placement.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Anchors as extra fixed pins
- Where the targets come from
- Choosing the anchor weight

Sample problem:

> A movable cell connects to fixed pins at x = 56 with weight 1, x = 91 with weight 1, x = 22 with weight 3 (um), so the plain quadratic solution puts it at x = 42.6. A spreading step computed a target position x = 7 for it in a less crowded area. The placer adds an anchor: a pseudo-net of weight 2 from the cell to a fixed point at the target. Where does the cell land now? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 32.43

Why: The anchor is one more fixed connection: (213 + 2 x 7) / (5 + 2) = 32.43.

<a id="c-place-global-force-directed"></a>

#### Force-directed placement

`place.global.force_directed`

Force-directed placement models connections as springs that pull connected cells together and, in its modern forms, density as a force that pushes cells out of crowded regions.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Springs and the zero-force target
- Net force on a cell
- The ripple-move algorithm

Sample problem:

> In force-directed placement each connection acts as a spring pulling with force equal to its weight times the distance. Cell c sits at (36, 19) and connects to cells at (0, 7) with connection weight 3, (38, 9) with connection weight 2. What is the x coordinate of c's zero-force target location? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 15.2

Why: The forces balance at the weighted centroid: x = 76 / 5 = 15.2.

<a id="c-place-global-density"></a>

#### Bin density and overflow

`place.global.density`

A global placer controls spreading through density: the cell area in each bin of a grid laid over the placement region, compared with a target.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Bin density
- Overflow of a bin and of the design
- Using overflow well

Sample problem:

> A 20 x 20 um placement region is divided into four 10 x 10 um bins. Cells (width x height, um): a 6 x 6 cell with lower-left corner (2, 6); a 5 x 6 cell with lower-left corner (6, 0); a 5 x 6 cell with lower-left corner (15, 12); a 8 x 3 cell with lower-left corner (8, 16). Cells may overlap each other in global placement. What is the density of the upper-left bin, the cell area inside it divided by the bin area? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 0.18

Why: Clip each cell to the bin and add the overlap areas: 18 um^2 over 100 um^2 gives 0.18.

<a id="c-place-global-smooth-wirelength"></a>

#### Smooth wirelength models

`place.global.smooth_wirelength`

Gradient-based placers need a wirelength that is differentiable, but HPWL is built from max and min, which have kinks wherever two pins tie for an extreme.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Smoothing the maximum
- Log-sum-exp wirelength
- Choosing gamma

Sample problem:

> A net's pins are at x = 13, 1, 10 (um) and the smoothing parameter is $\gamma$ = 1 um. The smooth maximum is $\gamma \ln \sum_i e^{x_i/\gamma}$. What is its value? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 13.049

Why: Factor out the largest term: 13 + 1 ln(sum of $e^{(x_i - 13)/\gamma}$) = 13.049, a little above the true maximum 13.

<a id="c-place-global-lse-gradient"></a>

#### The gradient of log-sum-exp wirelength

`place.global.lse_gradient`

A nonlinear placer moves each cell along the negative gradient of the objective, so it needs $\partial W/\partial x_i$ for every pin of every net, millions of times per iteration.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Softmax weights
- The full gradient of a net
- From pins to cells

Sample problem:

> A net's pins are at x = 9, 20, 7 (um), and its LSE wirelength in x is $W = \gamma \ln \sum e^{x_j/\gamma} + \gamma \ln \sum e^{-x_j/\gamma}$ with $\gamma$ = 2. What is the derivative of the first (smooth-maximum) term with respect to the pin at x = 20, listed in position 2? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 0.9944

Why: The derivative of $\gamma \ln \sum e^{x_j/\gamma}$ is the softmax weight $e^{x_i/\gamma}/\sum_j e^{x_j/\gamma}$ = 0.9944. Pins near the maximum get most of the weight.

<a id="c-place-global-wa-wirelength"></a>

#### Weighted-average wirelength

`place.global.wa_wirelength`

The weighted-average (WA) model, proposed by Hsu, Chang and Balabanov, estimates a net's maximum as an exponentially weighted average of its pin coordinates rather than a log-sum.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The weighted-average maximum
- The WA wirelength
- WA versus LSE in practice

Sample problem:

> A net's pins are at x = 4, 18, 14 (um) and $\gamma$ = 1. The weighted-average model estimates the maximum as $\sum x_i e^{x_i/\gamma} / \sum e^{x_i/\gamma}$ and the minimum as $\sum x_i e^{-x_i/\gamma} / \sum e^{-x_i/\gamma}$, and the x wirelength as their difference. What is the weighted-average estimate of the maximum? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 17.928

Why: Weight each pin by its softmax weight and average: 17.928, just below the true maximum 18.

<a id="c-place-global-nonlinear"></a>

#### Nonlinear placement with a density penalty

`place.global.nonlinear`

Nonlinear analytical placement minimises smooth wirelength plus a weighted density penalty, $W(x) + \lambda D(x)$, by gradient methods, raising $\lambda$ until the cells are spread.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- One step on the penalised objective
- Raising the penalty weight
- Balancing the two forces at the start

Sample problem:

> A nonlinear placer minimises $W(x) + \lambda D(x)$ with $\lambda$ = 0.1. A cell sits at x = 32 um, where $\partial W/\partial x$ = 12 and $\partial D/\partial x$ = -33. With step size 0.1, where does one gradient-descent step move it? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 31.13

Why: The combined gradient is 12 + 0.1 x -33 = 8.7, so x becomes 32 - 0.1 x 8.7 = 31.13.

<a id="c-place-global-electrostatic"></a>

#### Electrostatics-based placement

`place.global.electrostatic`

Electrostatics-based placement, introduced by ePlace and extended by RePlAce and DREAMPlace, models every cell as a positive charge equal to its area.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Cells as charges, density as energy
- Density force as electric force
- Fillers and the overflow target

Sample problem:

> In electrostatics-based placement each cell is a charge equal to its area, and the density penalty is the system's potential energy $N = \frac{1}{2}\sum_i q_i \psi_i$. Cells have charges 6, 10, 8 and sit at points where the potential is 0.4, 1.2, 1.6. What is N? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 13.6

Why: Sum charge times potential, 27.2, and halve it: 13.6.

<a id="c-place-global-poisson-fft"></a>

#### Solving the density Poisson equation by FFT

`place.global.poisson_fft`

Electrostatic placement solves Poisson's equation for the potential on the bin grid at every iteration.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Cosine modes diagonalise the Laplacian
- The field from the same coefficients
- Why the FFT makes it scale

Sample problem:

> A placer solves $\nabla^2 \psi = -\rho$ on an m x m bin grid (m = 64, unit bins) with a cosine expansion, $\omega_u = \pi u / m$. The zero-mean density contains the mode $0.9 \cos(\omega_5 x)\cos(\omega_2 y)$. What is the coefficient of the matching mode $\cos(\omega_u x)\cos(\omega_v y)$ in the potential $\psi$? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 12.8797

Why: Each cosine mode is an eigenfunction of the Laplacian with eigenvalue $-(\omega_u^2 + \omega_v^2)$, so the coefficient is divided by 0.069878: 0.9 / 0.069878 = 12.8797.

<a id="c-place-global-nesterov"></a>

#### Nesterov's method with Lipschitz step estimates

`place.global.nesterov`

ePlace solves the penalised placement problem with Nesterov's accelerated gradient method, whose momentum gives faster convergence than plain gradient descent on smooth problems.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Step length from a local Lipschitz estimate
- The momentum sequence
- One full Nesterov update

Sample problem:

> ePlace-style Nesterov placement estimates the step length as the inverse of a local Lipschitz constant, $\alpha_k = \|v_k - v_{k-1}\| / \|\nabla f(v_k) - \nabla f(v_{k-1})\|$. For a one-cell toy, $v_{k-1} = (32, 29)$, $v_k = (29, 32)$, $\nabla f(v_{k-1}) = (3, 15)$ and $\nabla f(v_k) = (-9, 21)$. What is $\alpha_k$? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 0.3162

Why: The position changed by 4.2426 and the gradient by 13.4164, so the local Lipschitz estimate is 3.1623 and the step is 0.3162.

<a id="c-place-global-dreamplace"></a>

#### DREAMPlace and GPU-accelerated placement

`place.global.dreamplace`

DREAMPlace recast electrostatics-based global placement as training a neural network: cell positions are the trainable parameters, wirelength plus density is the loss, and a deep-learning toolkit (PyTorch) provides the optimisation loop and GPU execution.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Placement as training
- Custom operators and GPU kernels
- What it changed for tool designers

Sample problem:

> Which placement algorithm does DREAMPlace implement on the GPU?
>
> A) Min-cut placement
>
> B) An electrostatics-based nonlinear placer in the style of ePlace and RePlAce
>
> C) Simulated annealing
>
> D) Force-directed placement with ripple moves

Answer: An electrostatics-based nonlinear placer in the style of ePlace and RePlAce

Why: It keeps the ePlace formulation (smooth wirelength, electrostatic density, Nesterov) and accelerates it.

<a id="floorplanning-and-placement-legalization"></a>

### Legalization

<a id="c-place-legal-displacement"></a>

#### Legalization and displacement

`place.legal.displacement`

Legalization takes the overlapping, off-grid output of global placement and produces a legal placement: every cell in a row, on a site, without overlap.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What legalization must achieve
- Measuring displacement
- Why the metric matters downstream

Sample problem:

> A legalizer moved cells from their global-placement positions to legal sites (um): c1 from (32, 5) to (27, 6); c2 from (38, 30) to (39, 28); c3 from (31, 17) to (33, 18). Displacement is Manhattan distance. What is the total displacement, in um?

Answer: 12

Why: Add the Manhattan moves: 12 um.

<a id="c-place-legal-tetris"></a>

#### Tetris legalization

`place.legal.tetris`

Tetris legalization is the simplest practical legalizer: sort cells by x and drop each into the row where it moves least, at the leftmost free position.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Sort, then place greedily
- Choosing the row
- Strengths and failure modes

Sample problem:

> Tetris legalization processes cells in order of increasing desired x. Each cell goes into the row where its displacement $|\Delta x| + |\Delta y|$ is smallest (ties to the lower row), at x = max(desired x, the right edge of the cells already in that row). The region has a single row at y = 0, starting at x = 0 with no right limit. Cells (lower-left corners): c1 (width 6) wants x = 0; c2 (width 4) wants x = 12; c3 (width 4) wants x = 3; c4 (width 3) wants x = 4; c5 (width 6) wants x = 18. Where does c2 end up: what is its legal x?

Answer: 13

Why: Packing left to right in x order, each cell starts at the larger of its wish and the row's current right edge. c2 lands at x = 13.

<a id="c-place-legal-abacus"></a>

#### Legalization with Abacus

`place.legal.abacus`

Abacus improves on Tetris by letting cells already placed in a row shift to make room, choosing positions that minimise total squared displacement in that row.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Clusters and their optimal position
- Adding cells and merging clusters
- Choosing rows and the full algorithm

Sample problem:

> Abacus legalizes one row spanning x = 0 to 33, keeping the cells in their order and minimising the sum of squared x displacements, where $x_i'$ is the desired position. Cells are added left to right; when a cell overlaps the last cluster it joins it, the cluster moves to its optimal position (clamped to the row) and merges with its left neighbour if they then overlap. Cells: c1: width 3, desired x 24; c2: width 4, desired x 25. The two cells overlap, so they form one cluster. What is the cluster's optimal left edge x? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 23

Why: For a cluster the optimum is $x_c = \sum e_i (x_i' - o_i)/\sum e_i$, where $o_i$ is the cell's offset inside the cluster: (24 + (25 - 3))/2 = 23, then clamped to the row.

<a id="c-place-legal-rules"></a>

#### Legality rules: sites, rails and regions

`place.legal.rules`

At advanced nodes, legal means much more than "in a row and not overlapping". Power rail alignment, multi-row cells, fence and guide regions, blockages and neighbour-dependent spacing all constrain where cells may go.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Rows, sites and rail alignment
- Regions and blockages
- Neighbour rules and why legality is core

Sample problem:

> A legalizer places a cell in an odd row without flipping it. What rule does that break?
>
> A) Timing closure
>
> B) Maximum fanout
>
> C) Site alignment
>
> D) Power rail alignment: the cell's VDD and VSS rails no longer match the row's rails

Answer: Power rail alignment: the cell's VDD and VSS rails no longer match the row's rails

Why: Rows alternate orientation; cells must be flipped to match the rails of the row they sit in.

<a id="floorplanning-and-placement-detailed-placement"></a>

### Detailed placement

<a id="c-place-detail-swap"></a>

#### Detailed placement by cell swapping

`place.detail.swap`

Detailed placement improves a legal placement with local moves that keep it legal.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Evaluating a swap
- Shared nets and double counting
- Global swap and search strategy

Sample problem:

> Detailed placement considers swapping equal-width cells a at (9, 17) and b at (43, 16) (um, treat each cell as one pin). In the placement, a net joins a with fixed pins at (39, 8); a net joins b with fixed pins at (20, 35). What is the change in total HPWL if they swap, new minus old, in um?

Answer: -40

Why: Only nets touching a or b change. Before and after: 39 to 12, 42 to 29. The change is 41 - 81 = -40 um; a swap is accepted only if this is negative.

<a id="c-place-detail-optimal-region"></a>

#### The optimal region of a cell

`place.detail.optimal_region`

For a single cell with every other cell fixed, the positions that minimise the total HPWL of its nets form a rectangle, its optimal region, found from medians of the other pins' bounds.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Why medians appear
- The gain from moving there
- Using optimal regions in detailed placement

Sample problem:

> Cell c is on 3 nets: net n1's other pins are at x = 14, 45, 17; net n2's other pins are at x = 39, 15, 30; net n3's other pins are at x = 56. Ignoring c, each net's other pins span an x interval. The x positions of c that minimise the total x span of its nets form an interval. What is its lower end?

Answer: 39

Why: Collect each net's lower and upper x bound, 6 values, and sort them: 14, 15, 39, 45, 56, 56. Any x from the third to the fourth value is optimal: [39, 45].

<a id="c-place-detail-sliding-window"></a>

#### Sliding-window reordering

`place.detail.sliding_window`

Local reordering takes a small window of consecutive cells in a row, tries every order of them packed into the same span and keeps the best.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Packing a window in a new order
- Trying every order
- Window size and sweeping

Sample problem:

> A sliding window covers 3 adjacent cells in one row, packed from x = 18 in the order A B C, with widths A 2, B 6, C 6 um. Each cell's pin is at its centre. The nets touching the window are: A to fixed x = 49; B to fixed x = 44, 66; C to fixed x = 57, 6. Only the x span of these nets changes when the window is reordered; the cells stay packed from x = 18. What is the total x span of these nets in the current order, in um?

Answer: 124

Why: Place the centres, then sum each net's x span: 124 um.

<a id="c-place-detail-ism"></a>

#### Independent-set matching

`place.detail.ism`

Independent-set matching picks a set of same-size cells that share no nets, so their wirelength costs are independent of each other, and reassigns them among their own locations by solving a minimum-cost bipartite matching.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Why the cells must be independent
- Solving the matching
- ISM in a detailed placer

Sample problem:

> Independent-set matching picks equal-size cells that share no net, so their costs are independent, and reassigns them to their own locations by minimum-cost matching. The cells are A at (8, 12), B at (45, 43), C at (24, 23) (um). A has a net to fixed pins at (55, 5), (43, 17); A has a net to fixed pins at (25, 48), (14, 49); B has a net to fixed pins at (20, 53), (21, 23); B has a net to fixed pins at (17, 40), (24, 41); C has a net to fixed pins at (60, 24). The cost of putting cell i in slot j is the HPWL of i's nets with i at j. What is the cost of putting cell A in C's current location?

Answer: 86

Why: Move A's pin to (24, 23) and recompute each of its nets: 86 um.

<a id="floorplanning-and-placement-timing--and-congestion-driven-placement"></a>

### Timing- and congestion-driven placement

<a id="c-place-driven-net-delay"></a>

#### Net delay as a function of placement

`place.driven.net_delay`

Placement fixes the length of every wire before any wire exists, and wire length sets wire delay.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Wire delay from placed pins
- Adding the driver and the load
- What this means for a placer

Sample problem:

> A driver at (500, 350) and its only sink at (310, 530) (um) are joined by a wire estimated at their Manhattan distance, with 1 ohm/um and 0.2 fF/um. Ignoring the driver and the load, what is the wire's distributed Elmore delay $rcL^2/2$, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 13.69

Why: L = 370 um, so the delay is 1 x 0.2 x 370^2 / 2 = 13690 ohm-fF = 13.69 ps.

<a id="c-place-driven-timing"></a>

#### Timing-driven placement

`place.driven.timing`

A wirelength-driven placer treats all nets alike, so critical paths end up no shorter than any other.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Criticality and net weights
- Weighted wirelength and its effect
- Keeping weights current

Sample problem:

> A timing-driven placer weights each net by $w = 1 + 4 c^{1}$, where the criticality $c = \min(1, \max(0, -s/|WNS|))$ uses the net's worst slack s and the design's WNS of -82 ps. What weight does a net with slack -25 ps receive? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 2.2195

Why: c = 0.3049, so w = 1 + 4 x 0.3049^1 = 2.2195.

<a id="c-place-driven-routability"></a>

#### Routability-driven placement

`place.driven.routability`

A placement with short wires can still be unroutable if too many wires must pass through one region.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- RUDY wire density
- Demand per bin
- From demand to congestion and action

Sample problem:

> RUDY spreads each net's HPWL uniformly over its bounding box, so a net with box w x h has wire density $(w + h)/(wh)$ inside the box. Coordinates are in um. What is the RUDY density, in um of wire per um^2, of a net whose pin bounding box spans x 17 to 21 and y 8 to 29? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 0.2976

Why: The box is 4 x 21, so the density is (4 + 21)/(4 x 21) = 0.2976. Small boxes get high density, which flags local pin crowding.

<a id="c-place-driven-inflation"></a>

#### Cell inflation for congestion

`place.driven.inflation`

Cell inflation is the simplest way to make a density-driven placer care about congestion: temporarily enlarge the cells that sit in congested regions, so the density force pushes them apart and leaves more room for wires.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The inflation rule
- Total area after inflation
- When inflation helps and when it does not

Sample problem:

> A routability-driven placer inflates each cell by the factor $f = \min(2.5, r^{1})$ when its bin's congestion ratio r (demand over capacity) exceeds 1, and leaves it alone otherwise. A cell of area 11 um^2 sits in a bin with r = 1.39. What is its inflated area, in um^2? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 15.29

Why: f = min(2.5, 1.39^1) = 1.39, so the area becomes 15.29 um^2.

<a id="c-place-driven-buffering"></a>

#### Buffering and sizing during placement

`place.driven.buffering`

Placement and logic optimisation are not separate in modern flows. Long wires that placement cannot shorten are split by buffers, and gates driving heavy loads are upsized, during and right after global placement, so that timing estimates stay realistic.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Delay of a long unbuffered wire
- A repeater at the midpoint
- Buffering and sizing inside the placement flow

Sample problem:

> A driver with resistance 200 ohm drives a 2100 um wire (2 ohm/um, 0.15 fF/um) into a 4 fF sink. A repeater can be placed at the midpoint: input capacitance 4 fF, output resistance 400 ohm, intrinsic delay 29 ps. Use the Elmore model $R(cL + C) + rL(cL/2 + C)$ for each driven segment, with 1 ohm x 1 fF = 0.001 ps. What is the unbuffered delay from driver to sink, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 742.1

Why: Driver term 63.8 ps plus wire term 678.3 ps gives 742.1 ps.

<a id="floorplanning-and-placement-frontier-agent-first-futures"></a>

### Frontier: agent-first futures

<a id="c-place-frontier-core-vs-surface"></a>

#### The placer's core and change surface

`place.frontier.core_vs_surface`

An agent-first placer is built so that most change requests never touch its hardest code.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What belongs in the placer's core
- Strategy, parameters and hooks
- Routing a request to a layer

Sample problem:

> Where does the target density of global placement belong?
>
> A) Core
>
> B) Strategy
>
> C) Observation hooks
>
> D) Parameters

Answer: Parameters

Why: It is a value the engine already uses; changing it needs no new code.

<a id="c-place-frontier-rule-plugin"></a>

#### A placement rule as a Tier 2 plug-in

`place.frontier.rule_plugin`

Customers often want placement behaviour no general placer offers: keep datapath bit-slices abutted, align regular arrays, cluster cells of one power domain near its switch.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The seam and its context
- Computing the rule's cost
- Proving the plug-in

Sample problem:

> Why is "abut regular cells" not a core change?
>
> A) It modifies DEF units
>
> B) It changes the site grid
>
> C) Gaps between group members are legal; the rule only prefers fewer of them
>
> D) It forbids overlap

Answer: Gaps between group members are legal; the rule only prefers fewer of them

Why: A preference expressed as cost leaves the legality invariant untouched.

<a id="c-place-frontier-objective-weights"></a>

#### Objective weights as Tier 1 configuration

`place.frontier.objective_weights`

A placer's objective blends wirelength with congestion, timing and density terms through weights.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- A weighted objective as configuration
- Comparing runs
- The break-even weight

Sample problem:

> A placer exposes its objective weights as Tier 1 configuration: cost = HPWL + $\beta$ x overflow + $\gamma$ x |TNS|, with HPWL in um, overflow in percent and TNS in ps. Run P gives HPWL 1009000, overflow 14%, TNS -297 ps; run Q gives HPWL 1046000, overflow 9%, TNS -133 ps. With $\beta$ = 2000 and $\gamma$ = 100, what is the cost of run P?

Answer: 1066700

Why: 1009000 + 2000 x 14 + 100 x 297 = 1066700.

<a id="c-place-frontier-qor-differential"></a>

#### Golden and QoR differential tests for a placer

`place.frontier.qor_differential`

No change to a placer, whether a parameter, a plug-in or a core edit, should be promoted on faith.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Golden tests for placer kernels
- Measuring QoR change
- Promotion gates

Sample problem:

> A placer change is run on a reference design: baseline HPWL 431000 um, new HPWL 424104 um. What is the HPWL change, in percent (negative is better)? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: -1.6

Why: (424104 - 431000) / 431000 x 100 = -1.6%.

<a id="c-place-frontier-fast-loop"></a>

#### Fast placement inside a modeling loop

`place.frontier.fast_loop`

Placement exists in fast and accurate forms: a GPU global placer with loose stopping rules and RUDY congestion, versus full global and detailed placement followed by global routing.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What the fast placer trades away
- Deciding what to run accurately
- Pitfalls of the loop

Sample problem:

> Why keep both a fast and an accurate placer instead of only the accurate one?
>
> A) Many candidates can be screened cheaply, and only promising ones pay for accurate runs
>
> B) Agents can only call fast tools
>
> C) The accurate placer is always wrong
>
> D) Fast placers produce legal layouts for tape-out

Answer: Many candidates can be screened cheaply, and only promising ones pay for accurate runs

Why: Screening reserves expensive compute for decisions that matter.

---

## Analog, Mixed-Signal and RF Design Automation

Layer 6. Small-signal design, op-amps, data converters and PLLs, sizing as optimization, matching and analog layout, RF and mixed-signal simulation.

Builds on: Circuit Simulation, CMOS Circuits and Cell Libraries, Semiconductor Devices and Compact Models, Circuits and Electromagnetics, Optimization for EDA, Variability, Yield and Reliability Statistics.

Topics covered:

- Analog integrated circuit design and its automation gap
- Small-signal models, gm/Id methodology, intrinsic gain, common-source and differential pairs, current mirrors
- Operational amplifiers, comparators, stability and compensation (phase margin)
- Data converters (ADC, DAC), phase-locked loops, voltage-controlled oscillators
- Analog sizing as optimization: equation-based, simulation-based, Bayesian optimization, PVT robustness
- Matching, mismatch (Pelgrom), common-centroid and interdigitated layout, analog layout automation (MAGICAL/ALIGN style)
- RF IC design, microwave circuits, S-parameters, noise figure
- Mixed-signal design and simulation, Verilog-A, real-number modeling, behavioral models
- Specialized branches: photonic integrated circuits and electronic-photonic design automation, MEMS design, power electronics and power semiconductor devices, neuromorphic hardware
- Open analog flow: xschem, ngspice, Magic, Netgen

Subdomains: [Small-signal analysis](#analog-mixed-signal-and-rf-design-automation-small-signal-analysis), [Amplifiers](#analog-mixed-signal-and-rf-design-automation-amplifiers), [Analog layout](#analog-mixed-signal-and-rf-design-automation-analog-layout), [Analog sizing](#analog-mixed-signal-and-rf-design-automation-analog-sizing), [Data converters](#analog-mixed-signal-and-rf-design-automation-data-converters), [PLLs](#analog-mixed-signal-and-rf-design-automation-plls), [RF design](#analog-mixed-signal-and-rf-design-automation-rf-design), [Mixed-signal flows](#analog-mixed-signal-and-rf-design-automation-mixed-signal-flows), [Special topics](#analog-mixed-signal-and-rf-design-automation-special-topics), [Frontier: agent-first futures](#analog-mixed-signal-and-rf-design-automation-frontier-agent-first-futures)

<a id="analog-mixed-signal-and-rf-design-automation-small-signal-analysis"></a>

### Small-signal analysis

<a id="c-analog-ss-automation-gap"></a>

#### Why analog automation lags digital

`analog.ss.automation_gap`

Digital implementation runs from RTL to GDS with little human intervention. Analog design still relies on experts who size transistors by hand, draw matched layouts and iterate with SPICE.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- No abstraction that hides the devices
- Many specs, expensive evaluation
- Where automation works today

Sample problem:

> Which property of digital design is the deepest enabler of its automation, and is largely missing in analog?
>
> A) The use of CMOS rather than bipolar transistors
>
> B) Noise margins that let each gate restore signals, so stages can be designed and verified independently
>
> C) Faster simulators
>
> D) The availability of more engineers
