## Extraction, Signal Integrity and Signoff

Layer 8. Parasitic extraction, SPEF, RC reduction, crosstalk and noise, ECOs and the signoff checklist.

Builds on: Routing, Circuits and Electromagnetics, Numerical Methods for EDA, Static Timing Analysis, Circuit Simulation, Clock Trees and Power Delivery, Fabrication and Design-Technology Co-optimization.

Topics covered:

- Parasitic extraction: resistance, capacitance (ground, coupling, fringe) and inductance extraction
- Pattern-matching (rule-based) extraction vs field solvers (random-walk, boundary element, FEM)
- SPEF: what it records; RC network reduction
- Signal integrity: crosstalk, coupling-induced delay change, glitch/noise analysis, Miller factor
- Signoff: timing, power, EM/IR, SI, physical; engineering change orders (ECO), PPA closure, the signoff checklist

Subdomains: [Resistance extraction](#extraction-signal-integrity-and-signoff-resistance-extraction), [Capacitance extraction](#extraction-signal-integrity-and-signoff-capacitance-extraction), [Extraction methods](#extraction-signal-integrity-and-signoff-extraction-methods), [Inductance](#extraction-signal-integrity-and-signoff-inductance), [Parasitic formats](#extraction-signal-integrity-and-signoff-parasitic-formats), [Parasitic reduction](#extraction-signal-integrity-and-signoff-parasitic-reduction), [Signal integrity](#extraction-signal-integrity-and-signoff-signal-integrity), [Signoff](#extraction-signal-integrity-and-signoff-signoff), [Frontier: agent-first futures](#extraction-signal-integrity-and-signoff-frontier-agent-first-futures)

<a id="extraction-signal-integrity-and-signoff-resistance-extraction"></a>

### Resistance extraction

<a id="c-extract-res-sheet-resistance"></a>

#### Sheet resistance and counting squares

`extract.res.sheet_resistance`

Every resistance an extractor reports starts from the same idea: a metal layer of fixed thickness has a sheet resistance, and a wire's resistance is that number times how many squares of its own width fit along it.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Resistance per square
- From resistivity to ohms
- Corners and current crowding

Sample problem:

> A straight wire on one metal layer is 20 um long and 0.1 um wide. How many squares does it contain?

Answer: 200

Why: Squares are length over width: 20 / 0.1 = 200. Sheet resistance times squares gives the resistance, whatever the absolute size of each square.

<a id="c-extract-res-wire-resistance"></a>

#### Wire and via resistance

`extract.res.wire_resistance`

A routed net is a chain of wire segments on several layers joined by vias. Its resistance is the series sum of every segment and every via level, with parallel via cuts dividing a via level's resistance.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Resistance from dimensions
- Vias in series and in parallel
- When vias dominate

Sample problem:

> A copper wire has effective resistivity 0.04 ohm-um, width 0.05 um, thickness 0.08 um and length 70 um. What is its resistance, in ohms? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 700

Why: $R = \rho L/(WT)$ = 0.04 x 70 / (0.05 x 0.08) = 700 ohm.

<a id="c-extract-res-temperature"></a>

#### Temperature dependence of wire resistance

`extract.res.temperature`

Metal resistance rises with temperature, roughly linearly over the operating range.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The linear temperature coefficient
- Moving between corners
- What scales and what does not

Sample problem:

> A wire measures 100 ohm at 25 C. Its temperature coefficient of resistance is 0.0035 per C. What is its resistance at 125 C, in ohms? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 135

Why: $R(T) = R_0[1 + \alpha (T - T_0)]$ = 100 x (1 + 0.0035 x 100) = 135 ohm.

<a id="c-extract-res-barrier-scattering"></a>

#### Barrier layers and size effects in copper

`extract.res.barrier_scattering`

A modern copper wire is not all copper. A thin barrier liner, needed to stop copper diffusing into the dielectric, coats its sides and bottom and conducts poorly.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The conducting cross-section
- Resistance penalty of the liner
- Width-dependent resistivity

Sample problem:

> A copper wire is drawn 0.024 um wide and 0.05 um thick. A resistive barrier liner of 0.002 um coats both sidewalls and the bottom, and it carries no current. What percentage of the drawn cross-section is conducting copper? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 80

Why: The copper is $(W - 2b)(T - b)$ = 0.02 x 0.048 = 0.00096 um^2 out of 0.0012 um^2, which is 80%. The liner does not shrink with the wire, so its share grows at every node.

<a id="extraction-signal-integrity-and-signoff-capacitance-extraction"></a>

### Capacitance extraction

<a id="c-extract-cap-parallel-plate"></a>

#### Area capacitance to the layer below

`extract.cap.parallel_plate`

The simplest capacitance a wire has is the parallel-plate part: the field running straight down from its bottom face to a wide conductor below, such as the substrate or a dense layer of crossing wires.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The parallel-plate formula
- Capacitance per unit length
- Scaling and its limits

Sample problem:

> A wire 0.2 um wide and 120 um long runs 0.08 um above a wide grounded plane, in a dielectric of relative permittivity 2.7. Using the parallel-plate formula with $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-3}$ fF/um, what is its area capacitance, in fF? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 7.17

Why: $C = \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r W L / h$ = 0.008854 x 2.7 x 0.2 x 120 / 0.08 = 7.17 fF.

<a id="c-extract-cap-fringe"></a>

#### Fringe capacitance

`extract.cap.fringe`

The field from a wire does not stop at its bottom face. Field lines leave its sidewalls and top and curve down to the conductor below, adding fringe capacitance along each edge.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Area plus edges
- The fringe share
- The crossover width

Sample problem:

> A wire 0.1 um wide and 30 um long has area capacitance 110 aF/um^2 to the plane below and fringe capacitance 35 aF/um along each of its two edges. What is its total capacitance to ground, in fF? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 2.43

Why: Area: 110 x 0.1 x 30 = 0.33 fF. Fringe: 2 x 35 x 30 = 2.1 fF. Total 2.43 fF.

<a id="c-extract-cap-coupling"></a>

#### Coupling capacitance

`extract.cap.coupling`

Two wires side by side form a capacitor through the dielectric between their facing sidewalls.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Facing sidewalls
- Spacing dependence
- Parallel run length

Sample problem:

> Two parallel wires of thickness 0.05 um face each other across a spacing of 0.03 um for 40 um, in a dielectric with $\varepsilon_r = 3$. Treat the facing sidewalls as a parallel-plate capacitor with $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-3}$ fF/um. What is the coupling capacitance, in fF? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 1.77

Why: $C_c = \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r T L / s$ = 0.008854 x 3 x 0.05 x 40 / 0.03 = 1.77 fF. Fringe fields add to this, so a field solver would report somewhat more.

<a id="c-extract-cap-cap-matrix"></a>

#### The Maxwell capacitance matrix

`extract.cap.cap_matrix`

A set of conductors over ground is described exactly, in electrostatics, by its capacitance matrix: the linear map from conductor voltages to conductor charges.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Couplings off the diagonal
- Ground capacitance as a row sum
- Building the diagonal

Sample problem:

> A field solver returns the Maxwell capacitance matrix of three conductors over a ground plane, in fF: row 1: [20, -7, -1]; row 2: [-7, 19, -1]; row 3: [-1, -1, 6]. What is the coupling capacitance between conductors 2 and 1, in fF?

Answer: 7

Why: Off-diagonal entries are the negatives of the coupling capacitances: $C_{c} = -C_{21}$ = 7 fF.

<a id="c-extract-cap-total-net"></a>

#### Total capacitance of a net

`extract.cap.total_net`

A driver's load is the sum of everything it must charge: wire capacitance to ground, coupling to every neighbour, and the input capacitance of every sink pin.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Summing the components
- The coupling share
- Grounded versus dropped coupling

Sample problem:

> A net is 130 um of wire with 72 aF/um to ground (area plus fringe), 45 aF/um of coupling to the neighbour on one side and 28 aF/um to the neighbour on the other. It drives one sink pin of 2 fF. What is the net's total capacitance with all coupling counted to quiet neighbours, in fF? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 20.85

Why: Wire: 130 x (72 + 45 + 28) aF = 18.85 fF. Pins: 2 fF. Total 20.85 fF.

<a id="c-extract-cap-field-solver"></a>

#### Field-solver capacitance extraction

`extract.cap.field_solver`

A field solver computes capacitance from first principles: it solves the electrostatic potential around a set of conductors and integrates the resulting surface charges.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What the solver computes
- Reading a solve
- When the reference is golden

Sample problem:

> Why does a capacitance solver only need the geometry and permittivities, and not the frequency?
>
> A) Because the solver averages over all frequencies
>
> B) At on-chip dimensions far below the wavelength, the quasi-static electric field decouples from the magnetic field
>
> C) Because dielectrics have no frequency dependence
>
> D) Because capacitance is defined only at DC by convention

Answer: At on-chip dimensions far below the wavelength, the quasi-static electric field decouples from the magnetic field

Why: When structures are electrically small, capacitance is an electrostatic quantity. Frequency effects enter through inductance and resistance (skin effect), extracted separately.

<a id="extraction-signal-integrity-and-signoff-extraction-methods"></a>

### Extraction methods

<a id="c-extract-method-pattern-matching"></a>

#### Rule-based extraction by pattern matching

`extract.method.pattern_matching`

Full-chip extraction cannot solve a field problem for billions of wire segments.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Table lookup along one index
- Two indices and a run length
- Fracturing a varying net

Sample problem:

> A rule-based extractor's coupling table (aF/um of parallel run) has, at width 0.06 um: 68 aF/um at spacing 0.02 um and 31 aF/um at spacing 0.03 um; at width 0.08 um: 71 aF/um at spacing 0.02 um and 34 aF/um at spacing 0.03 um. It interpolates linearly in each index. A wire of width 0.06 um runs 120 um beside a neighbour at spacing 0.025 um. What coupling per length does the extractor use, in aF/um? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 49.5

Why: On the width-0.06 row, interpolate in spacing: $t = 0.5$, giving 68 + 0.5 x (31 - 68) = 49.5 aF/um.

<a id="c-extract-method-random-walk"></a>

#### Floating random-walk capacitance solvers

`extract.method.random_walk`

The floating random-walk method computes capacitance by Monte Carlo instead of meshing.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Walks and scores
- The standard error
- Walks needed for a target

Sample problem:

> A floating random-walk solver estimates the coupling between conductors i and j. Each walk starts on a surface around conductor i, hops through the dielectric, and contributes a score (in fF) when it lands on conductor j, and zero otherwise. 6 walks scored 3.1, 2.1, 0.3, 0.4, 3.6, 2.8. What is the coupling estimate, in fF? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 2.05

Why: The estimate is the sample mean of the walk scores: 12.3 / 6 = 2.05 fF. Each walk is independent, so the estimate is unbiased and its error shrinks as walks are added.

<a id="c-extract-method-bem-fem"></a>

#### Boundary-element versus finite-element solvers

`extract.method.bem_fem`

Deterministic field solvers come in two main families. Boundary-element methods discretize only conductor surfaces and produce small, dense systems.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Surface panels
- Dense matrices
- Volume meshes and sparsity

Sample problem:

> A boundary-element solver meshes only conductor surfaces, into square panels of side 0.05 um. A wire is a box 1 um long, 0.1 um wide and 0.15 um thick. How many panels cover its whole surface?

Answer: 212

Why: Surface area is $2(LW + LT + WT)$; in panel units that is 2 x (20 x 2 + 20 x 3 + 2 x 3) = 212 panels. A finite-element mesh of the surrounding volume would need far more unknowns.

<a id="c-extract-method-calibration"></a>

#### Calibrating extraction to a golden solver

`extract.method.calibration`

A fast extractor is trusted only because it has been compared with a golden field solver on many structures and adjusted until the two agree within a stated tolerance.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Measuring the error
- Least-squares scale factor
- Residual error after calibration

Sample problem:

> A fast rule-based extractor is compared with a 3D field solver on a set of nets: net 1: fast 5.9 fF, golden 5.84 fF; net 2: fast 2.2 fF, golden 2.27 fF; net 3: fast 3.6 fF, golden 3.53 fF; net 4: fast 6.5 fF, golden 6.31 fF. What is the largest relative error of the fast extractor against the golden values, in percent of the golden value? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 3.08

Why: For each net compute |fast - golden| / golden. The largest is 3.08%.

<a id="extraction-signal-integrity-and-signoff-inductance"></a>

### Inductance

<a id="c-extract-ind-partial-inductance"></a>

#### Loop and partial inductance

`extract.ind.partial_inductance`

Inductance belongs to a current loop, not to a wire, so it depends on where the return current flows.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Partial self and mutual terms
- Where the return current flows
- Non-additivity and dense matrices

Sample problem:

> A signal wire has partial self inductance 550 pH, its return wire has partial self inductance 630 pH, and their partial mutual inductance is 210 pH. Current flows out on the signal and back on the return. What is the loop inductance, in pH?

Answer: 760

Why: With opposite currents the mutual term subtracts: $L_{loop} = L_s + L_r - 2M$ = 550 + 630 - 2 x 210 = 760 pH.

<a id="c-extract-ind-significance"></a>

#### When on-chip inductance matters

`extract.ind.significance`

Most on-chip nets are resistive enough that an RC model is accurate. Inductance matters on wide, low-resistance wires carrying fast edges: global clocks, wide buses and power distribution.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The knee frequency
- Inductive versus resistive impedance
- Time of flight and damping

Sample problem:

> A clock driver produces edges with a 10 to 90 percent rise time of 80 ps. Using the knee-frequency rule $f \approx 0.35/t_r$, what is the highest significant frequency in the signal, in GHz? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 4.37

Why: 0.35 / 80 ps = 4.37 GHz. Above this frequency the edge carries little energy, so this is the frequency at which to compare inductive and resistive impedance.

<a id="extraction-signal-integrity-and-signoff-parasitic-formats"></a>

### Parasitic formats

<a id="c-extract-format-spef"></a>

#### SPEF

`extract.format.spef`

The Standard Parasitic Exchange Format (SPEF, IEEE 1481) is how an extractor hands parasitics to timers, signal-integrity tools and power analysis.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The structure of a D_NET
- The header total
- What SPEF does and does not carry

Sample problem:

> Which information does a standard SPEF D_NET not record?
>
> A) Resistances between nodes
>
> B) Ground capacitances
>
> C) Coupling capacitances to other nets
>
> D) The wire's layer geometry and coordinates, unless optional extensions are used

Answer: The wire's layer geometry and coordinates, unless optional extensions are used

Why: SPEF is an electrical netlist of R and C elements. Geometry is abstracted away, which is why a tool cannot re-extract from SPEF alone.

<a id="c-extract-format-spef-counts"></a>

#### Reading a SPEF net section

`extract.format.spef_counts`

Reading SPEF fluently means predicting its contents from a net's topology and computing timing quantities directly from its entries.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Counting entries from topology
- Totals and units
- Elmore delay from the entries

Sample problem:

> An extractor writes the D_NET of a net with one driver pin and one sink pin. Its resistor network is a tree spanning the pins and 5 internal nodes. It puts one ground capacitor on every internal node and none on the pins, and the net has one coupling capacitor to other nets. How many entries does the CAP section have?

Answer: 6

Why: 5 ground capacitors plus 1 coupling capacitors: 6 entries.

<a id="c-extract-format-name-map"></a>

#### SPEF name maps and file size

`extract.format.name_map`

Full-chip SPEF files run to tens of gigabytes, and most of their bytes are names: long hierarchical instance and net names repeated in every entry.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Bytes saved per net
- Scaling to a whole chip
- The break-even point

Sample problem:

> In a SPEF file, a net's full hierarchical name is 53 characters long. With a name map, each reference is replaced by an index token of 4 characters (the asterisk and digits), and the map adds one line per net: the token, a space, the full name and a newline. The net's name appears 11 times in the body. How many bytes does the name map save for this net?

Answer: 480

Why: Each reference saves 53 - 4 = 49 bytes: 11 x 49 = 539. The map entry costs 4 + 1 + 53 + 1 = 59 bytes. Net saving 480 bytes.

<a id="extraction-signal-integrity-and-signoff-parasitic-reduction"></a>

### Parasitic reduction

<a id="c-extract-reduce-rc-reduction"></a>

#### RC network reduction

`extract.reduce.rc_reduction`

A detailed extraction can produce tens of millions of RC nodes, far more than a timer needs.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Why reduce
- Choosing the reduced model
- Accuracy, passivity and locality

Sample problem:

> Why must a reduced RC network be passive?
>
> A) Timers reject any network with resistors
>
> B) Passivity guarantees zero error
>
> C) A non-passive model can generate energy and make a downstream simulation unstable
>
> D) Passivity makes the file smaller

Answer: A non-passive model can generate energy and make a downstream simulation unstable

Why: RC interconnect is passive. A reduced model that is not can produce growing responses when combined with drivers, which is why PRIMA's passivity guarantee matters.

<a id="c-extract-reduce-moments"></a>

#### Moments of an RC tree

`extract.reduce.moments`

The moments of a network's impulse response are the coefficients of its transfer function's Taylor expansion in $s$.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The first moment
- The second moment
- Why lumping fails

Sample problem:

> An RC tree has resistors 0.2 kohm from the driver to node 1 (6 fF), 0.3 kohm from node 1 to node 2 (2 fF), 0.4 kohm from node 1 to node 3 (6 fF), each node with the stated capacitance to ground. One kohm times one fF is one ps. What is the first moment of the impulse response at node 3 (its Elmore delay), in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 5.2

Why: $m_1(i) = \sum_k R_{ik} C_k$, where $R_{ik}$ is the resistance shared by the paths to i and k. At node 3 this is 5.2 ps.

<a id="c-extract-reduce-node-elimination"></a>

#### Node elimination by star-mesh transform

`extract.reduce.node_elimination`

The workhorse of local RC reduction is eliminating one internal node at a time. Removing a node is Gaussian elimination on the network's nodal equations, which for a resistive star becomes the star-mesh transform: new resistors between every pair of former neighbours.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The star-mesh resistors
- Redistributing the capacitance
- Which nodes to eliminate

Sample problem:

> Internal node x has 7.5 fF to ground and resistors 90 ohm to node a, 130 ohm to node b, 190 ohm to node c. A reducer eliminates x with the star-mesh transform, which connects every pair of former neighbours i, j by $R_{ij} = R_i R_j \sum_k 1/R_k$ and splits x's capacitance among them in proportion to their conductances. What is the new resistance between nodes c and b, in ohms? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 594.44

Why: $\sum 1/R_k$ = 0.02407 S. $R_{cb}$ = 190 x 130 x 0.02407 = 594.44 ohm.

<a id="c-extract-reduce-elmore-preserving"></a>

#### Elmore-preserving elimination in an RC chain

`extract.reduce.elmore_preserving`

The conductance-proportional split of an eliminated node's capacitance is not just a heuristic: on an RC chain it preserves the Elmore delay at every downstream node exactly.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Splitting the eliminated capacitance
- The Elmore delay is unchanged
- The cost of naive lumping

Sample problem:

> An RC chain runs from a driver through 0.3 kohm to node n1 (5 fF), then 0.7 kohm to node n2 (9 fF). kohm times fF is ps. A reducer eliminates n1: it replaces the two resistors around n1 with one of 1 kohm and splits n1's capacitance between the driver end and n2 in proportion to the conductances of the two removed resistors. How much capacitance is added to n2, in fF? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 1.5

Why: n2's share is $(1/R_2)/(1/R_1 + 1/R_2) = R_1/(R_1+R_2)$ = 0.3 / 1, so n2 gains 1.5 fF; the driver end gets the remaining 3.5 fF.

<a id="c-extract-reduce-pi-model"></a>

#### The moment-matched pi model

`extract.reduce.pi_model`

A cell's delay depends on its load, but a resistive wire shields the driver from the far capacitance, so the total capacitance overstates the load.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The uniform line
- Admittance moments of a chain
- The resistance and its use

Sample problem:

> A uniform distributed RC line has total resistance 1600 ohm and total capacitance 48 fF. Its driving-point admittance has moments $y_1 = C$, $y_2 = -RC^2/3$ and $y_3 = 2R^2C^3/15$. The pi model matching them has $C_{far} = y_2^2/y_3$, $C_{near} = y_1 - C_{far}$ and $R_{\pi} = -y_3^2/y_2^3$. What is $R_{\pi}$, in ohms? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 768

Why: $R_\pi = (4R^4C^6/225)/(R^3C^6/27) = 12R/25$ = 768 ohm.

<a id="extraction-signal-integrity-and-signoff-signal-integrity"></a>

### Signal integrity

<a id="c-extract-si-miller-factor"></a>

#### The Miller factor of a coupling capacitor

`extract.si.miller_factor`

A coupling capacitor's effect on its victim depends on what the other end does. If the neighbour is quiet, the capacitor acts like one to ground.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Effective coupling
- Charge through the coupling
- Bounding with unknown aggressors

Sample problem:

> A victim net rises while its neighbour, coupled through 0.5 fF, switches in the opposite direction at the same time. Modelling the coupling capacitor as a grounded capacitor scaled by a Miller factor, what effective capacitance does it add to the victim's load, in fF? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 1

Why: The Miller factor is 2: the voltage change across the capacitor is 2 times the victim's own swing. Effective coupling 0.5 x 2 = 1 fF.

<a id="c-extract-si-effective-cap"></a>

#### Switching-dependent effective capacitance

`extract.si.effective_cap`

Once each coupling has a Miller factor, a victim's effective load is its ground and pin capacitance plus every coupling scaled by its factor.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- A specific switching scenario
- The worst case
- The spread between cases

Sample problem:

> A victim net has 3.6 fF of wire capacitance to ground and 3.6 fF of sink pin capacitance. During its transition, aggressor 1 (3.9 fF) switches in the same direction at the same time, aggressor 2 (2.4 fF) stays quiet, aggressor 3 (0.8 fF) stays quiet. Using Miller factors 0, 1 and 2, what effective load capacitance does the victim's driver see, in fF? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 10.4

Why: Add ground and pin capacitance, then each coupling times its Miller factor: 10.4 fF.

<a id="c-extract-si-crosstalk-delay"></a>

#### Crosstalk-induced delay

`extract.si.crosstalk_delay`

When an aggressor switches during a victim's transition, the victim's delay changes: slower if the aggressor opposes it, faster if it helps.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Delay with a quiet aggressor
- The delta delay
- Effect on setup and hold

Sample problem:

> Model the victim's driver as 2.2 kohm driving a lumped load, with 50% delay $t = 0.69 R C$ (kohm times fF is ps). The victim has 6.4 fF to ground (including pins) and 3.4 fF of coupling to one aggressor. What is the victim's delay with the aggressor quiet, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 14.88

Why: A quiet aggressor acts as ground, Miller factor 1: 0.69 x 2.2 x (6.4 + 3.4) = 14.88 ps.

<a id="c-extract-si-glitch"></a>

#### Crosstalk glitches

`extract.si.glitch`

A quiet net is not safe from its neighbours. When an aggressor switches, charge injected through the coupling capacitor bumps the victim's voltage, a glitch.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The capacitive divider
- Several aggressors
- Shielding

Sample problem:

> A quiet victim with 7.7 fF to ground is coupled through 0.5 fF to an aggressor that switches from 0 to 0.8 V. Treating the victim as floating (its driver too weak to respond during the fast edge), what glitch peak appears on the victim, in mV? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 48.8

Why: The capacitive divider gives $V_p = V_{DD} C_c/(C_c + C_g)$ = 0.8 x 0.5 / 8.2 = 48.8 mV. This is the upper bound on the glitch; a holding driver reduces it.

<a id="c-extract-si-noise-immunity"></a>

#### Glitch peak with a holding driver and noise immunity

`extract.si.noise_immunity`

A real victim is not floating: its driver holds it at its rail through a finite resistance, and that resistance drains injected charge during the aggressor's edge.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The holding-resistance model
- Noise margin
- Rise time versus the bound

Sample problem:

> A quiet victim is held low by a driver of resistance 3.9 kohm and has 3.4 fF to ground. An aggressor coupled through 3.6 fF ramps from 0 to 1 V in 30 ps. For a linear ramp, the victim voltage peaks at the end of the ramp at $V_p = V_{DD} \frac{R C_c}{t_r}\left(1 - e^{-t_r/\tau}\right)$ with $\tau = R (C_c + C_g)$; kohm times fF is ps. What is the glitch peak, in mV? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 312

Why: $\tau$ = 3.9 x 7 = 27.3 ps. $V_p$ = 1000 x (3.9 x 3.6 / 30) x (1 - exp(-30/27.3)) = 312 mV.

<a id="c-extract-si-timing-windows"></a>

#### Timing windows and aggressor filtering

`extract.si.timing_windows`

Assuming every aggressor switches against every victim at the worst moment is safe but very pessimistic.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Window overlap
- Pessimism removed
- The windowed delta and the iteration

Sample problem:

> A victim switches somewhere in the window 250 to 300 ps. Its aggressors are aggressor 1: 1.7 fF, switching window 210 to 240 ps; aggressor 2: 2.6 fF, switching window 120 to 130 ps; aggressor 3: 1.8 fF, switching window 240 to 250 ps. An aggressor can affect the victim's delay only if its window overlaps the victim's (windows that touch count as overlapping). Non-overlapping aggressors are treated as quiet. How many aggressors survive the timing-window filter?

Answer: 1

Why: Check each window against [250, 300]: 1 overlap.

<a id="extraction-signal-integrity-and-signoff-signoff"></a>

### Signoff

<a id="c-extract-signoff-rc-corners"></a>

#### RC corners and signoff scenarios

`extract.signoff.rc_corners`

Interconnect varies with the process just as transistors do: metal width, thickness and dielectric height all have tolerances.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Counting scenarios
- Corner geometry
- Which corner is worst

Sample problem:

> A chip has 4 functional modes. Setup is signed off at 2 PVT corners, each with 3 RC corners; hold is signed off at 5 PVT corners, each with 2 RC corners. Every mode is checked at every corner combination for its check type. How many timing scenarios must be run?

Answer: 64

Why: Setup: 4 x 2 x 3 = 24. Hold: 4 x 5 x 2 = 40. Total 64. Multi-mode multi-corner analysis multiplies quickly, which is why extraction runs once per RC corner and its results are shared across the PVT corners that use it.

<a id="c-extract-signoff-em-ir"></a>

#### Electromigration and IR-drop signoff

`extract.signoff.em_ir`

Extracted resistance feeds two reliability and power checks. Electromigration (EM) signoff checks that current densities in wires and vias are low enough for the chip to last its rated lifetime.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Current density
- IR drop along a strap
- Lifetime scaling

Sample problem:

> A power strap 0.2 um wide and 0.08 um thick carries a DC current of 3.6 mA. Its electromigration limit is 200 mA/um^2. What is the current density in the strap, in mA/um^2? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 225

Why: $J = I/(WT)$ = 3.6 / (0.2 x 0.08) = 225 mA/um^2, which exceeds the 200 mA/um^2 limit.

<a id="c-extract-signoff-checklist"></a>

#### The signoff checklist

`extract.signoff.checklist`

Signoff is the set of checks a design must pass before tape-out, each run with the qualified tools at the worst conditions for what it checks.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The categories
- Matching checks to conditions
- The checklist after changes

Sample problem:

> Which signoff check proves that the layout implements the netlist that was timed?
>
> A) Layout versus schematic (LVS)
>
> B) Design rule checking (DRC)
>
> C) Logical equivalence checking between RTL and netlist
>
> D) Static IR-drop analysis

Answer: Layout versus schematic (LVS)

Why: LVS extracts devices and connectivity from the layout and compares them with the netlist. DRC checks manufacturability, not connectivity.

<a id="c-extract-signoff-eco"></a>

#### Engineering change orders

`extract.signoff.eco`

An engineering change order (ECO) is a targeted change to a nearly finished design: a logic fix found late in verification, or a timing or noise fix found at signoff.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Functional and timing ECOs
- Metal-only ECOs and spare cells
- Side effects and re-verification

Sample problem:

> Why are late changes made as ECOs rather than by re-running synthesis and place-and-route?
>
> A) A full re-run perturbs the whole design and throws away its closure, while an ECO touches only what must change
>
> B) ECOs are always more optimal
>
> C) Synthesis cannot be run twice on one design
>
> D) Re-running the flow is forbidden by the foundry

Answer: A full re-run perturbs the whole design and throws away its closure, while an ECO touches only what must change

Why: Timing, SI and physical closure took weeks. A local change preserves them everywhere else.

<a id="c-extract-signoff-spare-cells"></a>

#### Metal-only ECOs with spare cells

`extract.signoff.spare_cells`

A metal-only ECO is a small physical design problem with tight constraints: find spare cells of the right types close to where the fix belongs, wire them in with new metal, and change as few mask layers as possible.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Finding the nearest spare
- Wirelength of the new net
- Masks changed

Sample problem:

> A metal-only ECO needs one NOR2 near the point (330, 50) um. The unused spare cells are: NAND2 at (400, 60), NOR2 at (460, 300), NOR2 at (140, 370), NOR2 at (190, 280), INV at (40, 480). Using Manhattan distance, how far is the nearest usable spare cell, in um?

Answer: 370

Why: Only NOR2 spares qualify. The nearest is 370 um away by Manhattan distance, which is what a router would roughly have to wire.

<a id="c-extract-signoff-ppa-closure"></a>

#### PPA closure

`extract.signoff.ppa_closure`

Closing a design means meeting its performance target within its power and area budgets, all measured by signoff tools: PPA closure.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The trade-offs
- Choosing a fix
- Closure with margins

Sample problem:

> What does PPA closure mean at signoff?
>
> A) Meeting the timing target while keeping power and area within budget, all at signoff accuracy
>
> B) Passing DRC and LVS
>
> C) Minimizing area while ignoring timing
>
> D) Meeting timing at any power cost

Answer: Meeting the timing target while keeping power and area within budget, all at signoff accuracy

Why: Power, performance and area trade against each other. Closure means all three meet their targets together, measured by signoff tools.

<a id="extraction-signal-integrity-and-signoff-frontier-agent-first-futures"></a>

### Frontier: agent-first futures

<a id="c-extract-frontier-core-vs-surface"></a>

#### The extractor's core and change surface

`extract.frontier.core_vs_surface`

An extractor built for an agent-first flow is split into a small immutable core and a change surface that agents and engineers can adjust without touching the core.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Core and change surface
- Tiers for extraction requests
- Designing the capacitance-model seam

Sample problem:

> Why must netlist correctness stay in the extractor's core, not in a plug-in?
>
> A) Netlist building is the slowest step
>
> B) A parasitic attached to the wrong net corrupts every downstream analysis, whatever the accuracy mode
>
> C) Customers never ask to change it
>
> D) Plug-ins cannot read layout

Answer: A parasitic attached to the wrong net corrupts every downstream analysis, whatever the accuracy mode

Why: Connectivity is an invariant. A fast or approximate mode may trade accuracy, but never which net a resistor or capacitor belongs to.

<a id="c-extract-frontier-calibration-tier1"></a>

#### Calibration as a Tier 1 change

`extract.frontier.calibration_tier1`

Calibration is the extractor's most frequent change, and it should never require a recompile.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Fitting the table entry
- Applying the calibrated table
- Validation before promotion

Sample problem:

> An extractor's fast mode applies one scale factor per pattern class, stored in a configuration table. For the class M2 coupling at minimum spacing, new golden 3D-solver samples give: 2.2 fF fast vs 2.22 fF golden; 1 fF fast vs 1.01 fF golden; 7.6 fF fast vs 7.91 fF golden. What least-squares scale factor $k$ (minimizing $\sum (k x_i - g_i)^2$) should the Tier 1 table entry hold? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 1.0379

Why: $k = \sum x_i g_i / \sum x_i^2$ = 66.01 / 63.6 = 1.0379. Writing it into the table is a configuration change: no recompile, only a validation run.

<a id="c-extract-frontier-fast-accurate"></a>

#### Fast and accurate extraction in an agent loop

`extract.frontier.fast_accurate`

An agent that optimizes a layout cannot wait for signoff extraction after every move.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Error bounds on fast results
- Which nets to recurse on
- What the loop saves

Sample problem:

> Fast extraction is within 4% of the accurate extractor on net capacitance. A net's interconnect-driven delay is 53 ps and scales linearly with its capacitance. What delay error bound, in ps, should an agent attach to this net's fast-mode timing? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 2.12

Why: 4% of 53 ps = 2.12 ps. Slack within this band of zero cannot be trusted from fast mode.

<a id="c-extract-frontier-differential-eco-check"></a>

#### Differential parasitic checks for ECOs

`extract.frontier.differential_eco_check`

When an agent claims that an ECO rerouted three nets, the claim is checkable: re-extract, compare every net's parasitics before and after, and confirm that only the claimed nets and their geometric neighbours moved.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Which nets moved
- Unexpected movers
- The pass rule

Sample problem:

> An agent's metal-only ECO claims to reroute n15. Its geometric neighbours, whose coupling may legitimately change, are n11. Re-extraction gives total net capacitance before and after, in fF: n10 3.1 to 1.1; n11 11.1 to 11.1; n12 3.1 to 3.09; n13 2.9 to 2.89; n14 4.3 to 4.3; n15 1.7 to 1.71; n16 10.7 to 10.71. A net has moved if its capacitance changed by more than 0.01 fF. How many nets moved?

Answer: 1

Why: Compare |after - before| with 0.01 fF for each net: 1 moved.

<a id="c-extract-frontier-agentic-signoff"></a>

#### Agentic signoff and ECO loops

`extract.frontier.agentic_signoff`

An agentic signoff loop reads the engines' reports, timing and SI violations, IR and EM hot spots, DRC markers, proposes ECOs, runs them through extraction and analysis, and iterates until the checklist is clean, with a human approving the final change.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Reports in, verified ECOs out
- Guarding against bad loops
- Fast engines, accurate signoff, and the flywheel

Sample problem:

> In an agentic signoff loop, what does the agent read at each iteration?
>
> A) Typed reports from the engines: timing and SI violations, IR and EM hot spots, DRC markers
>
> B) Only the final tape-out checklist
>
> C) The RTL source code
>
> D) The raw layout polygons of the whole chip

Answer: Typed reports from the engines: timing and SI violations, IR and EM hot spots, DRC markers

Why: The agent reasons over the engines' outputs. Compact, structured reports let it localize problems and propose targeted ECOs.

---

## Physical Verification and DFM

Layer 8. GDSII and OASIS, DRC engines, LVS as graph matching, antenna and fill, hotspots and tape-out.

Builds on: Computational Geometry for Layout, Fabrication and Design-Technology Co-optimization, Routing, Graph Algorithms for EDA, Floorplanning and Placement, CMOS Circuits and Cell Libraries.

Topics covered:

- Physical verification overview; GDSII and OASIS: what a layout stream preserves
- Design rule checking: width, spacing, enclosure, extension, density, antenna; rule decks; edge-based and hierarchical DRC engines
- Layout versus schematic: device recognition, netlist extraction, graph-isomorphism matching (Netgen-style partition refinement)
- Electrical rule checking
- Antenna effects and fixes, metal fill and density rules
- DFM: lithography hotspot detection, double-patterning coloring checks, critical area, recommended rules
- Tape-out, mask data handoff, signoff physical checks
- KLayout, Magic, Netgen in practice

Subdomains: [Layout formats](#physical-verification-and-dfm-layout-formats), [Design rule checking](#physical-verification-and-dfm-design-rule-checking), [Layout versus schematic](#physical-verification-and-dfm-layout-versus-schematic), [Antenna rules](#physical-verification-and-dfm-antenna-rules), [Metal fill](#physical-verification-and-dfm-metal-fill), [Design for manufacturing](#physical-verification-and-dfm-design-for-manufacturing), [Tape-out](#physical-verification-and-dfm-tape-out), [Frontier: agent-first futures](#physical-verification-and-dfm-frontier-agent-first-futures)

<a id="physical-verification-and-dfm-layout-formats"></a>

### Layout formats

<a id="c-pv-format-gds-records"></a>

#### GDSII records and stream structure

`pv.format.gds_records`

Physical verification starts from the layout stream that will become masks. GDSII, the oldest and most widely exchanged stream format, is a flat sequence of binary records that describe libraries, structures (cells) and the elements inside them.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Records and element sizes
- Counting records in a structure
- The byte size of a structure

Sample problem:

> A GDSII BOUNDARY element is written as the records BOUNDARY, LAYER, DATATYPE, XY and ENDEL. Every record has a 4-byte header (2-byte length, record type, data type); LAYER and DATATYPE each carry one 2-byte integer, and XY carries 4-byte x and y integers for every point, with the first point repeated at the end to close the ring. How many bytes does a polygon with 8 vertices occupy?

Answer: 96

Why: BOUNDARY 4 + LAYER 6 + DATATYPE 6 + XY (4 + 8 x 9 points) + ENDEL 4 = 96 bytes. The XY record lists 9 points because the ring is closed by repeating the first vertex.

<a id="c-pv-format-gds-oasis"></a>

#### GDSII and OASIS

`pv.format.gds_oasis`

OASIS is the newer stream format designed to replace GDSII for very large layouts, especially post-OPC mask data.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Variable-length integers
- Storing a regular array
- Why OASIS files are smaller

Sample problem:

> OASIS writes an unsigned integer in 7-bit groups, one group per byte, with the top bit of each byte marking whether another byte follows. GDSII writes every coordinate as a fixed 4-byte integer. How many bytes does OASIS need for the value 5 (for example a coordinate delta in DBU)?
>
> A) 0 bytes
>
> B) 4 bytes
>
> C) 1 bytes
>
> D) 2 bytes

Answer: 1 bytes

Why: 5 needs 3 bits (it lies in [2^2, 2^3)), and each byte carries 7 payload bits, so ceil(3 / 7) = 1 bytes. Small deltas between neighbouring vertices therefore cost one or two bytes instead of four.

<a id="c-pv-format-units-grid"></a>

#### Database units and the manufacturing grid

`pv.format.units_grid`

Layout databases store integers, not lengths. The stream's UNITS record says how long one database unit (DBU) is, and every coordinate counts those units.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Database units
- The coordinate range
- The manufacturing grid

Sample problem:

> A layout's UNITS record sets the database unit to 0.25 nm, and every coordinate is stored as an integer count of database units. A vertex sits at x = 31.5045 um. What integer is stored for its x coordinate?

Answer: 126018

Why: One um is 4000 database units of 0.25 nm, so 31.5045 um is 31.5045 x 4000 = 126018.

<a id="c-pv-format-hierarchy"></a>

#### Hierarchy with SREF and AREF

`pv.format.hierarchy`

A layout is a directed acyclic graph of cells: a cell holds shapes and placements of other cells.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Flattening a cell tree
- Placements as paths in the cell DAG
- AREF versus SREF

Sample problem:

> Cell LEAF holds 29 shapes. Cell MID holds 14 shapes and 3 SREFs of LEAF. Cell TOP holds 13 shapes, 7 SREFs of MID and one AREF of LEAF with 8 columns and 2 rows. How many shapes does TOP contain once fully flattened?

Answer: 1184

Why: Flatten bottom-up: MID expands to 14 + 3 x 29 = 101 shapes. TOP = 13 + 7 x 101 + 8 x 2 x 29 = 1184. The hierarchy stores only 56 shapes.

<a id="physical-verification-and-dfm-design-rule-checking"></a>

### Design rule checking

<a id="c-pv-drc-rule-types"></a>

#### Design rule types

`pv.drc.rule_types`

Design rules are the foundry's contract with the designer: if every rule passes, the layout is manufacturable with acceptable yield.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Single-layer rules
- Two-layer rules
- Context-dependent rules

Sample problem:

> One U-shaped metal polygon has its two prongs 25 nm apart, inside the same shape. Which rule type covers that gap?
>
> A) Notch, the spacing between facing edges of one polygon
>
> B) Enclosure of the prongs
>
> C) Minimum width of the prongs
>
> D) Minimum area of the polygon

Answer: Notch, the spacing between facing edges of one polygon

Why: A notch is same-polygon spacing. Engines that check spacing only between different shapes must check notches separately.

<a id="c-pv-drc-width-spacing"></a>

#### Width and spacing checks

`pv.drc.width_spacing`

Width and spacing are the bulk of any rule deck and the first checks an engine must get exactly right.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Width violations
- Euclidean spacing
- Width-dependent spacing

Sample problem:

> The minimum width rule on metal 1 is 40 nm. The layer holds the separate wires W1 = $[71, 87] \times [0, 257]$, W2 = $[10, 375] \times [400, 474]$, W3 = $[18, 92] \times [800, 1123]$, W4 = $[69, 309] \times [1200, 1233]$ (nm). How many wires violate the width rule?

Answer: 2

Why: A rectangle's width is its shorter side. 2 of the wires have a shorter side below 40 nm; their length does not matter.

<a id="c-pv-drc-enclosure-extension"></a>

#### Enclosure and extension rules

`pv.drc.enclosure_extension`

Enclosure and extension rules relate two layers. They keep a via cut inside the metal it lands on despite misalignment, and keep a poly gate long enough past diffusion that the transistor does not leak at its ends.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Enclosure
- Two-sided enclosure rules
- Extension and endcaps

Sample problem:

> A via cut is $[261, 311] \times [159, 209]$ and the metal above it is $[254, 321] \times [138, 211]$ (nm). What is the via's enclosure by the metal, the smallest distance from a via edge to the corresponding metal edge, in nm?

Answer: 2

Why: The four margins are left 7, right 10, bottom 21, top 2 nm; the enclosure is the minimum, 2 nm.

<a id="c-pv-drc-notch-eol"></a>

#### Notch, end-of-line and run-length rules

`pv.drc.notch_eol`

Simple spacing rules treat every pair of facing edges alike. Edges of the same polygon, wire ends, and long parallel runs of wide wires all have their own rules, because lithography and etch treat them differently.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Notches
- End-of-line spacing
- Parallel-run-length tables

Sample problem:

> A comb-shaped polygon is one horizontal spine with 5 vertical prongs rising from it; the prongs span x-ranges [0, 70], [140, 280], [350, 410], [510, 570], [680, 800] (nm). The notch rule requires at least 90 nm between two edges of the same polygon that face each other. How many notches violate it?

Answer: 2

Why: Each gap between neighbouring prongs is a notch: the edges belong to one polygon, so a merged-shape spacing check sees it. 2 of the 4 gaps are below 90 nm.

<a id="c-pv-drc-area-via"></a>

#### Minimum area and via rules

`pv.drc.area_via`

Area and via rules are where routers most often produce violations: short wire stubs are too small, and wide wires need more than one via cut.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Minimum area
- Fitting a via array
- Minimum-cut rules

Sample problem:

> An isolated metal stub is 50 nm wide and 72 nm long. The minimum area rule is 8000 square nm. By how many nm must the stub be lengthened, keeping its width, to meet the rule? Give the smallest whole number of nm.

Answer: 88

Why: The stub has area 50 x 72 = 3600. It needs length ceil(8000 / 50) = 160 nm, so 88 nm more.

<a id="c-pv-drc-engine"></a>

#### How a DRC engine works

`pv.drc.engine`

A DRC engine turns a rule deck and a layout into a list of violations. Its core is a small set of geometric primitives (merging, Boolean operations, sizing, edge-pair distance queries) driven by spatial data structures so that each shape is compared only with nearby shapes.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Candidate pairs and spatial filtering
- Polygon-based checks by sizing
- Edge-based and polygon-based engines

Sample problem:

> A DRC engine checks a 27 nm Euclidean spacing rule. Before computing exact distances it keeps only pairs whose bounding boxes, one of them expanded by 27 nm on every side, overlap with positive area. The shapes are R1 = $[18, 56] \times [80, 94]$, R2 = $[79, 103] \times [95, 111]$, R3 = $[33, 72] \times [14, 27]$, R4 = $[127, 141] \times [60, 86]$, R5 = $[11, 32] \times [49, 59]$, R6 = $[27, 57] \times [104, 131]$ (nm). How many pairs reach the exact distance test?
>
> A) 15 pairs
>
> B) 5 pairs
>
> C) 6 pairs
>
> D) 7 pairs

Answer: 6 pairs

Why: A pair survives when both its x gap and its y gap are below 27 nm. That keeps 6 of the 15 pairs. The exact test then confirms 6 of them as violations: a diagonal pair can pass the box filter yet be 27 nm or more apart.

<a id="c-pv-drc-plane-sweep"></a>

#### Sweep-line spacing checks

`pv.drc.plane_sweep`

Batch DRC engines process a layer with a sweep: a vertical line moves across the die, and only shapes near the line are compared.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The active set
- Querying the active set
- What the sweep saves

Sample problem:

> A sweep-line spacing check for a 22 nm rule moves a vertical line left to right. A shape enters the active set at its left edge and leaves at its right edge plus 22 nm, so it stays available for comparison with shapes starting within the rule distance (closed intervals). The shapes are R1 = $[15, 33] \times [67, 124]$, R2 = $[43, 99] \times [10, 30]$, R3 = $[159, 169] \times [9, 19]$, R4 = $[119, 173] \times [69, 114]$, R5 = $[92, 140] \times [95, 151]$ (nm). What is the largest number of shapes active at once?

Answer: 3

Why: Each shape is active on [x1, x2 + 22]. The maximum number of overlapping intervals, found by scanning the event points, is 3. The active set, not the whole layer, bounds the memory and the per-event work.

<a id="c-pv-drc-hierarchical"></a>

#### Hierarchical DRC

`pv.drc.hierarchical`

A modern chip repeats a few thousand cells billions of times. Hierarchical DRC checks each cell once and reuses the result wherever the surroundings are the same, checking only the regions where instances interact.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Reporting errors once per cell
- Interaction regions between instances
- The context problem

Sample problem:

> Cell A has 3 internal spacing violations and is placed 123 times; cell B has 2 internal violations and is placed 26 times; the top cell adds 4 violations between instances. No instance's context changes the internal results. How many violations does a hierarchical DRC run report, listing each cell's errors once in the cell's own coordinates?
>
> A) 9
>
> B) 10
>
> C) 425
>
> D) 5

Answer: 9

Why: Each cell's internal errors are reported once: 3 + 2, plus the 4 top-level ones, 9. A flat run would report 425.

<a id="c-pv-drc-rule-deck"></a>

#### Rule decks and derived layers

`pv.drc.rule_deck`

A rule deck is a program. It names the stream's layers, derives new layers by Boolean and sizing operations, and runs checks on them, each tagged with a rule name.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Derived layers by Boolean operations
- Sizing inside a deck
- What a rule deck is

Sample problem:

> A rule deck derives GATE = POLY AND ACTIVE. POLY is $[71, 90] \times [1, 113]$ and ACTIVE is $[11, 112] \times [50, 85]$ (nm). What is the area of GATE, in square nm?
>
> A) 4998 square nm
>
> B) 3535 square nm
>
> C) 665 square nm
>
> D) 2128 square nm

Answer: 665 square nm

Why: AND keeps the region covered by both layers: the intersection, area 665.

<a id="physical-verification-and-dfm-layout-versus-schematic"></a>

### Layout versus schematic

<a id="c-pv-lvs-device-recognition"></a>

#### Device recognition from layer Booleans

`pv.lvs.device_recognition`

LVS compares the circuit drawn in the layout with the schematic. The layout has no devices, only shapes, so the first step is recognizing devices from layer combinations: a transistor is wherever poly crosses diffusion, typed by the well and implant layers around it, with W and L measured from the gate region.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Gates from poly and diffusion
- Channel width and length
- Device types from wells and implants

Sample problem:

> An LVS deck recognizes a transistor wherever POLY crosses DIFF completely (GATE = POLY AND DIFF). The diffusion regions are D1 = $[82, 464] \times [50, 190]$, D2 = $[68, 448] \times [350, 485]$ and the vertical poly lines are P1 = $[495, 515] \times [-7, 531]$, P2 = $[201, 221] \times [-2, 224]$, P3 = $[166, 186] \times [308, 530]$, P4 = $[284, 304] \times [321, 521]$ (nm). How many transistors does device recognition find?

Answer: 3

Why: A poly line that spans several diffusion rows makes one gate in each row it crosses inside the row's x-range, and none where it passes beside a row. Counting crossings gives 3 transistors from 4 poly lines.

<a id="c-pv-lvs-extraction"></a>

#### Layout netlist extraction

`pv.lvs.extraction`

After devices are recognized, the extractor builds the nets: which shapes are electrically connected through overlaps and vias.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Connectivity by union-find
- Labels, shorts and net names
- Critical vias and opens

Sample problem:

> Metal 1 wires (horizontal centerlines): h1 at y = 1 from x = 3 to 8; h2 at y = 3 from x = 2 to 6; h3 at y = 2 from x = 1 to 7. Metal 2 wires (vertical): v1 at x = 9 from y = 0 to 4; v2 at x = 2 from y = 5 to 8; v3 at x = 3 from y = 0 to 2. Vias between metal 1 and metal 2 at: none. Two wires on the same layer and the same track connect when their ranges overlap or touch; a metal 1 and a metal 2 wire connect only through a via at a point on both, never by merely crossing. How many nets does connectivity extraction find?

Answer: 6

Why: Union the wires that overlap on a track and the wire pairs joined by each via; 6 wires collapse into 6 connected components, each one net. Crossings without a via stay separate.

<a id="c-pv-lvs-reduction"></a>

#### Device reduction and property comparison

`pv.lvs.reduction`

Layouts draw devices differently from schematics: one schematic transistor becomes four parallel fingers, a resistor becomes a serpentine of segments.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Parallel merging
- The merged device's width
- Resistors and property tolerance

Sample problem:

> An extracted netlist (W and L in nm) is: M1 nmos g=C s=Y d=VDD W=160 L=60; M2 nmos g=C s=Y d=VDD W=130 L=60; M3 nmos g=C s=Y d=VDD W=130 L=60; M4 pmos g=B s=Z d=Y W=250 L=60; M5 pmos g=A s=Y d=Z W=240 L=30; M6 pmos g=A s=Y d=Z W=150 L=30; M7 pmos g=A s=Y d=Z W=130 L=30; M8 pmos g=B s=Z d=Y W=140 L=40; M9 pmos g=B s=Z d=Y W=300 L=40; M10 pmos g=A s=Y d=Z W=260 L=30; M11 nmos g=C s=Y d=VDD W=370 L=60. The LVS tool merges devices in parallel: same type, same gate net, the same pair of source and drain nets in either order (source and drain are interchangeable), and equal L; the merged device's W is the sum. How many devices remain after parallel merging?

Answer: 4

Why: Group the devices by (type, gate, unordered source/drain pair, L). There are 4 groups; a device with a different L stays separate. Merging is what lets a 4-finger layout transistor match one schematic device.

<a id="c-pv-lvs-graph-matching"></a>

#### LVS as graph matching

`pv.lvs.graph_matching`

LVS asks whether the layout netlist and the schematic netlist describe the same circuit.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The device-net bipartite graph
- Isomorphism and invariants
- From mismatch to diagnosis

Sample problem:

> LVS models a netlist as a bipartite graph with one vertex per device and one per net, and one edge per device terminal (gate, source, drain; bulk ignored). For the netlist M1 pmos g=A s=VDD d=Y1; M2 pmos g=B s=VDD d=Y1; M3 nmos g=A s=GND d=n1; M4 nmos g=B s=n1 d=Y1, how many edges does the graph have?
>
> A) 16
>
> B) 8
>
> C) 12
>
> D) 10

Answer: 12

Why: Each of the 4 transistors contributes three terminal edges: 12. The graph has 6 net vertices.

<a id="c-pv-lvs-partition-refinement"></a>

#### Partition refinement in netlist comparison

`pv.lvs.partition_refinement`

Partition refinement is the algorithm at the heart of LVS tools such as Netgen and Gemini.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- One round of refinement
- Rounds until stable
- The stable partition

Sample problem:

> A transistor netlist is: M1 pmos g=A s=VDD d=Y1; M2 nmos g=A s=GND d=Y1; M3 pmos g=Y1 s=VDD d=n1; M4 pmos g=B s=n1 d=Y2; M5 nmos g=Y1 s=GND d=Y2; M6 nmos g=B s=GND d=Y2. Treat the netlist as a bipartite graph of devices and nets. Initially devices are coloured by type, VDD and GND each form a class of their own (they are matched by name), and every other net is coloured by its number of device terminals. In each round, every vertex gets a new colour made of its current colour plus the multiset of (terminal kind, neighbour colour) over its edges, where the terminal kinds are gate and source/drain (source and drain are interchangeable). The initial partition has 7 classes. How many classes are there after one round?

Answer: 12

Why: Recolouring by (colour, neighbour multiset) splits classes whose members see different neighbourhoods. The class counts by round are 7, 12, 13.

<a id="c-pv-lvs-ambiguity"></a>

#### Symmetry and ambiguity in LVS matching

`pv.lvs.ambiguity`

Refinement cannot separate vertices that are truly symmetric: two identical inverters with private inputs and outputs look the same from every angle.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Classes refinement cannot split
- Breaking ties
- Names, permutations and regular arrays

Sample problem:

> A layout netlist is: M1 pmos g=A s=VDD d=Y1; M2 nmos g=A s=GND d=Y1; M3 pmos g=B s=VDD d=Y2; M4 nmos g=B s=GND d=Y2. Treat the netlist as a bipartite graph of devices and nets. Initially devices are coloured by type, VDD and GND each form a class of their own (they are matched by name), and every other net is coloured by its number of device terminals. In each round, every vertex gets a new colour made of its current colour plus the multiset of (terminal kind, neighbour colour) over its edges, where the terminal kinds are gate and source/drain (source and drain are interchangeable). Refinement runs until the number of classes stops changing. Only VDD and GND are matched by name; no other port names are used. How many classes of the stable partition still contain more than one vertex?
>
> A) 2
>
> B) 6
>
> C) 4
>
> D) 0

Answer: 4

Why: Identical gates with private inputs and outputs are automorphic images of each other, so refinement can never separate them. The stable partition has 6 classes, 4 of them with more than one member; the matcher must break each tie by an arbitrary choice and refine again.

<a id="c-pv-lvs-errors"></a>

#### Diagnosing LVS errors

`pv.lvs.errors`

An LVS report is a list of symptoms: unmatched nets, unmatched devices, property errors.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Shorts and opens
- Device and property errors
- Debugging order

Sample problem:

> Schematic net OUT appears in the layout as two nets, one with the driver and one with the loads. What is the error?
>
> A) A short between OUT and another net
>
> B) An open: a missing via or a gap breaks OUT in two
>
> C) A swapped gate connection
>
> D) A floating well

Answer: An open: a missing via or a gap breaks OUT in two

Why: One schematic net matching two layout nets is the signature of a break in connectivity.

<a id="c-pv-lvs-erc"></a>

#### Electrical rule checking

`pv.lvs.erc`

Electrical rule checks look for circuits that are connected as drawn but electrically wrong: floating gates, untapped wells, two drivers on one net, devices exposed to voltages beyond their rating.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Floating gates
- Well taps
- Other electrical rules

Sample problem:

> An ERC deck flags a floating gate net: a net that reaches only gate terminals and is not a port of the cell. The netlist is M1 pmos g=A s=VDD d=Y1; M2 pmos g=B s=VDD d=Y1; M3 nmos g=A s=GND d=n1; M4 nmos g=B s=n1 d=Y1; M5 pmos g=C s=VDD d=n2; M6 pmos g=Y1 s=n2 d=Y2; M7 nmos g=C s=GND d=Y2; M8 nmos g=Y1 s=GND d=Y2. Besides VDD, GND and the outputs, the cell's input ports are: B, C. How many floating gate nets are flagged?
>
> A) 0
>
> B) 3
>
> C) 1
>
> D) 2

Answer: 1

Why: The nets that touch only gates are A, B, C. Those not listed as input ports have no driver at all: 1 floating nets, which would leave both transistors partly on.

<a id="physical-verification-and-dfm-antenna-rules"></a>

### Antenna rules

<a id="c-pv-antenna-rules"></a>

#### Antenna rules

`pv.antenna.rules`

During manufacturing, plasma etching of each metal layer charges the exposed metal.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The area antenna ratio
- The longest safe wire
- Side-wall ratios

Sample problem:

> When metal 2 is etched, a net's metal 2 pieces 85 by 0.28 um, 16 by 0.4 um are connected to the gates W = 0.65 um, L = 0.13 um; W = 1 um, L = 0.13 um and to no diffusion. Using the area antenna ratio (connected metal area over total gate area), what is the net's metal 2 antenna ratio? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 140.8

Why: Metal area = 30.2 square um; gate area = 0.2145 square um (W x L summed over the gates). Ratio = 140.8. All gates on the net share the collected charge, so their areas add.

<a id="c-pv-antenna-cumulative"></a>

#### Partial and cumulative antenna ratios

`pv.antenna.cumulative`

Antenna damage happens layer by layer. When metal $i$ is etched, the layers above it do not yet exist, so only metal connected to the gate through layers 1 to $i$ is electrically attached.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Partial ratios
- Cumulative ratios
- The worst layer

Sample problem:

> A gate of area 0.07 square um connects to this metal: metal 1: 54 square um connected through layers up to 1; metal 2: 21 square um connected through layers up to 2; metal 3: 15 square um connected through layers up to 3; metal 4: 49 square um connected through layers up to 4; metal 3: another 55 square um that reaches the gate only through metal 4. The partial ratio of layer i counts only the layer-i metal already connected to the gate when layer i is etched, that is, connected through layers 1 to i. The cumulative ratio at layer i is the sum of the partial ratios of layers 1 to i. What is the partial antenna ratio of metal 4? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 700

Why: Metal 4 counts 49 square um. Ratio = 49 / 0.07 = 700.

<a id="c-pv-antenna-diode"></a>

#### Antenna diodes

`pv.antenna.diode`

The standard antenna fix is a reverse-biased diode on the gate's net: a small diffusion region that leaks the plasma charge to the substrate before it can stress the oxide.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Removing excess metal
- Sizing the diode protection
- Diodes on nets with several gates

Sample problem:

> A net has 241 square um of metal 3 connected to a single gate of area 0.225 square um. The metal 3 area ratio limit without protection is 450. How much metal 3 area, in square um, would have to be moved off the net's metal 3 to meet the limit? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 139.75

Why: The allowed area is 450 x 0.225 = 101.25 square um, so 241 - 101.25 = 139.75 square um must go (in practice by a layer jump rather than by deleting wire).

<a id="c-pv-antenna-jumper"></a>

#### Layer jumpers and antenna repair

`pv.antenna.jumper`

A layer jumper breaks a long lower-layer route near the gate and carries it over a higher layer.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- How a jump cuts the antenna
- Where to jump
- Jump or diode

Sample problem:

> A 276 um long metal 1 route, 0.2 um wide, connects to a gate of area 0.065 square um. The router breaks it 12 um from the gate and carries the rest over metal 2, dropping back to metal 1 only at the far end. What is the metal 1 partial antenna ratio seen by the gate after the jump? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 36.9

Why: Before the jump the gate saw 849.2; after it, only the 12 um stub is connected when metal 1 is etched: 0.2 x 12 / 0.065 = 36.9. The far metal 1 piece joins only through metal 2, too late to charge the gate.

<a id="physical-verification-and-dfm-metal-fill"></a>

### Metal fill

<a id="c-pv-fill-density"></a>

#### Metal fill and density

`pv.fill.density`

Chemical-mechanical polishing removes material at a rate that depends on the local pattern density: sparse regions dish, dense regions erode.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Density of one window
- Checking a tiling of windows
- Density from routing pitch

Sample problem:

> A density window is $[0, 70] \times [0, 70]$ um. The metal shapes near it are R1 = $[13, 41] \times [1, 23]$, R2 = $[38, 51] \times [22, 53]$, R3 = $[-8, 24] \times [41, 54]$ (um); some overlap each other and some extend past the window. What is the metal density of the window, in percent? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 27.1

Why: Clip every shape to the window (AND), merge the clipped shapes (OR) so overlaps count once, and take the union area: 1328 square um out of 4900, 27.1 percent.

<a id="c-pv-fill-insertion"></a>

#### Fill insertion to a density target

`pv.fill.insertion`

Fill tools add electrically inactive metal shapes to windows below the minimum density.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Fill needed for a target
- Legal fill sites
- The best reachable density

Sample problem:

> A $170 \times 170$ um window holds 7819 square um of metal, and the minimum density is 50 percent. Fill squares are 1 by 1 um and are placed only in empty space. How many fill squares are needed?

Answer: 6631

Why: Target area 50 percent of 28900 = 14450 square um; deficit 6631; ceil(deficit / 1) = 6631 squares.

<a id="c-pv-fill-windows"></a>

#### Sliding density windows and gradients

`pv.fill.windows`

Density rules apply to windows that slide across the die with a fixed step, not to a fixed tiling.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Counting window positions
- The minimum window by tile sums
- Density gradients

Sample problem:

> A density rule uses a 50 by 50 um window stepped by 25 um in x and y over a 250 by 675 um die. How many window positions are checked?

Answer: 234

Why: Per axis (D - w) / t + 1: (250 - 50) / 25 + 1 = 9 in x and 26 in y, so 234 positions.

<a id="c-pv-fill-side-effects"></a>

#### Fill side effects and fill-aware flows

`pv.fill.side_effects`

Fill is metal, so it changes capacitance, and it lives in the same layout as signal wiring, so it must be removed and regenerated when routing changes.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Coupling added by fill
- Timing-aware and grounded fill
- Where fill lives in the flow

Sample problem:

> A signal wire has a neighbour 50 nm away on one side and empty space on the other. Fill is inserted on the empty side, 40 nm from the wire. Using a sidewall model in which each side's coupling capacitance is proportional to 1 / spacing (same run length and thickness), by what percent does the wire's total sidewall capacitance increase?
>
> A) 80 percent
>
> B) 125 percent
>
> C) 63 percent
>
> D) 20 percent

Answer: 125 percent

Why: Before: k / 50. The fill adds k / 40, which is 50 / 40 = 125 percent of the original. Fill-aware flows keep fill away from critical nets or extract it before signoff timing.

<a id="physical-verification-and-dfm-design-for-manufacturing"></a>

### Design for manufacturing

<a id="c-pv-dfm-hotspots"></a>

#### Lithography hotspot detection

`pv.dfm.hotspots`

Design rules are a simplified contract with lithography. Some rule-clean patterns still print badly: lines pinch, spaces bridge, line ends pull back, especially at the edges of the process window.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Precision and recall of a detector
- What makes a hotspot
- Detection methods

Sample problem:

> A hotspot detector is run on clips whose true status is known from lithography simulation. It flags 69 true hotspots and 9 clips that print correctly, and it misses 25 true hotspots. What is its recall, in percent, rounded to 1 decimal place?
>
> A) 80.2 percent
>
> B) 73.4 percent
>
> C) 26.6 percent
>
> D) 88.5 percent

Answer: 73.4 percent

Why: Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 69 / 94 = 73.4 percent: the share of real hotspots caught. Missed hotspots become yield loss, so recall is the metric a signoff flow cannot trade away.

<a id="c-pv-dfm-pattern-matching"></a>

#### Pattern matching for DFM

`pv.dfm.pattern_matching`

Pattern matching scans a layout for every occurrence of a known problematic pattern.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Exact matching of a raster pattern
- Orientation-invariant matching
- Don't-care pixels

Sample problem:

> A layer is rasterized into a 6 by 5 grid of pixels (1 = metal), rows top to bottom: 01110, 01110, 10101, 00010, 01001, 01000. A hotspot pattern is the 2 by 2 block 10, 10. At how many positions does the pattern match the grid exactly (no rotation)?

Answer: 2

Why: Slide the block over all 20 positions and compare every pixel: 2 match. Production matchers hash each window so a lookup replaces the pixel comparison.

<a id="c-pv-dfm-dp-coloring"></a>

#### Double-patterning coloring conflicts

`pv.dfm.dp_coloring`

When features are packed tighter than one exposure can print, double patterning splits a layer onto two masks.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Building the conflict graph
- Odd cycles
- Counting mask assignments

Sample problem:

> In double patterning, two features closer than 43 nm (Euclidean) cannot be printed on the same mask, so a conflict edge joins them. The features are F1 = $[96, 123] \times [2, 16]$, F2 = $[98, 130] \times [24, 52]$, F3 = $[5, 28] \times [55, 95]$, F4 = $[51, 82] \times [14, 39]$, F5 = $[74, 94] \times [94, 105]$, F6 = $[111, 140] \times [60, 91]$ (nm). How many conflict edges does the graph have?

Answer: 8

Why: Test all 15 pairs against the same-mask spacing 43 nm: 8 pairs are closer, each one an edge that forces the two features onto different masks.

<a id="c-pv-dfm-critical-area"></a>

#### Critical area of a layout

`pv.dfm.critical_area`

Random particle defects cause shorts and opens. Whether a defect of a given size kills the chip depends on where it lands: the critical area is the area of positions where its centre causes a failure.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Critical area at one defect size
- Averaging over defect sizes
- From critical area to yield

Sample problem:

> Two parallel wires run side by side for 360 um with a 125 nm gap. A circular conducting defect of diameter 225 nm shorts them if it touches both. Ignoring end effects, what is the critical area for shorts at this defect size, in square um? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 36

Why: The defect centre must fall in a band of width x - s = 100 nm along the run (zero if the defect is smaller than the gap): 360 um x 100 nm = 36 square um.

<a id="c-pv-dfm-recommended-rules"></a>

#### Recommended rules and DFM scoring

`pv.dfm.recommended_rules`

Beyond mandatory rules, foundries publish recommended rules: larger spacings, longer extensions, redundant vias.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Scoring recommended rules
- Wire spreading and critical area
- How tools use recommended rules

Sample problem:

> The minimum metal spacing is 50 nm and the recommended spacing is 80 nm. A block's neighbouring-wire spacings, in nm, are 85, 60, 55, 70, 75, 80. What percent of them meet the recommended value? Round to 1 decimal place.
>
> A) 100 percent
>
> B) 66.7 percent
>
> C) 28.6 percent
>
> D) 33.3 percent

Answer: 33.3 percent

Why: 2 of 6 spacings are at least 80 nm: 33.3 percent. All of them pass the mandatory rule; the recommended rule measures margin.

<a id="physical-verification-and-dfm-tape-out"></a>

### Tape-out

<a id="c-pv-tapeout-handoff"></a>

#### Tape-out

`pv.tapeout.handoff`

Tape-out is the handoff of the final layout to the foundry for mask making. Everything physical verification does converges here: the signed-off stream, the agreed layer map, documented waivers, and proof that nothing changed after signoff.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What is delivered
- The signoff checks
- After the handoff

Sample problem:

> Why does a tape-out require a single top cell in the stream?
>
> A) LVS needs exactly one transistor
>
> B) GDSII cannot store more than one cell
>
> C) Mask generation starts from one root of the hierarchy; extra top cells are ambiguous
>
> D) Fill requires it

Answer: Mask generation starts from one root of the hierarchy; extra top cells are ambiguous

Why: Orphan top cells in a stream are a classic tape-out mistake, often flagged by the foundry's intake checks.

<a id="c-pv-tapeout-mask-prep"></a>

#### Mask data preparation and fracturing

`pv.tapeout.mask_prep`

Between tape-out and the mask writer lies mask data preparation: deriving mask layers, applying OPC, and fracturing polygons into the simple figures a writer exposes.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Shot count of a rectangle
- Choosing a fracture
- Vertex growth after OPC

Sample problem:

> A variable-shaped-beam mask writer exposes rectangles of at most 2000 by 2000 nm per shot. How many shots does it need for one 3255 by 5018 nm rectangle, split on a regular grid of maximal shots?

Answer: 6

Why: ceil(3255 / 2000) = 2 columns and ceil(5018 / 2000) = 3 rows: 6 shots. Write time grows with the shot count, not the area.

<a id="c-pv-tapeout-xor-check"></a>

#### Layout XOR between versions

`pv.tapeout.xor_check`

An XOR compares two versions of a layout: it reports the area covered by exactly one of them.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- XOR of two shapes
- XOR of two versions of a layer
- The signature of a shift

Sample problem:

> A tape-out XOR compares a shape in the signed-off layout, $[7, 20] \times [19, 27]$, with the same shape in the final stream, $[6, 24] \times [14, 27]$ (um). What area, in square um, does the XOR report?

Answer: 130

Why: XOR = A + B - 2 (A AND B) = 104 + 234 - 2 x 104 = 130 square um. Any nonzero XOR on a layer that should be unchanged stops the tape-out until it is explained.

<a id="c-pv-tapeout-open-tools"></a>

#### KLayout, Magic and Netgen in practice

`pv.tapeout.open_tools`

Open-source physical verification rests on three tools. KLayout is a layout viewer and editor with DRC and LVS engines scripted in a Ruby-based language.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- KLayout
- Magic
- Netgen and the open flow

Sample problem:

> How does a KLayout LVS script build the layout netlist?
>
> A) With device-extraction and connect statements over derived layers, then it compares against a SPICE netlist
>
> B) It simulates the layout
>
> C) It reads the netlist from the GDS file
>
> D) It asks the router for connectivity

Answer: With device-extraction and connect statements over derived layers, then it compares against a SPICE netlist

Why: Like any LVS flow, it recognizes devices from layer Booleans and extracts connectivity before comparing.

<a id="physical-verification-and-dfm-frontier-agent-first-futures"></a>

### Frontier: agent-first futures

<a id="c-pv-frontier-agentic-fix-loop"></a>

#### Agentic DRC fix loops

`pv.frontier.agentic_fix_loop`

Signoff DRC on a large block can report thousands of violations after routing. An agentic fix loop reads the report, classifies each violation, routes it to the engine that owns the geometry, reruns the checks and iterates, with a human approving the final ECO.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Routing violations to the right fixer
- Classifying violations
- Closing the loop safely

Sample problem:

> A signoff DRC report lists 23 metal spacing, 3 short, 6 minimum-area and 2 via-enclosure violations on routed metal, 11 antenna violations and 0 density-window violations. Of the spacing violations, 4 lie entirely inside standard-cell layouts. The agent's policy: violations on routed metal go back to the detailed router as a Tier 1 rerun of the affected region; antenna violations go to the antenna-repair step; density goes to the fill step; anything inside a cell layout is escalated to a human. How many violations does the agent send to the router?
>
> A) 30
>
> B) 41
>
> C) 34
>
> D) 45

Answer: 30

Why: Routed-metal violations: (23 - 4) + 3 + 6 + 2 = 30. The 4 in-cell spacing violations are not the router's to fix: the router treats cell layouts as fixed, so changing them is a core library change.

<a id="c-pv-frontier-change-tiers"></a>

#### Change tiers for verification engines

`pv.frontier.change_tiers`

Verification engines follow the same four-layer model as implementation engines: an immutable geometry and matching core, policies such as check plug-ins and device extractors, parameters such as rule values and switches, and observation hooks over results.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Tier 1 changes in verification
- Tier 2 plug-ins
- Tier 3 core edits

Sample problem:

> A new foundry rule changes the density window from 50 to 100 um with a 50 um step. Which tier?
>
> A) Tier 3: a change to the Boolean core
>
> B) Tier 1: window size and step are parameters of the density check
>
> C) A layout change
>
> D) Tier 2: a new density algorithm

Answer: Tier 1: window size and step are parameters of the density check

Why: Density engines take window and step as parameters.

<a id="c-pv-frontier-golden-clean"></a>

#### Clean results as golden and differential tests

`pv.frontier.golden_clean`

For physical verification, the golden test is simple to state: the reference designs must stay DRC-clean and LVS-clean, and the regression designs must produce exactly the expected markers.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Introduced markers
- Fixed markers
- Matching with tolerance

Sample problem:

> An agent's change is checked by a differential DRC run. The baseline markers are M2.S.1 at (100, 200), M3.S.2 at (200, 200), M2.S.1 at (300, 300), M2.S.1 at (400, 300). The new run's markers are M2.S.1 at (100, 200), M2.S.1 at (350, 350), M3.S.2 at (200, 200). A marker matches only if the rule and the position are identical. How many markers did the change introduce?

Answer: 1

Why: Introduced = new markers with no identical baseline marker: 1. A golden test for a fix requires this to be zero, whatever happened to the old markers.

<a id="c-pv-frontier-fast-hotspot"></a>

#### Fast hotspot prediction versus signoff

`pv.frontier.fast_hotspot`

Learned hotspot predictors are the fast engine of lithography verification: milliseconds per clip against seconds for simulation.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Screen then verify
- Escapes at a threshold
- Gaming the proxy

Sample problem:

> A full lithography simulation takes 5200 ms per clip and a learned hotspot predictor 2 ms per clip. A layer has 80000 clips. The fast flow runs the predictor on every clip and simulates only the 8000 clips it flags. What is the speedup of the fast flow over simulating every clip? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 10

Why: Full: 80000 x 5200 ms. Fast: 80000 x 2 + 8000 x 5200 ms. Ratio 10. The speedup is bounded by the flag rate: if the predictor flags more, the accurate engine dominates again.

<a id="c-pv-frontier-ip-boundary"></a>

#### Rule decks and the IP boundary

`pv.frontier.ip_boundary`

Physical verification touches the most sensitive data in the chain: the foundry's rule decks, device recognition and hotspot libraries, and the customer's complete layout.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Whose IP is whose
- Architecture of the boundary
- Boundary decisions in practice

Sample problem:

> An agent fixes DRC violations on site. Which data may leave the site under a strict IP boundary?
>
> A) The GDS of the failing region
>
> B) The full DRC results with cell names
>
> C) The rule deck
>
> D) Nothing design-specific; at most generic, reviewed skills or anonymized metrics agreed in advance

Answer: Nothing design-specific; at most generic, reviewed skills or anonymized metrics agreed in advance

Why: Design and process data stay on site. Know-how can flow back only as skills and approved metrics.

## PCB Design

Layer 9. Schematic to layout, stackups and controlled impedance, differential pairs, vias, manufacturing outputs and board-level SI.

Builds on: Circuits and Electromagnetics, Computational Geometry for Layout, Routing, Graph Algorithms for EDA, The EDA Landscape, Physical Verification and DFM.

Topics covered:

- Printed circuit boards, schematic capture, component libraries, footprints and land patterns, bill of materials
- PCB layout, autorouters, PCB stackup, controlled impedance, differential signaling and differential pairs, length matching
- Vias: through-hole, blind, buried, microvias; HDI; flexible and rigid-flex PCBs
- Through-hole vs surface-mount technology, design for assembly, pick-and-place, reflow soldering
- PCB DRC/ERC, design for test, Gerber and ODB++ outputs, IPC standards
- Board bring-up and hardware debugging; signal and power integrity at board level (IBIS, IBIS-AMI, Touchstone)
- Tools: open-source (KiCad, LibrePCB, gEDA/Lepton) and commercial PCB suites
