Subdomains: [PCB flow and tools](#pcb-design-pcb-flow-and-tools), [Stackups](#pcb-design-stackups), [Vias](#pcb-design-vias), [PCB layout](#pcb-design-pcb-layout), [Differential pairs](#pcb-design-differential-pairs), [Signal integrity](#pcb-design-signal-integrity), [Assembly](#pcb-design-assembly), [PCB verification](#pcb-design-pcb-verification), [Manufacturing outputs](#pcb-design-manufacturing-outputs), [Frontier: agent-first futures](#pcb-design-frontier-agent-first-futures)

<a id="pcb-design-pcb-flow-and-tools"></a>

### PCB flow and tools

<a id="c-pcb-flow-schematic-to-layout"></a>

#### The PCB design flow

`pcb.flow.schematic_to_layout`

A printed circuit board flow takes a circuit drawn from purchased parts and turns it into copper, holes and assembly instructions.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Stages of the board flow
- What crosses each boundary
- Iteration and failure propagation

Terms: Schematic capture, Footprint assignment, Netlist transfer, routing, DRC, output generation, netlist, board database, fabrication outputs, assembly outputs.

Sample problem:

> Which statement draws the boundary between chip EDA and board EDA correctly?
>
> A) Chip EDA ends at the package; board EDA designs the transistors
>
> B) Board EDA interconnects off-the-shelf packages on a few to a few dozen layers; chip EDA creates the devices and wiring on the die
>
> C) Board EDA and chip EDA use the same standard-cell placer and differ only in units
>
> D) Board EDA has no design rules because fabrication is cheap

Answer: Board EDA interconnects off-the-shelf packages on a few to a few dozen layers; chip EDA creates the devices and wiring on the die

Why: The board flow starts where the chip flow ends: the die is already packaged, and the board tool wires packages together and models the board's own interconnect.

<a id="c-pcb-flow-symbols-footprints"></a>

#### Symbols, footprints and land patterns

`pcb.flow.symbols_footprints`

Every board part exists in two views. The schematic symbol is logical: pins with names, numbers and electrical types.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Two views of one part
- Pin-to-pad errors and footprint layers
- Land patterns from package tolerances

Terms: symbol, footprint, courtyard, land pattern, paste, mask, toe, heel and side fillet.

Sample problem:

> In IPC terms, what is the land pattern of a component?
>
> A) The schematic symbol of the part
>
> B) The copper pad geometry on the board that the component's terminations solder to
>
> C) The silkscreen outline drawn around the part
>
> D) The paste stencil aperture only

Answer: The copper pad geometry on the board that the component's terminations solder to

Why: A land is a pad; the land pattern is the set of pads for one package. The footprint adds mask, paste, silkscreen, courtyard and assembly data around it.

<a id="c-pcb-flow-bom"></a>

#### Bills of materials

`pcb.flow.bom`

The bill of materials (BOM) lists what must be bought and placed to build one board: one line per manufacturer part number, with its quantity, reference designators and approved sources.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- One line per part number
- Rolling up an order
- Variants and DNP

Terms: manufacturer part number, variant, DNP.

Sample problem:

> A schematic contains these placements: C1: 4.7 uF 0805 X5R capacitor; Y1: 12 MHz 3225 crystal; U1: SOT-23-5 LDO regulator; R1: 10 kohm 0603 resistor; C2: 4.7 uF 0805 X5R capacitor; U2: QFN-48 microcontroller; R2: 1 kohm 0402 resistor; U3: SOT-23-5 LDO regulator. The BOM has one line per manufacturer part number, and each distinct value-and-package description above is one part number. How many lines does the BOM have?

Answer: 6

Why: Group the 8 placements by description. Same value in a different package is a different part number, so it gets its own line. There are 6 distinct descriptions.

<a id="c-pcb-flow-netlist-handoff"></a>

#### Netlist handoff and annotation

`pcb.flow.netlist_handoff`

The netlist is the contract between schematic capture and layout. It lists each net as a set of pins, written as reference designator and pin number, and binds each designator to a footprint.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Nets, labels and annotation
- Forward and back annotation
- Consistency checks across the boundary

Terms: Net labels, Forward annotation, Back annotation, connectivity check, IPC-D-356.

Sample problem:

> What does annotation do in schematic capture?
>
> A) Assigns a unique reference designator such as R12 or U3 to every component
>
> B) Generates a footprint for each symbol
>
> C) Assigns net names to every pin
>
> D) Adds explanatory notes to the printed schematic

Answer: Assigns a unique reference designator such as R12 or U3 to every component

Why: Reference designators are the keys that join schematic, netlist, BOM, layout and assembly data.

<a id="c-pcb-flow-erc"></a>

#### Electrical rule checking of schematics

`pcb.flow.erc`

Electrical rule checking (ERC) runs on the schematic before layout. It reads each net's pins and their declared electrical types and flags combinations that cannot work: two outputs fighting, an input that nothing drives, a power input with no source, a net with a single pin.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Pin types and the conflict matrix
- Evaluating the rules net by net
- What ERC cannot see

Terms: pin conflict matrix.

Sample problem:

> An ERC flags a net if (a) the net has only one pin, or (b) it has two or more pins of type output or power output. The nets are: N1: U1 pin 16 (output), U4 pin 18 (output); N2: U3 pin 24 (output); N3: U3 pin 5 (passive), U5 pin 18 (output), U2 pin 2 (output); N4: U4 pin 5 (passive). How many nets does the ERC flag?

Answer: 4

Why: Test every net against each rule and count a net once even if it breaks two rules. Flagged: N1, N2, N3, N4.

<a id="c-pcb-flow-tools"></a>

#### The PCB tool landscape

`pcb.flow.tools`

Board design tools range from open-source suites to enterprise platforms. For a tool designer the useful questions are not which buttons they have, but what data model each exposes, how open its file formats and scripting are, how it represents constraints, and how designs move between tools.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Open-source tools
- Commercial families
- Data models and interoperability

Terms: gEDA, Lepton EDA, PADS, CR-8000, eCADSTAR, EAGLE.

Sample problem:

> A team wants to run a custom board check over hundreds of designs with an open toolchain. Which KiCad property helps most?
>
> A) Output limited to Gerber files
>
> B) Cloud-only design storage
>
> C) An encrypted binary database
>
> D) Readable text board files plus a Python scripting interface

Answer: Readable text board files plus a Python scripting interface

Why: Text files can be parsed, diffed and version-controlled, and scripting exposes the board model to custom checks.

<a id="pcb-design-stackups"></a>

### Stackups

<a id="c-pcb-stackup-layers"></a>

#### Stackup build: thickness, layer count and symmetry

`pcb.stackup.layers`

A stackup is the ordered list of copper layers and dielectrics that make up the board: cores, prepregs, copper weights and the finished thickness.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Cores, prepreg and copper
- Layer count and construction
- Symmetry and why boards warp

Terms: core, foil build, symmetric.

Sample problem:

> A 6-layer stackup from top to bottom is: L1 copper 1 oz, dielectric 14.5 mil, L2 copper 1 oz, dielectric 4.5 mil, L3 copper 1 oz, dielectric 7.5 mil, L4 copper 0.5 oz, dielectric 16.5 mil, L5 copper 1 oz, dielectric 15 mil, L6 copper 2 oz. Take 1 oz copper as 1.37 mil thick and ignore solder mask. What is the finished board thickness, in mil? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 66.91

Why: Dielectrics sum to 58 mil. Copper totals 6.5 oz, which is 6.5 x 1.37 = 8.91 mil. The board is 66.91 mil thick.

<a id="c-pcb-stackup-copper-resistance"></a>

#### Trace resistance from copper weight

`pcb.stackup.copper_resistance`

A trace is a resistor of rectangular cross-section. Its resistance sets the DC voltage drop on power traces, the loss at low frequency, and the self-heating that limits current.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Resistance from geometry
- Voltage drop on power traces
- Temperature and frequency effects

Terms: remote sense, skin effect.

Sample problem:

> A trace is 200 mm long and 0.5 mm wide in 0.5 oz copper. Use $\rho = 1.72 \times 10^{-8}\ \Omega\cdot$m and take 1 oz copper as 35 micrometres thick, so $R = \rho L / (w t)$. What is its resistance, in milliohms? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 393.1

Why: Thickness is 17.5 micrometres. $R = 1.72 \times 10^{-8} \cdot 0.2 / (0.0005 \cdot 0.0000175) = 393.1$ milliohms, with every length in metres.

<a id="c-pcb-stackup-current-capacity"></a>

#### Trace current capacity rules of thumb

`pcb.stackup.current_capacity`

How wide must a trace be to carry a given current? The trace heats from $I^2 R$ loss and cools through the laminate and the air, so the answer is a temperature-rise limit, not a hard current limit.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The IPC-2221 chart fit
- Inverting the rule for width
- Limits of the rule

Terms: IPC-2152.

Sample problem:

> Use the IPC-2221 rule of thumb $I = k\, \Delta T^{0.44} A^{0.725}$, with $I$ in amperes, temperature rise $\Delta T$ in C, cross-section $A$ in square mils, $k = 0.048$ for outer layers and $k = 0.024$ for inner layers, and 1 oz copper 1.37 mil thick. An outer-layer trace is 50 mil wide in 0.5 oz copper. What current gives a 10 C rise? Answer in amperes, rounded to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 1.71

Why: $A = 50 \cdot 0.685 = 34.25$ square mils. $I = 0.048 \cdot 10^{0.44} \cdot 34.25^{0.725} = 1.71$ A.

<a id="c-pcb-stackup-controlled-impedance"></a>

#### Stackups and controlled impedance

`pcb.stackup.controlled_impedance`

A fast edge on a board trace travels as a wave on a transmission line made of the trace and its reference plane.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Microstrip impedance
- Stripline impedance
- Sensitivities and fabrication tolerance

Terms: microstrip, stripline, rises with height, falls with width, falls with the dielectric constant.

Sample problem:

> Use the IPC-2141 microstrip approximation $Z_0 = \frac{87}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r + 1.41}} \ln\frac{5.98 h}{0.8 w + t}$, where $h$ is the dielectric height to the plane, $w$ the trace width and $t$ the copper thickness. A surface trace has $w = 9.8$ mil, $t = 2.1$ mil, $h = 6.5$ mil and $\varepsilon_r = 4.6$. What is $Z_0$, in ohms? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 48.4

Why: $87/\sqrt{6.01} = 35.488$ and $\ln(38.87 / 9.94) = 1.3637$, so $Z_0 = 48.4$ ohms.

<a id="c-pcb-stackup-prop-delay"></a>

#### Propagation delay and effective dielectric constant

`pcb.stackup.prop_delay`

A signal on a board trace moves at the speed of light divided by the square root of the effective dielectric constant the field sees.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Delay in a homogeneous dielectric
- Effective dielectric constant of microstrip
- Delay of a mixed route

Terms: effective, delay.

Sample problem:

> Light travels 11.8 inches per nanosecond in vacuum, so a line's delay is $t_{pd} = \sqrt{\varepsilon_{eff}} / 11.8$ ns per inch. A stripline is fully embedded in a dielectric with $\varepsilon_r = 3$, so $\varepsilon_{eff} = \varepsilon_r$. What is its delay, in ps per inch? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 146.8

Why: $\sqrt{3} = 1.7321$, and $1000 \cdot 1.7321 / 11.8 = 146.8$ ps per inch.

<a id="c-pcb-stackup-flex-rigid-flex"></a>

#### Flex and rigid-flex boards

`pcb.stackup.flex_rigid_flex`

Flexible circuits put copper on thin polyimide film so the board can bend, either once at installation or repeatedly in service.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Flex materials and construction
- Bend radius rules
- Routing and features in flex regions

Terms: polyimide, rolled-annealed, coverlay, rigid-flex, dynamic, static, perpendicular, cross-hatched.

Sample problem:

> In a rigid-flex board, what forms the flexible region?
>
> A) Flexible polyimide layers that run out of the rigid sections with no rigid material laminated over them
>
> B) A cable soldered between two rigid boards
>
> C) FR-4 milled down to a thinner section
>
> D) Copper wires molded into silicone

Answer: Flexible polyimide layers that run out of the rigid sections with no rigid material laminated over them

Why: The flex layers are continuous through the rigid sections, where they are laminated with rigid material, and left bare between them.

<a id="pcb-design-vias"></a>

### Vias

<a id="c-pcb-via-types"></a>

#### Via types

`pcb.via.types`

A via is a plated hole that connects copper on different layers. Its type is defined by which layers it spans and how it is made: through vias span the whole board, blind vias start at an outer layer and stop inside, buried vias join only inner layers, and microvias are small laser-drilled blind structures spanning one dielectric.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Through, blind, buried and micro
- Pads, antipads and fanout structures
- Via stubs and resonance

Terms: through via, blind via, buried via, microvia, pad, antipad, via-in-pad, stacked, staggered, stub, backdrill.

Sample problem:

> Which via joins an outer layer to an inner layer without passing through the whole board?
>
> A) A thermal via
>
> B) A blind via
>
> C) A buried via
>
> D) A through via

Answer: A blind via

Why: A blind via is visible on one surface only and ends at an inner layer.

<a id="c-pcb-via-aspect-ratio"></a>

#### Via aspect ratios and drill limits

`pcb.via.aspect_ratio`

The aspect ratio of a plated hole is its depth divided by its drilled diameter. It limits how well plating solution reaches the middle of the barrel, so fabricators cap it, and the cap ties the board thickness to the smallest through via.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Through-hole aspect ratio
- Minimum drill from a fab limit
- Microvia aspect ratio

Sample problem:

> A 93 mil thick board has through vias drilled at 10 mil. The aspect ratio is board thickness divided by drilled hole diameter, written $x$:1. What is $x$? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 9.3

Why: $93 / 10 = 9.3$. High ratios make it hard for plating solution to reach the middle of the barrel, so the copper there thins.

<a id="c-pcb-via-hdi"></a>

#### HDI build-ups and microvia stacking

`pcb.via.hdi`

High-density interconnect (HDI) boards add thin build-up layers to a conventional core, connected by laser-drilled microvias, so fine-pitch BGAs can escape without through vias.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The i plus N plus i notation
- Sequential lamination and drilling
- Stacked connections and reliability

Sample problem:

> HDI build-ups are written $i + N + i$: an $N$-layer core with $i$ sequential build-up layers on each side. A 12-layer board uses 3 build-up layers on each side. How many layers does its core have?

Answer: 6

Why: $12 - 2 \cdot 3 = 6$ core layers, so the board is 3+6+3.

<a id="pcb-design-pcb-layout"></a>

### PCB layout

<a id="c-pcb-layout-placement"></a>

#### Board placement and ratsnest length

`pcb.layout.placement`

Board placement positions a few hundred to a few thousand heterogeneous packages under mechanical, thermal, electrical and assembly constraints.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What drives board placement
- Ratsnest as a minimum spanning tree
- What the ratsnest misses

Terms: fixed, Decoupling capacitors, minimum spanning tree, noise coupling, thermal, assembly.

Sample problem:

> Where should a decoupling capacitor be placed?
>
> A) Next to the voltage regulator only
>
> B) Near the board edge to save space
>
> C) As close as possible to the power pin it serves, with a short low-inductance path to its vias and plane
>
> D) Anywhere on the net, since the plane is ideal

Answer: As close as possible to the power pin it serves, with a short low-inductance path to its vias and plane

Why: The capacitor's benefit at high frequency is limited by the loop inductance of its connection, which grows with distance.

<a id="c-pcb-layout-autorouter"></a>

#### Board autorouters versus chip routers

`pcb.layout.autorouter`

Board and chip routers share algorithms (maze search, rip-up and reroute, negotiated congestion) but face different problems.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Shape-based routing on few layers
- Shared algorithms
- Completion is not correctness

Terms: shape-based, fanout and escape, push-and-shove, maze router, rip-up and reroute, lock, net classes.

Sample problem:

> Which early step dominates routing a large BGA board?
>
> A) Choosing the copper weight
>
> B) Fanout and escape: bringing every ball out to a via and a routing channel
>
> C) Drilling the mounting holes
>
> D) Placing the silkscreen

Answer: Fanout and escape: bringing every ball out to a via and a routing channel

Why: Escape determines how many layers the board needs. Once the balls are out, the remaining routing is comparatively open.

<a id="c-pcb-layout-bga-escape"></a>

#### BGA fanout and escape routing

`pcb.layout.bga_escape`

A ball grid array puts hundreds or thousands of connections under one package. Escape routing brings each ball out from under the package to a routing channel, through traces between balls and vias down to other layers.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Traces between adjacent balls
- Rows escaped per layer
- Counting balls in the outer rows

Sample problem:

> A BGA has a 650 micrometre ball pitch and 300 micrometre pads. Traces are 75 micrometres wide with 125 micrometre clearance to pads and to each other. $N$ traces fit between two adjacent pads when $N w + (N + 1) s \le p - d$. How many traces fit between adjacent pads?

Answer: 1

Why: The gap is $650 - 300 = 350$ micrometres. $N \le (350 - 125)/(75 + 125) = 1.125$, so $N = 1$.

<a id="pcb-design-differential-pairs"></a>

### Differential pairs

<a id="c-pcb-diff-odd-even"></a>

#### Odd and even modes of coupled lines

`pcb.diff.odd_even`

Two traces routed side by side over a plane are coupled: each has mutual capacitance and mutual inductance to the other.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Two modes of a coupled pair
- Differential and common-mode impedance
- Velocities, crosstalk and reference planes

Terms: odd mode, even mode, differential impedance, common-mode impedance, microstrip, stripline.

Sample problem:

> Two traces of a pair are brought closer together. What happens to the even-mode impedance?
>
> A) It becomes infinite
>
> B) It rises above the impedance of one uncoupled trace
>
> C) It stays equal to the uncoupled impedance
>
> D) It falls below the uncoupled impedance

Answer: It rises above the impedance of one uncoupled trace

Why: In the even mode both lines swing together, so the mutual capacitance carries no charge and the mutual inductance adds to each line's inductance.

<a id="c-pcb-diff-pairs"></a>

#### Differential pairs

`pcb.diff.pairs`

A differential pair carries one signal as the voltage difference between two traces.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- From odd mode to differential impedance
- Common-mode impedance
- Coupling from measured impedances

Sample problem:

> A field solver reports an edge-coupled pair with odd-mode impedance 41.7 ohms and even-mode impedance 62.7 ohms. What is the differential impedance, in ohms? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 83.4

Why: $Z_{diff} = 2 Z_{odd} = 2 \cdot 41.7 = 83.4$ ohms. The even-mode value does not enter.

<a id="c-pcb-diff-length-matching"></a>

#### Length matching from a skew budget

`pcb.diff.length_matching`

Signals that must arrive together, the two traces of a differential pair or the data lines of a memory byte lane and their strobe, are given a skew budget in picoseconds.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Skew from a length mismatch
- Length tolerance from a budget
- Matching a group to a strobe

Terms: intra-pair skew, serpentines.

Sample problem:

> The two traces of a differential pair differ in length by 95 mil, and the layer's delay is 175 ps per inch. What is the intra-pair skew, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 16.62

Why: 95 mil is 0.095 in, times 175 ps per inch is 16.62 ps. Skew converts part of the differential signal into common mode.

<a id="pcb-design-signal-integrity"></a>

### Signal integrity

<a id="c-pcb-si-reflection"></a>

#### Reflections at board impedance discontinuities

`pcb.si.reflection`

When a wave on a board trace meets a change of impedance, at a load, a via, a connector or a width change, part of it reflects.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The reflection coefficient
- Launch voltage and the first arrival
- Terminations and discontinuities

Sample problem:

> A 85 ohm trace ends in a 100 ohm load. The reflection coefficient is $\Gamma = (Z_L - Z_0)/(Z_L + Z_0)$. What is $\Gamma$? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 0.081

Why: $\Gamma = (100 - 85)/(100 + 85) = 0.081$. A load above $Z_0$ reflects a same-sign wave; a load below it reflects an inverted one.

<a id="c-pcb-si-ibis"></a>

#### IBIS models

`pcb.si.ibis`

IBIS (I/O Buffer Information Specification) is the standard behavioral model of a chip's I/O buffers for board-level signal integrity.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What an IBIS model contains
- Reading drive strength from a V-I table
- Corners, power and the limits of IBIS

Terms: V-I tables, V-t tables, typ, min and max.

Sample problem:

> Why do silicon vendors publish IBIS models instead of SPICE netlists?
>
> A) IBIS is more accurate than SPICE in every case
>
> B) SPICE cannot model I/O buffers
>
> C) IBIS hides the transistor design and simulates much faster while still predicting the waveform at the pin
>
> D) IBIS contains the layout database

Answer: IBIS hides the transistor design and simulates much faster while still predicting the waveform at the pin

Why: Behavioral tables protect IP and make board-level simulation of many nets practical.

<a id="c-pcb-si-touchstone"></a>

#### Touchstone files and channel S-parameters

`pcb.si.touchstone`

Passive board structures at high frequency, such as traces, vias, connectors and packages, are described by scattering parameters measured or simulated over frequency.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The Touchstone format
- Insertion loss in decibels
- Return loss and mismatch

Terms: Insertion loss, Return loss.

Sample problem:

> A Touchstone file named channel.s12p holds the data of a 12-port network. How many complex S-parameters does it store at each frequency point?

Answer: 144

Why: An $N$-port network has an $N \times N$ scattering matrix: $12^2 = 144$ entries per frequency.

<a id="c-pcb-si-ibis-ami"></a>

#### IBIS-AMI and SerDes channel simulation

`pcb.si.ibis_ami`

Multi-gigabit serial links depend on equalization: transmit FFE, receive CTLE and DFE, and clock-data recovery.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The AMI model structure
- Transmit FFE as a filter
- Statistical and time-domain flows

Terms: algorithmic, statistical, DFE, time-domain.

Sample problem:

> In a statistical, Init-only AMI flow, what does the model process?
>
> A) The bill of materials
>
> B) The board's Gerber files
>
> C) A long bit-by-bit waveform with adaptation
>
> D) The channel impulse response, returning an equalized impulse response, under a linear time-invariant assumption

Answer: The channel impulse response, returning an equalized impulse response, under a linear time-invariant assumption

Why: If the equalizer is linear and fixed, its effect on the impulse response is enough to build an eye and BER statistically.

<a id="c-pcb-si-pdn-target"></a>

#### Power delivery: target impedance and decoupling

`pcb.si.pdn_target`

A power delivery network (PDN) carries current from the regulator through planes, capacitors, package and die to every transistor.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Target impedance
- Capacitors and their resonance
- Counting capacitors for an inductive limit

Terms: anti-resonance.

Sample problem:

> A 1.8 V rail may ripple by at most 3% while its load current steps by 34 A. The PDN target impedance is $Z_t = V \cdot \text{ripple} / \Delta I$. What is $Z_t$, in milliohms? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 1.59

Why: $1.8 \cdot 0.03 / 34 = 1.59$ milliohms. The PDN must stay below this from DC up to the frequency where the package and die take over.

<a id="pcb-design-assembly"></a>

### Assembly

<a id="c-pcb-assembly-tht-smt"></a>

#### Through-hole versus surface-mount technology

`pcb.assembly.tht_smt`

Components attach to a board in two ways. Through-hole technology (THT) passes leads through plated holes and solders them, usually by wave or selective soldering.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Two ways to attach a part
- Consequences for layout and process
- Assembly defects and their causes

Terms: through-hole, surface-mount.

Sample problem:

> How is a surface-mount component attached to a board?
>
> A) Its leads are crimped to the traces
>
> B) Its terminations sit on surface lands printed with solder paste and are joined in a reflow oven
>
> C) Its leads pass through plated holes and are wave soldered
>
> D) It is clipped into a socket

Answer: Its terminations sit on surface lands printed with solder paste and are joined in a reflow oven

Why: SMT prints paste through a stencil, places parts on the wet paste and melts it in a controlled oven profile.

<a id="c-pcb-assembly-dfa"></a>

#### Design for assembly

`pcb.assembly.dfa`

Design for assembly (DFA) is the set of layout rules that make a board cheap and reliable to build: fiducials and handling edges for the machines, spacing and orientation for placement and inspection, thermal and via rules for good joints, and BOM and side choices that cut setups.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Rules the machines need
- Spacing, panels and joints
- Cost and yield trade-offs

Terms: Thermal reliefs, Polarity and pin-1 marks, panelized, Open vias in lands.

Sample problem:

> Why do through-hole pads on planes use thermal reliefs?
>
> A) To raise its current capacity
>
> B) To lower the pad's impedance
>
> C) Spokes limit heat flow into the plane so the joint can reach soldering temperature
>
> D) To keep solder mask off the pad

Answer: Spokes limit heat flow into the plane so the joint can reach soldering temperature

Why: A solid connection to a large plane sinks heat, giving cold joints and hard rework.

<a id="c-pcb-assembly-pick-place"></a>

#### Pick-and-place data and throughput

`pcb.assembly.pick_place`

Placement machines pick parts from feeders and place them at coordinates from the centroid (pick-and-place) file: reference designator, X, Y, rotation and side.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Machine time from CPH
- Balancing a placement line
- Centroid data and rotations

Terms: components per hour.

Sample problem:

> A board has 1450 SMT placements. A build of 10 boards runs on a placement machine that sustains 28000 components per hour (CPH) on this job. How many hours of placement time does the build need? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 0.52

Why: $1450 \cdot 10 / 28000 = 0.52$ hours. Rated CPH is measured on ideal parts; real jobs with large or fine-pitch parts run slower.

<a id="c-pcb-assembly-reflow"></a>

#### Reflow soldering profiles

`pcb.assembly.reflow`

Reflow soldering melts printed solder paste in an oven that moves the board through heated zones.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Profile stages and ramp rates
- Time above liquidus
- Soak, thermal mass and profiling

Terms: preheat, soak, reflow, cooling, Time above liquidus.

Sample problem:

> A reflow profile is piecewise linear through (0 s, 25 C), (62 s, 150 C), (129 s, 194 C), (173 s, 238 C peak), (216 s, 206 C) and (273 s, 100 C). What is the preheat ramp rate from 25 C to 150 C, in C per second? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 2.02

Why: $(150 - 25)/62 = 2.02$ C per second. Ramps much above a few C per second risk thermal shock to ceramic capacitors.

<a id="pcb-design-pcb-verification"></a>

### PCB verification

<a id="c-pcb-verify-drc"></a>

#### Board design rule checking

`pcb.verify.drc`

Board DRC checks the layout against the fabricator's geometric rules and the design's electrical constraints: clearance between copper on different nets, trace widths, annular rings, drill sizes, hole-to-hole spacing, mask slivers, courtyard overlaps, plus connectivity against the netlist.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Clearance as edge-to-edge distance
- Corner-to-corner distance
- Scaling the check

Terms: spatial index, incrementally.

Sample problem:

> Board DRC measures clearance between copper shapes as the shortest edge-to-edge distance. A pad on net A covers the rectangle (19, 18) to (43, 36) and a trace segment on net B covers (48, 23) to (65, 36), in mil. What is their clearance, in mil? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 5

Why: The x gap is 5 mil and the y gap is 0 mil. The shapes overlap in one axis, so the clearance is the other gap, 5 mil.

<a id="c-pcb-verify-dft"></a>

#### Design for test on boards

`pcb.verify.dft`

A built board must be tested for assembly defects: opens, shorts, missing or wrong parts.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Test access and coverage
- The JTAG chain and instruction registers
- Bypass and test pattern length

Terms: test points, chain, instruction register, boundary-scan register, BYPASS.

Sample problem:

> A board has 1140 nets. 537 nets have a probe-able test point for in-circuit or flying-probe test, and 338 other nets have no test point but are reachable through boundary-scan cells. What percentage of nets has some test access? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 76.8

Why: $(537 + 338)/1140 = 76.8\%$. Boundary scan recovers access to nets under BGAs that no probe can reach.

<a id="c-pcb-verify-bringup"></a>

#### Board bring-up and hardware debugging

`pcb.verify.bringup`

Bring-up is the first power-on and functional test of a new board, where design errors that every check missed finally appear.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- A safe power-up order
- Measurement and localization
- Closing the loop

Terms: resistance from each rail to ground, current-limited, JTAG, TDR, margin.

Sample problem:

> Before a new board is powered for the first time, what should be measured?
>
> A) The clock frequency
>
> B) The trace impedance of every net
>
> C) The resistance from each supply rail to ground, to catch shorts
>
> D) The firmware checksum

Answer: The resistance from each supply rail to ground, to catch shorts

Why: A rail-to-ground short from a solder bridge or a rotated part is common on first articles and is cheap to find unpowered.

<a id="pcb-design-manufacturing-outputs"></a>

### Manufacturing outputs

<a id="c-pcb-output-gerber-odb"></a>

#### Gerber and ODB++

`pcb.output.gerber_odb`

Fabrication data leaves the board tool in one of a few formats. Gerber (RS-274X, and its attribute-carrying extension X2) describes each layer as a 2D vector image, with drill data in separate Excellon files.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The Gerber image model
- Coordinates and units
- Attributes and unified databases

Terms: D01, D02, D03, Gerber X2, IPC-2581.

Sample problem:

> In an RS-274X Gerber file, what does a D03 operation do?
>
> A) Draws a line from the current point with the current aperture
>
> B) Moves the current point without drawing
>
> C) Ends the file
>
> D) Flashes the current aperture at the coordinate, creating a pad image

Answer: Flashes the current aperture at the coordinate, creating a pad image

Why: D01 draws (interpolates), D02 moves, D03 flashes. Pads are usually flashes, traces draws.

<a id="c-pcb-output-ipc-standards"></a>

#### IPC standards for design, fabrication and assembly

`pcb.output.ipc_standards`

IPC standards are the shared vocabulary of the board industry: design rules, land patterns, current capacity, acceptance criteria for bare boards and assemblies, soldering requirements, and data formats.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Design standards
- Fabrication, assembly and data standards
- Product classes

Terms: IPC-2221, IPC-2223, IPC-2226, IPC-7351, IPC-2152, IPC-2141, IPC-6012, IPC-A-600, J-STD-001, IPC-A-610, IPC-2581, IPC-D-356, Class 1, Class 2, Class 3.

Sample problem:

> Which IPC standard gives visual acceptance criteria for electronic assemblies, such as solder fillets?
>
> A) IPC-A-610
>
> B) IPC-2581
>
> C) IPC-2152
>
> D) IPC-A-600

Answer: IPC-A-610

Why: IPC-A-610 is the assembly acceptability standard used by inspectors.

<a id="pcb-design-frontier-agent-first-futures"></a>

### Frontier: agent-first futures

<a id="c-pcb-frontier-constraint-agent"></a>

#### Agents for board constraint setup and placement

`pcb.frontier.constraint_agent`

A large share of board-design effort goes into setting up constraints (net classes, matching groups, impedance targets, keep-outs) from datasheets and design guides, and into interactive placement.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The four layers of a board placer
- Change tiers for constraint requests
- Evidence for accepting agent changes

Terms: immutable core, policy, Observation hooks, Tier 1, Tier 2, Tier 3.

Sample problem:

> In a board placer built on the four-layer engine model, what belongs in the immutable core?
>
> A) The weight between ratsnest length and thermal spreading
>
> B) Courtyard non-overlap, keep-out and board-outline legality
>
> C) A rule that keeps decoupling capacitors within 2 mm of power pins
>
> D) A hook that streams live congestion maps to an agent

Answer: Courtyard non-overlap, keep-out and board-outline legality

Why: Legality is the invariant every placement must satisfy. Objectives, rules and hooks vary per design and sit above it.

<a id="c-pcb-frontier-autorouter-golden"></a>

#### Judging an AI autorouter by DRC and SI

`pcb.frontier.autorouter_golden`

Learned and agentic autorouters are judged the same way as any engine change: by deterministic checks against golden references.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Acceptance gates
- Signal-integrity gates
- Differential tests on reference designs

Terms: differential.

Sample problem:

> An AI autorouter produced candidate routings of one board. A candidate is accepted only with zero DRC violations and worst intra-pair skew at most 3 ps. The results are: R1: 1 DRC violation, worst intra-pair skew 2 ps; R2: 0 DRC violations, worst intra-pair skew 6 ps; R3: 3 DRC violations, worst intra-pair skew 5.5 ps; R4: 0 DRC violations, worst intra-pair skew 1.5 ps; R5: 0 DRC violations, worst intra-pair skew 3 ps. How many candidates are accepted?

Answer: 2

Why: Apply every gate to every candidate; failing any one rejects it. Accepted: R4, R5. The checks are deterministic tools, so the router cannot talk its way past them.

<a id="c-pcb-frontier-schematic-review"></a>

#### Schematic-review agents

`pcb.frontier.schematic_review`

Design review of schematics is skilled, tedious work: checking every power pin's decoupling, every regulator's capacitors against its datasheet, every bus's pull-ups, every level crossing between voltage domains.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What the agent checks and from what
- Precision and recall
- Grounding and the review loop

Terms: seeded defects, precision, recall, grounding.

Sample problem:

> Which schematic check is best left to a deterministic rule engine rather than the language model in a review agent?
>
> A) Whether a block's comments describe it well
>
> B) Whether a filter's design intent matches the vendor's application note
>
> C) Whether every input has a driver and every power input has a source (ERC)
>
> D) Whether an alternative part would be cheaper

Answer: Whether every input has a driver and every power input has a source (ERC)

Why: Connectivity rules are exact and cheap to compute. The model's value is in the judgment calls the rules cannot express.

<a id="c-pcb-frontier-routing-reward"></a>

#### Tool-grounded rewards for board routing

`pcb.frontier.routing_reward`

Training a routing policy with reinforcement learning needs a reward computed by tools: DRC counts, via counts, wirelength against a baseline, skew from the constraint reporter.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- A tool-grounded reward
- Weights encode priorities
- Reward hacking against signoff

Sample problem:

> A routing agent is trained with the tool-grounded reward $R = 100 - 20 V - 0.1 N - 2 W - 5 S$, where $V$ is the DRC violation count, $N$ the via count, $W$ the wirelength excess over the baseline in percent, and $S$ the worst intra-pair skew in ps. Candidate A has 0 DRC violations, 172 vias, 6.5% wirelength excess and 2.5 ps worst skew. What is its reward? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 57.3

Why: $100 - 20 \cdot 0 - 0.1 \cdot 172 - 2 \cdot 6.5 - 5 \cdot 2.5 = 57.3$.

<a id="c-pcb-frontier-package-codesign"></a>

#### PCB and package co-design agents

`pcb.frontier.package_codesign`

The die, its package and the board are designed by different teams in different tools, yet one decision couples them all: which signal sits on which ball.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What crosses the package boundary
- Agent actions and tiers
- Verifying a co-design change

Terms: ball map, Tier 1.

Sample problem:

> Which data must stay consistent across the die, package and board databases?
>
> A) The Gerber aperture tables
>
> B) Net names and the mapping from die bumps to package balls to board pads
>
> C) The BOM quantities
>
> D) The silkscreen fonts

Answer: Net names and the mapping from die bumps to package balls to board pads

Why: The three databases describe one connected system. A mismatch in the mapping is an open or short across the boundary.

---

## Packaging, Chiplets and 3D Integration

Layer 10. Flip chip and BGA, interposers, TSVs, hybrid bonding, UCIe, thermal, mechanical and reliability physics.

Builds on: PCB Design, Circuits and Electromagnetics, Fabrication and Design-Technology Co-optimization, Clock Trees and Power Delivery, Numerical Methods for EDA, Variability, Yield and Reliability Statistics, Physical Verification and DFM, Semiconductor Devices and Compact Models.

Topics covered:

- Electronic and IC packaging: wire bonding, flip chip, BGA, package substrates, organic and glass substrates
- Wafer-level packaging, fan-out WLP, redistribution layers
- System in package, multi-chip modules, chiplets, heterogeneous integration, 2.5D integration, interposers, silicon interposers, 3D ICs, TSVs, microbumps, hybrid bonding
- Die-to-die interconnect, UCIe, advanced packaging, package-board co-design
- Thermal: heat transfer, conduction, thermal resistance, thermal simulation, self-heating, Joule heating, power density, hot spots, thermal management
- Mechanical: thermomechanical stress, CTE mismatch, package warpage, FEA
- Reliability: electromigration, stress migration, interconnect reliability, dielectric breakdown, aging; multiphysics simulation; thermal-electrical co-design

Subdomains: [Package basics](#packaging-chiplets-and-3d-integration-package-basics), [Wafer-level packaging](#packaging-chiplets-and-3d-integration-wafer-level-packaging), [Advanced packaging](#packaging-chiplets-and-3d-integration-advanced-packaging), [Chiplets](#packaging-chiplets-and-3d-integration-chiplets), [Thermal analysis](#packaging-chiplets-and-3d-integration-thermal-analysis), [Mechanical stress](#packaging-chiplets-and-3d-integration-mechanical-stress), [Package reliability](#packaging-chiplets-and-3d-integration-package-reliability), [EDA for 3D integration](#packaging-chiplets-and-3d-integration-eda-for-3d-integration), [Frontier: agent-first futures](#packaging-chiplets-and-3d-integration-frontier-agent-first-futures)

<a id="packaging-chiplets-and-3d-integration-package-basics"></a>

### Package basics

<a id="c-pkg-basic-package-roles"></a>

#### What a package does

`pkg.basic.package_roles`

A package is the structure between a bare die and a printed circuit board. It carries signals and power from the die's fine on-chip pitch out to the board's coarse pitch, removes the die's heat, protects the die mechanically and chemically, and lets the die be tested and handled.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Four jobs of a package
- The interconnect hierarchy
- What the package feeds back into design

Sample problem:

> A team thins a package substrate to shorten its vias for signal integrity. Which package job is most likely to suffer as a side effect?
>
> A) Mechanical: the thinner, less stiff substrate warps more under CTE mismatch
>
> B) Environmental: thin substrates absorb no moisture
>
> C) Thermal: substrates carry most of the heat to the sink
>
> D) Electrical: thinner vias always add inductance

Answer: Mechanical: the thinner, less stiff substrate warps more under CTE mismatch

Why: Stiffness falls steeply with thickness, so the same CTE mismatch bends a thin substrate more. Package jobs are coupled, and a change aimed at one moves another.

<a id="c-pkg-basic-wire-bonding"></a>

#### Wire bonding

`pkg.basic.wire_bonding`

Wire bonding connects die pads to package leads with thin gold, copper or aluminium wires, bonded by heat, force and ultrasonic energy.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Perimeter-limited pad count
- Bond wire resistance
- Inductance and ground bounce

Sample problem:

> A square die of side 7 mm has wire-bond pads in two staggered rows along every edge, each row at a pad pitch of 65 um. Each row holds $\lfloor$side/pitch$\rfloor$ pads per side. How many pads does the die hold in total?

Answer: 856

Why: Per side and row: $\lfloor 7000/65 \rfloor = 107$. Total: $4 \times 2 \times 107 = 856$ pads. Pad count grows with perimeter, not area.

<a id="c-pkg-basic-flip-chip-bga"></a>

#### Flip chip and BGA packages

`pkg.basic.flip_chip_bga`

In flip chip the die is turned face down and joined to the package by solder bumps spread over its whole area.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Area-array bump count
- Area array against perimeter
- BGA ball maps

Sample problem:

> A flip-chip die is 8.5 mm by 17 mm. Bumps sit on a full square grid at 180 um pitch, the first bump half a pitch in from each edge. How many bumps does the die carry?

Answer: 4418

Why: $\lfloor 8500/180 \rfloor \times \lfloor 17000/180 \rfloor = 47 \times 94 = 4418$ bumps.

<a id="c-pkg-basic-substrates"></a>

#### Package substrates: organic and glass

`pkg.basic.substrates`

A package substrate is the small wiring board under the die. Most are organic: a glass-fibre core with build-up dielectric layers and copper traces, made by semi-additive plating.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Wiring capacity per layer
- Layers needed for a signal count
- CTE and dimensional stability

Sample problem:

> A package substrate routes at 15 um line and 6 um space. How many traces can cross a 9 mm die edge using 7 signal layers?

Answer: 2961

Why: Per millimetre per layer: $\lfloor 1000/21 \rfloor = 47$. Total: $9 \times 7 \times 47 = 2961$.

<a id="c-pkg-basic-escape-routing"></a>

#### BGA escape routing

`pkg.basic.escape_routing`

Escape routing is the problem of bringing every signal out from inside a dense ball or bump array to the array's edge, so it can be routed onward.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Traces through one channel
- Rows per layer and layer count
- Balls escaped on the first layer

Sample problem:

> A BGA has 800 um ball pitch and 320 um pads. The board routes at 60 um trace width and 75 um space. How many traces fit through one channel between adjacent pads, if $n$ traces need $n$ widths and $n+1$ spaces?

Answer: 3

Why: $n = \lfloor (800 - 320 - 75)/(60 + 75) \rfloor = \lfloor 405/135 \rfloor = 3$.

<a id="packaging-chiplets-and-3d-integration-wafer-level-packaging"></a>

### Wafer-level packaging

<a id="c-pkg-wlp-wafer-level"></a>

#### Wafer-level and fan-out packaging

`pkg.wlp.wafer_level`

Wafer-level packaging builds the package on the wafer itself, before or instead of dicing into a separate substrate.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Fan-in capacity
- Fan-out area expansion
- Reconstituted wafers and panels

Sample problem:

> A fan-in wafer-level package places balls on a full grid under a 7.2 mm by 4.3 mm die at 0.35 mm pitch. How many balls fit, counting $\lfloor$side/pitch$\rfloor$ per side?

Answer: 240

Why: $\lfloor 7.2/0.35 \rfloor \times \lfloor 4.3/0.35 \rfloor = 20 \times 12 = 240$ balls.

<a id="c-pkg-wlp-rdl"></a>

#### Redistribution layers

`pkg.wlp.rdl`

A redistribution layer is a thin copper wiring level, insulated by polymer or inorganic dielectric, that moves connections from where the die's pads are to where the bumps or balls must be.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- RDL trace resistance
- IR drop on RDL power routes
- Density against resistance

Sample problem:

> An RDL copper trace is 6300 um long, 2 um wide and 2 um thick, with resistivity 2.4 micro-ohm cm. What is its resistance, in ohms? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 37.8

Why: 2.4 micro-ohm cm is 0.024 ohm um. $R = 0.024 \times 6300/(2 \times 2) = 37.8$ ohm.

<a id="packaging-chiplets-and-3d-integration-advanced-packaging"></a>

### Advanced packaging

<a id="c-pkg-adv-sip-mcm"></a>

#### System in package and multi-chip modules

`pkg.adv.sip_mcm`

A system in package (SiP) places several dies, often from different processes, and passive components in one package.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Compound module yield
- Known-good die
- Cost per good module

Sample problem:

> A multi-chip module holds 3 untested dies with yields 0.99, 0.92, 0.93. Each die attach succeeds with probability 0.995, independently. What is the module yield, as a percentage? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 83.44

Why: $Y = 0.995^{3} \times 0.99 \times 0.92 \times 0.93 = 83.44\%$. Every part must be good, so yields multiply.

<a id="c-pkg-adv-interposer-25d"></a>

#### 2.5D integration on interposers

`pkg.adv.interposer_25d`

In 2.5D integration several dies sit side by side on an interposer, a thin slab carrying fine wiring between them, which in turn sits on a package substrate.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Interposer area and the reticle
- Wires across the die edge
- The bump bottleneck

Sample problem:

> A silicon interposer carries 3 dies of 29.5 mm by 10 mm in a row, 0.2 mm apart, with a 0.5 mm margin on every side. A reticle field is 26 mm by 33 mm. Counting by area alone, at least how many reticle fields must be stitched?

Answer: 2

Why: Width $3 \times 29.5 + 2 \times 0.2 + 2 \times 0.5 = 89.9$ mm, height 11 mm, area 988.9 mm^2. $\lceil 988.9/858 \rceil = 2$.

<a id="c-pkg-adv-bridges"></a>

#### Embedded silicon bridges

`pkg.adv.bridges`

An embedded silicon bridge is a small piece of silicon with fine wiring, placed only under the facing edges of two dies, inside an organic substrate or a mold layer.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Silicon area saved
- Wires per bridge
- Bandwidth through bridges

Sample problem:

> A full silicon interposer for a multi-die package would be 1200 mm^2. Instead, 6 embedded bridges of 7.5 mm by 2.5 mm connect the facing die edges. By what factor does the silicon area fall? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 10.7

Why: Bridge silicon: $6 \times 7.5 \times 2.5 = 112.5$ mm^2. Factor $1200/112.5 = 10.7$.

<a id="c-pkg-adv-3dic-tsv"></a>

#### 3D ICs and TSVs

`pkg.adv.3dic_tsv`

A 3D IC stacks dies vertically and connects them through the silicon with through-silicon vias (TSVs): copper-filled holes insulated by an oxide liner.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Aspect ratio and die thickness
- TSV resistance
- TSV area overhead

Sample problem:

> A TSV process fills holes reliably up to an aspect ratio (depth over diameter) of 12. For 4 um diameter TSVs, what is the thickest die, in micrometres, that the TSVs can pass through? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 48

Why: $t = AR \times d = 12 \times 4 = 48$ um.

<a id="c-pkg-adv-tsv-keep-out"></a>

#### TSV keep-out zones

`pkg.adv.tsv_keep_out`

Copper expands about six times more than silicon per kelvin, so after the anneal and cool-down a TSV leaves residual stress in the silicon around it.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Blocked area per TSV
- Fraction of a block lost
- Sizing the keep-out from stress decay

Sample problem:

> A placer blocks a square keep-out around each TSV. The TSV is 5 um in diameter and the keep-out extends 3 um beyond the TSV edge on every side. What area does one TSV block, in square micrometres? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 121

Why: Side $5 + 2 \times 3 = 11$ um; area $11^2 = 121$ um^2.

<a id="c-pkg-adv-tsv-capacitance"></a>

#### TSV capacitance and delay

`pkg.adv.tsv_capacitance`

A TSV is a copper cylinder inside an oxide liner inside silicon, which makes it a coaxial capacitor to the substrate.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The coaxial capacitance
- TSV RC delay
- Liner thickness as a design lever

Sample problem:

> A TSV has a copper core of radius 1 um, an oxide liner 0.15 um thick ($\varepsilon_r = 3.9$) and a length of 85 um. Using the coaxial formula $C = 2\pi\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r L/\ln(r_{out}/r_{in})$ with $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-3}$ fF/um, what is its oxide capacitance, in fF? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 132

Why: $\ln(1.15/1) = 0.1398$. $C = 2\pi \times 8.854 \times 10^{-3} \times 3.9 \times 85 / 0.1398 = 132$ fF.

<a id="c-pkg-adv-microbumps"></a>

#### Microbumps

`pkg.adv.microbumps`

Microbumps are small solder-capped copper pillars, at pitches of roughly 25 to 55 um, that join dies to interposers, bridges or other dies.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Bump density from pitch
- Power bumps from current limits
- Bump resistance

Sample problem:

> A 40 mm^2 interface region is filled with microbumps on a square grid at 40 um pitch. Using density times area, about how many bumps does it hold? Round to the nearest whole number.

Answer: 25000

Why: Density $(1000/40)^2 = 625$ per mm^2, times 40 mm^2 gives 25000.

<a id="c-pkg-adv-hybrid-bonding"></a>

#### Hybrid bonding

`pkg.adv.hybrid_bonding`

Hybrid bonding joins two dies or wafers face to face with no solder: polished dielectric surfaces bond directly, and recessed copper pads expand during an anneal to form metal joints.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Connection density
- Gain over microbumps
- Overlay and pad overlap

Sample problem:

> A hybrid-bonding interface places pads on a square grid at 6 um pitch. How many connections per square millimetre does it offer? Round to the nearest whole number.

Answer: 27778

Why: $(1000/6)^2 = 27778$ per mm^2.

<a id="packaging-chiplets-and-3d-integration-chiplets"></a>

### Chiplets

<a id="c-pkg-chiplet-disaggregation"></a>

#### Chiplet disaggregation and yield

`pkg.chiplet.disaggregation`

Disaggregation splits what would be one large die into several smaller chiplets, joined in a package.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Poisson yield of a large die
- Chiplet yield with interface overhead
- Silicon per good system

Sample problem:

> A 240 mm^2 monolithic die is made in a process with 0.26 killer defects per cm^2, randomly scattered. Using the Poisson model $Y = e^{-AD_0}$, what is its yield, as a percentage? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 53.58

Why: $A = 2.4$ cm^2, $AD_0 = 0.624$, $Y = e^{-0.624} = 53.58\%$.

<a id="c-pkg-chiplet-d2d-interfaces"></a>

#### Die-to-die interface choices

`pkg.chiplet.d2d_interfaces`

A die-to-die interface is the circuit and protocol that moves data between chiplets in one package.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Parallel and serial interfaces
- Shoreline and reach
- Protocol, latency and test

Sample problem:

> Two chiplets on a silicon interposer are 2 mm apart. Which interface style suits them best?
>
> A) An optical transceiver per signal
>
> B) A single shared bus with tri-state drivers
>
> C) A wide parallel interface of many single-ended wires at moderate rates, without equalization
>
> D) A few long-reach SerDes lanes with heavy equalization

Answer: A wide parallel interface of many single-ended wires at moderate rates, without equalization

Why: Short dense interposer wires allow simple, low-energy parallel signalling.

<a id="c-pkg-chiplet-ucie"></a>

#### Chiplets and UCIe

`pkg.chiplet.ucie`

Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) is an open die-to-die interconnect standard.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Lanes, rate and module bandwidth
- Shoreline bandwidth
- Sizing for a target

Sample problem:

> A UCIe standard-package module has 16 data lanes per direction, each at 12 GT/s (one bit per transfer). What is its raw bandwidth per direction, in Gb/s?

Answer: 192

Why: $16 \times 12 = 192$ Gb/s each way, before protocol overhead.

<a id="c-pkg-chiplet-energy-per-bit"></a>

#### Energy per bit and link power

`pkg.chiplet.energy_per_bit`

Energy per bit is the energy an interface spends to move one bit from one die to another, usually quoted in picojoules per bit.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Link power
- On-package against off-package
- Energy from capacitance

Sample problem:

> A die-to-die link spends 1.75 pJ per bit and carries 25.5 Tb/s in one direction. What power does it draw, in watts? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 44.62

Why: 1 pJ/bit at 1 Tb/s is 1 W. $1.75 \times 25.5$ per direction gives 44.62 W in total.

<a id="c-pkg-chiplet-package-board-codesign"></a>

#### Package-board co-design

`pkg.chiplet.package_board_codesign`

Package-board co-design treats die, package and board as one system. The ball map, the power delivery path and the high-speed channels cross all three, and a choice made in one level, such as a ball assignment, fixes constraints for the others.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Power ball count
- Target impedance
- Parallel paths and inductance

Sample problem:

> A core rail draws 122 A, and each package ball may carry at most 0.9 A. How many supply balls are needed for this rail, not counting the ground return?

Answer: 136

Why: $\lceil 122/0.9 \rceil = 136$ balls, with as many ground balls again.

<a id="packaging-chiplets-and-3d-integration-thermal-analysis"></a>

### Thermal analysis

<a id="c-pkg-thermal-conduction"></a>

#### Heat conduction and Fourier's law

`pkg.thermal.conduction`

Heat leaves a chip mainly by conduction through solids: silicon, solder, thermal interface material, lid and heat sink, before convection carries it away.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Fourier's law
- Resistance of a layer
- Sizing a material for a budget

Sample problem:

> A layer of mold compound (k = 0.9 W/(m K)) is 710 um thick and 450 mm^2 in area. What is its one-dimensional thermal resistance $L/(kA)$, in K/W? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 1.7531

Why: With $L$ in um and $A$ in mm^2 the factors of $10^{-6}$ cancel: $710/(0.9 \times 450) = 1.7531$ K/W.

<a id="c-pkg-thermal-resistance-network"></a>

#### Thermal resistance networks

`pkg.thermal.resistance_network`

A thermal resistance network models a package as resistors between temperature nodes, with power as current and temperature as voltage.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Layers in series
- Parallel paths
- Heat split between paths

Sample problem:

> All the heat of a 70 W die flows in series through: die 0.35 K/W, TIM1 0.34 K/W, lid 0.12 K/W, TIM2 0.4 K/W. Ambient is 48 °C. What is the junction temperature, in °C? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 132.7

Why: Series sum 1.21 K/W; $T_j = 48 + 70 \times 1.21 = 132.7$ °C.

<a id="c-pkg-thermal-junction-temperature"></a>

#### Junction temperature and theta values

`pkg.thermal.junction_temperature`

Datasheets summarise package thermal behaviour with theta values: thermal resistances between the junction and a reference such as the ambient air, the case or the board, measured under standard conditions.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Junction from power and theta
- Maximum allowed power
- Case and sink resistances

Sample problem:

> A part dissipates 4 W with $\theta_{ja} = 7.9$ K/W in 42 °C ambient. What is its junction temperature, in °C? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 73.6

Why: $T_j = 42 + 4 \times 7.9 = 73.6$ °C.

<a id="c-pkg-thermal-power-density"></a>

#### Power density and hot spots

`pkg.thermal.power_density`

Power density is power per unit area, and its spatial variation, not the total power, decides the peak temperature on a die.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Average power density
- Hot-spot density ratio
- Temperature above the average

Sample problem:

> A 90 W die has an area of 290 mm^2. What is its average power density, in W/cm^2? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 31.03

Why: 290 mm^2 $= 2.9$ cm^2; $90/2.9 = 31.03$ W/cm^2.

<a id="c-pkg-thermal-joule-heating"></a>

#### Joule heating and self-heating

`pkg.thermal.joule_heating`

Joule heating is the power $I^2 R$ dissipated when current flows through resistance.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Power in a conductor
- Temperature rise of a wire
- Transistor self-heating

Sample problem:

> A power bump of 18.5 milliohm carries 490 mA. How much power does it dissipate, in milliwatts? Round to 4 decimal places.

Answer: 4.4418

Why: $P = I^2 R = 0.49^2 \times 0.0185 = 4.4418$ mW.

<a id="c-pkg-thermal-simulation"></a>

#### Thermal simulation

`pkg.thermal.simulation`

Thermal simulation solves the heat equation over the package and die to find the full temperature field, not just a few node values.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- One Jacobi update
- A chain with distributed heating
- Grid size and sparsity

Sample problem:

> In a 1-D finite-difference thermal model, each node joins its two neighbours through 1.5 K/W. An interior node receives 0 W of power. Its neighbours currently hold 46 °C and 88.5 °C. What is the node's new temperature after one Jacobi update, in °C? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 67.25

Why: Energy balance gives $T_i = (T_{i-1} + T_{i+1} + Q R)/2 = (46 + 88.5 + 0)/2 = 67.25$ °C.

<a id="c-pkg-thermal-transient"></a>

#### Transient thermal response

`pkg.thermal.transient`

Temperature does not respond instantly to power. Every material stores heat, which acts as a thermal capacitance, so a power step produces an exponential rise with a thermal time constant.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Thermal capacitance
- The thermal time constant
- Response to a power step

Sample problem:

> A silicon die is 13 mm by 8 mm and 425 um thick. Silicon has density 2330 kg/m^3 and specific heat 700 J/(kg K). What is the die's thermal capacitance, in mJ/K? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 72.1

Why: $V = 44.2$ mm^3 $= 4.42e-08$ m^3. $C = \rho c_p V = 2330 \times 700 \times 4.42e-08 = 72.1$ mJ/K.

<a id="c-pkg-thermal-management"></a>

#### Thermal management: TIMs and heat sinks

`pkg.thermal.management`

Thermal management is the set of materials and devices that move heat from the package to the environment: thermal interface materials (TIMs), lids and spreaders, heat sinks, fans, heat pipes, vapour chambers and liquid cooling.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Interface materials
- Required heat-sink resistance
- Convection and fin area

Sample problem:

> A thermal interface material with conductivity 6 W/(m K) has a 115 um bond line over 100 mm^2. Ignoring contact resistance, what temperature drop does it cause at 110 W, in kelvin? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 21.08

Why: $R = 115/(6 \times 100) = 0.19167$ K/W; $\Delta T = 110 R = 21.08$ K.

<a id="packaging-chiplets-and-3d-integration-mechanical-stress"></a>

### Mechanical stress

<a id="c-pkg-mech-thermal-stress"></a>

#### Thermomechanical stress from CTE mismatch

`pkg.mech.thermal_stress`

Every package joins materials that expand at different rates with temperature: silicon at about 2.6 ppm/K, copper near 17, organic substrates around 14 to 17, mold compounds from under 10 to over 20, and solder near 20.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Mismatch strain
- Biaxial stress in a constrained film
- Temperature swing to a stress limit

Sample problem:

> Silicon nitride (3.2 ppm/K) is bonded to a build-up substrate (14 ppm/K) and cooled 230 K from its stress-free temperature. What mismatch strain must the bond accommodate, in ppm? Round to the nearest whole number.

Answer: 2484

Why: $\Delta\alpha\Delta T = 10.8 \times 230 = 2484$ ppm.

<a id="c-pkg-mech-cte-warpage"></a>

#### CTE mismatch and warpage

`pkg.mech.cte_warpage`

Warpage is the out-of-plane bending of a package, wafer or panel caused by CTE mismatch between layers bonded at an elevated temperature.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Curvature of a symmetric bilayer
- Timoshenko's general formula
- From curvature to warpage

Sample problem:

> Two bonded layers of equal thickness and equal modulus, 1.3 mm thick in total, differ in CTE by 15.5 ppm/K and cool 220 K from stress-free. Using $\kappa = 3\Delta\alpha\Delta T/(2h)$, what is the radius of curvature, in metres? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 0.25

Why: $\kappa = 3 \times 0.0000155 \times 220/(2 \times 0.0013) = 3.9346$ per m; radius $1/\kappa = 0.25$ m.

<a id="c-pkg-mech-solder-fatigue"></a>

#### Solder joint fatigue

`pkg.mech.solder_fatigue`

Solder joints between a die and a substrate, or a package and a board, are sheared every time the temperature cycles, because the two sides expand by different amounts.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Shear strain in a joint
- Coffin-Manson scaling
- Geometry levers for life

Sample problem:

> A solder joint of height 110 um sits 2 mm from the neutral point between parts whose CTEs differ by 13.4 ppm/K. For a 70 K temperature swing with no underfill, what is the joint's shear strain $\Delta\alpha\Delta T \cdot DNP/h$, as a percentage? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 1.71

Why: Displacement $0.0000134 \times 70 \times 2000 = 1.876$ um over 110 um gives 1.71%.

<a id="c-pkg-mech-fea"></a>

#### Finite element analysis of packages

`pkg.mech.fea`

Finite element analysis (FEA) solves the equations of elasticity, and often plasticity and creep, over a meshed model of the package.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Modelling choices
- Mesh, elements and convergence
- Validation and use in the flow

Sample problem:

> A package FEA model must predict corner solder-joint strain. How are thousands of joints usually handled?
>
> A) Joints modelled as rigid links
>
> B) A homogenized joint layer globally, with a detailed submodel of the critical corner joints
>
> C) Every joint meshed finely in the global model
>
> D) Joints ignored entirely

Answer: A homogenized joint layer globally, with a detailed submodel of the critical corner joints

Why: Global-local modelling keeps the full model tractable while resolving the joints that fail first.

<a id="packaging-chiplets-and-3d-integration-package-reliability"></a>

### Package reliability

<a id="c-pkg-rel-electromigration"></a>

#### Electromigration and Black's equation

`pkg.rel.electromigration`

Electromigration is the slow transport of metal atoms by the momentum of conducting electrons.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Current density
- Black's equation
- Allowed current for a lifetime

Sample problem:

> A copper line 1.9 um wide and 0.55 um thick carries 5.5 mA. What is its current density, in MA/cm^2? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 0.526

Why: Area 1.045 um^2 $= 1.045 \times 10^{-8}$ cm^2. $J = 5.5 \times 10^{-3}/(1.045 \times 10^{-8}) = 0.526$ MA/cm^2.

<a id="c-pkg-rel-em-temperature"></a>

#### EM temperature acceleration and Blech length

`pkg.rel.em_temperature`

Electromigration accelerates strongly with temperature through the Arrhenius factor in Black's equation.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Arrhenius acceleration
- Extrapolating a stress test
- The Blech length

Sample problem:

> Electromigration in copper has an activation energy of 0.95 eV. At fixed current density, by what factor is the median life at 95 °C longer than at a 300 °C stress? Use $k = 8.617 \times 10^{-5}$ eV/K. Round to the nearest whole number.

Answer: 44845

Why: $AF = \exp\left(\frac{0.95}{8.617 \times 10^{-5}}\left(\frac{1}{368.15} - \frac{1}{573.15}\right)\right) = 44845$.

<a id="c-pkg-rel-stress-migration"></a>

#### Stress migration and voiding

`pkg.rel.stress_migration`

Stress migration, also called stress-induced voiding, moves metal atoms under a gradient of mechanical stress rather than electron current.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Mechanism and driving force
- The temperature peak
- Design and verification response

Sample problem:

> A via lands on a narrow line in one layout and on a wide plate in another. Which is more vulnerable to stress voiding?
>
> A) Neither, stress voiding needs current
>
> B) Both are equal, since width does not matter
>
> C) The via on the narrow line, because current density is higher
>
> D) The via on the wide plate, because the plate supplies many vacancies

Answer: The via on the wide plate, because the plate supplies many vacancies

Why: Vacancy supply scales with the metal volume feeding the via, which is the reverse of electromigration intuition.

<a id="c-pkg-rel-dielectric-breakdown"></a>

#### Time-dependent dielectric breakdown

`pkg.rel.dielectric_breakdown`

Time-dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB) is the gradual degradation of an insulator under an electric field until a conductive path forms and it shorts.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The electric field
- Field acceleration models
- Weibull statistics and area scaling

Sample problem:

> A dielectric 19 nm thick has 1.25 V across it. What is the electric field, in MV/cm? Round to 3 decimal places.

Answer: 0.658

Why: 1 V/nm is 10 MV/cm, so $E = 10 \times 1.25/19 = 0.658$ MV/cm.

<a id="c-pkg-rel-aging"></a>

#### Aging and lifetime guard bands

`pkg.rel.aging`

Aging is the slow drift of transistor parameters over a product's life, chiefly threshold voltage shifts from bias temperature instability and hot-carrier injection.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Power-law threshold shift
- Time to a shift limit
- Delay guard bands

Sample problem:

> BTI shifts a transistor's threshold by 23.5 mV after 100 hours of stress, following $\Delta V_{th} \propto t^n$ with $n = 0.22$. What shift is predicted after 15 years of continuous stress (8760 hours per year), in mV? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 114.07

Why: $23.5 \times (131400/100)^{0.22} = 114.07$ mV.

<a id="c-pkg-rel-multiphysics"></a>

#### Electro-thermal multiphysics coupling

`pkg.rel.multiphysics`

Electrical, thermal and mechanical behaviour are coupled. Current heats conductors, heat raises resistance, higher resistance changes the heat, and temperature drives both stress and electromigration.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Iterating the coupling
- The converged temperature
- Thermal runaway

Sample problem:

> A conductor has $R(T) = R_0(1 + \beta(T - T_a))$ with $R_0 = 0.1$ ohm and $\beta = 0.0041$ per K, and $T = T_a + \theta I^2 R(T)$ with $\theta = 62$ K/W and $T_a = 52$ °C. It carries 2.7 A. Starting from $T = T_a$, alternate power and temperature updates. What temperature does the second iteration give, in °C? Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer: 105.57

Why: Iteration 1: $T_1 = 52 + 62 \times 7.29 \times 0.1 = 97.198$. Iteration 2: $R = 0.11853$ ohm, $T_2 = 105.57$ °C.

<a id="packaging-chiplets-and-3d-integration-eda-for-3d-integration"></a>

### EDA for 3D integration

<a id="c-pkg-eda3d-partitioning"></a>

#### Partitioning a design across dies

`pkg.eda3d.partitioning`

A 3D or multi-die design must be partitioned: each cell or block is assigned to a die so that the vertical connections stay within budget while area, power and timing balance.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Cut nets between two dies
- Vertical connections in a stack
- Move gain

Sample problem:

> A design is split across two dies. Nets: N1 = {b, d, f, h}; N2 = {f, g, h}; N3 = {a, b, d, g}; N4 = {b, d, e, h}; N5 = {f, g}; N6 = {b, d, g, h}; N7 = {b, h}. Assignment: die 0 holds a, b, c, e, g; die 1 holds d, f, h. Each net with cells on both dies needs a vertical connection. How many nets are cut?

Answer: 7

Why: A net is cut when its cells are not all on one die; counting them gives 7.

<a id="c-pkg-eda3d-inter-die-timing"></a>

#### Inter-die timing

`pkg.eda3d.inter_die_timing`

A timing path that crosses dies passes through drivers, bumps or TSVs, and receivers, and its launch and capture clocks are distributed by separate clock trees on separate dies.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Setup slack across a die boundary
- Independent die corners
- Hold across dies

Sample problem:

> A path launches on die A and captures on die B. Clock period 1450 ps; launch clock latency on die A 350 ps; capture clock latency on die B 380 ps. Data delay: 240 ps of logic on die A, 165 ps for the die crossing, 310 ps of logic on die B. Setup time 45 ps. What is the setup slack, in ps?

Answer: 720

Why: Required $1450 + 380 - 45 = 1785$; arrival $350 + 240 + 165 + 310 = 1065$; slack 720 ps.

<a id="c-pkg-eda3d-thermal-floorplan"></a>

#### Thermal-aware 3D floorplanning

`pkg.eda3d.thermal_floorplan`

In a 3D stack, dies far from the heat sink must push their heat through the dies nearer to it, and thinned dies spread heat poorly.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Peak temperature of a stack
- Ordering dies in the stack
- Lateral placement of hot blocks

Sample problem:

> Two dies are stacked under a heat sink. The die next to the sink connects to ambient (26 °C) through 0.4 K/W, and the far die connects to the near die through 0.2 K/W. All heat leaves through the sink. The near die dissipates 140 W and the far die 20 W. What is the peak temperature in the stack, in °C? Round to 1 decimal place.

Answer: 94

Why: Near die $26 + 160 \times 0.4 = 90$ °C; far die adds $20 \times 0.2$ to reach 94 °C.

<a id="c-pkg-eda3d-multi-die-verification"></a>

#### Multi-die assembly verification

`pkg.eda3d.multi_die_verification`

Single-die DRC and LVS prove one die correct against its own netlist. A multi-die package adds new ways to fail: bumps that do not line up between dies, a die flipped or rotated the wrong way, nets connected to the wrong neighbour pin, or package wiring that does not match the system netlist.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- The assembly description
- Interface DRC
- Assembly LVS

Sample problem:

> Why must the assembly description itself be checked against design intent?
>
> A) It is only used for documentation
>
> B) It replaces the system netlist
>
> C) It is generated by the foundry
>
> D) The checkers treat it as the source of truth, so an error in it hides real errors

Answer: The checkers treat it as the source of truth, so an error in it hides real errors

Why: If the description is wrong, a check can pass on the wrong assembly.

<a id="packaging-chiplets-and-3d-integration-frontier-agent-first-futures"></a>

### Frontier: agent-first futures

<a id="c-pkg-frontier-multiphysics-engine-layers"></a>

#### Multiphysics engines in the four-layer model

`pkg.frontier.multiphysics_engine_layers`

Package and 3D-IC analysis runs on multiphysics engines: thermal solvers, mechanical FEA, power-integrity and electromigration checkers, and the coupling between them.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Core and change surface of a multiphysics engine
- Placing a request in a tier
- Seam design for coupled physics

Sample problem:

> Which item is an observation hook rather than a parameter in a coupled electro-thermal engine?
>
> A) The maximum number of coupling iterations
>
> B) The choice of loose or monolithic coupling
>
> C) The thermal conductivity of silicon
>
> D) The live coupling residual and per-die peak temperature exposed during a run

Answer: The live coupling residual and per-die peak temperature exposed during a run

Why: Hooks let an agent read live state; the others are settings chosen before the run.

<a id="c-pkg-frontier-thermal-surrogate"></a>

#### Fast thermal surrogates versus accurate solvers

`pkg.frontier.thermal_surrogate`

An agent exploring package and 3D floorplans cannot run a full thermal solve for every candidate.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What a fast thermal engine trades away
- When to recurse to the accurate solver
- Measuring surrogate error honestly

Sample problem:

> Which nonlinearity do fast thermal models often linearize?
>
> A) The geometry of the die
>
> B) Temperature-dependent conductivity and leakage-power feedback
>
> C) The number of dies
>
> D) Fourier's law itself

Answer: Temperature-dependent conductivity and leakage-power feedback

Why: Both make the problem nonlinear; fast models commonly freeze them at a nominal point.

<a id="c-pkg-frontier-chiplet-partition-agent"></a>

#### Chiplet partitioning agents and their rewards

`pkg.frontier.chiplet_partition_agent`

A chiplet partitioning agent proposes how to split a system into dies, which process each die uses, and how they connect, then scores the result with tools: cost and yield models, a partitioner for cut size, die-to-die bandwidth and energy models, and thermal checks.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- A tool-grounded reward
- How the reward gets gamed
- Proxy reward against signoff quality

Sample problem:

> A partition exceeds the reticle limit for one chiplet. How should the reward treat it?
>
> A) Reject the candidate as infeasible rather than subtracting a small penalty
>
> B) Ignore it until signoff
>
> C) Reward it for using more area
>
> D) Subtract a small penalty and keep it

Answer: Reject the candidate as infeasible rather than subtracting a small penalty

Why: Soft penalties for hard constraints teach the agent to trade violations for gains.

<a id="c-pkg-frontier-golden-multiphysics"></a>

#### Golden multiphysics checks

`pkg.frontier.golden_multiphysics`

Before an agent's change to a multiphysics engine or flow is accepted, it must pass golden and differential tests.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Golden cases from closed-form physics
- Differential checks on reference designs
- Measured ground truth

Sample problem:

> Which case makes a good golden test for a new 3-D thermal solver?
>
> A) A customer package with no reference result
>
> B) The solver's own previous output on any design
>
> C) A 1-D slab with fixed face temperatures, whose resistance is L/(kA)
>
> D) A random power map with no known answer

Answer: A 1-D slab with fixed face temperatures, whose resistance is L/(kA)

Why: Golden tests need an exact, independent answer.

<a id="c-pkg-frontier-codesign-loop"></a>

#### Agentic package co-design loops

`pkg.frontier.codesign_loop`

An agentic package co-design loop reads the reports of package, board, thermal and power-integrity tools, proposes changes such as ball reassignments, decap placement, die order or TIM choice, runs them through the engines and iterates until signoff passes, with a human approving the final change.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- What the loop reads and proposes
- Seams the loop needs
- Convergence and approval

Sample problem:

> How should the loop express a proposed ball reassignment?
>
> A) As a typed edit to the design database, validated before any engine runs
>
> B) As a paragraph describing the change
>
> C) As a new RTL module
>
> D) As a hand-edited GDS file

Answer: As a typed edit to the design database, validated before any engine runs

Why: Typed edits are checkable and reviewable.

---

## Building EDA Software

Layer 11. Design databases, format parsers, incremental computation, deterministic parallelism, regression and QoR, and the open-source RTL-to-GDS flow hands-on.

Builds on: The EDA Landscape, HDLs and Hardware Compilers, Logic Synthesis, Technology Mapping and Sizing, Static Timing Analysis, Floorplanning and Placement, Routing, Clock Trees and Power Delivery, Extraction, Signal Integrity and Signoff, Physical Verification and DFM, Graph Algorithms for EDA, Computational Geometry for Layout, Fabrication and Design-Technology Co-optimization, Circuit Simulation, Formal Verification, Functional Verification and Simulation.

Topics covered:

- EDA software architecture: design databases (OpenDB, OpenAccess), object models, hierarchy and instancing
- Parsing industry formats: Verilog netlists, Liberty, LEF/DEF, SDC, SPEF, GDS; EDIF, IP-XACT, UPF; Si2 standards
- Tcl and Python APIs, domain-specific languages, plug-in architectures, APIs
- Incremental computation and dependency graphs (incremental STA, incremental legalization), memory management, cache locality, serialization
- Parallel algorithms, concurrency, determinism and reproducible builds, distributed task scheduling, workflow orchestration, cloud computing, containers, Linux
- Software engineering for tools: version control, regression testing, continuous integration, QoR tracking, build systems, C++ and Rust in EDA
- Open-source EDA hands-on: Yosys, ABC, OpenROAD (OpenDB, OpenSTA, RePlAce, TritonRoute, OpenRCX), OpenROAD-flow-scripts and its GCD design, OpenLane 2, OpenTimer, KLayout, Magic, Netgen, ngspice, Xyce, Xschem, Verilator, cocotb, SymbiYosys
- Open PDKs: SKY130, GF180MCU, SG13G2; open-source hardware; what open access does not give you (production readiness, fab access)
- License management, commercial tool economics

Subdomains: [Design databases](#building-eda-software-design-databases), [APIs and scripting](#building-eda-software-apis-and-scripting), [Parsers](#building-eda-software-parsers), [Tool architecture](#building-eda-software-tool-architecture), [Incremental computation](#building-eda-software-incremental-computation), [Parallelism](#building-eda-software-parallelism), [Testing and QA](#building-eda-software-testing-and-qa), [Open PDKs](#building-eda-software-open-pdks), [Flow orchestration](#building-eda-software-flow-orchestration), [Frontier: agent-first futures](#building-eda-software-frontier-agent-first-futures)

<a id="building-eda-software-design-databases"></a>

### Design databases

<a id="c-infra-db-design-database"></a>

#### Design databases

`infra.db.design_database`

A design database is the in-memory model that every engine of a physical design tool reads and edits: placement, routing, timing, extraction and verification all work on the same objects.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Why tools share one database
- What the database stores and links
- Derived results, change and persistence

Sample problem:

> A placer, a router and a timer each read the design from files written by the previous tool. What is the main cost a shared in-memory design database removes?
>
> A) The need for a netlist at all
>
> B) The cost of timing analysis itself
>
> C) The need for technology data such as layers
>
> D) Re-parsing and rebuilding the design between every step

Answer: Re-parsing and rebuilding the design between every step

Why: With file handoff every tool parses LEF, DEF, Verilog and Liberty again and builds its own model. A shared database is built once and every engine reads and edits the same objects.

<a id="c-infra-db-object-model"></a>

#### Blocks, instances, nets and terminals

`infra.db.object_model`

Every netlist database names the same handful of objects: a block (the design), instances of master cells, nets, and terminals where nets meet pins.

Key ideas and worked examples:

- Instance terminals and block terminals
- Nets as hyperedges of terminals
- Expanding nets into graphs

Sample problem:

> A block holds 23 instances of BUF_X2 (2 signal pins), 7 instances of NOR2_X1 (3 signal pins) and 39 instances of OAI22_X1 (5 signal pins), and the block itself has 4 ports. In an OpenDB-style object model, every signal pin of every instance is one instance terminal (ITerm) and every block port is one block terminal (BTerm). How many ITerms does the block hold?

Answer: 262
